items.s: Young Athletes' Results Young athletes' section for 1992: Leo Coy's review of the Thameside League and Woolworths Young Athletes League seasons (second in Division One South, promotion to the Premier Division), followed by results from inter-club, YA League, Thameside League and Surrey Championships meetings. Thameside League The performances of our teams this year was down on last year but we nevertheless finished well up in each League. The outstanding performance was by Ben Cascoe with a Club Record Javelin throw of 51.16 metres which would have won him the English Schools. Also noteworthy was the Shot Putt of Damian Daldin which measured 12.40 metres. Woolworths Young Athletes League For many years we have dreamed of competing in the Premier Division of this League and this season our dreams have been fulfilled by finishing in second place in Division One South. Promotion in successive years does not just "happen" and it is the result of hard work by a number of people. In particular: Billy Bull, Chris Bentley, Martin Milner, Bart Mathias, Selemi Simcek, Bob Bridges, Jon Coy, Chris Knight, Karen Drake and Tony Ganio. The success would not be possible without the support of the competitors and just a casual glance through the results will highlight the fact that we have some outstanding, talented, athletes, who have supported their club throughout the league campaign. They have performed well at all levels and have broken Club Records in abundance. Well done everybody and thanks for your support. A special mention for Stuart Booth who has competed in the YAL since he was a Colt and for the past three years has been YA Captain. This is his final winter as a Youth as next summer he will be a Junior on the track. Thanks for your continued support Stuart. Your dedication to Belgrave is an example to everybody. Youth Gavin Mason prepares to strike in the Tonbridge 1500 metres. Gavin has had a great season over events ranging from 200 to 1500 metres. In the Surrey Schools he ran to 3rd place in the 800 metres with 1:58.0. Sprints, throws and relays; keep throwing them Dave Baffoe's way and he's happy. Stevie Scott set many personal bests in '92 - look out for plenty more when next summer comes around Voted "Man of the Match" at the Horsham YA Meeting for his 1.78 high jump, James Ganio has made a big impact on the jumps, sprints and shot in our Boy's team. Es Hassan has been showing great promise in the sprints, hurdles and long jump, representing Surrey in the Colts' Inter-County match at Battersea. Whatever the meeting you can be sure that at some stage a baton wielding Richard David will be seen running down the opposition. Above: A long but superb season has come from 400 metre man Robert Milner. As early as April 18th he clocked 40.0 for a 300 at Tooting and then, as the summer wore, on he chipped away at his one lap times with his best of 53.6 coming in June at Kingsmeadow. He was "Man of the Match at Tonbridge, placed 3rd in the South of England Boys' Champs in 53.92, won the Inter-County match at Battersea and placed 2nd in the Southern Inter-Counties at Hayes in late August with 53.7. items.s: The old firm back in the medals Charlie Dickinson's review of the 1992 veterans' summer: the M60 team's successes (Laurie O'Hara, Bert Stroud, Charlie Walker, Pat Newall, Arthur Bruce) and a disappointing season for the over-40s and over-50s. VETERANS' RESULTS The old firm back in the medals The Over Sixties It has been the marvellous performances of the Belgrave M60's which have dominated the 1992 summer season of road and track. With Bert Stroud and Laurie O'Hara both turning 60 in June, an already strong team has now become truly world class. They won the Southern 4 stage road relay at Aldershot by an amazing NINE minutes. They won the silver team medal in the first World 10km road Championships in Birmingham; Laurie also came second in the individual race and has been selected to represent England in the international cross country race in Belfast in November. These performances give a stark reminder of the strength of the Belgrave running teams of the fifties and sixties. But it is not only the ability of Laurie O'Hara, Charlie Walker, Pat Newall, Bert Stroud, and Arthur Bruce which is evident, it is their lifelong enthusiasm for Belgrave and the team which shines through and overshadows the other running sections of the club. As a Veteran, Laurie O'Hara has always been outstanding. He has won National, European and World Championship gold medals on Track, Road and Cross Country and he still holds many British age group records for 1,500m, 5,000m, and 10,000m. In his first major outing as an M60 at the National Vets Track and Field Championships at Copthall in July, Laurie broke the British record in the 5,000m. Charlie Walker is an inspiration to us all. Always trying to improve, always looking forward to the next race. It was Charlie who persuaded an unfit Arthur to turn out at Cardiff to make up the scoring three in the National last March. It was he who got Dennis Jones out at Dunsfold aerodrome when they won the silver in the National 5km road Championships. And every Sunday during the winter he gets Pat Newall to run with him from Clapham to Richmond, round the park and back! Arthur Bruce has neglected his own fitness to spend at least two sessions per week coaching an ever increasing group of all ages. Under Arthur's eagle eye seniors such as Roger Alsop, Mark Anderson, and James Ryle have all produced PB's on the track this season. His training group includes many Vets too, of all speeds and abilities, and there is always room for others to join. Arthur's approach is very straightforward, but he also has an uncanny way of reading an athletes state of fitness and finding the recipe to bring out the best. Bert Stroud has been a revelation at 60. With his long loping stride he appears to be running just as he did 20 or so years ago. It's just that everyone else at 60 is now running slower. Bert won the VAC 5 mile road race in June, his first Championship win, and achieved the fifth fastest time in the South of England relay at Aldershot, faster than Bob Belmore and Derek Wood of Barnet. Although they race less competitively nowadays, mainly half Marathons, the influence of John Davies and Charlie Henn should not be overlooked. Both are mainstays of the 'Saturday Pack' which is an important feature of the club in its own right, but has also been a route to greater heights for many new members. (Helen Maskrey has been a recent example). And finally there is the number one supporter, Fred Paget. Although Fred's injured foot prevents him from running competitively, he still joins the pack on Saturday and Sunday mornings and remains as enthusiastic as ever. Fred is very knowledgable about running and fitness and also loves to watch and talk about races. He was wonderful company on the trip to Norway last June for the European Veterans' Track & Field Championships. The 40's and 50's Although there have been a number of encouraging individual performances from our over 40's and over 50's it has, on the whole, been a rather disappointing summer season. The M50 team had to scratch from the National Vets' six stage relay in Manchester at the last moment, even though we had Tony Verdie and Laurie O'Hara, and we were similarly unable to field a team in the South of England 4-stage relay at Aldershot. Belgrave did manage to get a team out in the Surrey relays at Crystal Palace and were rewarded with the silver medal. Tony Verdie has had some good road results this summer, and Tony Stone has recovered from a jaded patch to compete as often and as competently as ever. There were not enough M40's to even enter a team for the National and South of England relays. However, Alan Painter has produced some good track form, especially at 800m, Snowy Brooks is competing as well as ever, and it is good to see Alan Mead back on the track for the first time in fifteen years. We look forward to seeing him and new Vet Derek Clack next season. WORLD VETERANS' ROAD RACE CHAMPS., BIRMINGHAM NEC, 29/30 AUG A small group of Belgravians made the journey up to Birmingham on a cold, wet Saturday in late August for the first World Veterans' Road Race Championships. Most of the familiar British runners took part despite the hefty entry fees and an awesome 10k M40 field, the race being won by Mick McLeod. Entries from overseas, however, were very low, making this a domestic rather than truly International event. Also, the NEC was hardly an inspired choice as venue, with long walks to and from the car park and much of the organisation was, quite frankly, an embarrassment in front of our colleagues from overseas. Highlight was the M60 silver team medal won by the Belgrave team of Laurie O'Hara, Charlie Walker and Pat Newall. Arthur Bruce also ran but didn't score. Laurie came second in the individual M60 race in a time of 35:59, overtaking two other M60 runners in typical Laurie style in the final sprint finish. He was also a member of the winning Great Britain M60 team, so came home with a crop of three medals! 10k M40 1, M.McLeod 30:40; 2, M.Fromant 30:51; 3, I.Senzburg (GER) 30:53. M50 49, A.Stone 37:36. Fresh from his exertions at Crystal Palace the previous day Tony Stone ran to a surprising 2nd M50 place in the hilly Wimbledon Half-Marathon with 85:36. The surprise was because he was beaten by 2 minutes by J.Long of Stragglers - someone he had not previously ever encountered. RON HILL SOUTH OF ENGLAND VETS 4x6k ROAD RELAY, ALDERSHOT, 26 SEP BELGRAVE SMASH BARNET IN THE OVER 60'S The long reign of Barnet in the over 60's team came to an abrupt end when they were beaten by no less than nine minutes by the Belgrave squad. Led off by Charlie Walker, the Bels led throughout the four stage race and their dominance was such that they produced four out of the five fastest individual legs. Although, perhaps, Charlie swept off a little too fast running first leg with the M40's and M50's, he handed over a minute and a half clear of the next team in 24:14 to Pat Newall on stage two. Pat ignored the Barnet warnings that Laurie Forster was catching him and ran a blinder, pulling away even further and producing the second fastest leg of the afternoon (24:08). On stage three, Bert Stroud was only a fraction slower in 24:19, leaving Laurie O'Hara to complete the rout on stage four with an outstanding 21:46 fastest leg. It is interesting to note that the M60 team would have finished in the top dozen in the M50 section. It was unfortunate that Belgrave were unable to field teams in any of the other races - Seniors, M40's and M50's. FLYING FOX BVAF VETERAN MARATHON CHAMPS., STONE, 4 OCT The two Belgrave Marathon specialists, Richard Pearson and Tony Verdie made the long trip up to Stone for the BVAF championships very worthwhile with two excellent performances. Tony often competes in this particular event. The timing is just about right for Summer and early Autumn evening long training runs, with sufficient recovery time from the London in the Spring. The Flying Fox is well organised too with a good course. This year, Tony won the M55 title in a time of 2:49:04, and Richard came 7th in the M45 category in 2:46:53. items.s: Notice that Belgrave will enter the Southern Veterans' Track & Field League for the first time next summer, appealing for over-40 and over-50 competitors. Watch out for a new departure next summer. For the first time Belgrave will be entering the Southern Veterans' Track & Field League. Full details are not yet to hand but there will be about four matches, each taking place on a Monday night on the tracks of South London. We need two over 40s and one over 50 competitor in all standard events and although not every event will be included in every match, we are looking for triple jumpers, sprinters, pole vaulters, hammer throwers etc.! Southern Veterans' Track & Field League South London

items.sum: Arthur Bruce looks back at the 1946 athletics season, from the National cross-country at Leamington Spa (won by Belgrave's team) and Sydney Wooderson's 3 miles record to the European Games in Oslo, then Belgrave's own successes that year, including Derek Burfitt, Tom Carter, Len Herbert, Charlie Smart and walker Harry Churcher.
items.s: 1946: The first post-war athletics season Arthur Bruce looks back at the 1946 athletics season, from the National cross-country at Leamington Spa (won by Belgrave's team) and Sydney Wooderson's 3 miles record to the European Games in Oslo, then Belgrave's own successes that year, including Derek Burfitt, Tom Carter, Len Herbert, Charlie Smart and walker Harry Churcher. ARTHUR BRUCE looks back nearly fifty years to review a season of athletics in a world returning to normality. From the early copies of "Athletics Weekly" we were assured that for some time we would have to rely on pre-war stars returning from the services to represent Great Britain in the forthcoming international clashes. These were to climax in 1946 in the European Games to be held at the Bislet Stadium in Oslo. The situation at the end of the war indicated the pre-eminence of those countries untouched by the conflict, especially Sweden with their great middle-distance stars Gundar Haegg and Arne Anderson, soon to fade from the scene, and the heir apparent Lennart Strand. Finland still appeared to maintain it's reputation at the longer distances with the current world 10,000 metres record holder Viljo Heino, a worthy successor to that country's pre-war stars. The remainder of Europe was generally in the same formative stage as the United Kingdom with just a few established stars and promising newcomers. Across the Atlantic the United States were still showing the same excellence at sprints and field events as before, although no established middle distance stars had yet appeared. A noteworthy change in the athletics scene there were the foreign athletes, especially Jamaican and Irish, on Athletic Scholarships at American Universities. The contrast with today in the structure of athletics was marked by the absence of all-weather tracks, no grand prix series, World or European Cup, not even a closed UK championships!, and naturally no money despite capacity crowds at the White City for such events like the British Games, Inter-Counties and AAA Championships. International events were limited to perhaps one or two matches against such traditional rivals as France or Germany. The early months of 1946 brought the climax of the first Cross-Country season at Leamington Spa - "The National". Jack Holden reasserted his pre-war dominance despite his mature years on a tough, muddy, ten mile course. A Junior Championship did not yet exist but the Youths' Championship was won easily by G.B. Saunders who went on to win the "International" a few years later. Belgrave won the senior team race with six in twenty-four! and Leeds Harehills, in a close run finish against TVH and Belgrave, took the Youths' title. Our National shortcomings were later exposed in the International Cross-County Championships at Ayr racecourse when the French and Belgians, reared on a diet of fast, flat courses, triumphed over our rugged ten-milers. The track season was ushered in by the traditional Oxford v. Cambridge clash at the White City and it was evident that the pre-war preponderance of strength at the Universities had been eroded. The season progressed through county, district and AAA Championships which were highlighted by a magnificent win by Sydney Wooderson, who despite a lapse of five years and army service, moved up to a new distance and broke the British 3 mile record, defeating the formidable Willie Slykhuis of Holland in the process. The third man was over half a minute behind the leading two. The new sprint star was McDonald Bailey, probably the first of many world class Caribbean performers. Arthur Wint brought off the difficult 440/880 double prior to his Olympic success. Jim Peters emerged with a win in the 6 miles having not yet moved up to the marathon distance. The AAA were followed by the first International match of the season against France at the White City, in which we surprisingly won by 72 to 57 points with Sydney Wooderson producing yet another classic 3 mile performance in defeating the future European Steeplechase Champion Raphael Pujazon. We also uncharacteristically won both the high and long jump. The climax to the season was, as previously mentioned, the European Games at Oslo, the British team providing a surprisingly competent performance. A grand finale to his season came from Sydney Wooderson in the 5,000 metres. His time was the second best ever, coupled with the defeat of such great athletes as Gaston Reiff, Emil Zatopek, Viljo Heino and Slykhuis. The surprise win for Great Britain was Jack Archer in the 100 metres. He was so often domestically in the shadow of McDonald Bailey but came into his own in Oslo. Other excellent British performances were: Tom White - a three second improvement on his best for a close 5th in the 800 metres, Derek Pugh's 3rd spot in the 400 metres, Alan Paterson's 2nd in the high jump, Forbest and Megnin 2nd and 3rd in the long walk and a close up 2nd in the 4x400 metre relay. The small women's team performed well with Winnie Jordan being runner up in both 100 and 200 metres. Noteworthy was the appearance for the first time in international athletics of the Soviet Union team. In meetings subsequent to the "Europeans" both Arthur Wint and McDonald Bailey produced best European times for the year at 400 and 100 metres. It is interesting to note that in the British top ten rankings for the year that despite their reputation of primarily being a harrier club, Belgrave had one in the 800, two in the 1500, two in the 5,000, two in the 10,000 and one (Tom Carter) in the steeplechase. Belgrave's share of athletics success during the year started with wins in both the Surrey and Middlesex Cross-Country team Championships, the Surrey win with only 16 points!, and an individual win by Derek Burfitt in the Middlesex Junior. This was followed by Tom Carter in the Southern Championships at Wimbledon, the team going to Belgrave with six in twenty. Derek matched the win with success in the Southern Junior. The cross-country season was rounded off with the National team win previously described, with Len Herbert making the international team. Our Youths, in finishing 3rd with three in nineteen, came within nine points of success. The summer season showed Belgrave to be powerful on the track but showing the usual British weakness in the field. The County Championships provided plenty of success in our usual varied counties. Jimmy Wood and Len Herbert were winners of the Surrey mile and 3 miles with a number of places gained in the field events. The Juniors showed equal success with Derek Burfitt and Arthur Bruce winning the Middlesex and Surrey miles respectively. Derek continued his success with wins in the Southern and AAA Junior miles, the latter in record time. Len Herbert just failed to catch Maurice Bingham in the Southern 3 miles at the White City. The AAA Championships produced a number of finalists but unhappily no winners. Our serving members abroad continued Belgrave success with Bill Nankeville's 1500 win in the International Services 1500 at the Berlin Olympic Stadium and several good wins by Charlie Smart in Germany with the Control Commission. The newly instituted London Championships produced a number of Belgrave successes, prominent among which was Charlie Smart's 3 miles win following his recent German successes. Our walkers, led by Harry Churcher, recapturing his pre-war form, showed solid success throughout the season from the 20 miles to 50 kilo Road Championships to the track 2 and 7 mile championships. One final thought on that promising season were the number of well supported Club Handicaps right through the spectrum, providing exciting finishes and some quality performances as in Len Marchant's 1:56 880 yards from scratch at the end of the season. Blackheath's 31 year old Sydney Wooderson, a comparative novice at 3 miles, leads the Dutchman Willie Slykhuis on his way to victory in the 1946 AAA Championships in a British Record time of 13:53.2. "Athletics" magazine of November 1946 depicts the "new Wooderson" - Belgrave's outstanding Junior of the day -Derek Burfitt. Belgrave's leading walker of 1946 was Harry Churcher. He went on to take 5th place in the 10,000 metres Walk at the 1948 Wembley Olympics. items.sum: Paul Warburton's profile of Tommy Green, the Belgrave walker who overcame rickets, war wounds and a factory accident to win the first Olympic 50k walk at Los Angeles in 1932, Belgrave's only Olympic gold medal. It covers his homecoming at Eastleigh, his cigarette card, his years as publican of the Meadowbank Hotel and his death one day short of his 81st birthday.
items.s: A very unlikely Olympian Paul Warburton's profile of Tommy Green, the Belgrave walker who overcame rickets, war wounds and a factory accident to win the first Olympic 50k walk at Los Angeles in 1932, Belgrave's only Olympic gold medal. It covers his homecoming at Eastleigh, his cigarette card, his years as publican of the Meadowbank Hotel and his death one day short of his 81st birthday. Looking at a picture of TOMMY GREEN, it's hard to believe that this man won Belgrave Harriers' only Olympic gold medal. PAUL WARBURTON tells us more. It comes as a surprise to find out that Britain's premier club, currently riding the crest of a wave in track and field success, must look to a 38 year old, father of four, lucky to have walked at all, for its sole golden moment of Olympic success. Thomas William Green was born on 30th March, 1894. Because of rickets, he was unable to walk until he was five years old. In 1906 he falsified his age in order to join the army but was invalided out of the Royal Hussars four years later as a result of injuries received from a falling horse. Then, after the start of World War 1 prompted the Army reserve into calling him back to action, he was wounded three times and badly gassed amongst the mud and blood of northern France. After the War and a return to Civvy street, he resumed his earlier checkered life and went through a number of jobs before ending up at the Eastleigh Railway works, where he was again the victim of an accident sustained in the line of duty. This time, Green had his right thumb torn off by a piece of machinery. Throughout his athletic career, the Olympic gold medallist always wrapped a handkerchief around the disfigured hand during races. Percy Wright, who as a junior, first saw Green race the year after his L.A. triumph, was never sure if this was a touch of vanity; an aid to wiping the sweat; or some other mental "support" But other competitors, thinking it must magical properties, aped the champion and arrived at the start line with handkerchiefed hands. Finally, to complete this less than athletic scene, I have also never seen a picture of Green when he had his own teeth. Presuming he wore dentures, they must have been stowed prior to the starter's gun. Given this catalogue of physical mishap, it takes some imagination to see this balding, toothless, bow-legged little man walking all the classic distance races, and winning the lot, in times that would hold up well today, while sweating in a foundry week after week. To all that are alive today and remember him, he was a 'natural'. I've always been suspicious of that tag. It never quite gives you the real picture of the relentless, tedious slog required by any champion. Most athletic 'naturals' are actually at pains to support Edison's reminder of "1% inspiration and 99% perspiration." But Green realised early on that he had the indefinable extra the Gods reserve for the few mortals whom they decide will be Olympic champions. His first experience of walking was as the guide for a war-blinded friend whom he had been helping to train for the St. Dunstan's London to Brighton. In 1926 and his first race, he surprised the locals by winning the 12 miles Worthing to Brighton. It was after this encouraging start, that he joined Belgrave, then as now a top club; Gordon Doubleday remembers that he didn't want for supporters at big races. There was always a club 'retinue' as he puts it, who looked after Tommy. His second daughter, Lily, used to cycle alongside her father on his long training walks and from this base support the railwayman built up the impressive record which was to lead to the ultimate excursion: the 1932 Games in Los Angeles. On the afternoon of August 3rd, 15 competitors paid the obligatory scant attention to the starter's orders before the first Olympic 50k walk. There had been no walks at the Amsterdam Games four years earlier and, not for the first or last time, walking had to justify its inclusion at the Olympics. The result was one long walk rather than the more contentious shorter 'sprints' which Italy's Ugo Frigerio had dominated in the early 20's. The colourful Italian was here in L.A. and keen to add to his three medal haul, but not relishing the prospect of a distance well beyond his normal scope. Germany's Paul Sievert, however, was the unofficial record holder of the distance at 4:34:00 and the Latvian, Janis Dalinsch, was also considered to be a part of the threat to Green's chances. Apart from each other, the walkers also had to combat the intense heat. The temperature was in the 90's and on one part of the road course near the Coliseum, the tarmac was blistering and sticking to shoes during the race. But Green had prepared well. In June, he had walked conservatively in the Manchester to Blackpool 50 miles, securing the third of his six successive victories 28 minutes quicker than the 1992 winning time! He allowed another Italian, Francesco Pretti, to dominate the first few kilometres, but by 10k, Green and Frigerio had drawn level and were joined at the half-way point, reached in 2:23:11, by Dalinsch, who had wisely avoided the earlier pace. Shortly after, Frigerio fell away, realising that both distance and conditions were not the cakewalk of his earlier Olympic victories. At 35k Green was also having a bad time and had lost nearly a minute on Dalinsch when, not for the first time, his revival was as dramatic as his subsequent victory was certain. Gordon Doubleday remembers in one distance race, he was assisting Green, and reached into the tin bath on the roadside for a sponge. The walker who was going through a bad patch waved it away: "Never mind that - throw the bloody lot over me!" And here again in L.A. an impromptu douche provided the resurrection which added Tommy Green's name to the record books. He caught Dalinsch, and applied the pressure in the last 10k which forced the Latvian to complain of stomach cramps, but just held off a resuscitated Frigerio for the silver medal. Meanwhile, 7 minutes down the road, the Briton, in the days before crowd control became necessary, walked into the arms of the spectators as he crossed the finishing line, and after his initial shock at the rapturous reception, recovered sufficiently to send one very important telegram. Back in Eastleigh, Rose Green raced to the door to receive the envelope which brought news from a country that was a week's travel from Hampshire. How long now would it take for the entire World to hear of a sporting triumph? She had brought up four children on an often reduced pay packet, because although the railway were able to let him go to races all over Europe - they certainly didn't pay her husband while he was away. And now she had more than a share in his fate ... "I won the Gold Medal. Very hot. See you all soon. love Tom!" A week later the streets of Eastleigh were lined six and seven deep to hail the most unlikely conquering hero, who on three days a week training, and at the age of 38, had won the Olympic title. Mrs. Lily Coakes, as she is now, remembers the police stopping her at the entrance to Eastleigh station. ' "You can't go in there. Only special dignitaries" they said. I said, "But I want to greet my Dad!" Fortunately, they believed me and let me through ... ' Green was soon awarded the ultimate accolade when Players added him to their cigarette card issue. You had to be a famous film star or a famous footballer or a famous something to emerge from a cardboard packet of ten. And here a walker had managed to become a collector's item. I suppose in the days before prize money and trust funds, a pub was a sound venture to make the most of your popularity and Green became publican of the Meadowbank Hotel on the Romsey Road. His sociable, generous spirit allowed him to make awards of trophies to local athletic organisations in later years, that at first sat behind the bar. Before that he returned to his original sporting passion, boxing. Because of the size of some of the rooms at the Meadowbank, he was able to help out a fellow railwayman who was also a promising middleweight, by turning them into a makeshift gym. Vince Hawkins also received a new trainer and the walker turned publican took the young boxer to the giddy heights of challenging the legendary Randolph Turpin for the British title. Green himself continued to remain fit by organising local sporting events, and simply because he wanted to keep active, he had a rent collector's job at the age of 78. One morning on his round he was struck by a sports car while crossing a road. His first reaction was to ask his son Ray, to help him continue the collections. According to Lily, this injury prompted the stroke from which he was to die three years later on, one day short of his 81st birthday. Some years before, Green had been presented by his club with a sculpted model, which was based on his cigarette card pose. At the foot was the inscription: "To Tommy Green - the best of them all." items.sum: Note on George Piddington, team manager for Havant AC, Hampshire and the YA cross country, who now also manages Havant's women and passes on a message from Gerry North about the Victory '5' at Portsmouth.
items.s: George a glutton for punishment! Note on George Piddington, team manager for Havant AC, Hampshire and the YA cross country, who now also manages Havant's women and passes on a message from Gerry North about the Victory '5' at Portsmouth. George Piddington is a busy man down in the Hampshire area. Already Press Liaison Officer and Young Athletes' League Team Manager for Havant AC, Team Manager for Hampshire and Team Manager for the YA Cross Country, George found himself taking on a little extra responsibility when Havant lost their Women's Cross-Country Team Manager. So that the Minors, Girls and Intermediates would not get neglected, George said he would help if someone else could keep an eye on things as well. A week later a file of papers, entry forms, etc. were given to him with a message from the Committee that they had unanimously agreed that he should be Team Manager for all the Young Athletes, male and female, and for the Senior Ladies as well. George's reaction? "I love it," he says, "It gives me great satisfaction when I see how our young lads' section has come on over the past four years. The squad has built up nicely with Colts coming into the side every year through contacts with local schools. I am now intending to build up our ladies' section." He reckons that the early signs are that his ladies are going to be very good within another year and will be a match for any club including the Belgrave girls! George sends his regards to all and relays a message from Gerry North. Gerry would like to know if Gary Staines is coming down with a Belgrave team to the Victory '5' at Portsmouth in December. Perhaps he might care to have a go at the course record held by Nick Rose who will be running - as will Mark Rowland, Steve Brace, Tom and Jack Buckner. items.sum: Roundup of Belgrave men's road running in summer 1992, from Steve Halliday's wins at Halifax, Almondbury and Burnsall to relay and Belgrave 5k/10k results, with Gary Staines fastest on the first leg of the Blackheath 6x3M relay.
items.s: Men's Road Roundup Roundup of Belgrave men's road running in summer 1992, from Steve Halliday's wins at Halifax, Almondbury and Burnsall to relay and Belgrave 5k/10k results, with Gary Staines fastest on the first leg of the Blackheath 6x3M relay. The organisers of the "Run for Rumania" 10 kms race at Blackheath on May 10th aimed to raise £1,000 for the needy orphans of Eastern Europe by putting on this cross-country race. Owain Lewes supported them with a winning 34:03 timing, a full minute ahead of second man Smythe of Cambridge H. On the same day in the Alton '10' Martin Lake was clocked at 55:59 for 6th place with Don Anderson just over the hour at 60:22 for 24th. The LARA Long Grove races have given many a Belgravians the chance of a mid-week outing. John Barry availed himself of the 2 miles event on May 13th when he placed 6th with 10:42. A week after running the 'A' 1500 in BAL match 1 at Birmingham Steve Halliday was back on the roads for the Halifax Courier 10k. He won it by a minute and a half in 30:53. The City of Canterbury Half-Marathon on May 17th saw Steve Willimont get up to 23rd with 76:29. In a sweltering 80 degrees Farenheit, Jim Estall came home 21st for Surrey in the Inter-Counties 20 miles race at Corby. Pete Gardner ran a 5:02 in the Capital Road Mile in Hyde Park on May 20th. Cool and overcast conditions for the Lensbury 10k at Teddington on June 7th resulted in some fast times for the leaders of the 800 strong field and Jim Estall's 31:19 gained him 21st place. The Turk's Head '10' was held along the towpath of the River Thames at Twickenham and hot conditions prevailed once more. Jim got up to 11th in 55:22. He was also up among some classy opposition in the Southwark '5' where his 25:09 gained him 5th. As usual, Marcello likes to mix a bit of road running in with his track work and June 1st saw him winning the Sri Chinmoy 2 miles at Battersea in 9:29. Unfortunately it was about this time that "March" got struck down with a virus that gave him trouble on and off for the rest of the summer. The Chemical Corporate Challenge was held in heat-wave conditions at Battersea Park on July 15th. Our second-claim member Chris Sweeney (16:16) was beaten to the tape by just 1 second by a team mate from British Gas. In fact the first three home all represented BG. Roger Alsop, running for Nat West Bank, was =28th in 17:40. There must have been some other Belgravians among the 3,500 runners but we don't know any other details. At Davos in Switzerland on July 19th Paul Evans raced to 3rd in 23:37 behind Kenyans Omwoyo, 23:21, and Maritim, 23:29. Behind were Dos Santos and Steve Brace. In the Sri Chinmoy races Marcello Bizio placed 3rd over 2 miles on July 13th, 9:43, and Marco Mazzotta was 7th, 9:56. A week later over 1 mile Roger Alsop was also 3rd, in 4:27. Marco got under 10 minutes again on 3rd August, with 9:59 while Tony Stone took 2nd in the M50's with 11:33. In September's race it was the turn of Gary Pitts to score with 3rd in 9:49. Steve Halliday clocked 4:11 for the Leeds City Open Mile on August 11th but this was just a pipe opener for the Almondbury 10k at Huddersfield a week later. Here he came home well over a minute clear of the field in 32:14 to remove 9 seconds from the course record. Within four days he was in action again in the Burnsall 10 miles. This gave him his third win in the event, earlier victories coming in '88 and '89. His time was 51:16 from Otley's I.Fisher, 52:57. items.label: April 1993
items.sum: Editorial arguing that, despite the men's cross-country demotion and financial worries, the winter brought much good news, and explaining the committee's plan to set up new sub-committees to run the club.
items.s: Editorial arguing that, despite the men's cross-country demotion and financial worries, the winter brought much good news, and explaining the committee's plan to set up new sub-committees to run the club. Many members have said that this winter's results have been a disaster, with demotion from Division One of the Surrey Cross Country League such a contrast to the track and field successes of last summer. Certainly our Cross Country Secretary Colin Pearson has been pretty fed up with the lack of support from team members over the ``country''. This, together with our Treasurer's warnings about the state of finances within the club and lack of any of the sponsorship deals enjoyed by other clubs have made it seem like a very dismal winter. But is this really the case? One of the benefits of editing the club magazine is the gathering of news from all areas of the club and there is no doubt that, on the whole, there is far more good news to report in this edition than bad. Our Ladies, with their wonderful team spirit, have done well to gain promotion to Division One of the Surrey League in such a positive manner, and Belgrave's young stars in the Youths and Boys team convincingly won their section of the Surrey League with the Colts also doing well to finish third. We haven't had successes like that from our youngsters since the days of Gladwin and Co. Even in the Men's Cross Country we have a new star in Kaesse Tadesse who warmed the hearts of many on a freezing day at Parliament Hill with his second place in the Junior race. There has been a feeling on the committee for a while that some aspects of the management of the Club might need to be reviewed. Athletics has changed so much over the last ten or twenty years with the introduction of open Athletics and sponsorship and it is important that Belgrave should reflect those changes. It is also important for the club to review areas which are not doing so well and become pro-active in helping those areas. At an extra committee meeting held specially to discuss this topic on March 1st it was decided to set up a number of sub-committees whose areas of responsibility are to cut right across the traditional sections of the Club. For instance, it is intended that the Track and Field group should cover both genders, all age groups and include track walking; the Road Running, Cross Country and Road Walking sub-committee would have a similar structure. Sub-committees are also being created for Finance, Social Activities, Sponsorship and Public Relations, Membership Services, Belgrave Hall, Relationships with external bodies and, finally, Planning and Development. The idea is that each of these groups' activities will still need to be ratified by the General Committee which, it has been suggested, should be restructured along slimmer lines than at present. The Planning and Development sub-committee would be a sort of ``think tank'' for the club. It has already played a great role in developing and presenting the ideas of Club members who felt that it was time for our administration and organisation to be looked at critically. Some of the ideas that have come up have, to say the very least, been radical. Some, even if accepted by the current General Committee, would require changes to be made at the Annual General Meeting. There have already been those who have said that we tried to form sub-committees before and it didn't work, while some older members have commented that the ideas are nothing new, the club used to be run this way in the past. Well, no good ideas are truly original, so hopefully Belgrave can learn from the past, make changes where they will benefit our Club and look forward to continued progress into the next century. Colin Pearson Colin Pearson Cross Country Secretary Gladwin Gladwin 'the days of Gladwin and Co.' — earlier successful young athletes Kaesse Tadesse Kaesse Tadesse second in the Junior race at Parliament Hill (National); spelt Kaessa elsewhere in the issue Surrey League National Cross Country Championships Parliament Hill

items.s: Help! Appeal for officials to cover the club's duties at Southern T&F League away meetings, continued on page 19 with contacts Jean Hutcherson and Bob Bridges. Help! We are desperately in need of help! At Southern T&F League away meetings we are supposed to provide a track judge, a timekeeper, and a team of judges for a field event. The trouble is that our two men's SL teams have eleven away matches between them this summer and so far we have no judges or timekeepers whatsoever for these meetings. Please, we have got to do something about this predicament. Couldn't you lend a hand - even just for one match? Perhaps you are a normally active athlete but currently on the injured list. It doesn't matter if you have no experience, it's willing hands that we need. items.sum: Look-back column reprinting news of members in the services from May 1943 and cross-country and road-relay reports from June 1968.
items.s: From "THE BELGRAVIAN" Look-back column reprinting news of members in the services from May 1943 and cross-country and road-relay reports from June 1968. From "THE BELGRAVIAN" 50 YEARS AGO ..... May 1943 News from members in the services:- Lieutenant F.W. 'Billy' Pritchard of the anti-tank regiment has been killed in action in North Africa. He will be remembered as a sprinter of merit. Captain Tommy Green recently met with a bombing accident and suffered three slight wounds. Wally Ives, out in India, writes ``Always I am waiting for the call which means HOME and WIMBLEDON''. His letter took eleven weeks to arrive. Arthur Beaumont says he is now in Tripoli for a rest after the big advance. Tells unusual tales about the Arabs and tent life. Percy Wright, in South Wales, acknowledging 'The Belgravian', says ``It's equal to a flash of cockney in the heart of this place and believe me that's saying something. When the mag arrives it carries me back to stale sinks and an overcrowded bath tub''. Alf Orton says that after 8 1/2 months in the desert he can now get in to Cairo. Hasn't felt like training; though a 2:06 time for 800 metres has nearly made him change his mind. Flying Officer Bill Lucas found time to look in at Belgrave Hall when on leave from instructional flying duties. Joe Flower, writing from West Africa, says of 'The Belgravian' ``What pleasure that little journal brings''. Dan Patience, after having been stationed in the wilds of Ayr, bemoaning his fate because he couldn't get a run, now writes from North Africa! Says that all he does is marching, bathing and eating oranges. Len Fletcher says that if he asks for leave for walking ``The beaks of this Fred Karno outfit think you want to take a WAAF out''. Flight Sergeant Colin Sutton has hopped from the Middle East to India. He has started training again and met the Indian Champion, Simba, over 1500 metres but was beaten. There will be a return match. Reg Shepherd, back from Canada with his ``wings'' is now in Scotland. (News has just been received that Reg has been posted missing after a reconaissance over Europe). Knut Moe our Norwegian member, according to rumour from a neutral source, has escaped to England. Les Bennett is still amongst the missing in Malaya. His wife Olive writes ``It is over a year since I last heard from my husband. I have not given up hope and have great confidence that he is safe and well''. 25 YEARS AGO ..... JUNE 1968 Cross-Country ``Many of our members will consider that 4th place in the ``National'' at Sutton Coldfield was a good performance but to those of us who know the potential of our runners this was a most disappointing result. This is the THIRD year in succession that we have occupied 4th position and although we move nearer and nearer to the leaders year by year there is no doubt that this year's team could have won handsomely given the right preparation and right approach. Tony Fairclough was unlucky to suffer two bad falls. 11th Gerry North, 31st Geoff North, 45th John Thresher, 78th Adrian Major, 87th Bill Dance, 102nd Peter Whewell, 139th Laurie O'Hara, 160th Trevor Hart, 179th Tony Fairclough.'' Road Relays ``Two firsts, two seconds and two thirds. Our best for many years. That must be the undisputed verdict on a spring road-relay season that saw our team do battle on six occasions and return home with awards every time. The peak of this brief but high powered season was undoubtedly the National 12-stage Relay at Leicester where Coventry Godiva, aided and abetted by our ``own'' Mel Thorpe, ran out deserved winners. That Derby should edge us out of the silver by just 11 seconds may seem rough justice. Including our reserve (Dabbs) five of our thirteen runners are over 30 years of age, headed by Bill Kerr, 36. The average age of the team is 28yrs 4mths. It will be up to our three under-24's Bicourt, Major and Donnison to share an ever increasing degree of responsibility in our future teams, especially with the loss of Peter Whewell to South Africa, Gerry Williams to Venezuela, Chris Steer to Canada and Geoff North to retirement (again). items.s: We're looking good! Ted Pallant thanks members for adopting the official Belgrave strip and invites orders for a new batch of track suits. We're looking good! My effort to co-ordinate the official Belgrave strip seems, with your support, to be progressing quite successfully. You must all by now be aware of my feelings that, as one of the country's leading clubs, we were not looking the part of the Champion team that we are. Now there's no excuse. The complete strip is available to all and many of you have taken to wearing it with pride and as a result are giving the club the increased publicity it deserves after the successes of recent years. Thanks for your help There was a great response to my request for your assistance in helping me complete my sets of athletics magazines. Thanks to the following people I am now only 8 issues short of every "Athletics Weekly" going back to when it actually became a weekly in 1950: John and Pam Davies, Leo Coy, Pete Mulholland (Hercules Wimbledon AC), Colin Pearson, Tom Morell, Tommy Thomas (South London H), Charlie Jones, Arthur Penstone, Win Shepherd, Nina Mills, Bob Bridges, Charlie Dickinson and Martin Duff (Aldershot F&D). Nina dug out some copies of "Women's Athletics" which make for some interesting reading. This was a short-lived sister magazine to "AW" lasting just twelve issues from May '68 to April '69. It contains some gems like, "... following a beauty routine both during the week and on the day of competition ..." and featured a male track pin-up each month! Maybe "The Belgravian" could pick up a few tips here. Arthur Penstone came up with a nice little run of "The Belgravian" from the early '30s and Tom Morell has passed on some copies of "Amateur Athlete", a weekly produced by Armour Milne during the War years. Thanks again to you all - and if anyone can come up with the following then I'll be ecstatic: "Athletics Weekly" 1954 No. 43. 1956 No. 34 1960 Nos. 3, 6, 7, 9, 17, 44. items.sum: Report on the English Cross Country Championships at Parliament Hill on 27 February, led by Kaesse Tadesse's second place in the Junior race, with Youth, Junior and Senior race accounts and results.
items.s: Kaessa breaks the drought Report on the English Cross Country Championships at Parliament Hill on 27 February, led by Kaesse Tadesse's second place in the Junior race, with Youth, Junior and Senior race accounts and results. Kaessa breaks the drought ENGLISH CC CHAMPS., PARLIAMENT HILL, 27 FEB A magnificent second place by Kaesse Tadesse in the Junior Men's race warmed the hearts of Belgrave supporters in the Arctic conditions of Parliament Hill fields. We have had a long, barren stretch as far as cross country goes. There have been relatively successful Belgrave Junior teams, and our Juniors and Seniors were near the front in the early to mid-sixties but how long is it since a Belgravian last took home a ``National'' cross country medal of any variety? Charlie Dickinson and Alan Mead report Returning to the famous course for the first time since Julian Goater won by nearly two minutes in 1981, and although the strength of the fields was perhaps weakened by the revamped Inter-Counties/ International Trial three weeks before, the National nevertheless produced three very exciting races. The course had been slightly altered because of gas maintenance work around Kenwood and therefore had even more twists, turns and undulations than in previous years. This together with numerous boggy patches left by the winter rain, the terrible uphill start, and a freezing wind bringing squalls of snow from the north, certainly produced a test of the ``traditional'' kind. Youth 7k The youngest age group was the one that promised most for Belgrave in the way of team positions. Our lads could mostly be classed as belonging to the shorter middle-distance group, perhaps not best suited to 7,000 metres over Parliament Hill. However, it was felt that a team place inside the top ten might just be on the cards. Imagine the excitement then, when after the charge up the starting hill, Ben Hamill was placed handily on the shoulder of joint favourite Scott West, leading the field as they went over the top. As if that wasn't enough the cheeky blighter had the audacity to wink to the Belgrave supporters cheering him on. Unfortunately even bold Ben couldn't sustain this sort of action for the full distance. The loss of a shoe together with his extravagant start had him spinning back through the field to a position well below his potential. Adam Jones was another who would have expected to place a lot higher, so in spite of a brilliant 34th from Matt Hillier, who was really flying over the last section of the race, and an equally impressive 54th from Gavin Mason, the team had to settle for 17th. Nevertheless, we were still 4th Southern team home. 1, K.Farrow (Derby & C) 21:15; 2, W.Levett (Tonbridge) 21:35; 3, B.Noad (Bristol) 21:47; ... 34, M.Hillier 22:48; 54, G.Mason 23:09; 180, M.Anderson 24:48; 232, B.Hamill 25:36; 240, A.Jones 25:41; 335, T.Earle 30:39. Teams: 1, Derby & C 68; 2, Oxford City 155; 3, Royal Sutton Coldfield 181; ... 17, Belgrave 500; 39 teams closed in. Junior 10k In the Junior race, Kaesse was well to the front of a large leading group at the start, then began to force the pace in the long downhill sweep coming out of the South Meadow on the first lap. This broke the field, apart from Spencer Barden who had won so convincingly in the South of Thames a month before, Tim Dickinson, running a 'blinder' for Blackheath, and Stefan White of Coventry Godiva, runner up at Luton in 1991, and running for the third time as a Junior. These four continued to battle it out as the race entered the second lap with Barden, the favourite, now leading and Kaesse clinging to third place. But this effort visibly tired the strong looking GEC Avionics man, giving Stefan White his chance. With Kaesse hanging on like grim death, White made his move half way through the final lap and the pair quickly opened up a huge gap over Barden. As they swept around Kite hill to the finish, Kaesse made one final spirited effort to close a five yard gap, but White's strength and experience prevailed and he pulled away round the fields to the finish. For a man who dislikes the cold, dislikes the mud, and dislikes hills, Kaesse had run so very well. Danny Winson was our only other Junior. For a man who competes over 400 and 800 metres in our track teams, Danny has been showing good form in his last few cross country races but he too suffered from a shoe lost to the glutinous Hampstead mud. Interestingly, only four of the twenty-six teams that finished had a full complement of six runners. 1, S.White (Coventry Godiva 29:42; 2, K.Tadesse (Belgrave) 29:49; 3, S.Barden (GEC Avionics) 30:14; ... 161, D.Winson 35:27. Senior 15k The Seniors were led home by Jim Estall who ran what appeared to be a comfortable race. Owain Lewes was next scorer and ran probably his best race of the season. He ran in bare feet which seemed ideal for the conditions but strange for someone who sells running shoes. Perhaps he knows more than we do! Mike Lake ran another steady race. 1, R.Nerurkar (Bingley) 42:52; 2, D.Payne (Tipton); 3, P.Roden (Sale) 43:08; ... 230, J.Estall 48:13; 421, O.Lewes 50:03; 532, Mike Lake 50:55; 696, M.Mazzotta 52:01; 1011, R.Harding 54:36; 1099, S.Willimont 55:17; 1946, A.Stone 63:50. items.s: Dougie gets it wrong - and wins ! Result of the previous issue's photo competition (the picture was of Leo Coy, prize to Doug Maughan) and a new teaser asking readers to name the faces in a crowd photo of Belgrave supporters taken at a South Coast resort. Dougie gets it wrong - and wins ! We weren't exactly inundated with entries for the competition set in the last issue. Who was that smart young fellow depicted on page 49? Well, two people had a crack: Bert Stroud reckoned it was a young Don Anderson, thinking about slipping out to go train-spotting. Doug Maughan, on the other hand, thought it was Jim Heathfield. ``I've had my picture taken, read the lesson, what next? I thought I was joining a running club!'' (Incidentally, Doug thinks that Jim looks just as smart in 1993, even in his long trousers. Sorry lads, you're both wrong. The photo' was of Leo Coy and we reckon it was a shot of him learning his lines for reading out the season's best performances at the 1952 Club Dinner! Anyway, we had a prize lined up, and it was Doug's name that came out of the hat. He is now the proud owner of a copy of the Track Statistician's Bible - The ATFS Athletics 1992 Handbook. See, it was worth entering. Have a go at this issue's teaser. A prize will be awarded to the person who can put the most names to faces in the accompanying photograph below. As a tie-breaker you'd better tell us a bit about the occasion as well! We'll give you a clue - the picture was taken at a well known South Coast resort. Doug Maughan has promised to donate the prize, but just in case the winner is a bit long in the tooth for wearing a pair of the latest in lycra training tights, we'll have a standby prize of something a little more suitable. Of course we will have to bar the owner of the photograph (one of the crowd) from entering, but what we will do is make them the judge. All entries to be received at [address withheld], by 31st July. How many faces can you name? How many faces can you name? items.sum: Carl Lawton complains that over 80 members had not paid their subscriptions by 23 March, some of them well-known athletes, and sarcastically suggests making subscriptions optional.
items.s: Membership moans Carl Lawton complains that over 80 members had not paid their subscriptions by 23 March, some of them well-known athletes, and sarcastically suggests making subscriptions optional. Membership moans I am sure all club members will be pleased to be aware of the Club's financial problems and the efforts some of their elected officials go to, to ensure the careful management of our limited resources. We are not a sponsored Club and have to rely on subscription and generous donations from members. Unfortunately we are blighted, as no doubt other organisations are, by a proportion of ``members'' who decline to pay these subs. As at March 23rd over 80 ``names'' are outstanding. Regretably some of these are well known and, in cases, from their gains from the many major athletic meetings at which they compete, it is unfortunate that they cannot see their way to providing the Club with the small amount that is requested. For those of you that would criticise that some of these are poor and live a hand to mouth existence, well, this may be the case, but we can only help if we are informed. Non-reply to letters tells us nothing. One simple way out of this annual predicament is to make subscriptions optional: only send out one reminder per year and let the Club stew from lack of finance. This will make my job nice and easy and then I won't have an axe to grind about non-payers. Carl Lawton Carl Lawton Carl Lawton handles membership subscriptions

items.sum: Club gossip column with news of members old and new: reminiscences of trips to the 1936 Berlin and 1960 Rome Olympics, injuries to Paul King, Gary Staines and Lewis Samuel, a Merton civic reception for the European Clubs' team, and Julia Cockram's return to high jumping.
items.s: Sidetracks Club gossip column with news of members old and new: reminiscences of trips to the 1936 Berlin and 1960 Rome Olympics, injuries to Paul King, Gary Staines and Lewis Samuel, a Merton civic reception for the European Clubs' team, and Julia Cockram's return to high jumping. Sidetracks Tony Whatley, an old friend of Tony Verdie's from some way back, turned out for the Belgrave Half-Marathon, hoping to renew their acquaintanceship. He sends his regards and hopes to catch up with him soon at some other race. Colin Pearson bumped into Alf Horton a few months back. Alf is well and asks that his best wishes be passed on to all that remember him up at the Hall. We read in the Veterans Athletic Club Newsletter that Cecil Gittins has been elected President of that Club for 1992-93. The newsletter goes on to praise him as one of the hardest working officials in our sport, something that we in Belgrave can only endorse. Congratulations, Cecil. Good old Marcello! Together with his willing band of helpers, his hard work in organising another Sunday afternoon Italian ``binge'' at the Hall netted the Club nigh on £200. Tom Carter has been corresponding with one of his old colleagues Dave Main, who is now living in Tournon in France where he is converting a barn to a small house. Previously he had lived in Karpathos, Greece for seven years. Dave recalls the lads of '46. ``Oh! What happy days they were. I can still re-live our training runs around the Common and sometimes into Richmond Park, you pushing as all to the limit (except for the odd day when you were not feeling so good) and then Len Herbert or myself would try and push you - great fun it was. It does not seem to have done the members any harm either, they all seem to be steaming past the eighties and into the nineties - long may they go on.'' Dave keeps fit by hitting the odd golf ball. One of his sons has run the Boston and London Marathons and he has a nephew who has also completed the ``London''. Hearing about the prospective trip by a Belgrave party to Stuttgart for the World Championships, Charlie Jones recalls the trip he made with fellow Belgravians to the Berlin Olympics in 1936. He had to save for two and a half years to rake together the £35 they each needed for the jaunt. Charlie remembers the rail and boat fare figure to this day - five pounds, nine shillings and seven pence halfpenny! They combined the athletics with a walking holiday along the Rhine, staying at Youth Hostels. Charlie had a fall just a year ago and doesn't get out as regularly as he used to but both he and Betty are well. Win Shepherd too recalls a Belgrave trip on the Continent - to the Rome Olympics of 1960. They had trouble from the start when they couldn't get into their hotel room due to its occupancy by a group of Polish swimmers who were refusing to leave as one of their number had got to the finals. They managed to get put up elsewhere and Harry Shields ended up in the hotel Manager's flat - immaculate decorations including a marble floor - and the first thing he did was set up a primus stove on the floor to brew up a cup of tea. We understand that Sheena Lucas underwent a hip replacement operation a few months ago but has been making a good recovery. Our best wishes go to her and we look forward to seeing her at one or other of our summer competitions. A fractured limb has been the lot of walker Paul King this winter. Motorcyclist Paul now shares a little more in common with Barry Sheene, having had an assortment of steel pins inserted in his leg to hold it together after a collision with a car. Actually Paul was lucky he didn't get his other leg broken as well, for when Messrs. Warburton and Lawton arranged to go and see him in hospital, they only found out by chance that he had discharged himself without telling anyone. Believe it or not it wasn't too long before 'Kingy' was managing to get up to the Hall again on training nights - and even if he couldn't get out for a spin, he took advantage of the Club showers. But amazingly, as we go to print, we find that not only is Paul out training again but is planning to enter one of the Veterans Walks at Battersea in a few days! Unfortunately a little more news about those on the injured list. Poor Gary Staines is, if nothing else, learning how to be patient. Having completed the long haul back to fitness after his achilles tendon problems and operation and with the track season all but upon him, he has now suffered troubles with a calf muscle and at best is likely to have to put his season back a bit. But for 400 metre star Lewis Samuel the season is already over due to a ruptured achilles tendon, perhaps the worst of athletic injuries and one which hit him, we believe, while playing basketball in Lanzarote. To Lewis and all others on the injured list we send our hopes for a speedy recovery and return to the team. An interesting document to come the way of ``The Belgravian'' Editorial Offices is a copy of a completed application for a US National Collegiate Championships record. Mike Edwards, representing his Texas outfit Abiline Christian University, vaulted 5.25m to help his team win the competition at the Dakotadome, Vermilion, on March 13th. A dozen or so members of our track and field team gathered in the Mayor of Merton's Parlour on the evening of Monday 5th April. The Mayor had been thrilled to find out that Great Britain was being represented in the European Clubs' Championship by a team from his own borough and wanted to be introduced to the Bels. He presented a Merton Borough flag for us to fly in Budapest and the Council made a most generous donation towards the costs of transporting the team to Hungary. Haringey's Dalton Grant is a fine ambassador for our sport and we have him to thank - although he probably doesn't know it - for the re-launching of the athletic career of Julia Cockram. Julia's 1.59m High Jump, set as an Under-13 in May 1980, has stood the test of time and still ranks as the equal 9th best performance ever by a British Minor Girl. Third on that list is current international Debora Marti's 1.65m, also from 1980. As a 15 year old Julie competed for Surrey in the English Schools Championships, clearing 1.75m, but like many others it was not long before she dropped out of the sport. Luckily, however, that was not the end of the story. A chance meeting with Dalton and the exchange of a few enthusiastic words about the jumping that she used to do when she was a schoolgirl was all that was required to make her think about getting fit again. And looking for a club, she fortunately decided upon Belgrave. Good old Dalton! items.sum: Obituary of F.A. 'Mickey' Walker (1908-1992), a supporting cross-country runner of the 1930s and 1940s who won the Surrey County 20-mile title and later lived in Cornwall.
items.s: OBITUARY F.A. "Mickey" Walker (1908-1992) Obituary of F.A. 'Mickey' Walker (1908-1992), a supporting cross-country runner of the 1930s and 1940s who won the Surrey County 20-mile title and later lived in Cornwall. OBITUARY F.A. ``Mickey'' Walker (1908-1992) Mickey Walker was a contemporary of Tom Carter's. Both were born in 1908; they joined Belgrave within nine months of each other and later in their lives went into business together. He was not one of the stars who featured in our formidable teams of the '30s and '40s, but he was a sound supporting runner who frequently featured in 12-to-score teams and on one occasion was just pipped for sixth scorer by Alf Taylor when the ``Southern'' was held at Taplow. In the late 1930s he concentrated on distance running with some success. He gained a 1st Class standard in the Polytechnic Marathon of 1938 and the following year won the Surrey County '20' title ahead of the legendary Bert Footer who was making his debut at the distance. His success in this race led to an over-confident start in the Polytechnic Marathon where ``he blazed through the first five miles in sub-28 minutes'' (Belgravian) - quite a pace in those days. He faded to a creditable 12th. Seeing Footer finish 3rd made him wonder what might have been. Unlike Carter, Walker did not regard Belgrave as a major part of his life and when he moved to Cornwall he allowed his membership to lapse. He re-joined the Club in 1963, at Tom's instigation, and visited Belgrave Hall very occasionally. He died at his Cornwall home in 1992 at the age of 84 years. Our commiserations are extended to his family and friends. Clive Shippen F.A. "Mickey" Walker F.A. Indoor Track & Field BIRMINGHAM GAMES, NIA, 8/9 JAN Fred Salle had a clear margin over Cannock & Stafford's Barrington Williams and sharpened up with a bit of speedwork in the 60m as well. The sprints were dominated by young pretenders but Phil Goedluck showed he was in good shape, reaching the final and ending up only 1/10th off his best outdoor time for last season. 60m: (heats) P.Goedluck 6.94; F.Salle 7.10. 200m: 5, P.Goedluck 21.59; (semis) J.Ridgeon 22.08. 3000m: 15, R.Turner 8:30.90. 60mH: 7, N.Owen 8.17. HJ: 6, A.Hutchinson 2.00. LJ: 1, F.Salle 7.60. PV: 6, D.McDermott 4.60. SP: 3, L.Marar 15.75. PEARL INTERNATIONAL GAMES, KELVIN HALL, GLASGOW, 30 JAN Fred Salle had the indoor jump of a lifetime when in the first round he cut the sand at 7.96 metres for a Club Record, only 9cm behind the UK best and just 1cm shy of his outdoor pb set in 1986. He followed up with a no jump but still held the lead going into the 3rd round when World Record holder Mike Powell managed to register a lacklustre (for him) 8.07. Powell went on to record an all-comers record of 8.36 with his last leap. Fred also got in a 7.82 to back up but slipped to 4th as Russians Bogrianov and Tarasenko crept past him. Paul Edward's series in the shot read 18.17, 18.20, x, 17.86, 17.82, x, but he too suffered at the hands of two Russians; Nikolayev and Smirnov reached 20.38 and 19.83. VAUXHALL INTERNATIONAL, NIA, BIRMINGHAM 13 FEB The GB versus USA indoor match always generates a lot of excitement on this side of the Atlantic but unfortunately rather less in the hearts of the away team. Once again the American outfit was devoid of many of the top names in T&F and they suffered a resounding defeat as a result. Marcus Adam and John Regis returned from off-season training in sunny California to don British singlets and lined up together in the one lap race against the rising young Briton Darren Campbell. The two Belgravians had no trouble in putting him and the Americans down with John just shading Marcus as they crossed the line. Unfortunately the former had clearly taken a shorter than legal route to the line and was disqualified. These three later teamed up with Windsor's Mark Richardson to defeat the USA team in the 4x200 relay, 1:23.56 to 1:23.79. As usual Paul Edwards had far too much muscle for his domestic opposition but was in turn well beaten by the three Americans with Olympic Champion Stulce setting an all-comers record of 21.77. Fred Salle continued his solid indoor season and had every right to be pleased with his 2nd place, but the winner only recorded 7.76 and a repeat of his Glasgow form would have given him victory. 200m: 1, M.Adam 21.06; J.Regis dsq unofficial time 21.0. LJ: 2, F.Salle 7.51. SP: 4, P.Edwards 18.56. TSB INTERNATIONAL, NIA, BIRMINGHAM, 20 FEB Neither John Regis or Marcus Adam had the World Indoor Championships pencilled into their programmes but their performances at the NIA showed that they would most certainly have been medal contenders. Marcus was edged in the final straight by Bulgaria's Antonov as they set the 3rd and 4th fastest times in the World this winter, 20.84 and 20.89. (A Russian was to go a fraction faster in Bercy on the same afternoon and an American performed similarly next day in Boston.) But John was not to be outdone. At the 200m point in his 300m race he was hand-timed at 20.9 and went on to win as he pleased in 32.98 - 8/100ths behind the British best. TSB AAA INDOOR CHAMPS., NIA, BIRMINGHAM, 27 FEB The Shot competition gave the Bels their only ``gold'', courtesy of Paul Edwards of course, but it is really worth taking note of Leith Marar's performances this winter. His best outdoor mark of 15.40 dates from 1990 and is surely due for revision. In indoor meeting after meeting he has peppered the 15.50 area - might we see a 16m plus effort when summer comes around? Warren Caswell had the pleasure of sharing 3rd place in the high jump with Geoff Parsons, and Phil Goedluck put two fine runs together in the one lap race, 21.64 to win heat 3 by five metres and then 21.62 for 5th in the final. 60m: ht. 6, L.Campbell 7.26. 200m: 5, P.Goedluck 21.62. 60mH: ht. 5, R.Hunter 8.40; 3, N.Owen 7.99. HJ: =3, W.Caswell 2.15. SP: 1, P.Edwards 18.47; 9, L.Marar 15.57. WORLD INDOOR CHAMPS., TORONTO, 12-14 MAR Fred Salle had every reason to be pleased with his indoor season, culminating in his selection for this fourth edition of the World Championships. A reproduction of his Kelvin Hall form should have seen him in the final and another few centimetres on top might even have put a medal within his grasp. But sometimes luck just runs the wrong way. Two ``no jumps'' left him with one last attempt to force his way into the final and how galling it was to find that red flag going up yet again for a marginal violation of the plasticene. No distance recorded for Fred while the 'bronze' went at 7.98 with Fred's best of the season 7.96! Better luck had come Belgrave's way on day one when Shot Putter Paul Edwards was in action. Nineteen-sixty was required to guarantee progression to the final but only four athletes could reach that and Paul's second round effort of 18.23 saw him comfortably into the last twelve. The USA's Stulce had led the way in the qualifier and although fellow American Doehring led for four rounds, Stulce did the business again with a 5th putt of 21.27. Paul, meantime, confirmed his rating of 9th at these games with a 3rd round 18.32. items.s: Hunter aims for 7,000 points Decathlete Richard Hunter, a West London Institute student, describes his background as a hurdler, his injuries and finances, and his aim to score 7,000 points, with his training week, decathlon scores and 110m hurdles progression. Hunter aims for 7,000 points In September 1992 multi-eventer Richard Hunter upped his decathlon pb beyond the 6,000 mark for the first time. We invited Richard, a student at the West London Institute to tell us about himself and his aims for the future. I came to London, Isleworth in 1990 to study at W.L.I.H.E. where I am presently in my final year of a sports science degree. Having moved to the area from the North East I wanted to join a good ``local'' club. At the time I was only doing 110 metre hurdles and saw Belgrave as the ideal choice in terms of getting the races when I needed them. Unfortunately I have been hindered by injuries since coming to London. As a 110 metre hurdler I competed for my old club Gateshead Harriers and was second in two English Schools finals, 1987 and 1989. I also gained a GB Junior international vest in 1989. While I was still a Junior in 1990, I won the AAA 60 metres hurdles indoor title, but was again hampered by injuries in the summer season of that year. I then spent 1991 hurdling and messed about in two decathlons to get an idea of what I could do. In the winter of 1991 I decided to train for the multi-events, without having a coach to help me. I guess my favourite events are the 110 metre hurdles, long jump, 400 metres, but I actually enjoy them all. The only event that frustrates me is the javelin, for obvious reasons. In terms of aims, I have many long term and short term goals some of which include first of all breaking 6,500 points and 7,000 points. Then from there I would like to keep improving in 1994 and beyond. Athletics is a vital part of my life and I love the training as much as the competitions but the last two to three years have been hard, with injuries, lack of a coach (until Greg Richards came along), living off a student grant, and change of environment from the North East, where facilities are so good and free, with great people to train with and motivate you, to London where the tracks take so long to get to (eg. Haringey sessions involve three hours travelling time) and sometimes cost far too much! Then at the moment I have got to get orthotics for my shoes, which are going to cost me £170! On top of this I made sure I could go warm weather training in 1991 and 1992, both out of my own funds. This year my coach has gone with the group to Cyprus again but I was not able to go due to financial reasons. As far as my life outside athletics is concerned, I also have a part-time job as a gym instructor at a club in Twickenham. I also like music, clubs, movies, and travelling - there's always something to do. Training for week ending 4th April 1993 Mon No training - college work. He also clocked 49.96 in the 'B' 400m. Sharing a joke behind him are Belgrave's Ian Wells and Haringey's Dalton Grant. items.sum: Paul Warburton invites members to try racewalking at Tuesday evening 2.7k races in Battersea Park, arguing walkers have better chances of representative honours, with the summer race dates.
items.s: WALKING TO SUCCESS Paul Warburton invites members to try racewalking at Tuesday evening 2.7k races in Battersea Park, arguing walkers have better chances of representative honours, with the summer race dates. WALKING TO SUCCESS A chance to try something different - From small acorns grow unexpected opportunities of athletic stardom. This summer if you're in the vicinity of Battersea Park on certain Tuesday evenings listed at the end, why not give racewalking a try? Now just before you turn the page because you wouldn't be seen dead bum wiggling, at least give me the rest of the paragraph. What are your current chances of county, international or major championship honours? I would reckon that if you are athletically fit and open-minded the British walker has six times greater chances of doing one of the above than the British runner. Six times? A top road running field is 300 - a top walking field is 50. Every current Belgravian walker (aged between 30 and 60) has won a representative honour of some sort. Candidly, the British walking standard is not that strong. Some international vests in recent years have been won, especially by females, with remarkable ease. I was an average runner in 1982: 25:50 was my best for 5 miles. Giving walking a go was a means of recovering from injury. I decided to stick with it. By 1986 I had won National team medals, Southern area championships, county championships, and a sackfull of open race medals and prizes. Kerry Saxby was part of the excellent 'Little League' system in Australia where young children have a dabble at all athletic events, and discovered her event when she had a go at walking after an average showing at running, throwing, etc. At the time of writing she has just won another major championships medal indoors at Toronto to go with the 28 world records or bests already posted by the Queensland girl. Of course, anybody that knows anything, knows that walking is not a soft option. It's not easier than running. For a start it's the only event that combines technique and aerobic effort. And so it has cardio-vascular benefits the equal of running without the threat of accompanying injury. I'm not saying walking is for you. But it's like eating something new. If you've never tried it, how can you say you don't like it? Why not give walking one try before rejecting it? You might discover a new athletic career ... Jordan. Women's Road and Country SURREY CC LEAGUE, DIV. 2 RACE 1, TILFORD, 24 OCT Times are changing. In the opening match last season Jacinta Moore had to take on the other Surrey clubs single-handed and not surprisingly, as a team, we ended up in last position. This time around, however, our ladies started the season in the mood to battle for promotion back up to Division One, and on the sandy hills of the Tilford course, the toughest on which we compete, we turned out a full squad of five to score plus three more backing up. Helen Maskrey led the way and with some of our sprinters getting into the scoring positions we were pleased to finish as 2nd team, not too far behind Tadworth. In the intermediate race over 3.5k Jessica Dash was 18th in 17:49 and Laura Wilson was 5th in the minor's event, taking 10:03 for the 2.5k. 1, C.Hodgson (Hercules Wimb) 21:52; 2, H.Maskrey (Belgrave) 22:06; 3, J.Lodge (Hercules Wimb) 22:15; ... 9, J.Smiter 23:46; 20, N.Mills 25:25; 28, J.Stone 26:06; 39, B.Kulidzan 27:23; 69, P.Mead 32:01; 71, S.Porter 32:07; 73, A.Patten 32:40. PRIORY 3x2.5m RELAY, REIGATE, 7 OCT It took Helen 16:29 to tour the testing hills of the Reigate Priory and she was just under a minute slower than the fastest time of the day for her 4th place on leg one. Nina Mills was next away, clocking 19:02 to bring the team in 9th, and a now constantly improving Jacqui Smiter enjoyed herself on the final leg, picking off two of the opposition with her 17:56 effort. This was good running from our ladies - 7th place out of the 20 teams that finished. 1, Croydon 47:38; 2, Cambridge H 50:58; 3, Herne Hill 51:13; ... 7, Belgrave 53:27. SURREY CC LEAGUE, DIV. 2 RACE 2, EWELL COURT, 28 NOV With Morag Andrew and Gabby Collison drafted into the team it became a fight to get into the scoring five and the overall result was a resounding win for the Bels. and a fine individual victory for Helen. This course might be normally classed as flat and grassy but heavy rain had turned parts of the circuit into a leg-sapping quagmire - and then there was the descent down the slippery banks and through the muddy waters of the River Hogsmill to contend with on each lap! Eventually it was the two 'Js' who filled out the score sheet, pushing Nina Mills back to become our 6th placer. But watch out for the young woman who was next home and making her debut in Belgrave colours. Martina Ryan is no stranger to cross-country, having run regularly as a junior back in Ireland. It shouldn't take her too long to run off the few intervening years of inactivity, particularly as the Ryan family are in residence at the 'King of Denmark'; how convenient for training from Belgrave Hall just around the corner. 1, H. Jacqui Smiter's hard winter's training is beginning to pay off but what can you say about Jacinta Moore - a baby due in three months time and here she was closing off the scoring team to ensure that the Bels. claimed 2nd team prizes. 1, G.Collison (Belgrave) 17:46; 2, H.Imeson (Tadworth) 18:46; 3, J.Whyte (Tadworth) 19:51; 4, J.Smiter 19:59; 7, J.Moore 21:03; 8, S.Porter 24:31.
