items.h: SCVAC T&F League Mid-London Div., Match 2, Battersea Park 16 May
items.sum: Report and results of the second SCVAC veterans' track and field league match at Battersea Park on 16 May, with Leo Lyons' steeplechase club record and Jacinta Moore's winning medley relay leg.
items.s: SCVAC T&F League Mid-London Div., Match 2, Battersea Park 16 May Report and results of the second SCVAC veterans' track and field league match at Battersea Park on 16 May, with Leo Lyons' steeplechase club record and Jacinta Moore's winning medley relay leg. SCVAC T&F LEAGUE MID-LONDON DIV., MATCH 2 BATTERSEA PARK 16 MAY "Yep! Sometimes it's good being an old lady," chuckled Barbara Dunsford, nudging our team manager in the ribs after his congratulations to her on three more wins. It was another enjoyable evening for the Old Bels. although the men's team, looking for a win, were surprised to find themselves only third with Serpentine and Thames Valley getting the jump on them. Leo Lyons is running better than ever. The winter has seen him tearing away from the field at the start of every veterans' race in which he has taken part, laying down a challenge to all participants. It's a habit he's carried over onto the track and, running in flat shoes, he left the rest of the steeplechasers in his wake while removing a further half a minute off his M45 Club Record. What a treat it was, too, to see tough-guy Pete Gilbey back in action. A great technician over the barriers, Pete took the 'B' race by a street and was good enough to win this and probably any other SCVAC 'chase, but for clashing with an in-form Leo. He must have been pleased with himself too, because news of his run soon spread to the East Street Gym in Epsom where Pete does a lot of his workouts. Natalie Stracey and Nina Mills made their '94 debuts in individual events and both were involved in the final race, a medley relay that had competitors and officials from all clubs jumping with excitement. Pat Mead ran her socks off on the second 200 stint to keep us in contention with the "Serps" but they had a strong 400 runner who got away from Nina, still blowing hard after her 3k race. Now it was all up to Jacinta on the final 800 metre leg. Imperceptibly she closed over the first lap but was still 50 metres down at the bell. Remember, she had already won the 800 and 3,000. Surely this was just too much. But she continued to close ... quicker ... and quicker ... until, to the delight of all those present who were not wearing red vests with two yellow hoops, she tore past and into the lead. In match one our women ended up 115 points down on Serpentine Runners but here the gap was down to 51. Our women were on their way - and we had a secret weapon up our sleeves for match three! items.s: SCVAC T&F Championships, Swindon, 29 May Report of the SCVAC veterans' track and field championships at Swindon on 29 May, where Snowy Brooks, Leo Lyons and Charlie Dickinson each won gold. SCVAC T&F CHAMPIONSHIPS SWINDON, 29 MAY Only three Belgravians made the long journey to Swindon for this year's SCVAC Championships but Snowy Brooks, Leo Lyons and Charlie Dickinson all came away with a gold medal apiece, with Snowy collecting four second places as well. Although the rain mostly held off, it was a blustery day on a very exposed track next to the new Swindon Town football stadium. Although not too well supported in numbers there were many outstanding performances and championship bests, including a 10.16.7 run by Leo Lyons in the M45 Steeplechase where he sliced over a minute off the previous best. Elsewhere we were treated to a 54.78m hammer throw by BBC commentator Paul Dickenson, a 4.30m pole vault by Brian Hooper, and an 11.6/23.5 sprint double by Alastair Ross. Snowy won the M45 long jump with a leap of 5.31m, came second in the 100m and 200m in 13.0 and 27.1, and also gained 2nds in the discus and shot with throws of 33.60m and 10.34m. Charlie Dickinson was beaten in the 5000m by new vet Bill Bailey, an army man from Aldershot, but easily won the M45 category in 15:46.7. items.s: SCVAC T&F League Mid-London Div., Match 3, Hendon, 27 Jun Report and results of the third SCVAC veterans' track and field league match at Hendon on 27 June, where the Belgrave women consolidated second place and the men were third. SCVAC T&F LEAGUE MID-LONDON DIV., MATCH 3 HENDON, 27 JUN Our women's team had their best competition yet, beginning to look a sure bet to be our first ever Vets team to reach the SCVAC final as they consolidated 2nd position overall. With two ladies now operating in the W50 group we scored heavier than ever before, our points differential with the Serps now down to a mere 22 in this match. Barbara Dunsford rushed back from Bruges to set four pbs and was joined for the first time by our secret weapon, Cynthia James fresh into the age group. Another best ever came from Sally Scott, her 15.1 getting her frighteningly within range of a slot in Southern League relay teams. It was not such a happy story in the men's match. Work commitments kept a couple of our key competitors away and Leo Lyons ran with back trouble, making all the difference between 1st team place and 3rd in a tightly scored match. Bob Bridges and Snowy Brooks were able to put their rivalry to the test in the sprints and ended the evening being just tenths apart when the times were added up. Bob also broke new ground in the hammer - and what do you think of young Georgie Piddington - all the way up from Hayling Island on the South Coast for an evening filling in as reserve! items.h: SCVAC T&F League Mid-London Div., Match 4, Tooting, 25 Jul
items.sum: Report and results of the final SCVAC veterans' track and field league match at Tooting on 25 July, won by both the Belgrave men and women, with the women's 4x200m relay decided by Jacinta Moore on the last leg.
items.s: SCVAC T&F League Mid-London Div., Match 4, Tooting, 25 Jul Report and results of the final SCVAC veterans' track and field league match at Tooting on 25 July, won by both the Belgrave men and women, with the women's 4x200m relay decided by Jacinta Moore on the last leg. SCVAC T&F LEAGUE MID-LONDON DIV., MATCH 4 TOOTING, 25 JUL And so to the last matches in our division. The men had to win by miles to get through to the final but all our women needed to do was to turn up on the night. As it happened, both teams won handsomely for our first ever victories but as far as the men were concerned there just weren't quite enough points in the bag. A SCVAC T&F League Record for M50s came from Mike Edwards in the pole vault with a fine 3.20. Leo Lyons was back in form and good points were scored in the throws by Mike Small and Pani Zeniou. Paul Warburton did the business for us in the 2k walk, backed up well by Lionel Mann and Johnny Morris. Once again, however, poor Bob Bridges had to resort to the Koolpak - a pulled hamstring in the 100m! As for the women - they were great! We had just about every event covered for the first time, even the over 50's 5k where Pam Davies must have found it difficult to believe that she was back competing on Tooting track where her athletic career started in the 1950s. Sue Porter, Heather Miller and Margaret Stroud gave us a treble in the walk and Cynthia James mopped up points all over the arena but the hardest won victories came from Jacinta Moore. Jacinta took the 5,000 metres and then lined up for the 800, the very next event, and not surprisingly had to dig down exceedingly deep to stay ahead down the home straight - but it wasn't over yet. We needed to win the relay to clinch the match and that 4x 200 metres turned out to be so exciting that it was still being talked about months afterwards. Sally Scott was neck and neck with the Serpentine runner on leg one, passing the baton to Pat Mead just a stride down. Pat tore into the lead but our rivals crept back ahead on leg three as Natalie Stracey gave everything to keep close. The Serps. had a good sprinter in Jane Searle on their final stage and she must have fancied her chances against a Jacinta that was still blowing from the last two races. Both entered the straight together but with everyone from all the clubs leaping with excitement it was the Belgrave girl that got to the line first. Who could ever have imagined that veteran athletics could conjure up such thrills. Captain Snowy was delighted and Herne Hill's Byron Gray is still talking about it being the best race of the year - World Cup and all! items.h: Reebok Southern Veterans' Road Relay, Aldershot, 24 Sep
items.sum: Report and M60 result of the Reebok Southern Veterans' Road Relay at Aldershot on 24 September, where Laurie O'Hara's last leg won back the South of England M60 title from Barnet.
items.s: Reebok Southern Veterans' Road Relay, Aldershot, 24 Sep Report and M60 result of the Reebok Southern Veterans' Road Relay at Aldershot on 24 September, where Laurie O'Hara's last leg won back the South of England M60 title from Barnet. REEBOK SOUTHERN VETERANS' ROAD RELAY ALDERSHOT, 24 SEP The Belgrave over sixties stars won back the South of England title they lost last year to Barnet, but it was a pretty close thing with Laurie O'Hara outsprinting Ron Higgs in the final straight winning by a mere six seconds. Pat Newell had got Bels off to a great start with his fastest ever 60's leg in 23:57 nearly a minute ahead of Cambridge and two and a half minute clear of Bob Belmore of Barnet. But with Laurie Forster and John Wood back to their best, Charlie Walker not going too well and Bert Stroud rather unfit after his holiday, it was Barnet who had pulled into a 26 second lead by the end of the third leg. After the first lap Laurie had not appeared to have made much impression on the leader Ron Higgs, and even as the runners came into view at the top of the far hill there seemed too much for him to do. But as they raced down the hill on the far side of the playing fields the gap became visibly smaller and as Charlie screamed his instructions to Laurie to "get a move on", Laurie shifted gear at the final bend and the rest, as they say, was history. e: Surrey County Veterans Cross Country Championships
items.s: Surrey County Veterans CC Champs, Richmond Park, 8 Oct Report and results of the Surrey County Veterans' cross country championships at Richmond Park on 8 October, where the Belgrave M60 team won gold and the women were fourth. SURREY COUNTY VETERANS CC CHAMPS RICHMOND PARK, 8 OCT It was back to the usual lovely Autumn sunshine for this year's popular county championships after the cold day last year. New winners in all categories came from a somewhat reduced field of 157 runners. An equestrian event on part of the usual course forced the organisers to stage this year's race on the lower Petersham course. This meant climbing that terrible hill on each of the three laps. Another change was to allow the ladies race time to finish before starting the men's and this provided a far better atmosphere for the ladies. Jacinta Moore ran very well for 5th place, with Nina Mills in 15th and completing the team, Hilary Saw in 21st. Belgrave finished just outside the medals in 4th place. In the men's race it was again our over sixties who won the medals. Pat Newall, fit at the moment but hating the hill, won the bronze, but the team of Pat, Charlie Walker and Bert Slough again took the team gold with a mere ten points. We even had a fourth scorer in Derek Manning. Best of the rest was a very characteristically determined run from John Mather in 7th place and an epic struggle between Tony Stone and John Wasbrough in the M50's. John went faster up the hills and Tony overtook when they went down. In the end it was Tony's long legs that prevailed in the sprint to the line. Belgrave numbers were down on previous years and most hoped the race would return to the old course next year. Vets' T&F League up and running Richard Turner, organiser of the Southern Counties Veterans' T&F League was forced to stand down at the end of the '94 season due to pressure of work and it seemed for a while that the league might fold up. We are still not sure if there is going to be a final in 1995, or even if the other areas are going to continue with their divisions - but the Mid-London Division is up and running again. It is highly likely that each of the clubs we met last year will take part and the likely dates are as follows: Events are likely to be as in 1994 and once again all clubs are to provide a field judging team, track judge and timekeeper, with the host club taking on all the extra duties. items.s: Mann of the Mountains Item on the Scottish hill and road race results of royal chef Lionel Mann and his sons Robert and James during the summer of 1994. Mann of the Mountains If you examine the road running results shown in the pages of this magazine you'll spot the name Mann turning up with startling frequency. Shown below, however, are a whole series of results chalked up by the Mann family - Royal Chef Lionel with sons Robert and James - presumably while accompanying Ma'am on her hols. north of the border this summer. They certainly seem to pick out the tough ones! Two runners went missing on the downhill section of the Cairn William race. items.sum: Arthur Bruce's reminiscences of athletics in 1950: the cross country season, the Empire Games in Auckland and the start of the track season, illustrated with an Athletics Weekly cover from March 1950.
items.s: Athletics in 1950 Arthur Bruce's reminiscences of athletics in 1950: the cross country season, the Empire Games in Auckland and the start of the track season, illustrated with an Athletics Weekly cover from March 1950. Judging by the letters and comments we receive, Arthur Bruce's reminiscinces of athletics after World War II are among the most popular items in our magazine so we have pleasure in continuing with: ATHLETICS IN 1950 by Arthur Bruce The year of 1950 was one of transition for Great Britain. The rationing era was ending and the improvisation of the immediate post-war years was ending. More important, the generation of pre-war stars that had carried on after the war such as Sydney Wooderson and Don Finlay were now being supplanted by a new generation of athletes, some of whom were only at the beginning of high calibre careers. The climax to the year for British athletes would be the British Empire Games in New Zealand in February followed by the European Games at the Heysel Stadium, Brussels, in August. Both were to show the steady improvement of performances throughout the athletic world. The winter season preceding the Empire Games produced several new young cross country performers coupled with those making their mark from previous winters. The first major event of the year was the Inter-Counties Championship held at Leicester and it produced a clear win for Dr. Frank Aaron the Yorkshire Champion who pulled clear of the young prodigy Geoff Saunders who only four years previously had won the first National Youths' Championship. They were followed in by the T.V.H. star Alec Olney and another young rising luminary Walter Hesketh from Manchester A.C. Lancashire were clear in the team championship with a fifty points margin over Warwickshire. The Inter-Counties were followed in February by the district championships, the Southern at Eastbourne surprisingly won by Harry Hicks (Hampstead) in front of more experienced performers with T.V.H. taking the team honours in front of Aylesford Paper Mills, Blackheath and Belgrave. An interesting newcomer to the Juniors was Gordon Pirie, over a minute in front of his rivals, including brother Peter, South London H also taking the team honours. The Midland at Great Barr the same day went to the veteran performer Bobby Reid of Birchfield by only a second from team mate Ted Dalton with their club comfortably taking the team title. Inter-County Champion Aaron was the victor of the Northern at Horwich from Geoff Saunders and Don Birch of Leeds with the quality small club Sutton Harriers clear in the team event. The following month at Aylesbury the National Championships were resolved. The "Senior" produced another convincing win by Frank Aaron from Alec Olney, Reg. Gosney and Harry Hicks, with the team title going again to the excellent packing of the Northern Champions Sutton Harriers whose first five scorers were home in twentyfive places! Second were Harehill Liberals and then the Scottish Champions Shettleston Harriers. The "Junior" went to the powerful running of Walter Hesketh from Green of Reading and Jack Eastham of Bolton, team title going to East Cheshire Harriers. Youth winner was Ike Williams, clear of his rivals with Sutton Harriers taking the team title. Our team for the international at Brussels at the end of March, stronger and younger than immediate post-war years, was not fast enough to cope with the track oriented French and Belgian teams spearheaded by Alain Mimoun and Lucien Theys. Although Aaron and Olney ran well for 4th and 7th places respectively, the winning time of 45 minutes told it all - a different conception of cross-country running. The Empire Games The winter season was bisected by the timing of the Empire Games which took place in Eden Park, Auckland, New Zealand, in the first week of February. Despite competing out of season against the in season Australian and New Zealand performers the Home Countries did well with fines wins by John Parlett in the 880 yds, Len Eyre in the 3 miles, Dorothy Tyler in the high jump, Tim Anderson in the pole vault and Jack Holden in the marathon. Other sterling performances were those of Les Lewis, 2nd in the 440 yds, Alan Chivers, 2nd in the 6 miles, and Dr. Moody in the shot. Our teams took runners up spot in both relays. Our women's team, however, suffered from the very high level of performances set by the Australians and New Zealanders. The track season begins The track season was preceded by the usual short road relay period culminating in April with the London to Brighton Relay. A closely fought battle in the shortened version of the race, starting at Mitcham, resulted in a win by T.V.H. from Blackheath and Reading. The opening shots of the track season were fired at the White City on 18th March being the Inter-Varsity match between Oxford and Cambridge. The outstanding performer was Roger Bannister in the mile in 4:14.8, a new Inter-Varsity record and an indication of better things to come. Other names to go on to better things were John Wilkinson and J.M.K Finley in the sprints, Angus Scott in the 880 and Chris Brasher in the 3 miles. The first major meeting of the year at which the shape and strength of British Athletics would be expressed was the annual Inter-Counties Championship coupled with selected invitation international events; these were held at the White City over the Whitsun weekend. The first day again showed E. McDonald Bailey to be our outstanding sprinter, winning the invitation 200 metres in 21.3 by five metres and close to the British record. The other international event, the 800, was won by the massive Canadian performer Bob McFarlane. The domestic events resulted in good wins by Harry Whittle in the 440 hurdles, Alec Olney in the 3 miles and a new British 7 miles walk record in 51:21 by Lol Allen of Sheffield by four minutes. The second day's programme produced a record equalling run in the domestic 220 by McDonald Bailey in 21.2, a good 440 yds win by Olympic Champion Arthur Wint in 48.1 and the first of many wins by John Disley in the 2 mile steeplechase. Another prominent early season meeting, the Kinnaird Trophy, which some regarded as the English Club Championship meeting and was promoted by Polytechnic Harriers in conjunction with the annual Poly Marathon from Windsor to Chiswick, provided good early season competition and a British record equalling long jump of 25' 2¾" by S.Williams of the Polytechnic. Jack Holden won the marathon in confident style by over five minutes from A.Lawton of Leeds Harehill. Polytechnic Harriers took the team honours of their own promotion. A.A.A. Championships The A.A.A. Championships followed in July being the selection meeting for the forthcoming European Games in Brussels. The Friday night's events provided a usual hors d'oeuvre for the main events on the Saturday, with a sparkling 6 miles in which Frank Aaron fought an exciting duel with Van de Wattyne the Belgian Champion, finally drawing away for a new British Record of 29:33.6 with Mihalic of Yugoslavia 3rd. The other prominent final on Friday was Duncan McClarke's new British hammer record of 178'4½" from Gubijan of Yugoslavia. Saturday started with a British record in the 7 miles walk of 50:11.6 by Roland Hardy of Sheffield closely followed by his team mate Lol Allen. The half mile produced the expected battle between Arthur Wint the Olympic 400 metre Champion and Roger Bannister the future World mile record holder with John Parlett, the Empire Games 880 yds Champion thrown in for luck! Wint came home in 1:51.6 to equal the Championship Record from Bannister and Parlett. The field events continued to slowly improve with a close high jump battle between Alan Paterson and Ron Pavitt, victory going to the former with a record equalling leap. The 440 yds produced its usual tight finish with Les Lewis getting home from Derek Pugh in a record equalling 48.2. The mile, which was considered to be very open, showed a return to form of the holder Bill Nankeville who won in 4:12 from Empire Games Champion Len Eyre and Alan Parker. The 3 miles provided another great battle with Lucien Theys of Belgium, a popular visitor here, beating Alec Olney and a fast finishing Andy Ferguson in 14:09. Another title going overseas went to Segedin of Yugoslavia in the 2 mile steeplechase although John Disley, in finishing a close 2nd, indicated a future Olympic medal winner's potential. McDonald Bailey collected his usual double in the sprints to maintain his control of the British sprint scene. The final event, the 440 yds hurdles produced a class battle between Harry Whittle and Angus Scott and a win for the former but providing us with two good representatives at Brussels. Climax of the season And so to the climax of the season for British Athletics: The European Games at Stade Heysel in Brussels in late August. In the first final at which good results were expected, both British hopes Lol Allen and Roland Hardy were disqualified after finishing 2nd and 3rd respectively in the 10kms track walk. The less said about the standard of judging the better! Our lesser hopes in the 50kms walk were confirmed although Alf Cotton and John Proctor walked well to finish 5th and 6th. The superiority of the Russian women in the power events was early established by Nina Doumbadze in the women's discus, winning by some six metres from her nearest rival. However, British hopes were revived by Sheila Alexander and Dorothy Tyler in the high jump where they placed 1st and 2nd with our third string Betty Crowther finishing 5th. Our men swung into action in a nail-biting 800 metres in which Roger Bannister and Marcel Hansenne swept past new Norwegian discovery Audun Boysen only to have a flying John Parlett take the title right on the line in 1:50.5. Meanwhile Maureen Dyson, refighting her 1948 Olympic battle with Fanny Blankers-Koen, again collected the silver medal in the 80 metres hurdles, although the margin was greater. Zatopek! Zatopek's 10,000 metre win on the first day was significant in that on a 400 metre track he would have lapped the whole field, showing his tremendous superiority at this distance. The 5,000 metres final was eagerly awaited by the home crowd supporting their hero Gaston Reiff, the Olympic Champion renewing his Olympic battle with Emil Zatopek. The race took on a predictable course with the elegant Reiff stretching Zatopek on the rack for eleven laps only to have him race past in irresistable style with only a lap to go, a dismayed Reiff fading to be caught on the line for second place by a fast finishing Mimoun of France. Alex Olney ran his usual solid race for 8th place in 14:51. Our fortunes in the sprints were mixed. Despite looking a finallist in the 100 metres, won by Bally of France, Brian Shenton, showing the best form of his life, repeated his 21.5 best performance in semis and final for a totally unexpected win in the 200 metres. This was followed by the ever-consistent Alan Paterson taking the high jump in 1.96, one place better than his 2nd in Oslo in 1946. Another fighting performance from Harry Whittle gaining bronze in a good quality 400 metres hurdles final made you wonder what he would do if he could only hurdle! Fanny Blankers-Koen kept up her winning ways in the 200 metres, drawing away from Setchenov of the Soviet Union with Dorothy Hall taking third spot. The metric mile provided another storming finish with Bill Nankeville breaking clear of the field with 400 to go only to be collared close to home by Willi Slijkhuis of Holland and El Mabrouk of France in 3:47.2, the favourite Lennart Strand of Sweden not even finishing. The steeplechase produced another Czech in the Zatopek mould. Jan Roudny pulled clear of all the expected favourites in 9:05.4 including our own John Disley who finished 10th, having an uncommon off day. The relays again produced mixed fortunes for us as Britain did not make the first three in the sprint relay but were led by our new European Champion Derek Pugh in a tight finish with the Italians. A surprise win by our women's relay team after some sloppy baton changing by the Dutch and Soviet teams gave us an unexpected victory. Comparing our overall performances with the previous European Games indicated the progress made in our track and field standards, especially regaining our power in middle distance running, but our weaker events remained as before on the field. And what of Belgrave? And so we come to Belgrave's position in the span of British Athletics in 1950. The athletic scene over 40 years ago, our objectives and standards, were so different from what we observe today. No women's section, no British League, no Grand Prix Series and only a small percentage of the road races that we enjoy today. However, athletics in 1950 did have a structure which enabled athletes to fasten on to their priorities. For Belgrave 1950 was also a year of transition. Our strength, especially over the country, immediately after the War was the result of the quality performers from pre-war that were still available or inherited when athletics recommenced in 1945. By the year 1950 most of these stars were at the end of their careers and the junior talent that had joined immediately after the war had not yet come through. The cross country season indicated the situation as to this decline first in the County Championships. Belgrave were 2nd in the Surrey Champs. both in the team and individual, Len Herbert following Stone of Dorking St. Pauls and with only two in the first ten. Our performers in Middlesex under the name of Cadogan AC slipped to 4th team, only Derek Burfitt, 9th, and Vic Blowfield, 10th, making the county team. We did, however, have Jack Brown in 6th place in the Kent Championship. This situation was confirmed a few weeks later in the Inter-Counties, our first scorer in 52nd place being Bill Lucas - Surrey's third man. The Belgrave 10 mile Cross Country Championship at this time resulted in a win for Jack Brown in 59:31 from Steve Charlton and Bill Lucas. The Southern Champs the following month at Eastbourne at which the Club usually made a strong showing resulted in another 4th place behind T.V.H., Aylesford and Blackheath, our first man home being Les Stokell with a good performance by evergreen Ted Stimpson in 21st place. Our Juniors were a solid 5th with Charlie Walker 24th while our Youths were runners up with Don Maclean a good 4th in the individual. The National Cross Country Champs in March only reflected for Belgrave their previous performances. Eighth place would be considered today a good performance, especially with the scoring six in 100 places. Les Stokell was first home in 47th place. Sutton Harriers again proved their solidarity with their scoring six in 67 places. The Juniors were back in 21st with a solid run from Charlie Walker in 40th place and the Youths performed creditably in 7th spot with Don Maclean in 20th position. Meanwhile our walkers put up a good performance in the RWA 10 mile Championship, being 2nd to Sheffield with ever-consistant Harry Curcher second individual to Lol Allen and a good follow up performance by Charlie Churcher in 5th place. It's interesting to see the result of the '5¾' Road Championship that year with a win by Vic Blowfield in 29:09 from Bill Lucas and Charlie Walker. The Southern Clubs' London to Brighton Relay enabled Belgrave to display their strength in depth with a close up 4th and good runs by Derek Burfitt, Charlie Walker, Len Herbert and Bill Lucas. Our walkers continued their string of good performances with a close 2nd in the National 20 mile Championship to Woodford Green with Harry Clayton in 4th spot. The track season started annually with the County Champs. In the Surrey Bill Lucas won the 3 miles with 3rd places in the mile by Charlie Walker, the steeplechase by Eddie Short and in both sprints by Bas. Walden. Our only notable performances in the subsequent Inter-County Championships at the White City was a good win by Harry Churcher in the 2 mile walk and a fighting 2nd in the 3 miles by Len Herbert. Our performers in the other county champs. did well with Derek Burfitt and Vic Blowfield 1st and 3rd in the Middlesex 1 mile and Jack Brown 3rd in the Kent senior mile. In the RWA 50k Championship Belgrave maintained their good record in walking champs with 2nd team to Woodford Green, Clayton again walking well to take 3rd place. And so to the AAA Championships at the White City in July with a notable performance by veteran Charlie Smart in the 6 miles, finishing 5th overall but 3rd Englishman home! This was matched by Readman's 5th place in the 7 mile track walk behind Roland Hardy's British record. Our only other performance of note on the main day was from Bill Lucas, who always timed his best performances for championships. He finished a close 4th in the 3 miles, only 2 seconds behind winner Lucien Theys of Belgium, timed at 14:09. Bill subsequently represented Britain in the triangular meeting against USA and Turkey at the White City. Right: Gavin Mason pauses between reps while Clive Shippen gets busy with the camera. When Gavin clocked 48.89 to place 7th in the British League 'A' 400 metres on 2nd July he further complicated a little statistical anomaly. John Gladwin's Under 20 Club Record set in 1989 is a hand timed 48.9, but going back to 1977 Dave Mote also ran 48.9 as a Junior for Surrey AC. Surrey amalgamated with Belgrave in 1982 and therefore Dave had a 50% (and little known) claim on that record. Left: New under 17 Club Record holder at 56.39 and 10th best in the country for his age, Rob Milner also competed regularly over the 91.4cm barriers and set a Club Best for a 17 year-old of 58.3. Photo by Robin Nicholls Above: Aussie Mike "Mad Dog" Morgan was hoping to make the Commonwealth Games team for Wales in the Long Jump. Unfortunately he found out that they insist that their athletes must have competed in the Welsh Championships for at least two years. "It's bloody embarassing," he said, "I might have to consider becoming a flamin' Pom! items.s: Kassa beats huge field over 17.5k Kassa Tadesse wins the inaugural 17.5k Pont de Normandie Classic at Le Havre on 21 January, over a minute clear of Didier Bernard. Kassa beats huge field over 17.5k Kassa Tadesse produced further confirmation of his steady improvement as a road racer when he won the inaugural 17.5k Pont de Normandie Classic on 21st January, writes Bill Laws. Over 10,000 lined up as part of the celebrations to mark the opening of what is now the world's longest bridge spanning the Seine estuary at Le Havre. A six hour storm-swept ferry crossing did not deter the tough 21 year old from defeating a strong select field competing in a race held in high winds and driving rain. The bad weather ensured a steady start. After 4k a small group of five broke away with Kassa tucked in. At the 8k point Kassa surged up a sharp incline and a gap appeared which he gradually extended until by the finish he was over a minute clear of former French half marathon champion Didier Bernard. 1, 1, K.Tadesse 51:56; 2, D.Bernard 53:01. items.s: Tragic death of Michael Coleman Notice of the sudden death while jogging in Brockwell Park of Michael Coleman, Kassa Tadesse's mentor and manager, hours after Kassa's Pont de Normandie win. Tragic death of Michael Coleman Michael Coleman, who over the last few years has been mentor and manager to Kassa Tadesse, tragically collapsed and died while jogging. By a cruel twist of fate his untimely death occurred in Brockwell Park just hours after Kassa had won the Pont de Normandie Classic and Michael was never to receive the news which would have given him so much pleasure. items.s: BELGRAVE HARRIERS Inside-back-cover recruitment page for Belgrave Harriers, sponsored by Tilda Rice: the club's history, training venues, headquarters, membership fees, leagues contested and contacts. BELGRAVE HARRIERS Officially Sponsored by Tilda RICE • Some of the greatest athletes in the world compete for Belgrave Harriers. • Du'aine Ladejo (pictured over page) set the tracks of Europe alight in 1994, scorching around the 400 metre circuit to become European Champion. The powerful John Regis set a staggering British Record of 19.87 secs. for the 200 metres and a dozen others from our Club jumped, threw or ran at international level. • We in Belgrave are proud of them all but so too are we proud of our slower men and women, girls and boys. As long as there are people prepared to "have a go", to enjoy the thrill of competition or a simple jog or walk around the roads, commons or parklands, our mission will always be to help them and show them how. Belgrave Harriers was founded over one hundred years ago - in 1887 - and in those early days our headquarters actually were in Belgravia while our races were held along the Embankment of the River Thames and over the Common lands of South London. Nowadays our members come from all around the globe but our spiritual home is still South London. Battersea Park athletic track is where many of our track and field athletes train - come rain or shine, all the year round. We also use Kingsmeadow (near Kingston), Crystal Palace and various other stadiums. At Wimbledon, just a couple of hundred metres from Wimbledon Common and available to all members, is our own Club Headquarters with separate changing facilities and showers for men and women, a refreshment room and gymnasium (for which a complete upgrade is planned). We have coaches to assist you in whatever event you prefer but we are also looking for people who would like to help us to organise our club: timekeepers, judges, coaches, administrators . . . and then there are our social events. Membership will cost you: £25* a year if you are over 20, £15* if you are 17 to 20 and £10* if you are under 17. Special rates exist for husband/wife or family membership. (* £20, £12 and £6 if you apply before 1st July 1995) Main league events in which Belgrave Harriers compete: • Track & Field British League Division One - Senior Men. Southern Women's League Division Three - for ages 11 to adult. Southern Men's League Divisions Two and Six - for ages 15 to adult. Rosenheim League - for ages 15 to adult, men and women. Thameside League - for ages 11 to 14, boys and girls. Young Athletes (McDonalds) League - boys aged 11 to 16. National Junior League - boys aged 15 to 19. Southern Veterans' League - Men over 40 and over 50, Women over 35 and over 50. • Cross Country - Surrey Men's and Women's CC Leagues Division One - All age groups. • Road and Track Walking - many events - men and women all age groups.Road Running - Surrey Winter and Summer Leagues - men and women. Find us at: Belgrave Hall, Denmark Road (off Ridgway), Wimbledon, London SW19 4PG. Telephone 0181 946 6859. on Tuesday and Thursday evenings at 6.30pm, Saturday afternoons at 2pm and Sunday mornings at 10.15am for distance running, jogging or walking, or at Battersea Park Athletic Track, Tuesday and Thursday evenings at 6.30pm. items.s: Our Window on the Past Appeal for members to lend old programmes, photographs and other memorabilia to Clive Shippen, who is mounting and annotating the club's historical material. OUR WINDOW ON THE PAST Clive Shippen has been making great strides in his task of mounting, dating and annotating Belgrave memorabilia. Old photographs in particular enable us to step back through the years to join Belgravians now long gone and to follow the progress of the club from its early days in 1887 to the present time. There are some surprising gaps to be filled, however. If you have any items stored away - programmes, photographs, etc. - please contact Clive who will be able to advise on whether the material will compliment that already held and will arrange for copying as necessary. In particular Clive is keen to ensure that no material whatsoever is irrevocably lost. If you can arrange for items to be passed on to the Club one day then you will be doing your bit towards recording our history. Please 'phone Clive now to talk about it. His telephone number is [phone number withheld]. Clive Shippen Clive Shippen mounting, dating and annotating Belgrave memorabilia Clive Shippen Clive

items.label: November 1995
items.sum: Editorial reviewing the club's very successful 1995 summer across its league teams, noting the cost to the Men's Southern League teams, and thanking sponsors Tilda Rice.
items.s: Tilda Rice must be pleased Editorial reviewing the club's very successful 1995 summer across its league teams, noting the cost to the Men's Southern League teams, and thanking sponsors Tilda Rice. Tilda Rice must be pleased Have we ever seen, in all our 108 year history, such a successful summer; the result of extremely hard work by our team managers, officials, coaches, organising committees - and of course our athletes. Our Guardian Insurance British Athletic League Team again captured the Division One title and have earned themselves a trip to Turkey next year to represent Britain in the European Clubs' Cup. The Guardian Insurance Gold Cup just slipped from our grasp in the last event of the last match of the season but otherwise was another successful campaign by our first team. The Junior Men were unbeaten and have been promoted to Division Two (South Thames) of the National Junior League while our younger athletes romped away with their division of the McDonald's National Young Athletes League and have bounced straight back to the Southern Premier Division. The Mid-Weekers annexed the Eastern Division of the Rosenheim League and then resoundingly won the final. Our Men's Veteran Team were also unbeaten in every one of their Mid-London Division matches and they too were Champions in the high standard South of England final in only their third year of existence as a track & field team. Concentrating on each of the foregoing leagues has, however, proved to be to the detriment of our Men's Southern League teams where athletes have been pulled out to support the BAL outfit and we have avoided making up the numbers with youngsters due to compete on the same weekend in the age-group leagues. Recent recruitment levels indicate that this should be less of a problem next year but we really do need two or three times the number of middle and longer distance runners than we can currently boast. The Women's Southern League team showed signs early on in the year that promotion could be gained by them as well. A poor turn-out then put paid to those hopes but nevertheless they have held steady in the upper reaches of their division. Next year we will be entering a girls' team in the National Young Athletes League for the first time ever and if the team achieves anything like the momentum that the boy's team has then our Senior Women's teams are going to look a lot stronger in the years ahead. The Race Walking scene also seems to be picking up. From nowhere, thanks to a little talent and a lot of enthusiasm, we now seem to have one of the most thriving young walking teams in the country. Our sponsors, Tilda Rice, must be pleased with the partnership that they have entered. items.label: November 1995
items.sum: Report on the club's Tilda Rice-backed scheme sending coaches into schools, appealing for more qualified coaches and explaining that expenses are paid for day-time school work.
items.s: Coaching in schools Report on the club's Tilda Rice-backed scheme sending coaches into schools, appealing for more qualified coaches and explaining that expenses are paid for day-time school work. Coaching in schools Thanks to the support of Tilda Rice Ltd. there has been great activity on our part in encouraging young people to take up the sport of athletics. On a regular basis we send coaches into the schools during the day to give expert advice on training and competition. Our aim is to give young people the chance to sample our sport, to help them into it gently by assisting them with their training and for those who do take to it, encouraging them to join an athletics club. You won't be surprised to know, of course, that the club we hope continued on page 4 ... Editorial page continued they will join is Belgrave Harriers but what you will be surprised with is the fact that we do also send youngsters in the direction of other clubs where that club is more suitable. How do we manage to find coaches to do this work for us? The answer is "With great difficulty". We do pay their expenses for this day-time school work which particularly helps those who have to give up the chance of earning a living at these times but we can only do this for qualified coaches - and we desperately need more qualified coaches! If you have time that you can make available during the day and would like to become involved in this very worthwhile work then get in touch with our Coaching Secretary (address in Club Fixture Card) or any other Club official and we will organise things for you. If you are not qualified we will even arrange for you to attend the relevant coaching courses and pay the fees involved as well. Incidentally, we do not pay anyone for coaching, or carrying out any other Club work for that matter, when it takes place during the evenings or at other normal training times.

items.label: November 1995
items.sum: Column reprinting club news from 25 years ago (June/September 1970: Les Cohen and Bill Lucas presidencies, Cadogan A.C., Trevor Hart's Polytechnic Marathon club record) and 50 years ago (November 1945: post-war return and wartime achievements).
e: R.W.A. National Junior Ten Miles Championship
items.s: From The Belgravian Column reprinting club news from 25 years ago (June/September 1970: Les Cohen and Bill Lucas presidencies, Cadogan A.C., Trevor Hart's Polytechnic Marathon club record) and 50 years ago (November 1945: post-war return and wartime achievements). FROM THE BELGRAVIAN 25 years ago .... June/September 1970 OUR sincere congratulations go to Les Cohen on becoming President of the Southern Counties A.A.A. - an honour he deserves more than any other man in Athletics. The responsibility he assumes, the work he does, the wires he pulls in the service of our Sport have become a tradition and a legend; and we all hope he will long continue serving and enriching Athletics at all levels. WE CONGRATULATE also Bill Lucas on becoming President of the Surrey Co. A.A.A. - again an honour well deserved; and we wish him every success in his year of office. Incidentally, Bill is the first Belgrave man to become a Surrey President - which is just a little surprising for we have been members since the Association's inception. CADOGAN A.C., under whose name and colours many Belgravians served in Middlesex County events over a period of nearly 40 years, is no more. A recent change in A.A.A. Laws permits clubs such as ours to affiliate to more than one County Association (with permission); and so Belgrave has affiliated to Middlesex County A.A.A., as well of course continuing in affiliation with Surrey County A.A.A. THE POLYTECHNIC MARATHON, the premier marathon of the year, (run from Windsor Castle to Chiswick) was held in a heat wave. Lionel Mann was forced to retire when well placed and it was left to Trevor Hart to spearhead the team. This Trevor did in magnificent fashion. Running a well judged race, and refusing to be drawn out by the leading bunch, he led our team home with a new Belgrave record, knocking 2mins. 10 secs. off the time set by Barry Sawyer in 1963. Result: 20, T.Hart 2:25:58 (Club record); 70, C.Shippen 2:41:20; 71, P.O'Connor 2:41:30; 104, B.Joines 2:53:57; 114, A.Brien 2:58:04. (G.I.B) and, 50 years ago .... November 1945 SINCE the last issue events have moved quickly. The sudden ending of hostilities in the Far East has brought Peace to the World again. A number of our members have already been demobilised and many others hope to return to civilian life soon. We extend a hearty welcome to those who have been away from us and wish them the best of luck in the battles ahead for places in our teams. The Committee has decided that the Club shall return to its full pre-war programme, and a glance at the Fixture List will show that there is a busy season ahead. At the outbreak of war we occupied a position which had never before been attained by any club. We were National Road Walking Champions (20 miles) and English Cross-Country Champions (10 miles). We also won the R.W.A. National "Junior" (qualification basis) Ten Miles Championship, whilst our runners had been placed in the Southern, and the London-Brighton Relay. Of our best individual performances, Harry Churcher was our brightest star. A.A.A. Champion at Two and Seven Miles, Inter-Counties Road Walking and Track Champion, unbeaten in Open Road Walks for two seasons. Ted Stimpson and Arthur Penny represented England in the International Cross-Country Race. Tom Carter was Southern Six Miles Track Champion, he also held the Surrey Title, and was fourth in the A.A.A. Ten Miles Championship. Eddie Pack was Southern and Inter-Counties 440 yards Champion, and runner-up in the A.A.A. title. Charlie Melchior was second in the Southern and third in the A.A.A. Javelin Throw. Joe Coleman was third in the A.A.A. Seven Miles and third in the Southern Two Miles Walk. Stan Botwright was third in the Southern Furlong. Many other members gained A.A.A. and Southern Standards, and won honours in County Races. During the war our runners, walkers and field events men have striven hard to uphold the high position held by the Club, and we can say that no other club maintained such a high all-round level of performance. We can feel justly proud of our war-time record. Les Cohen Les Cohen President of the Southern Counties A.A.A. (1970) Bill Lucas Bill Lucas President of the Surrey Co. A.A.A. items.label: November 1995
items.sum: Editorial on the shortage of middle and longer distance runners and the new group training sessions from Belgrave Hall, Tooting and Battersea tracks.
items.s: Putting some sparkle back Editorial on the shortage of middle and longer distance runners and the new group training sessions from Belgrave Hall, Tooting and Battersea tracks. Putting some sparkle back We mentioned our shortage of middle and longer distance runners, and now that we are entering the winter season you may rest assured that we are doing all we can to nurse this side of our activities back into good health. What we must realise, though, is that while on paper we have some of the strongest runners in the country, individually they operate at such a high level, actually making their living through the sport, that we can hardly expect them to support our teams and give up the chance of earning money on anything more than an occasional basis. Of course we will be trying to get them all together whenever we can but we really do need to put some sparkle back into the middle order men. The more we can build up our packs of runners the more chance there is that from these groups will spring the talent that we need. It might take some time: two, three, maybe five seasons or more, but as long as the progression is there we can take comfort in the knowledge that we will eventually succeed. We now have a group of "engine-room" men training together on Saturday afternoons (races permitting) and they leave Belgrave Hall at 2pm sharp. Sunday morning runs start at 10.30am, also from the Hall and on Tuesdays we are attempting to build up a crowd who will set out on the roads at 6.30pm. For those who prefer to run on grass we have a group training from Tooting Track (using the commons) on Tuesdays and Battersea Track (running in the park or monthly 'Bridges' time trials) on Thursdays (both also at 6.30pm). Belgrave Hall Tooting Track Battersea Track

items.label: November 1995
items.sum: Farewell tribute to Clive Shippen, former Belgravian editor, results organiser and archivist, who is emigrating to Australia with his wife Elizabeth.
items.s: Au revoir Clive Farewell tribute to Clive Shippen, former Belgravian editor, results organiser and archivist, who is emigrating to Australia with his wife Elizabeth. Au revoir Clive Can it really be possible that we are about to say "au revoir" to Clive Shippen as he and Elizabeth make plans for a new life with their sons and grandchildren in Australia. Such high standards have been set by Clive in all that he has done for our Club that it has affected every single person who has followed in his footsteps. When he and Malcolm Robinson collaborated as Editors of The Belgravian in 1959 we saw the first issue bearing a front page photograph and two years later the cover became an eye-catching gold with claret titling. The most meticulous of workers, Clive has spent years masterminding the results of our major races and much of the excitement of the Southern Road Relay was due to the barrage of stage rankings and results appearing at the finish barely before the runners had caught their breath. Someone required as Meeting Organiser for a home British League Match? That person had to be Clive with his ability to ensure that every little wrinkle in the organisation was smoothed away. Our archives are bulging with information - 19th and 20th century photographs, cuttings, results, scrap books, maps - all so beautifully organised and researched. No man could have done this like Clive. And how fitting that during his time as Secretary of our External Relations Management Committee, when we had discussed and responded in writing to Professor Peter Radford's Consultation Document Athletics 21, that we received a letter from the Executive Chairman of the B.A.F. stating, "... if only all the comments I received were as constructive as yours ...". No doubt we will continue to hear from Clive and no doubt, also, we will read more of his contributions towards our Club's healthy state of affairs but in the meantime, Clive and Elizabeth, "Bon Voyage". Clive Shippen Clive Shippen co-editor of The Belgravian from 1959, results organiser, archivist, Secretary of External Relations Management Committee; emigrating to Australia Clive Shippen Clive Elizabeth Elizabeth Clive Shippen's wife Malcolm Robinson Malcolm Robinson co-editor of The Belgravian from 1959 Peter Radford Professor Peter Radford author of consultation document Athletics 21 Southern Road Relay British Athletics League Australia B.A.F.

items.sum: Two photo features on club officials: Johnny Morris, hit on the nose by a falling pole while judging the pole vault at the Rosenheim meeting at Tooting Bec, and Life Member Rex Bale, veteran runner and field-event judge.
items.s: Officials - where would we be without them ? Two photo features on club officials: Johnny Morris, hit on the nose by a falling pole while judging the pole vault at the Rosenheim meeting at Tooting Bec, and Life Member Rex Bale, veteran runner and field-event judge. Officials - where would we be without them ? JOHNNY MORRIS is one of those stalwarts who turn out to help us by officiating at Track & Field Meetings whenever he gets the chance but he got more than he bargained for at the Rosenheim Meeting at Tooting Bec on June 14th. Judging the Pole Vault, with our members Jamie Webb, Susie Drummie and Julia Cockram taking part, he stepped onto the runway behind Jamie to catch the pole as it fell back. Unfortunately Jamie's progression skywards was interrupted by the cross bar and as athlete, bar and pole descended at once, Johnny got caught a nasty whack across the nose by the bar. Sporting a pair of black eyes at the Thameside League a couple of days later he recounted the tale: "I'll give the buggers their due, though," he added, " at least none of them laughed." Elected a Life Member last year, REX BALE competes regularly in veterans' races on all terrains yet still finds time to appear at track and field matches, both at home and away, with his clipboard, pencil and tape measure to help judge the field events. items.sum: Profile of new club president Snowy Brooks: Royal Navy years, joining Belgrave in 1964 via sprints coach Ben Lulham, his decathlon career including representing Barbados at the 1972 Munich Olympics, his all-time PBs and his 1995 World Veterans' decathlon silver.
items.s: Snowy Brooks, President of Belgrave Harriers 1995 - 1996 Profile of new club president Snowy Brooks: Royal Navy years, joining Belgrave in 1964 via sprints coach Ben Lulham, his decathlon career including representing Barbados at the 1972 Munich Olympics, his all-time PBs and his 1995 World Veterans' decathlon silver. SNOWY BROOKS President of Belgrave Harriers 1995 - 1996 Turn up at the start of any of our main track fixtures, we wrote in 1973, and you are certain to see the muscular figure of Olympic Decathlete Snowy Brooks limbering up for the early events. Hours later as the meeting draws to a close he will still be there, holding together a relay team, having competed non-stop on the field and the track throughout the whole match. Well, twenty-two years later, the story is much the same. He no longer competes at British League level of course but at 51 years of age he is still a force to be reckoned with in Southern League throwing events and when it comes to the world of veteran athletics - the man is phenomenal. He was always respected as an athlete, and continues to be so, but his stature has increased over the years as he has gone on to advise athletes of all levels on their fitness, technique and recovery from injury. Snowy thought long and hard before accepting the role of President of Belgrave Harriers. Would he be able to devote the time to Club affairs that he felt he should as President? There is no way that he would take something on unless he was prepared or able to do his very best and he is still extremely committed as an athlete. Happily for us the answer was "Yes" and already we have seen him slip easily into roles of race starter, presenter of prizes and presider over social functions. As Snowy himself has said: "I'm a Decathlete - that's ten events to train for and compete in - and as far as being President is concerned I shall add that event onto the others and make it eleven for the coming year." Snowy was born in Camberwell on August 19th, 1944. At school he played football and cricket and as for most youngsters of that era, athletics was the once a year activity that took place in early summer - school sports day. At about fifteen or sixteen, while at St. Luke's Secondary Modern School in Kingston-upon-Thames he did make his way down to the local track to run in a few races for Kingston Athletic Club but just around the corner loomed a course of action that was to play a great part in his young life. In 1960 at sixteen years of age Snowy signed on with the Senior Service, the Royal Navy, and during the next eleven years he served as a steward on board the anti-submarine frigate HMS Plymouth and the aircraft carriers HMS Victorious and HMS Hermes. It was an enjoyable period of Snowy's life and his travels with the "Grey Funnel Line" gave him the chance to see a great deal of the world - the Mediterranean, the Far East, sights and cultures far removed from those to which most South London lads of the time were confined. But a little corner of his mind was still reserved for the sport of athletics and during a spell of leave and with home now being Victoria in central London, he made his way down to Battersea athletic track to do a little training. What a stroke of luck for us, for who should he meet there but sprints coach Ben Lulham who had recently become a member of Belgrave Harriers. Ben had been the mainstay of Kingston Athletic Club. They had trained at Norbiton and Kingstonian Football Gound in Richmond Road and had among their number some remarkable sprinters. Kingston A.C. had recently wound up its affairs, however, with some of its members joining Surrey Athletic Club and others, including most of Ben's squad, coming to Belgrave. It was natural, then, that the next step should be for Ben to ask Snowy to fill out a membership form. This he did and he was duly elected to the Club on May 15th 1964. Within a few weeks we were for the first time treated to a typical "Snowy performance". The Club Championships were held at Hurlingham and as a Junior Snowy won the High Jump and placed 3rd in the 100 yards but competing in Senior events on the same afternoon he also won the Long Jump and placed 2nd in the Triple Jump. The Decathlon beckons Being at sea much of the time meant that most of his training consisted of weight lifting which had to be done in a narrow space below deck in between the fuel tanks. Snowy's enthusiasm was not to be daunted, however, and in 1965, with his all-round ability, he made the natural progression to the ten-in-one event, the Decathlon, his first attempt being as a guest in the R. A. F. Championships. He was greatly influenced by his training companion and fellow matelot, international decathlete Peter Gabbett and by 1968 was beginning to make real progress. Sometimes this was to Belgrave's dismay, for in 1969 we lost one of the premier trophy meetings, the "Ryder Trophy" held at Southampton, to the Royal Navy. Their winning margin over us was just eight points and fifteen points were scored for the Navy that day by an athlete wearing a tracksuit with the name "Snowy" emblazoned across the shoulders! There used to be an athletics competition for small ships and as Snowy was the only man on his vessel that wanted to take part, he entered all the events. The number of events that he won and the performances that he recorded are not now known but surfice it to say that "HMS Snowy" single-handedly won the trophy for his ship. The Belgrave Club Record for the Decathlon was by now his own and in his final year with the service in 1971 he won their 400 metre hurdles championship, placed 3rd in the inter-services 400 hurdles and 2nd in the RN Decathlon behind Gabbett. Now a civilian, life took on a different routine, one that involved an almost daily trip to the National Recreation Centre at Crystal Palace. He trained with a group of four or five other decathletes and his best season followed in 1972 with an unexpected win in the Surrey County 400 metres Championship, representative honours for the Amateur Athletic Association and Southern Counties A. A. A. and eventually 7th place in the A. A. A. Decathlon Championships. A trip to Barbados, the easternmost island of the West Indies and the birthplace of his father, enabled him to compete in their athletics championships where he ran to a startling 10.7 for the 100 metres. It also gave the Barbadian authorities a timely reminder of some overseas talent that they could lay claim to and resulted in what must be the highlight of Snowy's career, selection to represent that Caribbean island in the Munich Olympic Games. The Munich Olympics Munich was the experience of a life time. The facilities and stadium were superb and in the athletes' village language problems were soon overcome and a friendly atmosphere prevailed among the competitors. Sadly, sportsmen and women are not left alone to befriend like-minded colleagues from other nations and the Games were marked by a tragedy growing out of political conditions in the Middle East. Members of a guerrilla organization killed two Israeli athletes and took nine hostages, who were later killed, along with five of the guerrillas and a West German policeman, in a gun battle with police at a Munich airport. Olympic activities were suspended for a day to hold memorial services for the murdered Israeli athletes. But back in the village, in spite of the shadow over the Games, Snowy was looking forward to his event and particularly enjoyed meeting the U.S. Decathlon team and Bill Toomey, World Record holder and winner from the Mexico Olympics. The competition took place on 7th/8th September and as he was not expected to excel in this company Snowy found himself quite relaxed and admits to having felt a lot more nervous prior to a Surrey Championship. In front of an 80,000 crowd, for many of whom with the German love of der Zehnkampf the Decathlon was the event of the Games, the competiton unwound. Snowy's overnight score was on a par with that set during his best ever performance and he was also able to take great delight in Peter Gabbett's superb first day which was terminated by a 46.1 400 metres to place him 5th. Day two dawned and they progressed through the Hurdles and Discus events but for both of them, the Pole Vault was to prove their undoing. Gabbett hit knee trouble and although getting in a clearance, had to withdraw from the competition. For Snowy there were no injuries; it was simply a case of the opening height being set in excess of his personal best and try as he might, the bar was beyond his reach and it was the end of any hope of improving his score. With the Javelin and 1500 metres remaining Snowy called it a day and sat back to watch the Soviet Union's Nikolay Avilov crush the world's best all-rounders to win with a World Record score of 8,454 points. A Fine Ambassador At the age of 28, Snowy had competed with the very best athletes the world could offer, in an event that more than any other, fulfills the Olympic motto - Citius, Altius, Fortius - Faster, Higher, Stronger. But as we know, this was far from the end of Snowy's career. On four further occasions he improved his Decathlon score, reaching 6,727 points in 1978, having advanced the Club Record by over 1,500 points during his prime; and still his encounter with the event goes on. With the aid of age-related tables to combat the onset of anno domini his score reached 7,299 in Buffalo this summer where he gained silver medal in the World Veterans' Decathlon Championship for over 50s. The old gang still occasionally meet up for training sessions that have become a way of life: Nick Phipps, Pan Zeniou, Greg Richards, Mike Corden and Daley Thompson. At Battersea now it's not just training partners that greet him but their sons and daughters as well. Even trackside toddlers pottering about outside the changing rooms while mum or dad complete their warm-down will throw their arms up and run to him calling "Snowy" when he makes his entrance. Snowy Brooks is a great Belgravian and a fine ambassador for our Club and sport. items.s: Sidetracks Club gossip column: news of Geoff Davis, Pat Lyttle's wedding, London Marathon ever-presents Lionel Mann and Dave McMillan, walker Nigel Whorlow, the Manning brothers, George Piddington, a donation marking Harry Hare's centenary, Brian Gorman, J. Blair-Fish, Gordon Doubleday's memory of Bill Rice, transplant athlete Barrie Laverick, John Dawson's return to Australia and Tony Stone's Yugoslavia trip. Sidetracks • Just because we don't see much of our Past President Geoff Davis now that he has retired to Peterborough it doesn't mean that that he is resting on his laurels. We note that he was the man taking entries for the Eastern Indoor Championships. • Pat Lyttle is getting married. A regular sprinter for the Bels in the 80s, Pat still competes for us in field events and often forms half of our Southern League throwing events duo 'Lyttle and Small' whose combined weight belies their names and must be well over 30 stone. Pat had the shock of his life on his first date with the lady due to become his wife. They had to sprint for a bus with Pat leading the way. He turned to see where his partner had got to and was staggered to find her right on his shoulder. It turned out that she was once a sprinter with Coventry Godiva! Congratulations to you both. • Lionel Mann and Dave McMillan are two of only 41 runners who have competed in every one of the fifteen London Marathons 1981-1995. Both received a commemorative medal and special tee-shirt after this year's event, together with a letter from Marathon organiser Alan Storey. Normally sharp-eyed scanners of the results at first missed Dave's name this year. He improved so much that we weren't expecting to find him in the 'just over 3hrs' section. He's not so far from picking up Club Championship medals now and another ten years should see him down to about 2:30! • One of our young walkers Nigel Whorlow has picked up the habit of 'lifting' rather frequently - but he's not worried. You see he saves his airborne activities for the high jump, not competition of the heel and toe variety. At Dartford in the McDonald's YA League he 'flopped' over 1.50m to win his high jump in a personal best but at the moment it is walking where it looks as if he is going to make a name for himself. 'Nige' has tried sprints, cross-country, jumps and throws in the past couple of years but when he tried a walking event a while back he took to it like a duck to water and has already earned a trip to the English Schools, picked up medals in area and representative races and even competed for an English team against Ireland. It just goes to show, there's an event for everyone in athletics. • Talking of 'lifting', we now have positive proof that runner (and we use the term loosely) Charlie Manning doesn't. He and brother Derek occasionally run over a six mile course from Sutton Arena. Charlie gets there half an hour before hand and sets out immediately. Derek comes along later, runs the same course and overtakes Chas. about a mile from the end. After a recent tour of this circuit by the brothers Manning, taken when a light shower had dampened the grass, Derek explained: "I couldn't see you Charlie but I knew you were out there ahead of me - I could see the ski marks on the grass!" • What a pleasant surprise to see our old friend George Piddington down at Horsham for the Women's Southern League match at Horsham in May. He was there supporting his Havant team and was managing to walk with the aid of a stick. He looked a little pale but how good to see him out and about - and in spite of the ribbing from his local team, wearing a Belgrave tracksuit. Keep it up George. • Harry Hare's daughter sent a donation for £100 to commemorate the 100th year since her father's birth on 9th May 1895. Harry was the founder of our Club magazine The Belgravian, its first Editor and the Club was a very great part of his life. What a delightful idea by his daughter and of course we are extremely grateful. • Brian Gorman was off his feet earlier this year, with a spell in hospital to sort out a foot problem. Happily he is on the mend now, back behind the tea counter and holding court on Saturday afternoons at Belgrave Hall. • Does anyone remember the name J.Blair-Fish, one of our cross-country runners from the 70s. He is still competing in his favourite event, fell running, winning the M40 section of the Carn Mor to Cairn Well Uphill Race at Glenshee by over 7 minutes. • Gordon Doubleday, a past Editor of this magazine, regularly keeps in contact with your current Editors. He reminds us that Tilda Rice isn't the only Rice connected with us. When Gordon joined the Club in 1934 the Track Captain was one Bill Rice - a good all-round runner - cross-country, track and road relays - also Social Secretary. He lived at Battersea and made good use of his local knowledge on the first leg (Westminster to Clapham) of the London to Brighton Relay. • Some of those who frequent Battersea Park Track, especially the veterans, will know of Barrie Laverick of Serpentine Runners. Barrie had a heart bypass operation in 1988 and a kidney transplant in 1992 but not one to let little incidents like that spoil his athletics he has come back to clock 57.2 for the 400m and won two gold medals at the World Transplant Games this summer. Many vets would be pleased with a time like that, transplant or not. • Sadly we have said goodbye to John Dawson who recently returned to his native Australia. Still a Junior, John made a great contribution to our Southern League and National Junior League teams and even made a showing in the British League team at one point. But he is probably going to be remembered just as much for one or two other exploits: the 'Aussie' who drank his wine straight from the bottle at the 1994 Club Dinner, the runner who seemed to get faster every time he came back from blistering those fragile feet and the man who wore his Australian Club's bow tie and started a trend in Belgrave (order your Belgrave bow tie now from Ted Pallant). Good luck to you John and keep in touch. • You know there's lot more to that man Tony Stone than at first meets the eye. All of us feel for the refugees in what was once Yugoslavia but Tony takes it a little further than that. In July he travelled by coach across Europe with a group of like minded souls to meet with and comfort the people that most of us only see, distressed, on our television screens. Tony has documented his trip in a 32 page booklet entitled My Time In War Torn Yugoslavia. Why don't you ask him for a copy? We are sure he'd be delighted to let you have one and no doubt the small donation that you offer will find its way to a very worthy cause. Management change Pictured left: For thirteen years Leo Coy (left) has been half of the two-man management team that took the Bels. on the long road from the Southern League to the heights of the British Athletics League Division One. His partner through all that time, Bill Laws, paid tribute to Leo after the opening BAL match this year ... "He is surely one of the the sport's all-time greats when it comes to team management." Leo intends to concentrate on our McDonalds Young Athletes' Team and we have no doubt that he will be just as successful there. Assistant GB Team Manager John Jeffery (right), who has been easing himself into our administrative ranks over the past season or two, will be taking Leo's place and helping Bill to lead our BAL team to even greater success. items.sum: Story of young members Steve and Sarah Scott helping police catch two of three thieves who snatched their cash at a cash machine, Steve chasing them down.
items.s: Great Scott ! Story of young members Steve and Sarah Scott helping police catch two of three thieves who snatched their cash at a cash machine, Steve chasing them down. GREAT SCOTT ! A TRIP to the cash dispensing machine by two of our young members Steve and Sarah Scott and their cousin proved to be the start of an exciting episode. Before the folding stuff could be stowed away three guys jumped them, grabbed the money and made off. Not one to suffer such an indignity quietly, Sarah immediately started bellowing at the top of her voice, "Call the police, call the police", and as it happened the men in blue were quickly on hand to find out just what was going on. It was decided that a tour of the vicinity in the squad car might enable the villains to be spotted - and so it proved. "There they are", yelled Steve, and as the driver jammed his foot on the brakes a policeman was already leaping out to give chase followed closely by Steve and Sarah. Now Steve isn't our Under 17 Track & Field Captain for nothing. Before you could say "Get Set" he was out of that car seat and overhauling the bobby in the dash for his cash. But when their victims started leaping walls and fences then they were in trouble in a big way: well how were they to know that they were being pursued by Belgrave's record breaking ace hurdler! Steve grabbed thief number one and quickly put him in an arm lock, handing him over to the law before setting off on the next stage of this chase and doing a similarly successful job on villain number two. Number three got away. The boys from the Met. were thoroughly impressed and suggested that Steve should be signed up to join the 'force' immediately. Steve's Dad was proud - but quite rightly had a few qualms. Suppose those crooks had been armed in some way ... He's right of course, but nevertheless, great work Steve! Steve Scott Steve Under 17 Track & Field Captain; record breaking hurdler Steve Steve Scott Sarah Scott Sarah Sarah Sarah Scott

Report on nine-year-old Paul Graham running 45:43 for 10k at Battle with his father Mick, and placing 4th in an under-12 race at Langham. 45:43 10k by 9 year-old Paul ! NINE YEAR-OLD Paul Graham (son of one of our veteran runners, Mick) failed to be daunted when he arrived at Battle expecting to take part in the 10 to 12 years-old category of a two mile road race but found that it was in fact to be 10k! Sensibly, the organisers would only let Paul take part if his Dad accompanied him - no mean feat for father as it turned out. They ran at steady 8 minute mile pace for the first three-quarters of the race but Paul insisted that he wanted to run free for the remainder of the course and cut loose to such good effect that he soon started pulling right back on a projected finish time of around 48 minutes. Into the finishing straight and he received much applause from the onlookers as he carried his claret and gold racing singlet across the line in 45:43 - first home in the 10-12 group. Was this enough for him? Not on your life. In spite of joining the Bels. because he wants to race the sprints in the under 13 age-group on the track next summer, he has accepted an invitation by the organisers of the Hastings 10k who were so impressed with Paul that they would like to see him in their race. Another race nearer to home saw Paul place 4th in the under 12 section of a 1½ miles race at Langham, Colchester. His time was 8:48. Well done Paul. Enjoy your running but don't take it too seriously just yet. There's plenty of time ahead of you and we look forward to seeing you in action over the shorter events as well. items.s: Clive wins photo competition Clive Shippen, the sole entrant, wins the previous issue's competition by naming twelve runners in a cross-country start photo; his prize book turned out to be one he already owned. Clive wins photo competition IN THE LAST issue of The Belgravian, on page 8, we featured a photograph of the start of a cross-country race headed by Colin Pearson and offered a prize for the person who could name the most runners in the picture. We had a clear winner in Clive Shippen who put names to no less than twelve of the faces in the field. There were another five or six that he recognised but could not name. Clive identified John Hanscombe, John Phelan, Adrian Trowell, Laurie O'Hara, David North, Ray O'Donoghue, Dick Piotrowski, Colin Pearson, Pat O'Connor, Bob Roath, John Lee and Tony Binda. The next best entry was received from ... er ... um ... well actually we only had the one entry. We told you he was a clear winner. Sadly, when Clive was told that he had won the prize, Alister Aitken's book More Than Winning, he felt moved to reveal that a copy of this volume was in fact already in his possession. A bit of a disaster as far as a competition was concerned wasn't it!
