items.s: Belgrave Harriers Club Records Belgrave Harriers club records as at 30 September 1995: introduction, a table of records set in 1995, key to the notes, and full record lists by age group. Belgrave Harriers Club Records What a statistical feast we are able to offer you. The compilers of the following lists of records have spent scores of hours poring over old Belgravians, Athletics Weekly magazines and British Athletics Annuals to establish the full details of the best ever performances by Belgrave athletes. Notes written by Steve Williams in the '80s have played their part, as too have helpful comments from Gordon Doubleday and additional information from Snowy Brooks and Laurie O'Hara. Conversions from imperial measurements have been checked, converted performances set over imperial distances shorter than the current metric ones have been removed (although kept as "other notable performances" until such times as the metric event is clearly superior), weights of implements used in throws have been ascertained, as far as possible, and similarly banished from the main list where superceded. We have even gone to the lengths of investigating and including Surrey AC performances from before the merging of our clubs, where they are still superior to any "pure" Belgrave ones. Imagine the vexation caused when a long investigation into the full details of, for example, Dave Mote's Under-20 400 metres from 1977 was finally concluded, only to find that some young upstart had gone and wiped out his record overnight! Men's records and all veterans' records were compiled by Hazel and Alan Mead. Women's records, apart from those for veterans, were compiled by Derek Jones. Where the best electronic and manual times are close (ie within 1/10th) then both are shown. Inter-club and area league meetings rarely benefit from the presence of a wind gauge and it is in these type of meetings that most age-group records are set. It is difficult to exclude a record when it has been marginally assisted by a recorded following wind when on other occasions performances may have been assisted but wind readings were not available. Therefore, unless patently assisted by the conditions, age-group records are not ruled out entirely if 'windy'. We still have further work to do: we are not entirely comfortable with the male veterans' road records that we offer (please let us know if you have any disagreements), and we have yet to think about female veterans' road records and veteran walks. In the meantime, if anyone can add any information where the asterisks are shown, or if there are any queries, then please get in touch with the compilers at: [address withheld]. The 1995 Ranking lists covering Track, Field, Road Running and Walking will appear in the next issue of The Belgravian, hopefully to be published late Spring 1996. If you have any performances that are unlikely to have been picked up by the compilers then please send them in to the address shown above. Nineteen-ninetyfive has been an astounding year for Club Records. No fewer than 115 best ever marks by Belgravians have been equalled, broken and broken again in the period starting 1st January and ending 30th September. A perusal of the table shown below soon shows that our veteran athletes have contributed 54 of these marks but even if you take them out (and they are very worthy performances as we are sure you will agree when you look at the lists) it still leaves a resounding 61 marks set in mainstream athletics. The table also quite clearly shows the areas that are not currently progressing. items.h: Club life at the turn of the century
items.sum: Ted Good's 1951 recollections of Belgrave club life around 1900: his first meetings, joining the club in 1901, club finances, training quarters and races around Battersea Park.
items.s: Club life at the turn of the century Ted Good's 1951 recollections of Belgrave club life around 1900: his first meetings, joining the club in 1901, club finances, training quarters and races around Battersea Park. Back in December 1951, encouraged by our Hon. Secretary of the time A.A. Harley, one of our older members Ted Good put pen to paper to describe the Club as he first knew it at the turn of the century. Ted's notes recently came to light again ... Club life at the turn of the century My first interests were awakened by reading the inscription on the biscuit bowl that stood on the "chiffonier" at home - "Presented to A.J. Good (my father) Bloomsbury Rifles 1 Mile Championship 1880. When I was about eight years old (1890) I remember being taken to the Scottish Highland Gathering. Highly coloured bills announced it was taking place at the Kennington Oval. I was much impressed by the brawny Scotsmen trying to upend a huge pole (tossing the caber). They reduced the length after all had failed, until one at last succeeded. The "slinging" the 56lb weight and the dancing to bagpipes must have taken my attention from the running events. This was my first meeting. About 1898 I remember visiting Old Stamford Bridge. It may have been the Championships but I remember that W.J.Sturgess won the Walking race. I was then living at Chelsea and I often went to sports meetings at the "Bridge". In 1901 I was introduced to the Club by Frank Bool, the Hon. Sec. I should like to place on record that the "Bels" owed their existence to Frank and his Committee. How they managed to keep the right side of the financial fence only they know. I was elected to the Committee quite early on in my career and Frank's persuasion to a possible prize donor or backward subs-dodger taught me all the approaches for when I took over with W.Mathewson the Co-Secretaryship. I am sure the present members are more regular in paying their subs. When I joined perhaps 25% of our members were working long hours for small wages. Shop assistants working to 8 pm with an occasional let-off for our races on Saturdays when in the ordinary way they may be working until 10 pm. We held our races according to the fixture card with prizes £1, 10/- and 5/-. We were supposed to start our evening races at 8 pm. sharp but seldom did - the late-comers entries and subs just managed to keep us solvent. Stop watch competitions only to members of course (don't make me laugh!), raffles, etc. All brought grist to the mill. Our evening training quarters was the William IV. This was about half a mile from where we started in 1887. I got the impression the landlord thought we burnt too much gas and did not drink enough beer. The distance races were held around Battersea Park, 3¼ miles out and home - twice if you wanted to. William IV was open till midnight anyway! And they were open again for rum and coffee at 5.30 am. I was told that just prior to my joining the Club some of the members went round the course with an official "chain measurement". Three miles 400 yds. they said. The 440 yds. started just above Grosvenor Road railway bridge - and what a lovely start down-hill for the short mark men! The 880 yds. and Boxing Day Sprint started in the opposite direction - the annual get-together of the old'uns. Imagine a damp, murky night. Just an occasional Handsome Cab with bells ringing as you went on your way, perhaps startling a courting couple. They must have had a lot to talk about because they were still there the second time round. I came back with my extremities numb and frozen. Our trainer said he would soon put some life into it (!). My goodness he did! How was I to know he had just been rubbing his previous clients chest with Sloans Liniment. How I walked - or shuffled - home I do not recall but I was in agony for days. But for all that Bill Harland, our trainer, was very loyal to us all. Many a time he has been at our Saturday quarters, the Railway Tavern ? Wandsworth Common, when only two have turned out, but always the hot tub when we returned. Hopefully we will be able to bring you more from Ted Good's notebook in the next edition of The Belgravian. Ted Good Ted Good wrote these notes in December 1951; joined the club in 1901; later Co-Secretary A.A. Harley A.A. Harley Hon. Secretary in 1951 A.J. Good A.J. items.sum: Arthur Bruce's history series reaches 1952: the Helsinki Olympic Games event by event, British athletics that year, and Belgrave's 1952 season in cross country, road relays and on the track.
items.s: The Athletics World of 1952 Arthur Bruce's history series reaches 1952: the Helsinki Olympic Games event by event, British athletics that year, and Belgrave's 1952 season in cross country, road relays and on the track. Arthur Bruce continues his series on the development of our sport and we reach the XVth Olympiad and ... The Athletics World of 1952 Nineteen-fiftytwo: What memories the year conjures up! The climax of course being the Olympic Games in Helsinki from July 19 to August 3. World Athletics had moved on since 1948 with a new array of world stars appearing on the scene. Over 69 countries took part in the XV Games with the Olympic torch carried into the stadium by that great legend of the past Paavo Nurmi. Watching the simple but dignified parade of athletes forming only an overture to the first day's competition one realises today how much the Games have been surrendered to commercial influences with a whole day now devoted to the glitzy opening ceremony. As for the progress of individual countries since the 1948 games, the United States retained its premier position, producing an excellent well balanced track & field team. Of the prominent countries in 1948 only Sweden slipped from their previous impressive showing. The Soviet Union, making their Olympic début, showed enough to indicate they would be a future power to be reckoned with. Of the smaller countries to show prominently Jamaica and Luxembourg were outstanding. The stadium, set among the pine forests on the edge of the city with its towering simplicity, provided a magnificent setting for the gladiatorial contests. The two sprint events maintained the United States' supremacy with a narrow win by Lindy Remigino in the shorter race with the first four given the same time and a clear win by Andy Stanfield in the 200 metres. Britain's MacDonald Bailey ran extremely well for 3rd place in the 100m and 4th in the 200m but did not quite recapture his form of the previous year when he equalled the World 100 metre Record. Herb McKenley, the World 400 metres Record holder surprised everybody by his performance in the 100 metres, losing by inches. The 400 metres seemed to be a straight contest between the usual strong USA trio and Jamaica with George Rhoden, Herb McKenley and Arthur Wint. The final produced a Jamaica 1-2 with Rhoden holding off McKenley by inches with the holder Wint 5th. This Jamaican superiority was confirmed in the 4 x 400 metres relay with a tremendous narrow win over the United States with Great Britain 5th. The middle-distance events provided their usual intriguing competition with the major protagonists of 1948 fighting it out again in almost identical times, Mal Whitfield again proving just too strong for Arthur Wint with Albert Webster excelling himself in 5th place. The 1500 metres provided the surprise of the Games in which semi-finals were introduced for the first time. Barthel of Luxembourg surprised all with his scintillating burst to win in a new Olympic Record of 3:45.1. Roger Bannister disappointed his supporters with 4th place in 3:46 which was still the fastest by an Englishman to that date. The Czech Locomotive The five and ten thousand metres went to the Czech Locomotive Emil Zatopek, who despite an appendix operation earlier that year was astounding in his defeat of the world's best. An ability to follow and finish or to front run made him a formidable opponent despite opposition from such brilliant performers as Alain Mimoun of France and Herbert Schade of Germany. The United Kingdom maintained their high standard in these events with 4th, 5th and 11th in the 5,000m final and 5th, 7th and 8th in the 10,000m; great performances by Gordon Pirie, Chris Chataway, Frank Sando, Alan Parker and Fred Norris. Chattaway's fall on the final bend in the 5,000m will long be etched on the memories of those who were there. That man Zatopek again turned out as a novice in the marathon and proceeded to trounce the world's best by over 2½ minutes despite a brave attempt by Jim Peters to run everybody into the ground. Geoff Iden ran a sensible race to finish a good 9th. The three hurdle or barrier events continued the superiority of the USA. Harrison Dillard came back after his sprint win in 1948 to take the high hurdles followed by the other two Americans. Charles Moore won a great battle with Lituyev of the USSR in 50.8 with our own Harry Whittle a fine, battling 5th place. The steeplechase provided a big improvement in standards compared to 1948 as more milers took to the barriers. Horace Ashenfelter of America drew away from Kazantsev of the USSR, who just prevailed over our own John Disley; the Olympic Record was improved by six seconds. The long and high jumps as expected went to the United States. Expectedly by Walt Davis in the High Jump but unexpectedly by J.Biffle in the Long Jump, the standard being surprisingly low. The Triple Jump, however, went to the World Record holder Ferreira Da Silva of Brazil, well clear of the field in 16.22. The Pole Vault provided its usual American dominance with a great fight between Bob Richards and Don Laz although Europe, spearheaded by the USSR, were beginning to show prominently. Finland were disappointed to lose the Javelin, their specialist event and on their own ground, to superior Americans. The USA continued their domination of the power events in both Shot and Discus but a mighty battle between the Europeans produced a victory for Czermak of Hungary from Storch of Germany in the Hammer. The glamour of the Decathlon was confirmed by the outstanding performances of the young American Bob Mathias and Milt Campbell who, together with Simmons, gave America a clean sweep and a new Olympic Record. Finally the Walks, especially the short track walk, produced the usual controversies as to the interpretation of rules. The disqualification of Roland Hardy and Lol Allen in their heats was most disappointing. However, George Coleman walked well in the final to finish 5th to Mikaelson of Sweden. The 50,000 metre Walk was more satisfying with Dordoni of Italy prevailing over Dolezal of Czechoslovakia with Britain's G.B.R. Whitlock a well merited 4th. When we examine the Women's results in the Games we realise what enormous strides we have made in women's athletics, both in range and in performance. The sprints produced the wonder Australian sprinter Marjorie Jackson who showed superiority in both 100 and 200 metres from European rivals and Hasenjager of South Africa. Russia showed their potential for the future in these events. The relay was not surprisingly won by Australia clearly from the Dutch team by a full second. The Australian wins were supplemented by the victory of Shirley Strickland in the 80 metre hurdles from Golubichnaya of the USSR with Jean Desforges 5th. The jumps high and long were won by Commonwealth athletes. Yvette Williams of New Zealand in the Long Jump and surprisingly Esther Brand of South Africa in the High Jump. Our girls performed well, Sheila Lerwill taking the silver in the High Jump and Shirley Cawley the bronze in the Long Jump. The family Zatopek collected their fourth gold with a good win by Emil's wife Dana in the Javelin from two Soviet performers. The Soviet women showed how post war women's power events would go with wins in the Shot and Discus (first three in the Discus), both events in Olympic Records. It's surprising the small range of women's events in 1952. The thought of women running 1:55.0 for 800 metres would have been considered amazing in the early 'fifties. Britain had made great advances We now come to the place of British Athletics as set in the World scene in 1952. The great pre-war stars had now passed from the scene and a new array of performers had arrived. Britain had made great advances since the austerity days of 1948. America was as powerful as ever, Germany had made a good athletic recovery and the athletic world inevitably had a more far flung range of talent, especially with the presence of the Soviet Union, with East Germany and Africa waiting in the wings. The A.A.A. Championships of 1952 showed the new standard reached. MacDonald Bailey retained his no. 1 position held since 1948 as shown by his close 3rd in the Olympic 100 metre final. Several talented newcomers were now on the scene, such as Ken Jones, Willie Jack, John Wilkinson and Nick Stacey but Bailey still remained King. Arthur Wint continued to dominate the scene in the 400m although Les Lewis, Alan Dick and Terry Higgins were beginning to show prominently. Our 800 metre competition was still commanded by Arthur Wint unless challenged by Roger Bannister and the two other performers Frank Evans and Albert Webster. The Great British middle distance event was of course dominated by Roger Bannister with new British mile and 1500 metre Records but perhaps a little disappointing in the Olympic Games. He was ably backed up by Bill Nankeville, four times British Champion, Len Eyre, John Parlett and Doug. Wilson. Other promising junior talent was emerging with D.Williamson, Derek Burfitt and Roger Dunkley. Britain's 5,000/10,000m challenge, thwarted by the presence of Zatopek, showed quality in depth. The rivalry between the hard school as pioneered by Gordon Pirie and the more cavalier approach of Chris Chattaway produced new British Records from 3,000 metres to 10,000. Frank Sando, Walter Hesketh, Alan Parker and Fred Norris provided strong opposition to our leading pair. British hurdling produced good competitors in the high hurdles by European standards but Peter Hildreth and Frank Parker were still the proverbial half second behind their American counterparts. The same could be said of our 400 metre hurdlers. Harry Whittle, despite his poor hurdling, made up for it in dogged persistence and reached most world class finals. Angus Scott and Douglas Gracie pushed Whittle hard in all the Championships. The steeplechase in Britain had shown dramatic improvement after the National Coach Geoff Dyson persuaded John Disley to turn to the event from miling, resulting in new British Records. The emergence of Chris Brasher in this event can be noted as reaching the Olympic final. The field events, apart from a few notable exceptions such as John Savidge in the Shot, Geoff Elliott in the Pole Vault and Ron Pavitt in the High Jump, proved to be the weak link in Track & Field. Standards were rising but generally lagged behind the world level. Our excellent walkers Roland Hardy and Lol Allen, whilst succeeding domestically, suffered from the controversial judging in Olympic and European Championships during this decade. Our good performances on the track at the large events was reflected in the continuing high standard of our Cross Country Running with Gordon Pirie, Walter Hesketh, Frank Sando and Fred Norris being individually, on their day, the best in the world. One should, perhaps, note for future reference the link between world class cross country performers and top grade 10,000 metre performers. Birchfield breathed a sigh of relief For Belgrave 1952 was a year of mixed fortunes. The Club was in a state of transition from the successful post-war teams which were aging and the slow emergence of young talent yet to appear in depth. The year started on a high note with a usual good win in the Surrey Cross Country Champs. at Oxted where we were led by Charlie Walker in 2nd spot and our scoring six were in 11 places. We were clear winners from Herne Hill and our juniors, led by Don Maclean finished 6th. The Club Ten Mile Championship following the Counties was won by Jack Brown from Charlie Walker and Bill Lucas, confirming our hopes for the big races ahead. Our expectancies rose again with our win in the Southern Championships at Hadleigh where we beat Aylesford Paper Mills by 10 points with our six scoring men in 43 places led by a good solo performance in 11th spot by Vern Blowfield. And so to the National at Great Barr where we had high hopes. Unfortunately, despite excellent runs by Vern Blowfield, 26th, Jack Brown, 40th, and Charlie Walker, 58th, we did not quite have the depth to succeed and finished 5th. Our Youths performed well in 4th place led home by Frank Wright in 7th. The short road relay season followed the National closely and at Ilford in the 10 x 3½ miles race we entered three teams. Our 'A' team were 1st of the 33 teams that took part, the 'B' team failed to close in, having only 8 men present, but the 'C' team, mostly composed of juniors, did well to place 14th. At Cranford for Thames Valley's 4 x 5 miles relay we placed 2nd to the host club with all five of our teams closing in and our 'B' team being strong enough to take 3rd place. Snow bound roads at Wimbledon meant that our 5 miles road race, a precursor to the National Road Relay over the London to Brighton course, had to be called off. In that National race Charlie Walker ran first leg but had been suffering from a poisonous hand and was well below par to finish in 16th place at the end of his stage. Great runs followed from Len Herbert and "Ginger" Newell, who had been brought in as a reserve, to take us back to 4th and then Bill Lucas went into 3rd. Ray Tooby equalled our own Charlie Smart's stage record and by now we were only 37 seconds behind the leaders. Bob Taylor and Vern Blowfield moved us closer and then Len Adams took us to 2nd. Eddie Short ran well against Birchfield's ace Freddie Green and finally Jack Brown took us to within 5 seconds of winning the event on that last stage with his Club Record breaking run. Only then could winners Birchfield breath a sigh of relief. The track season The Track Season; and the first significant indicator was the County Championships. Notable performances for us were the 1st and 2nd places in the Kent Mile by Ray Tooby and Jack Brown and over in Middlesex Bob Taylor in the 880 yards with Ron Holtum gaining the runner up's spot in the 100 yds. Over to Surrey where Basil Walden and D.J.Merrett placed 3rd in their sprints, Don Maclean found only Bill Paget too good for him in the mile and another 2nd was gained in the Steeplechase by Eddie Short. Harry Churcher had his usual win in the 2 mile Walk. We subsequently finished 2nd in the Brockman Trophy with record wins by Bill Lucas in the 3 Miles and Alan Sexton in the 440 yds. At the interclub Kinnaird Trophy Meeting (the British League match of the day) we finished 4th out of the top nine clubs with good performances from Alan Sexton, 3rd in the 440 yds., and Basil Walden, runner up in the 100. At the Southern Championships our best performers were Basil Walden, a surprise winner in the 100 yds., and G.Gregory in the 2 Miles Walk. Our Juniors won the 4x110 yds. relay. As we approached the climax of the season, the Club Championships were held at Battersea Park in cold and wet conditions. Denis Merrett sprang a surprise with an excellent double in both sprints, defeating Basil Walden and Ivan Mayers. The 440 went as expected to Alan Sexton in the good time of 50.6 in atrocious conditions with Jim Heathfield 2nd. Bob Taylor won the 880 yds. from Ian Badiali in 1:58.5 which was almost matched by Frank Wright in the Junior race with 1:59.5, both being meeting records. Jack Brown retained his mile title from Don Maclean and Bill Lucas in 4:19, just outside his meeting record made in 1951. Promising Geoff Goode took the Junior Mile in 4:31. Our Nigerian performer E.Bone took the High Jump from P.Luxon who had previously done the double with both the Javelin and Long Jump. Surprise winner of the Shot was Junior Alan Law. The meeting of the year from a domestic angle was of course the A.A.A. Championships held early in June for Olympic selection and these produced a number of good performances. Our two top sprinters Basil Walden and Denis Merrett reached the semi-finals in their respective events but then went out against strong British and foreign competitors. Both Bob Taylor and Jack Brown reached their finals with Jack finishing 5th to Bill Nankeville in an excellent 4:13.6 - a personal best. Both Bill Lucas and Len Herbert ran well in hot 3 and 6 Miles races, peppered with star performers, and both gained A.A.A. Standards. G.Gregory maintained his form with 2nd in the 2 Miles Track Walk. Only 3 seconds outside British Record At the subsequent L.A.C. 4 x 1 Mile Relay at the White City, the team of Ray Tooby, Don Maclean, Jack Brown and Len Herbert finished 2nd to Walton A.C. and only 3 seconds outside the British Record. The A.A.A. 4 x 440 Yards Relay at Uxbridge also gave us a well deserved 4th. The end of season meetings produced some sound results for the Club. In the London Championships we had winners in the 100 yds with Ron Holtum, 3 Miles, Arthur Bruce, Junior Mile, Geoff Goode, and 3rd in the Senior Mile with Don Maclean. The final track meetings were the two floodlight meetings held at the White City with excellent wins by Jack Brown in the Mile beating Gordon Pirie in 4:13 and Ray Tooby in the 2 Miles in 9:12 with Bob Taylor a close 2nd in the 880. The Autumn Road Relay season followed and started a little disappointingly in the Surrey Road Relay 6 x 3 miles. Our usual supremacy was missing and a weak team achieved only 5th. And so we came to the big one on October 11th, the London to Brighton Relay Southern Road Relay at which we always pulled out all the stops. After a brilliant start by Jack Brown we subsequently dropped to 6th place but record runs by Arthur Bruce, Ray Tooby, Len Adams and Eddie Short on their stages gave Bill Lucas a 9 second lead on the final stage and he made no mistake. Our time was only a few seconds outside the course record. A few words on the start of the 52/53 winter season: the opening Club 5 Mile cross country run at the end of October produced a weak field of 66 runners and this was followed two weeks later by fielding four teams in the South of the Thames "Junior" at Maidenhead with Pat Newell finishing an individual 2nd! items.s: Asthmatic? Notice explaining the British Athletic Federation exemption for prescribed beta-2-agonist inhalers and whom to contact for the exemption form. Asthmatic? Do you use a prescribed drug inhaler? Then read on. The group of drugs incurring a 4-year ban for a first offence includes those known as "beta-2-agonists". However, under a new amendment to British Athletic Federation rules:- "Exceptionally, the administration of the beta-2-agonists salbutamol or terbutaline is permitted by inhalation where prescribed for therapeutic purposes by properly qualified medical personnel and where prior clearance has been given by the Federation. Any exemption granted will be in effect during a maximum period of one year, unless renewed by the Federation." To claim exemption, you need to fill in the special two-part form obtainable from: Charlie Henn ([phone number withheld]) or Bob Bridges ([phone number withheld]). items.sum: Editorial on the special appeal of the Olympic Games and good wishes for a strong Belgrave presence in Atlanta.
items.s: The Games Editorial on the special appeal of the Olympic Games and good wishes for a strong Belgrave presence in Atlanta. The Games The Olympic Games. No matter how commercialised they become, or "over the top" with sports that would have been beyond de Coubertain's comprehension, the Games, when each Olympiad rolls around, bring something special to the world of athletics. Apart from the sporting feast beamed into our homes for a couple of weeks, real competition without a pacemaker in sight, there is the exciting prelude for fan and athlete alike - the need to qualify. Impressing selectors, achieving the qualifying standard and fulfilling requirements at the trials are dramas in their own right. The World Championships might be the athletic event for the connoisseur but as far as Joe Public is concerned the Olympic Games are what really count and therefore the urge for athletes to shine at this event is even greater. Luck and good health allowing, we hope for a strong Belgrave presence in Atlanta's Olympic Stadium in a whole range of events. Our distance runners will have the problem of 34°C temperatures and humidity of well over 90% to face but the sprinters and hurdlers will enjoy the Mondo track which is already acknowledged as being "lightning fast". We won't tempt fate at this stage by naming those likely to gain selection but we wish them all the very best of luck. Olympic Games World Championships Atlanta

items.sum: Editorial welcoming the completion of the club's gymnasium at the Hall and appealing for more volunteer officials and team managers.
items.s: Gymnasium project completed ... Editorial welcoming the completion of the club's gymnasium at the Hall and appealing for more volunteer officials and team managers. Gymnasium project completed ... Have you been up to the Hall recently and seen the gymnasium. There is probably not another athletic club in the country that has its own gym equipped to such a standard. Several new members have already come our way, attracted specifically by the chance to use the facilities for a mere £25 a year (£15 second-claim), and we wholeheartedly thank those who have kept this particular project on track. To have our own gym has been an aim that we have pursued for the last couple of years and it is good to see the plan draw to a successful conclusion. But this is just one of diverse schemes that we are following. Not everyone sees each project of being of equal in importance and some undertakings do not even gain immediate benefit for our club, being aimed more at assisting the community as a whole with the hope of a dividend being returned to Belgrave Harriers only in the longer term. One thing is sure, however, we have some very dedicated and hardworking officers. Although members of our Committee do not always see eye to eye when it comes to agreeing which road we should take next, it has been said recently that the Club has probably never been in such good shape. Nevertheless, while we are pleased with the progress we are making, there is no doubt that we could do with a lot more help. On a summer Saturday we might have as many as four track & field teams in action across the country, not to mention walking and road running groups; and there may be a couple of teams in action the following day as well. This is a tremendous drain on our small band of dedicated and enthusiastic officials and team managers. Goodness knows what we would do without them. If you can contribute towards helping to run our Club in any way then please get in touch with the Club Secretary who will be only too pleased to point you in the right direction. We would particularly like to see parents and younger members (exams permitting) getting involved.

items.sum: Editorial asking athletes to tell team managers in advance if they cannot turn up for a match.
items.s: Do us a favour Editorial asking athletes to tell team managers in advance if they cannot turn up for a match. Do us a favour One thing that our athletes, particularly the younger ones, can do to make life a little easier for team managers is, "let the Manager know if you can't turn up for a match". There is nothing worse for a team manager who has spent hours and hours on the phone trying to put a team together, than sitting in the coach on the morning of the match with time ticking away while waiting for athletes who simply fail to turn up. A 'phone call the night before or first thing in the morning is all that is required. Unless you actually have a problem on your way to the meeting place, it really is inexcusable to keep everyone waiting for no purpose.

items.s: Sidetracks Club news notes: the Shippens settling in Sydney, members in hospital, darts championship, new officials and Ted Moore back timekeeping. Sidetracks Clive and Elizabeth Shippen have safely arrived in Sydney, Australia, and are currently living in Dee Why with son Mark. Clive has been running several times a week, mostly in Dee Why Park but sometimes on a circuit of Long Reef that takes in stretches of beautiful coastline. After one session, warming down consisted of an hour of lying on the beach enjoying the sunshine. Tough eh! The Shippens soon met up with Ron Wyld and helped him to celebrate his 60th birthday along with other guests Dave Scott, Joy Gardener (Pete's mother), and Scott Wyld and almost before Clive's feet had touched the floor he was being inveigled into helping to coach pole vault at Homebush Stadium. Apparently Ron drives a claret Datsun Bluebird with yellow number plates! Clive and Elizabeth pass on their regards to all. Several Belgravians have been in hospital for one thing or another recently. Colin Pearson underwent gall bladder surgery just a couple of weeks ago while Keith Harris, a regular behind the tea bar on washing up duties is in nearby Atkinson Morley Hospital at the time of writing. Arthur Penstone who does so much to keep our Headquarters up to scratch has also been undergoing treatment. Our best wishes to you all and we look forward to hearing of continued good progress. George Piddington is now more mobile and has enjoyed being visited by various members. He is taken to his local track every Tuesday by his Havant AC colleagues where he helps with coaching. The 32nd holding of the Darts Championship for the "Denmark Pot" took place at Belgrave Hall on December 2nd and once again Bill Couzens was the victor. That makes it three years on the trot for Bill - a feat he last attained 1963-65. We are very pleased to welcome several new officials to our ranks. A series of training courses were held at Belgrave Hall during the winter followed by tests and the result was that we now have three newly qualified track judges in Pam Davies, Leslie Earle and Richard Hearn, and two new time keepers in Terry Earle and Phil Mason. Already these good people have lent a hand at our matches and we are more than grateful for their help. At one point during the Surrey County Championships we noted that on the Track Judges' Stand we had three Belgravians in action while across the other side of the straight three more were holding stop watches. With one or two out on the field as well, and several carrying out administrative tasks we can start to feel pleased that we are contributing a little more to our sport as a Club rather than leave it to a few individuals. But we need so many more (see our Editorial page). Talking of Timekeepers, it's great to see Ted Moore back in action and looking remarkably well after his stroke. Ted has been timing at several school's matches and has even been up to Battersea a couple of times for our home fixtures. You can't keep a good man down for long. items.s: From The Belgravian Column reprinting items from 25 years ago (June 1971: Southern cross country, RWA 10 miles walk, Carl Lawton, Surrey League) and 50 years ago (June 1946: post-war cross-country season). FROM THE BELGRAVIAN 25 Years Ago ... June 1971 BELGRAVE bounced back into form in the Parliament Hill mud this February, with a highly encouraging second place in the Southern Cross Country Championships. The most heartwarming sight of the afternoon for Belgrave supporters was that of the flying figure of Gerry North, who made a thrilling attempt to recapture his title, and had he not been hit by his old enemy 'stitch' might well have done so. As it was, his 4th place just 20 seconds behind the winner gave us a magnificent start and with another three men in the first 34 it was a good day for the Bels. Result: 4, Gerry North; 30, Tony Brien; 32, Lionel Mann; 34, John Bicourt; 42, John Thresher; 79, Tony Fairclough. Team: 1, Reading 137pts; 2, Belgrave 221pts; 3, Hillingdon 225pts. RWA NATIONAL 10 MILES WALK. In one of the closest races yet Belgrave only clinched the team title in the closing stages. There was never more than a few points in it as our boys battled for the vital places. Wilf Wesch, our reigning champion, was concentrating on staying safely in the race, and avoiding any possible trouble finished a comfortable fifth. Result: 5, Wilf Wesch; 13, Carl Lawton; 16, Allan Callow; 29, Ray Middleton. Team: 1, Belgrave 53pts; 2, Lancashire W 65pts; 3, Southend 68pts. CARL LAWTON walked brilliantly in the National 20km and clearly deserved his first selection to represent GB in a race abroad - competing over 20 kilos in Bucharest. TONY BINDA, Peter Carton and Bill Curtin yet again filled the first three places in the final Surrey League. With Mark Clancy (5th) and Paddy Breslin (7th) Belgrave were runaway winners of both match and League title. and, 50 Years Ago ... June 1946 THE FIRST post-war Winter season was a memorable one for the Belgrave Harriers. Our cross-country runners won every open championship. In November we had the first two teams home in the South of Thames "Junior," and the first three individuals. This in itself was a remarkable feat as all of our pre-war "cracks" cannot run this race owing to the barring clauses. In the New Year we won the Surrey County Title, whilst our Middlesex members, running for Cadogan A.C., took the Middlesex title. This was not regarded as very extraordinary as it had been done on various occasions before the war. The South of Thames "Senior" Race resulted in another win for us. Here again, a large number of our best men are "barred." The Southern Counties Cross-Country Championship, 7 ½ miles instead of the usual 10, was held from Belgrave Hall. Our Captain, Tom Carter, gained a well-earned and popular victory. With David Main third and four others in the first 20 positions, we gained a 99 points' margin over the second team. In fact our team of 12 was home before any other team had finished its six scoring men! Then to the much awaited English Championship, of which we were the proud holders. On March 9th our lads travelled to Leamington Spa and had another battle royal with our famous Midland rivals, Birchfield Harriers. Our team finished in the first 24 positions, and after a breath-taking adding up of the scores we were acclaimed winners with a ten-points' margin. We are indeed truly the Champion Club. Of individuals, Tom Carter deserves our thanks and praise for the successful training and nursing of his team, also, of course, for his own brilliant running. It was a cause for general regret that Tom did not get another International vest. Tom had had a cold the week before the race, which no doubt left its effect. Len Herbert, by finishing seventh, was awarded an England vest, and we congratulate Len on adding his name to the distinguished company of Belgravians so honoured in the past. items.s: Belgrave Dinner Dance Announcement that Bill Couzens is handing organisation of the Belgrave dinner-dance (Saturday 16th November) to Ron Severn, with a profile of Ron. BELGRAVE DINNER DANCE NEXT NOVEMBER - Saturday, 16th, to be precise - sees what newspaper journalists call "the end of an era." That is the date of this year's Belgrave dinner-dance (put the date in your diaries and start saving for it now) and, after thirteen years of organising it, Bill Couzens is taking a rest. He is handing this great event over to Ron Severn who will actually, with Bill's help and guidance, be responsible for this year. Some of you may not know Ron. He joined Belgrave in 1983 after leaving High Wycombe, where he had been successively Secretary, Chairman and Trustee of Wycombe Phoenix Harriers, as well as organiser for years of the famous "Furniture Five" road race. Soon after joining Belgrave he became Hon. Treasurer, which job he did for five years, and upon giving it up he was elected a Life Member of the Club. He has been away from the innermost affairs of the "Bels" for a while, but is back now, not only for the dinner-dance, but also as a new auditor of the Club, taking over from Ray Conway, another long servant. Ron says: "Following Bill with the dinner-dance will be almost impossible, he has made such a huge success of it for so long. All that I can say is that I plan no changes in the venue (Preston Cross Hotel) or the format, so I hope everyone can look forward to the same wonderful evening they have always enjoyed. But I need all the help I can get in the sale of tickets, so will everyone please make a special effort this year to buy them, not only to save me many sleepless nights, but also - and this is much more important - to see that Bill and his wife Gwen (who has herself made a great contribution to each year) get a grand 'send-off' and 'thank you'. items.s: Club record corrections Notes correcting and adding to the club records list published in the previous issue, thanking contributors; corrections themselves are on page 37. club record corrections OUR EXTENSIVE list of Club Records in the previous issue proved to be of great interest and we are grateful to those who were able to fill in some of the missing details or took the trouble to let us know of any inaccuracies. Many thanks in particular to Peter Matthews, Jacinta Moore, Steve Williams, Dave Sharpe, Charlie Dickinson, Helen Maskrey, Gary Staines and Derek Jones. We promised to reprint the younger age group Walking Records once we had more information but quite frankly, our lads and lasses are turning in record performances with such rapidity that they are moving from week to week. We will reprint them and what we hope to do for all events in all disciplines and age-groups is produce a check-list of records broken on a regular basis. Apologies to Rachael Parrot, whose first name we had spelled incorrectly. Incidentally, all her best walking times were believed to have been set on the track. It seems that all of Ian Gilley's U13B Records were set in South Africa and we have no knowledge whatsoever of the conditions, venues, timekeeping standards, etc. As a result we are relegating his performances to other notable performances status and have to carry out more investigation to find out what the best confirmed performances really are for this age-group. More news in the next issue. Michael Nicholls' correct age for under 17 records has been confirmed and we now have the correct spelling of Ian McDermott. We are informed that 1.5k walking events are no longer held so they will also be recorded as other notable performances. Charlie Gillett's M40 100m was patently wind assisted so it's back to the drawing board for that event although we suspect that Snowy Brooks' 12.0 from 1985 will probably stand up as the best on record. We missed Jacinta Moore's sprint times from '95 and including them now, we note that she holds every flat running record for W35 from 100m to 5000m. We recorded Jim Estall's '95 London Marathon as our best M40 time but had missed Charlie Dickinson's 1989 effort which was a little faster. As Chas. turned away after watching the 'London' this year he couldn't help commenting, with his tongue in his cheek "So I've still got the record then." We also omitted Helen Maskrey's best 10 miler on the road. Gary Staines reckons that he has a better 10k road time than Paul Evans' 28:13 but apart from the fact that he set it in Spain some time around 1989 we haven't any more details yet. Corrections, with the exception of name spellings only, are shown on page 37 - and yes we know some of these have been beaten since. items.label: June 1996
items.h: Marathon Dave faces his toughest challenge
items.sum: Dave McMillan, who had run all 15 London Marathons, was badly injured when hit by a car on a training run and vows to run again.
items.s: Marathon Dave faces his toughest challenge Dave McMillan, who had run all 15 London Marathons, was badly injured when hit by a car on a training run and vows to run again. Marathon Dave faces his toughest challenge JUST UNDER a year ago Fleet Street journalist Dave McMillan, a member of Belgrave Harriers for the last 34 years, was delighted to receive a commemorative medal and tee-shirt from the London Marathon organisers congratulating him upon being one of only 41 runners who had completed all 15 London Marathons. Dave's first athletic events had been the sprints back in the '60s but he was always ready to have a go at anything and was regularly to be seen in his teenage years, plugging away at the back of the "Southern" and "National" cross-country fields. He was so proud to receive that letter from Alan Storey because gradually, over the years, he had got faster and faster in 10ks, half and full marathons until at the age of 47 he had just set his latest pb over the London course with 3:03:05. Club-mates jokingly reckoned that by the time he was 60 he would be down to about 2:30! Dave was determined to carry on until he was the only person left who had completed every single 'London' but sadly fate does not always favour the nice guy. While out for a Sunday morning 13 miler in the Warwickshire country lanes near his home earlier this year and with just a mile or so to go before that hot shower, he was cruelly struck by a speeding car and received the most horrific injuries. With a leg shattered in four places, broken ribs, punctured lungs, a crushed arm ... his proud record of consecutive marathon runs was quite obviously over. But you know, runners are such a positive breed and no-one could be more determined than 'Dave Mac'. For a start he was pleased to be alive. The ambulance rushing him to the Radcliffe Infirmary in Oxford had to radio ahead to report that he was likely to be dead on arrival unless special surgery was carried out immediately. Another ambulance with the necessary equipment was dispatched and at a rendezvous in an Oxfordshire country lane an innovative emergency operation was carried out. A three month minimum predicted stay in hospital was then reduced to a month as Dave oh! so painfully carried out every exercise and more prescribed by the doctors. He had already told the hospital staff that he would be running again and they devised additional 'work-outs' to keep tendons and muscles in tone for that big day in the future. Incredibly, only two months later, he is already getting about in his wheelchair although the jarring caused by cracks in the pavements has him gritting his teeth and he has had to return to hospital for a bone graft. Once more he has vowed that he will run again and who can possibly doubt it. Dave McMillan Dave McMillan member for 34 years; one of 41 runners to complete all 15 London Marathons; pb 3:03:05 at age 47; seriously injured by a car Dave McMillan Dave 'Dave Mac' Alan Storey Alan Storey London Marathon London Marathon Southern Cross Country Championships National Cross Country Championships Warwickshire Radcliffe Infirmary, Oxford Oxfordshire

items.sum: Past President Reg Hopkins relays a BAF message on protecting young athletes and coaches from abuse and false accusation, and takes on the role of club contact, with his photo.
items.s: Safeguarding young athletes and coaches Past President Reg Hopkins relays a BAF message on protecting young athletes and coaches from abuse and false accusation, and takes on the role of club contact, with his photo. Safeguarding young athletes and coaches "THE DISCUSSION between BAF, Sports Council and other sports concerning statutory and recommended procedures for protecting young sports persons against abuse, and those working with them against malicious accusations of misbehaviour or abuse, continue. It is becoming increasingly apparent that the key agency in putting these safeguards into effect can only be the athlete's club. For it is here where young athletes and adults interact in an athletic context. Protocols are going to have to be established by which clubs vet appointees to positions in which they work with the young, and then monitor them in doing so. References and affidavits may be needed and sub-committees and confidential files safely and securely kept. Will your club be able to cope?" At a recent meeting of the Club's Management Committee the Secretary brought the above message from BAF to our notice. It was agreed by all present that we should give it our full attention. Having had to deal with this subject, in which I have received considerable training as part of my full time occupation as Youth and Community Officer, I readily offered to act for the Club in this matter. Following the request of the Committee and on the recommendation of BAF I have purchased the information pack concerned with our sport, and will consult it when and where necessary. I feel sure that all Belgravians will understand the need to give attention to this danger that can threaten both young person and adult, and will give me their full support in what can be at times a very sensitive situation. All I need to say at this time is ... you know whose responsibility it is to act in these matters on behalf of the Club and therefore whom to contact if you have any fears. Reg Hopkins, Past President. Telephone [phone number withheld]. Below: Past President Reg. Hopkins Snr. takes on the role of safeguarding our members. Reg Hopkins Reg Hopkins Past President; Youth and Community Officer; club contact for safeguarding Reg Hopkins Reg. Hopkins Snr.

items.sum: Report of the New York City Marathon on 12 November 1995, where Paul Evans finished second, four seconds behind German Silva.
items.s: An Englishman in New York Report of the New York City Marathon on 12 November 1995, where Paul Evans finished second, four seconds behind German Silva. An Englishman in New York NEW YORK CITY MARATHON 12 NOV 95 AS THE 26.2 mile charge through the streets of New York gradually drew to a conclusion and Central Park loomed ahead there were still 11 men battling it out for the top prizes. The Mexicans were out in force with Silva and the Garcias; Lopuyet, Kagwe and Koech were there from Kenya, Portuguese representatives were Matias and Pinhero and there were the South Africans Thys and Moqhali - oh! and of course the lone Briton and Belgravian Paul Evans. It was tough little German Silva making the running at 23 miles, piling on a pace that at last began to whittle down the leaders. Two miles to go and it was down to three: Silva, Evans and Koech. As the diminutive Mexican's searing pace bit harder and harder first the African fell away - and then Paul faltered, only to get back on terms again. Together they raced on until with 800 metres remaining the low geared Silva opened up just enough daylight on the Belgrave Harrier and at such a speed there was no coming back again. Exciting stuff! 1, G.Silva (Mexico) 2:11:00; 2, P.Evans 2:11:04; 3, W.Koech (Kenya) 2:11:19. Paul Evans Paul Evans 2nd, New York City Marathon 1995, 2:11:04 Paul Evans Evans Paul P.Evans G. items.s: Vets in Ireland Report of the home international veterans cross country races at Malahide Castle, Dublin, on 18 November, with Laurie O'Hara second in the M60s and Charlie Dickinson fourth in the open veterans race. Vets in Ireland THREE veteran Belgravians, Laurie O'Hara, Fred Paget and Charlie Dickinson flew to Ireland for the annual home international cross country races, this time held at Malahide Castle, Dublin on November 18th. Laurie was selected to run for the England M60 team while Charlie was a reserve for the England M45's. Fred went in an advisory capacity! It was indeed a splendid weekend. The hospitality was superb, the course beautifully cut green grassland in front of the magnificent castle, and the weather cold but with clear air and brilliant sunshine. The standard of running, particularly in the men's race, was awesome with Nigel Gates getting the better of Ireland's Jerry Kiernan and SLH's Barry Attwell. Laurie had to settle for silver in the M60s behind Scotland's Hugh Rankin and collected another silver in the team event. His time over the 9km course was 30:50. Charlie Dickinson came 4th in the Open Veterans race held over the same circuit in 27:50, a time that would have got him a team medal in the international race - but he did easily win the competition for drinking the most Guinness! items.h: Another Record Haul from President Snowy Brooks
items.sum: Club President Snowy Brooks wins the British Veterans Pentathlon Championship (M50) with 3647pts, setting M50 club records in the high and long jumps.
items.s: Another Record Haul from President Snowy Brooks Club President Snowy Brooks wins the British Veterans Pentathlon Championship (M50) with 3647pts, setting M50 club records in the high and long jumps. Another Record Haul from President Snowy Brooks BEING PRESIDENT of Belgrave Harriers doesn't seem to have slowed Super-Vet Snowy Brooks down at all. After last year's foray to the World Championships he had previously decided to take 1996 a little more easy but somehow the performances just seem to keep on coming. February 18th saw him at the Southern Counties VAC event at Crystal Palace where he clocked 8.3 for 60m and 9.7 for the 60m hurdles - but this was just a warm-up. At the British Veterans Pentathlon Championship at Birmingham Arena on March 2nd he led from the first event to the last, coming home over 700 points ahead of the second M50 with performances of 60mH/9.60, LJ/5.58, SP/11.90, HJ/1.51 and 1000m/3:50.86. Both the high jump and long jump were M50 Club Records and his final score of 3647pts was just 50pts shy of his best ever M50 pentathlon mark. items.s: Gabby set for a good summer Gabby Collison's spring road wins: Wimbledon Premier 10k in 36:08 and Arco Wessex 10k in 34:44, after an 81:53 half-marathon in Brighton. Gabby set for a good summer AFTER a record breaking 81:53 half-marathon in her home town of Brighton on 25th February , Gabby Collison took the Wimbledon Premier 10k on March 10th by over three minutes from Hare & Hounds' Rachel Disley, clocking 36:08. But the girl from the South Coast still had plenty in reserve. On April 14th at Totton near Southampton she ran to 34:44 in the Arco Wessex 10k race to gain an impressive victory over Bath's Zena Marchant in a time just 12 seconds short of her best ever. It looks as if the summer will see yet another revision of her best marks on road and track. items.s: Yacht '3', Wimbledon, 7 Oct 95 Report and handicap results of the club's Yacht '3' race at Wimbledon, won by S. Willimont, with nine-year-old Paul Graham the star. YACHT '3' WIMBLEDON, 7 OCT 95 "Hmph! Mystic Meg stands more chance of getting the handicaps right than you do ..." Every year Charlie Manning's ritual abuse of the Hon. Handicapper gets more inventive but never one to hold a grudge, Arthur Bruce this year gave him enough leeway to keep him off the back of the pack for a change. Entries were up for the second year in a row even if there was a Veterans' race over at Petersham and at last the field began to look like a race again. Even young Laurie was out scorching the SW19 roads again, sending the memories of onlookers drifting back over the years to races of days gone by. At the other end of the age-scale, nine years-old Paul Graham was having a great day. A jog in the morning at Battersea with Snowy and Daley Thompson loosened him up nicely for this three-miler and his determined sprinting down the finish stretch earned him the admiration of all. Pete Gilbey and Laurie O'Hara were so taken with the young man's efforts that they spontaneously awarded him their sports voucher prizes - at which Paul responded by offering them a go of his "power-ranger". But it was Misery Manning who had the last word when watching our President haul his decathlete's frame over the last yards: "What ... I thought he was supposed to be an athlete ..." items.sum: Report of the Surrey Cross Country League Division 1 race 1 hosted by Belgrave at Wimbledon on 14 Oct 1995, with course-marking mishaps and Belgrave 7th. Includes a team photo printed on page 10.
items.s: Hard pressed at home ! Report of the Surrey Cross Country League Division 1 race 1 hosted by Belgrave at Wimbledon on 14 Oct 1995, with course-marking mishaps and Belgrave 7th. Includes a team photo printed on page 10. Hard pressed at home ! REEBOK SURREY CC, LEAGUE DIVISION 1 RACE 1 WIMBLEDON, 14 OCT 95 Our officials were hard pressed on this day. As Don Anderson was running round the course laying out the trail of flags and tape he was unaware that mischievous youths were were busily adjusting his markings. With many of our Saturday afternoon runners happily ignoring the race as they ran past on their way to the Park, we were already short of pointsmen and as a result the youngsters' race was neatly diverted across a golfing green and off towards the horizon. After a long detour they approached the finish from completely the wrong direction. It didn't affect the result of the race as all except one lad followed the same route but it did affect the golf tournament which was called off ! Irate golfers had to be placated. When this was followed by a letter of complaint from one of the participating clubs with the suggestions that we should have people with radios at intervals around the course - we should have pointsmen stationed within sight of each other at every turn - that we should have a senior runner at the head of the field leading the way (any runner capable of doing that would currently be among our our scoring ten!) - well, it make's one wonder if there isn't a better way to spend a Saturday afternoon. In spite of all this, Amir Becirhodzic had great pleasure in getting home 2nd, and with fellow Bels Kevin Quinn, Steve Beaver and Peter MacDonald packing in close behind, Boro' of Hounslow only just pipped us for the Under 17 team win. Our mighty midgets the under 13s also gave us second place even though they had run way over the correct distance. While all this was going on senior Belgravians were still arriving at the start - some new faces - and some old - including Stu Paton and John Gladwin. No fewer than 29 claret and gold vests were among the initial charge as the starter sent around two hundred-odd runners on their way. Herne Hill's Taylor made the race his own from the very beginning although he never got right away. His clubmate Jon Solly was in close attendance after the first circuit with Aldershot's Jackson and Hare & Hounds' Oxborough strung out behind. Our second-claimer Adrian Passey led the Belgrave contingent but although we were strong in numbers, for most it was the first run of the winter season - and didn't it show. Far from gaining a good start in the series we found ourselves shunted right back to 7th place when the points were tallied. Even newly promoted Ranelagh got ahead of us. One man who was highly delighted was Stuart Paton. He sailed into the scoring ten to prove that there is plenty of life in his legs yet. New members Ray Foley and Nick Kello closed in our team. items.s: Surrey County Veterans CC Champs., Petersham, 7 Oct 95 Report and Belgrave results from the Surrey County Veterans cross country championships at Petersham, where turnout fell to a dozen runners. SURREY COUNTY VETERANS CC CHAMPS. PETERSHAM, 7 OCT 95 Only a few years ago this event was perhaps one of the most popular races for Belgravians with as many as thirty veterans taking part. This year it was down to a bare dozen runners with complete teams only from the ladies and M40's. The reasons are simple. Firstly, the date has moved progressively forward from its traditional spot at the end of October and this year clashed Surrey Vets continued . . . with Belgrave's own Yacht handicap. Secondly, for the last two years the course has been held over the very tough lower circuit which includes climbing the dreadful Petersham hill three times. Many who ran it last year opted out this year, and some who did it this year will never do it again (ask Doug Maughan). Belgrave ladies fielded the same team as last year but Jacinta Moore never felt happy and was well down from last year's fifth place. Nina Mills finished 6th W45 and Hilary Saw was only a minute and a half behind her. They placed 8th as a team. Again, John Mather was down from last year when he had a blinding run, but won the battle with Don Anderson to finish first Belgrave runner in 21st place. It was good to see the improving and very keen Tony Binda next, followed by Paul Roche. Chris Taplin had a good run in 49th and the M40 team finished 7th. John Wasbrough and Tony Stone renewed their M50 battle of last year. This time it was John who was just ahead at the finish. With Pat Newell injured and Arthur Bruce lining people up at Wimbledon for the 'Yacht' it was only Bert Stroud who ran in the M60's finishing 7th. items.sum: Team manager Alan Mead's review of the men's 1995-96 road and cross country season, culminating in the London Marathon team win.
items.s: Harriers once more Team manager Alan Mead's review of the men's 1995-96 road and cross country season, culminating in the London Marathon team win. Harriers once more We didn't expect our Men's Road and Cross Country team to set the world alight during the winter just past but nevertheless, things have begun to bubble nicely and looking back, the general feeling is one of satisfaction. A corner on the road to greater things has been turned and we have a clearer view of what we can do. In the Surrey League we came steadily from behind to end up at Coulsdon with our best team place in several years. We were well supported by Gary Staines but just as pleasing was the confidence beginning to creep into the team with half our scorers getting used to finishing in the 20s. What we must do next season is start off stronger - get a couple of low key events under our belts before the winter season begins in earnest - and then we can definitely aim for a final team place in the top half of the league. The South of Thames 'Junior' race at Crowthorne saw us in the medals while the 'Senior' event where we only belatedly entered a team gave us the individual winner. Both of these races could provide rich pickings for us next year. Few of our runners currently suffer from the barring clauses that prevail in these races - so let's go out next winter and get barred in a big way! We never did have the main championship events inked into our calendars but when one looks back one can see that with a little better organisation we could have won the Surrey title and with Matt Yates finishing in the 60s in the National one couldn't help getting excited about what we could achieve if we had enough runners with the same aim. By the time the relays came around things were looking better and better. Tackling the ECCU 4x5k cross-country event for the first time was an eye-opener. We had a hot team but those Northerners were hotter still. Who would've thought that clubs would turn out their top men two weeks in a row; 14k of cross-country at Newark followed by another 5k at Mansfield. We might have missed out on our dream of winning national medals in that four stage event but at least we featured again among the names of the traditional cross-country clubs - Bingley, Coventry, Border, Tipton, Belgrave ... with others like Birchfield in our wake. Then came our own road relay promotion where we swept the board. The Belgrave 6-Stage is beginning to look as if it might remain a regular event and it all adds to the pride and confidence that we need when it comes to showing that we are indeed still a harrier club as well as an outstanding track and field outfit. On to the Southern 12-Stage. Things got so exciting during the fortnight beforehand that our aim of a top ten spot got forgotten as we changed our target to top six and then saw ourselves as potential medallists. Sadly the wheels came off during the last few days but to end up 8th was a fine achievement and surely a herald of what is to come. Finally the London Marathon gave us the high profile win that we were looking for. Of course we had a brilliant start with 3rd and 9th from Paul Evans and Gary Staines but there had been prolonged negotiations between our management team and Nike, the BAF, the SEAA and the Race Referee, simply to ensure that out top two men would be eligible to score for us due to the fact that they were contracted by Nike to wear their Elite vest while in the team race club colours "should be worn". Our negotiations bore fruit and as a result we may well be pressing for an amendment to BAF's rules to make them more workable in today's sport. So now it's all before us. If we really do want to move on, we can. We have a good team running the show and as Team Manager I would like to thank Charlie Dickinson, Gordon Biscoe and Don Anderson for their help but most of all thanks to you the runners led by Captain 'Gerry' Adams and Vice-Captain Roger Alsop. Already I am looking forward to the prospect of next winter's campaign. There's the challenge of completing teams in the major championships, County and National 6-Stage Relays to have a crack at, the defence of what we have won this winter past. items.s: A 'stormer' from the Captain Report and results of the Priory 6x2½ mile cross country relay at Reigate Priory on 4 Nov 1995, where captain 'Gerry' Adams helped Belgrave to 6th. A 'stormer' from the Captain PRIORY 6x2½m CC RELAY REIGATE PRIORY, 4 NOV 95 Our best showing in recent years was in 1991 when a Gary Staines last leg of 12:19 took the Bels to 6th. No superstars this time out so our final position of 6th after half a dozen circuits of Priory Park has got to be considered highly satisfactory. Roger Alsop gave us a solid start by coming in 7th with Tonbridge making the running thanks to the day's fastest leg from Skelton. The young team from Kent held on to their lead on leg two with the first of the Graffin twins swinging into action but the field had closed up drastically behind with our own 'Gerry' Adams running a stormer to take the Bels up to 3rd. We should have been able to analyse our Captain's run over and over again at leisure but unfortunately Colin Pearson forgot to set the record button on his camcorder! Boxhill snuck past a fit looking Rob Turner and Bruce Barton, suffering from the sniffles held onto 4th as the last legs approached but Windsor were getting ominously close. Sure enough the Berkshire club's McHarg had the measure of Belgrave's Said Chettati and then Phil Carstairs had the pleasure of setting out for the final stage with Brighton's Andy Bristow breathing down his neck. Pick of the 'B' runners was City Dealer Nick Kello who'd have gone faster still had he arrived a little earlier and taken the 1st stage. Fastest in our women's team was Laura Wilson, still not quite 16 years of age and seemingly able to tackle any distance from 200m to 3k. items.s: We're in the medals Report and results of the South of Thames Junior cross country at Crowhurst on 11 Nov 1995, where Belgrave were second team and captain Graham Adams 4th (the season review on page 9 places this race at Crowthorne). SOUTH OF THAMES "JUNIOR" CROWHURST, 11 NOV 95 We're in the medals It was heartwarming for all those involved in cross country to watch a fine second place from our team and an inspired individual 4th from captain Graham Adams. Overnight rain, the first for several weeks, had softened the woodland paths which together with some very tough hills and more rain during the race made for a demanding course. A narrow downhill start produced the predictable manic rush with the Graffin twins from Tonbridge already heading the fray just ahead of Graham Adams. Then came a bunch of Belgravians, Roger Alsop, Nick Kello, Phil Carstairs, and Said Chettati nicely packed in the low twenties. The end of first short lap saw Graham maintaining his position in the leading bunch, Roger moving up, Nick dropping back slightly, and the others roughly the same. Futher back Steve Willimont looked unhappy but Tony Binda and Paul Cooper were running well. At the halfway stage a breakaway group of seven runners were forcing the pace with Graham Adams hanging on at the back. Roger Alsop continued to move up into the low teens and Phil Carstairs, not too well lately, was beginning to look uncomfortable. Graham made a huge effort after the long hill on the final lap picking off three tired bodies in a long run for home. An excellent effort. Roger showed that he is fast getting fit again after achilles tendon problems and a disappointing track season. He too finished strongly and got up to 11th. Next came Said who had got past Phil Carstairs and ran himself almost to a standstill in finishing 29th, another very good performance. Although suffering badly, Phil managed to hang on to the end without dropping too many places which was a good job as Belgrave only finished one point ahead of Basingstoke. Further down the field Nick Kello pulled a calf muscle but battled on gamely and cheerfully to the end. Tony Binda did well to finish 94th and we all know he has the potential to become a very good veteran. Paul Cooper too has a great deal of natural ability, he just needs to train harder and drink less! In all a very good day, well done Belgrave and well done Graham. 1, A.Graffin (Tonbridge) 28:57; 2, T.Hyde (Windsor S&E) 29:08; 3, S.Turvill (Basingstoke &MH) 29:25; 4, G.Adams 29:33; ... 11, R.Alsop 30:27; 29, S.Chettati 31:51; 37, P.Carstairs 32:29; 56, N.Kello 33:16; 94, A.Binda 34:44; 100, S.Willimont 34:54; 103, P.Cooper 34:58; 181, A.Stone 39:48; 203 finished. items.sum: Report and results of the second Surrey Cross Country League Division 1 match of 1995-96 at Richmond Park, where Belgrave's seniors were 7th but moved up the league, and the young athletes' teams placed second and third.
items.s: League hopes take a dive Report and results of the second Surrey Cross Country League Division 1 match of 1995-96 at Richmond Park, where Belgrave's seniors were 7th but moved up the league, and the young athletes' teams placed second and third. League hopes take a dive REEBOK SURREY CC LEAGUE DIVISION 1 RACE 2 RICHMOND PARK, 18 NOV 95 High hopes and hard work in attempting to round up a strong team counted for nothing. While we went through the list of Belgravians we had hoped to put on the starting line but who had failed to appear for one reason or another, Hounslow were at their strongest and romped to a clear win with 8 men finishing in 28. The Bels who were there all ran well, greatly improving on their first race positions but we simply had to go back too far to close in the team. Luckily for us, but unluckily for the "Irrepressibles," South London H crashed so badly that they dropped from 6th after match 1 to 8th here and as a result we actually moved up in the league! Jim Estall's 22nd came just the day before the Epsom '10' - there's no stopping this man when he's on song - and after two races he had put himself well in line for the vets title. A very warm welcome went to new member Dave Beaver, one time second placer in the National Junior Cross Country Champs for Polytechnic H. Dave's been around the club for a season or so while son Steve has been making a niche for himself in our under 15 team, and finally he took the plunge and signed the dotted line along with other son Chris. Dave then celebrated by going straight into the scoring ten even though far from fit. Before you read through the results, we must point out that Charlie Manning's "dnf" was not due to that gentleman's inability to complete the course - it was simply due to the fact that he was a little worried about keeping the timekeepers hanging about and a lot more worried about getting his car out of Richmond Park due to the gates being closed at dusk! Among the youngsters, great running came from Amir Becirhodzic who raced through strongly for 3rd with the rest of the team queuing up for points just behind. As a result second team place went the way of our under17s/under15s while the under 13s also scored well headed by David Bates, Chris Beaver and that mighty nine year-old, Paul Graham. At the halfway point in the league both these teams were lying in 2nd spot. items.s: Sweeney on his tod in 'Surrey' Report on the Surrey County Cross Country Championships at Frimley, won by second-claim Belgravian Chris Sweeney on his return from three years of injuries, with Graham Adams 7th and Steve Beaver 6th in the Under 15 Boys. Sweeney on his tod in 'Surrey' SURREY COUNTY CROSS COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIPS FRIMLEY, 9 DEC 95 Those who braved the icy conditions at Frimley were treated to a wonderful victory by Chris Sweeney, returning to competition after three years of injuries. Chris was running as a second claim member for Belgrave and was unfortunately unable to score for the team (not because second-claimers are barred but because he only entered at the last minute). The rest of the squad all ran well but just lacked sufficient depth to claim any medals although it is worth noting that had Chris stated his intentions earlier we would have been within a point or two of winning. Two times around the frozen playing fields and both Chris Sweeney and Graham Adams were well up in the leading pack; Chris looking very relaxed, Graham already working hard. Further back Jim Estall and Roger Alsop were nicely placed in the second group. Then the field climbed up the steep bank into the woods for three tough undulating circuits. By this time the sun had disappeared and with it any semblence of warmth. Many runners never really warmed up and found the hard rutty conditions very tiring. After the first lap Chris Sweeney had already forged a useful lead and he looked comfortable and confident as he floated over the ground with his economical style. As the race progressed so his lead grew, all the way to the finish. This was really the first indication of the form which later took Chris to a successful Grand Prix series and a Great Britain vest in the World Cross Country Championships. Graham Adams again led by example and battled around the course to finish in 7th, an excellent result which reflected his strong early winter form. Then Jim Estall, unhappy with the cold, but finishing a fine 14th, again ahead of BVAF National Champion Barry Atwell and also Bob Treadwell. Roger Alsop ran steadily for 27th, then a gap before Mike Nouch and Junior Galley in the late fifties. One more engine room runner here would have given the Belgrave team medals even without Chris Sweeney, but it was not to be and it was thanks to Tony Stone for completing the scoring six back in 185th position. Leo Coy's lads looked as if they would be on for a set of medals in the Under 17 Men's group but unfortunately Simon Alexander suffered an asthma attack, putting paid to those hopes. Highest placed first-claim Belgravian of the day was Steve Beaver whose 6th place in the Under 15 Boys race must be ranked as his finest run to date. Above: Out on his own, Chris Sweeney takes his first Surrey County Championship. Left: With the race not a minute old, Chris Sweeney (424) already heads the bunch with Hounslow's Hugh Brasher (16) our own Graham Adams (1) and Dorking's Bruno Witchalls in close attendance. items.sum: Account of Darren Mead being challenged by an official, then placed second on the same time as the winner, at the Norfolk Cross Country Championship while running for his second-claim club Thetford.
items.s: Darren 2nd at Norfolk Account of Darren Mead being challenged by an official, then placed second on the same time as the winner, at the Norfolk Cross Country Championship while running for his second-claim club Thetford. Darren 2nd at Norfolk At Caldecott Hall, Norfolk, Darren Mead ran into controversy when recording the same time as the winner in the Norfolk CC Championship. Turning out for his second-claim club as one is perfectly entitled to in County CC Champs., Darren found himself accosted by a Norfolk official who told him that he would not be allowed to run. After a heated discussion (not the best preparation for a race) it was agreed that the official was wrong and that he could indeed represent Thetford. But the day had more twists in store yet. Tucked in behind the leader as the finish was neared, Darren unleashed a sprint for the line and although our man felt he got his nose in front, as did his rival and various other onlookers, the decision went against him and second place in the same time as the winner was all he could claim. We believe that this is the first Norfolk CC title Darren has ever lost. Darren Mead Darren Mead 2nd, Norfolk CC Championship, same time as the winner Darren Mead Darren Norfolk Cross Country Championships Caldecott Hall, Norfolk Thetford

items.s: Reigate Priory Holly Run Report and results of the Reigate Priory Holly Run, where Belgrave's men won the 'Holly Run' Cup with the 'B' team second, with photos of young Belgravians Paul Graham and Christian Morris who also ran. REIGATE PRIORY HOLLY RUN REIGATE PRIORY, 17 DEC 95 This was intended as an unashamed "pot-hunt" for our engineroom men, having a final run out together before Christmas. Conditions were so slippery that most had trouble keeping their feet at some stage but Marcello seemed to suffer the most, looking as if he'd be much happier wearing a pair of skis. Phil Carstairs yo-yo'd up and down the top ten as the race progressed, gaining places on the rolling grassland and hills but losing them again every time the murderous descent was tackled when less cautious souls let the brakes off and dodged the rocks and trees like fell runners. Foxy old Charlie Dickinson worked his way through gradually while lightly built Dave Beaver just could not believe how well he was going. As tea and mince-pies were consumed in great quantity at the presentation we had pleasure in receiving the "Holly Run" Cup as first team (won nine times in the last ten years by Boxhill) with our second team just pipping Crawley to gain silver medals. With our veteran runners taking just about all the vets' medals, we'd cleaned up nicely.
