items.s: McDonalds YA League Southern Premier Div. Match, Oxford, 5 May 96 Report and results of Belgrave's first Young Athletes' League Southern Premier Division match at Oxford, which Belgrave won. MCDONALDS YA LEAGUE SOUTHERN PREMIER DIV. MATCH , OXFORD, 5 MAY 96 Having been promoted to the Southern Premier Division as a result of last summer's efforts it was important that we made a good start to consolidate our position. The trouble was, the week before the match so many of our youngsters pulled out due to being grounded prior to exams, having colds, and so on, that it looked as if a disaster was to be the more likely result. Not so, however. It seemed that each of the other clubs had similar problems and we came away from Oxford with a superb win - our first at this level of competition. Only Blackheath scored better of all clubs in the division so the Bels. immediately went into position two on the league table. Nice work boys! There were far too many fine performances to pick out individuals but looking through the results, one thing is certain: if we can hang on to just some of these lads as they become Juniors and eventually Seniors, then our future is assured. MATCH 2 CROYDON, 19 MAY 96 There were still quite a few gaps on the team sheet at Croydon - and we suffered a double disqualification in the Under 15 relays - but still we came up trumps with a second team win. Both "Man of the Match" awards went to Belgrave lads. To Shaun Eaton for his marvellous sprinting in the youngest age-group and Syful Ahmed whose triple jumping in the Under 17 group was out of this world- over 14 metres and only 16 years old! And when you consider that we had Young Athlete's Captain Peter Waterman launching his hammer out beyond the 50 metre line ... items.sum: Feature introducing three new Belgrave distance runners, Nigel Powley, Anthony Robertson and Donal O'Riordan, with panels of their best performances and Powley's championship wins.
items.s: Three of a Kind Feature introducing three new Belgrave distance runners, Nigel Powley, Anthony Robertson and Donal O'Riordan, with panels of their best performances and Powley's championship wins. THREE OF A KIND Three runners who have recently joined Belgrave Harriers are likely to strengthen our hand considerably when the cross country and road relay season comes round again. Suffolk based Nigel Powley, previously a member of Colchester Harriers, is sponsored by Mizuno and likes to compete regularly over anything from 5 to 20 miles. It was on a trip to Ewell for the 26.2 Club's 10k that he caught our eye, running "unattached" and placing 2nd in 31:29. According to AW he was looking for a club and had Belgrave in mind. So with a bit of detective work we tracked him down and found ... that he didn't know where AW had got that piece of information from ... he hadn't really been thinking of the Bels. ... but on the other hand why not ... and signed up within the week! Nigel was delighted to don Belgrave kit in his next road race and has every intention of joining our road relay and cross-country squads. His local press already feature him regularly and made a point of noting that he had teamed up with fellow Suffolk man Paul Evans and that Belgrave are the "currently the Manchester United of the athletics world". The last five months or so have seen Nigel steadily coming back from an achilles tendon problem. The signs are that he is over it now and raring to go. Just take a look through his cv in the accompanying panel and you'll know why we are so excited to have him on board. Anthony Robertson became a Belgravian just a few weeks ago. He hails from South Africa but his father was born in Ireland and athletically, that is his nationality. Living in Wimbledon now, he has great running country not so far from his doorstep with Wimbledon Common and Richmond Park and he's looking forward to teaming up with other runners to get himself into good shape and really motivated. A word of warning though, he's a 14:40 5,000m man and around 31½ minutes for 10k on the road so don't take any liberties on those 10 mile fartlek sessions. Anthony had heard about Belgrave from other South African runners who have been over here and now being a local man, is looking forward to using our gymnasium. Ideally Anthony likes to clock up 100 to 110k each week including 15 or 20x400m sessions and recently tried his first marathon - this Spring's London - where he ran 2:36-odd to finish just a little way down on Jim Estall. What an asset this man's going to be. Now we'd like to introduce you to another runner from across the Irish Sea - Donal O'Riordan. Watching Donal race in some of our opening meetings this year one cannot help but be struck by the fact that he really does look every inch "a runner". But it's not surprising really as his father is Tom O'Riordan, the first Irishman to run inside 14 minutes for 5k back in the 'sixties, a competitor who proudly bore his emerald green singlet in the Tokyo Olympics of 1964 alongside some great names - Jazy, Keino, Clarke. Tom is now a sports writer for the Irish Independant and will be in Atlanta this year to cover the Games. Donal only really started training at the age of 22 when he went to Loughborough University but within a couple of seasons he has logged up some classy runs over 1500 metres and the mile. He lives in London at the moment and has spent some time training with the Shaftesbury Barnet boys but it's Belgrave for him, influenced to a certain extent by Derek and Dave Kelleher. Donal hasn't really gone in for road racing so far but has some definite aims for the near future. He wants to run cross country in the County and Southern Championships next winter and has his eyes set on our indoor Club Record for 1500 metres - Stuart Paton's 3:46.65 from 1983. 800m 1:54.0 1500m 3:47.8 1 mile 4:08 5000m 14:40 10k Road 31:32 Marathon 2:36:34 1 mile 4:17 5 miles 24:07 10k 30:12 10 miles 49:42 Half-marathon 65:46 15 miles 77:15 20 miles 1:44:37 Marathon 2:35:50 10k 93, 94 10 miles 85, 91, 93, 94, 95 Half-marathon 91, 92, 93, 95 15 miles 91 20 miles 94 Cross country 93 10 miles 94 Half-marathon 91, 92, 93, 95 15 miles 91 Nigel Powley Nigel Powley new member from Suffolk, previously Colchester Harriers; 2nd in 26.2 Club 10k at Ewell in 31:29 Nigel Powley Nigel Paul Evans Paul Evans fellow Suffolk man Anthony Robertson Anthony Robertson new member from South Africa, living in Wimbledon; 14:40 5000m; 2:36:34 London Marathon Anthony Robertson Anthony Jim Estall Jim Estall Donal O'Riordan Donal O'Riordan new member; started training at Loughborough University; 1500m 3:47.8 Donal O'Riordan Donal Tom O'Riordan Tom O'Riordan Donal's father; first Irishman inside 14 minutes for 5k; Tokyo Olympics 1964; sports writer for the Irish Independant Tom O'Riordan Tom Jazy Jazy Keino Keino Clarke Clarke Derek Kelleher Derek printed 'Derek and Dave Kelleher' Dave Kelleher Dave Kelleher Stuart Paton Stuart Paton indoor club record 1500m 3:46.65 (1983) 26.2 Club 10k London Marathon Olympic Games Suffolk Championships Eastern Counties Championships Suffolk Ewell South Africa Ireland Wimbledon Wimbledon Common Richmond Park Tokyo Atlanta Loughborough University London Colchester Harriers 26.2 Club Shaftesbury Barnet

items.label: June 1996
items.sum: Dave Scott, a Belgravian and former British League 800m runner now Athletics NSW Development Officer, describes how athletics is organised in Australia and gives news of old Belgravians around Sydney.
items.s: From Belgrave to Bondi Dave Scott, a Belgravian and former British League 800m runner now Athletics NSW Development Officer, describes how athletics is organised in Australia and gives news of old Belgravians around Sydney. FROM BELGRAVE to BONDI DAVE SCOTT, BELGRAVIAN AND FORMER BRITISH LEAGUE 800M MAN, HAS SWAPPED LIFE IN LONDON FOR A BUSY ROLE AS ATHLETICS NSW DEVELOPMENT OFFICER After spending two years as the Development Officer for Athletics New South Wales, the track and field organisation for the largest state in Australia, (in terms of participation levels) I have come to terms with some major differences in the way the sport is conducted here, compared to the way that I was used to things being done when I was part of the English system up to 1993. To begin with, the system of administration of the sport is vastly different. Our national body, Athletics Australia, runs a highly successful Grand Prix series over here, which showcases domestic elite talent and some overseas stars in competitions in every state in Australia. Stars from overseas who have competed whilst I have been here include Gwen Torrence, Michael Johnson, Mike Powell and Sergei Bubka, as well as Linford Christie and Colin Jackson, who are regular visitors to Sydney to train in the European off season. Athletics Australia also organise the National Championships, overseas teams and major championships trials. In this respect Athletics Australia is similar to the BAF. When one gets to the state bodies, of which I am part, the situation differs greatly. The national body officially has no jurisdiction over the state organisations, who can (and sometimes do) go their own way in terms of local competition and development. In addition, these state bodies are funded in part by the state governments, but exist as independent entities, as opposed to the council-run system in England. From the development aspect of things, which is my specific area, this independence is valuable since it gives me the freedom to base a development programme on what I, as the "man on the ground" know needs attention rather than having to implement a programme passed down by politicians. Sponsorship dollars, becoming more readily available due to the Sydney Olympics in 2000, allows me to have a fairly ambitious programme, something which I know the money-starved development officers in England would sorely love to have. Co-operation between the states and national body is vital if progress in the sport is to occur here in Australia, and disharmony between the various bodies in the past has led to a dramatic slide in track and field participation numbers across Australia. From a low of 9,000 registered members nationally in 1990, the sport has recovered to have 15,000 registered in the 1994-95 season. This looks and indeed is pretty pathetic compared to England, but track and field here is a relatively low profile sport, with the media dominated by rugby league, cricket, surf lifesaving (ironman) and swimming. That is where the big money, and consequently the high profile, goes. The club system is very different too, for various reasons. To begin with, there is no national club competition like the British League or GRE Cup. The country is just too big for a club to compete in other states - Australia is a continent bigger than Europe, and Perth, the city furthest away from Sydney is one time zone and a 6 hour flight away. Makes a British League Division One bus trip to Edinburgh seem like a piece of cake! The clubs themselves are different too. Although some large clubs do exist, the nature of Australia, and New South Wales in particular, with a small population of 5 million living in an area 10 times the size of France, means that most clubs are very small with perhaps 100 members maximum. This makes even a state league competition based around clubs impossible, as most clubs couldn't field a full team. Also, use of many venues for the competition is impossible as there are only five all weather tracks in New South Wales, two of which are at the new Olympic site in Sydney. Instead, a competition is held on a weekly basis during the club season (September - January) in Sydney, based around teams comprising clubs from regions of NSW. This system is entirely unsatisfactory, and, along with the dire lack of facilities, is a major factor in the near terminal decline of grass-roots track and field in NSW and Australia as a whole. Sounds pretty depressing so far doesn't it? Well, I was fairly disgusted with things as I saw them in 1992, but so far I have only outlined the negative parts. There are some major advantages to the sport out here, which properly used, I believe will make Australia a strong international force, which has not been the case since Herb Elliott, Ron Clarke, Ralph Doubell, Alby Thomas and Betty Cuthbert dominated in the fifties and sixties. First and foremost is the fact that Sydney is hosting the Olympic Games. Aside from boosting my chances of actually getting a seat in the stand at the Games, the Olympics have provided an impetus for all that has been lacking in Australian track and field; profile, media coverage, sponsorship dollars and public appeal. At last the sport is moving in the right direction and all in the administration at the national level and within NSW are determined to capitalise on the opportunities arising. The aforementioned Grand Prix Series in Australia is a great boost to the sport too. Started in 1989, it is well supported by Australia's elite athletes, and provides much needed media and public exposure for the sport as well as revenue for the state organisations. Earlier this year the IAAF granted the Melbourne Grand Prix "B" status, putting it on a par with any meet held in England. This should help to boost the international profile of Australian track and field. This year I had a heavy involvement in the Sydney Grand Prix, held in February. There were sponsorship proposals to write, negotiations with potential sponsors, and I had to organise ticket offers to schools and think up incentives to get more people through the gate. One of the great features about my job is that I am gaining experience in aspects of sport other than purely development issues, such as sports marketing and event management, which will come in handy for future career moves. Probably the greatest innovation in Australian athletics in recent years, and a programme working well in NSW in particular, is in the area of junior elite development. On a state level, we have divided our area into six country regions, excluding the Metropolitan area of Sydney. Each of these regions has a Regional Academy of Sport supporting several sports, including track and field. A squad of 20 talented young athletes aged 12-19 are financially supported to attend training days, receive elite coaching and travel to competitions. Some of these regions have smaller "development" squads of younger athletes. These squads are determined through talent identification, testing and thorough analysis of schools competition results. Each regional programme costs roughly $6,000 (£3,000) to run for a year. In addition, the athletes have to be registered with a local club and compete at certain events. These programmes have the effect of retaining young talent in the sport at a crucial age when many leave to go to other sports, supporting athletes in remote country areas and raising the profile of the sport on a local level. The programme has been highly successful, with the first athletes to enter the programme now beginning to enter the World Junior team and compete well at senior level. At the next level above this is the NSW Academy of Sport track and field programme, run by a British Olympic bronze medallist and Belgrave adversary, Keith Connor. This programme handles the elite junior and senior athletes from NSW and funds them to compete around the country in the Grand Prix Series, or in organised trips overseas, such as on a tour to the USA to compete at the Penn State Relay Championships. This is really the transition point for our juniors to senior level, and allows that change to be smooth. Few of our elite juniors, once in the system, are lost. In addition to these administration structures, Athletics Australia have introduced a national junior elite programme, called the "Oz Squad". This programme is designed to identify talented juniors from the Under 14, Under 16 and Under 18 age groups from each state and maintain their interest in the sport through newsletters and track and field camps, forming a talent pool from which to draw athletes into the World Junior and eventually, World Championship, Olympic and Commonwealth representation. NSW currently has 102 athletes in the OZ Squad, of whom 16 are currently qualified to compete at the Sydney World Juniors in 1996. Every athlete in the Oz Squad has to fulfill tough performance standards, and are all linked to high performance coaches and clubs in every state. As far as I know, this system is unique to Australia, and is modelled roughly on the Eastern European model of the seventies and eighties. It is a very popular and effective programme, and a key element to Australia's future success, in my belief. I am heavily involved with the planning, organisation and administration of the above programmes and feel that other countries should try the same if they are to succeed in track and field in later years. Our model has only been running for three years and already the benefits are being felt through increased registration numbers, better international performances and higher public recognition of the sport. One of the great paradoxes of Australia is that because the population is so into sports, we have a reduced success at international level. In Australia a wider variety of sports are played per head than anywhere else in the world. Whilst this is great for public health, it results in the limited talent pool being diluted across many sports, hence the reduced success on a world scale. The above programmes retain talent within our sport, and help to boost overall participation in the sport through providing a media profile. In this way track and field is beating off the challenge from other sporting bodies, and has ensured its future. Britain and Europe are just beginning to feel the effects on track and field of "new" sports such as baseball, basketball and American football as they encroach upon the traditional talent resources. It is probable that, unless similar measures are taken to address the problem, then Britain too will begin to lose numbers and success. From what I have seen, the BAF and Belgrave in particular are taking steps to stop the slide. In addition to my involvement with all of the above programmes, I am also a member of the Organising Committee for the 1996 World Junior Championships in Sydney and the Organising Committee for the 1996 Pacific Schools Games to be held in Perth. I am also the meet organsiser for the NSW All Schools Championships, an event with over 3,000 competitors held over three days, and help organise the NSW State Open Championships (the equivalent of a county championships). All up, a pretty busy schedule. We have a small full time staff in our office of an Executive Director, a Media Liaison Officer, an Accounts Manager, an Admin. Assistant and myself, so its all hands to the pumps much of the time. Still, I guess this set-up would still make some county organisations jealous! I've only really touched on the highlights of what I do on an annual basis. There is the usual round of school coaching visits and athlete camps on top of this. One school I coached at this year was in Broken Hill, a mining town 11 hours drive out of Sydney, so that gives you some idea of the area I have to cover! On a personal note, I feel that Australia's potential is yet to be fulfilled, and I am certain that you will see more of our athletes kicking European butt around the tracks in years to come; and not just in the junior ranks, which we are already doing! News of old Belgravians in and around Sydney: a small community seems to have grown up here. About five minutes drive from me Wayne Larden has set up home with his wife and baby. Wayne is a regular visitor to Belgrave Hall each winter as he passes through to compete at the World Cross Country Champs. Andy Lloyd, an ex-Belgravian and ex-Commonwealth Games 10,000m Champion lives on the other side of town, providing the team boat when the boys want to go out fishing on Sydney harbour! Ron Wyld too has found his way over here and lives a few kilometres north of me. I bumped into Ron a while back in the NSW Academy of Sport weights room, puffing and blowing on a rowing machine whilst Steve Smith and Brendan Reilly stood there laughing at him. (The boys were over here training at the time of writing.) Brandon Reid, former British League 1500m rep. and Surrey County bronze medallist also pays visits to Sydney, mainly to be out-drunk and out-run by Wayne and Co.! items.label: February 1997
items.sum: Editorial on Tilda Rice extending its sponsorship for a year at a reduced level and the need for the club to cut spending.
items.s: Tighten your belts Editorial on Tilda Rice extending its sponsorship for a year at a reduced level and the need for the club to cut spending. We are pleased to report that Tilda Rice have agreed to extend their sponsorship of Belgrave Harriers for a further 12 months although we are sorry that their deal with Du'aine Ladejo has now run it's course. The main reason for Tilda's continued support of the Club is their recognition of the enormous efforts we have made in taking athletics to young people and the schools and encouraging them to become involved in our beloved sport. Sadly the extension is only for one year and furthermore Sportsmatch, who initially matched Tilda's sponsorship pound for pound, have now reduced their support to only 25%. Basically, therefore, we have £12,500 to continue our Youth Scheme into 1997. It might seem like quite a tidy sum but when you consider that this summer we may well make the National Young Athletes Final, involving the transportation of around 80 young athletes to Birmingham, we have a Women's Southern League match in Newquay which may again result in a large group of youngsters staying away from home overnight, and we have some fifteen away matches in various leagues which will require coach travel at around £250 per time, you can see that it is not going to go very far. Our crusade to carry athletics into the local schools week in week out will also take its toll but we are committed to doing this otherwise we will not earn even the aforementioned sponsorship. All this at a time when our subscriptions seem to be slower and slower in coming forth and the total received doesn't come anywhere near covering the cost of the normal activities that any athletic club is involved with. Additionally we have the ongoing cost of maintaining our Club Headquarters. Our financial wizards meet regularly to keep an eye on our affairs and at their most recent gathering went through the budgets for each section of our club with a fine tooth comb. It became quite obvious that if we don't come up with something soon then some cuts are going to have to be made - deep cuts which will probably affect every activity covered by Belgrave Harriers. So, the message is that we are all going to have to reduce our spending. Everyone will have to chip in more generously when it comes to collecting fares on coaches and mini-buses. Club kit needs to be paid for up front. Every effort must be made to reduce our spending in every area and even this very magazine may have to take on some other form. We are going to have to tighten our belts. Du'aine Ladejo Du'aine Ladejo his sponsorship deal with Tilda had ended National Young Athletes League Women's Southern League Birmingham Newquay Belgrave Harriers

items.label: February 1997
items.sum: Tribute to Leo Coy, nearly thirty years a runner, team manager, helper and 1988-89 Club President, who is moving back to Ireland (County Wexford).
items.s: Words are not enough Tribute to Leo Coy, nearly thirty years a runner, team manager, helper and 1988-89 Club President, who is moving back to Ireland (County Wexford). For nearly thirty years Leo Coy has been at the heart of our affairs, first as a runner and then as a team manager as we made our way up the ladders of both British and Young Athletes Leagues. Every Belgrave social gathering - from camping expeditions in the New Forest to Club Dinners has benefited from his presence. It hasn't all been just fair-weather support either. In the depths of winter young lads have been collected from all points of South London and driven to training and competition venues for cross country and road running; he has stood at the trackside all year round supervising warm-up drills, timing repetitions and coaching high-jump. He has been involved in everything we have done during three decades and of course became our Club President for 1988-89. Great success has come our way, due in no small part to Leo's efforts but he has admitted that all the hard work has been repaid by seeing our young athletes take their first competitive steps as eleven and twelve year-olds in the Thameside competitions - and finally gain selection for the British League team. All things must pass, however. Gradually over the last year Leo has been easing his way out of his club responsibilities, paving the way for a planned move back to his native Ireland. At first we didn't really believe he would carry it through but we should have known better. By Springtime Leo will have taken up residence in County Wexford and no more will we be able to rely on his efforts as a matter of course. He assures us that he will continue to make his way to Club functions and that we will see him cheering on our teams at venues around the country. We look forward to those occasions Leo but in the meantime we wish you every happiness in your new home - and mere words, written or spoken, cannot thank you enough for all you have done. Leo Coy Leo Coy runner then team manager for nearly thirty years; Club President 1988-89; moving to County Wexford, Ireland, in spring 1997 Leo Coy Leo British Athletics League Young Athletes League Thameside League New Forest South London Ireland County Wexford

items.sum: Notice of Bill Lucas's 80th birthday and 61 years' service to the club, with a celebration planned for 19 April at Belgrave Hall.
items.s: A celebration of service Notice of Bill Lucas's 80th birthday and 61 years' service to the club, with a celebration planned for 19 April at Belgrave Hall. Not only did Bill Lucas reach his 80th birthday a short while back but he's just completed 61 years of dedicated service to Belgrave Harriers. As fit as ever, thanks to his passion for golf, Bill's commitment to the Club is ongoing. It's almost unknown for him to miss a Committee Meeting, he is always on hand for our Finance Meetings and of course he always has a viewpoint on all our club matters. We don't intend to let a couple of anniversaries like these slip past without something special so a celebration is being planned for April 19th at Belgrave Hall. Contact Gordon Biscoe ([phone number withheld]) or Charlie Manning ([phone number withheld]) to find out more. items.h: Ridgeon heads '97 Club 800m rankings after "Fun Run"
items.sum: Light-hearted report of a BMC 800m 'fun run' for 400m men at Battersea Park on 18 January, where Jon Ridgeon was first Belgrave home in 1:54.7.
items.s: Ridgeon heads '97 Club 800m rankings after "Fun Run" Light-hearted report of a BMC 800m 'fun run' for 400m men at Battersea Park on 18 January, where Jon Ridgeon was first Belgrave home in 1:54.7. The 'race' had been talked about for months - an 800 metres - just for fun - featuring some of the top 400 boys. Roger Black might be tops over one lap - but who could hold it together best for TWO laps of the track? Eventually a date and place were set - Saturday 18th January at Battersea Park. Matthew Fraser-Moat of the BMC promoted the event and in turn asked Belgrave to provide the officials. Unfortunately 'Bamby' Black was having a course of knee treatment so it was left to Mark Richardson, Vince Rose and Jon Ridgeon to take on the challenge. Jon's coach Mike Whittingham turned out to watch the fun as did Peter and Mrs. Coe, while Frank Horwill was busy on the mike keeping everyone informed about recent form and best times. The weather was mild, the track was damp and the sun even broke through the January clouds for a few minutes. With nerves jangling the sprinters lined up to race the only two genuine middle-distance men in Thompson of Dartford (best of 1:50.1) and Clive Gilby (1:47.33). Snowy Brooks fired the starter's pistol and they were away. The pacemaker was aiming for times of 27, 54 and 82 and although bell time was just about right - 54.7 - the initial rush had been a bit ferocious so it was going to be a hard run for the sprinters. As it turned out the specialists had the race to themselves. The Valley's Vince Rose seemed to have 3rd sewn up until a tremendous dash down the straight topped off with a real sprint hurdler's dip saw Ridgeon just snatch the 'real race' on the line. With Richardson also under the qualifying time the BMC suddenly found itself with three new members. Seriously though, put him in the right race in early track season and that nice Mr. Ridgeon might just nip under 1:50. items.sum: Extracts from The Belgravian of 25 years ago (1971/72: Laurie O'Hara's club 5,000m and 10,000m titles, the seventh successive Surrey League title, John Moullin's 100 miles) and 50 years ago (1946/47: issue No. 100, the first post-war winter, the South of Thames Junior race won by W. items.s: From The Belgravian Extracts from The Belgravian of 25 years ago (1971/72: Laurie O'Hara's club 5,000m and 10,000m titles, the seventh successive Surrey League title, John Moullin's 100 miles) and 50 years ago (1946/47: issue No. 100, the first post-war winter, the South of Thames Junior race won by W. Lucas). 25 Years Ago ... 1971/72 LAURIE O'HARA has been in great form lately, and he skated away with our 5,000m championship in the fastish time of 15m 51.8s. Gerry North had to draw on his well-known ability to hold off Guy Monnet for second place ... Guy in turn had to show his sprinting powers to hold off the defending champion, Lionel Mann. Laurie ... was an easy winner of the 10,000m championship - adding the Tom Carter Trophy to the Griffen Cup. Last year's winner Lionel Mann was his closest challenger, but headed Adrian Major by only a few yards. SURREY CC LEAGUE Division One. So, Belgrave took their 7th successive league title by clinching the final race at Petersham on February 19th. But an ominous cloud has appeared on the horizon in the form of the young Aldershot, Farnham & District contingent. This was their first year in Division 1 and they showed flashes of brilliance, particularly in the second race, which indicated that Belgrave will have to be on their toes next season if they want to make it eight in a row. 1, Belgrave H (168, 252, 276, 235) 931pts; 2, Aldershot, Farnham & Dist. (394, 173, 244, 284) 1095pts; 3, Hercules Wimbledon (292, 414, 242, 494) 1442pts. [Editors' note: in fact this proved to be the last time that Belgrave were Division One Champions.] JOHN MOULLIN joined the ranks of the Centurions in a most spectacular fashion. With a truly magnificent display of fast, controlled walking, he finished first in the [Surrey W.C.'s Open 100 miles] race, with a remarkable time of 16hrs. 55m. 44s., only 1m. 29s. outside Frank O'Reilly's world best performance for 100 miles. ... A search through the Centurions' roll of honour shows that no one has entered their ranks with such a high class performance. To get inside 17hrs. at one's first attempt at the distance is indeed an unique achievement which makes John Moullin one of our top ultra-long-distance walkers. and, 50 Years Ago ... 1946/47 NUMBER 100. We are all rather inclined to accept an issue of The Belgravian when it arrives as something that just "happened," and seldom do we think of the hours of preparation that go into each issue, or the care and attention which somebody must devote to every sentence on every page before it passes into print. This issue of The Belgravian is No. 100, and an appropriate moment for wishing ourselves an ever-increasing measure of success for record in the next hundred issues ... WE ARE NOW at the end of what can be termed the first post-war winter season. From the afternoon of the season's opening meeting at Belgrave Hall the atmosphere was set: time seemed to have slipped back and the years of the war became, in many minds, non-existent. As one who "arrived back" that afternoon, not having been near Belgrave Hall since 1940, it was a startling joy to see again so many well-remembered faces and to be greeted with such a warmth of welcome. Many things have changed these past seven years and this club has lost some of its dearest and best members, but we are still a club with enthusiasm and unity about us. SOUTH OF THAMES "JUNIOR" RACE. Held at Nonsuch Park, Cheam on November 9th, a field of 209 runners, representing 29 teams, fought out a closely-contested race over a two-lap course. As winners of the race last season we thus had to find a new scoring team, and our hopes received a set-back when Vic Blowfield failed to arrive in time. However, at the half-way stage in the race, Bill Lucas and Len Marchant were in the leading bunch of four runners, which was a good start-off to our team's chances. When they came in sight of the finish Bill Lucas was clear away in front and in 2nd position came Len Marchant, a fine performance by both runners. 1, W.Lucas 26:55; 2, L.Marchant 27:03; 15, S.Jarlett 27:55; 23, L.Bishop 28:16. items.s: A message from The President New President Ted Pallant thanks members for his election and retiring President Snowy Brooks, and appeals for volunteers; printed beside an uncaptioned photo of a man holding a trophy. May I express my sincere thanks to everyone for my election as President. I am very proud of this honour and feel sure that we can look forward to another successful year. On your behalf I would also like to say thank you to the retiring President Snowy Brooks. During his year of office he worked untiringly, setting a fine example in the true Belgravian tradition. It was a year to remember, Snowy, and I know you are now looking forward to competing once again in the World Veterans Decathlon Championships in 1997. We all wish you every success. Looking ahead, the hope is to see us consolidating on the fine progress made in recent years. Much work has still to be carrried out and we must be prepared to adapt to changes in the sport if we are to stay at the top level. Fortunately we have a fine band of Officers and Coaches of high standards. They have been prepared to give their time and experience throughout the years but more help is always needed. With the ever-increasing workload of a club the size of ours, volunteers will always be welcome. Club Team Managers will also appreciate your support when it comes to turning out our strongest teams in competition. This makes all the difference between just losing a championship and winning. Finally I would like to thank all members in the Club who have made my membership of nearly 40 years such a happy time. I look back with pleasure on the friendships formed and hope that the future will bring many more. Best wishes, Ted Pallant Ted Pallant Ted Pallant newly elected President; member for nearly 40 years Snowy Brooks Snowy Brooks retiring President; to compete in World Veterans Decathlon Championships 1997 Snowy Brooks Snowy World Veterans Championships

items.h: Ted Pallant: President of Belgrave Harriers 1996-1997
items.sum: Profile of new President Ted Pallant: member since 1957, childhood in Battersea, wartime evacuation to Reading, national service, taxi business, club dinners, committee and kit work, and SEAA links with African athletics.
items.s: Ted Pallant: President of Belgrave Harriers 1996-1997 Profile of new President Ted Pallant: member since 1957, childhood in Battersea, wartime evacuation to Reading, national service, taxi business, club dinners, committee and kit work, and SEAA links with African athletics. "A real surprise, I was delighted". This was Ted Pallant's reaction to being nominated as this year's President. It was less of a surprise to many in the club who knew Ted to be experienced, courteous, wise and mature, all qualities of a good President. An active member since 1957 both as an ordinary club runner and a member of the committee, he is perhaps best know by the younger members as the person who sells the club kit. Few Belgrave members over the last five years will not have been approached by Ted and politely asked if they need a vest or a new tracksuit. This has put Ted in touch with all sections of the club and given him an overview few can match. Born at St George's Hospital, Hyde Park in 1929, Ted spent his childhood in Battersea, living in Warriner Gardens just a stone's throw from the park. The park became Ted's playground, almost a second home, and the track was to influence him to the present day. At that time, of course, the Battersea track was cinders and three laps to the mile. The 100 yards was run parallel to the power station with taped lanes, and the long jump pit was where the tennis courts are today. Ted first competed there at the age of eight representing his Primary school, Ethelburger, in the Battersea school sports. He remembers digging his starting blocks with a trowel. The church also played an important part in Ted's childhood. His family attended St Mary le Park Church near Albert Bridge. There were social activities, the youth club, dances, the cubs and later scouts. Ted made many friends and was to remain in the scout movement as a rover scout until the age of 28. The war came when Ted was ten. He was evacuated from Clapham Junction station on September 3rd 1939 and war was declared while he was on the train to Reading. Strangely, it was here that Ted was to find another connection with athletics and another important influence. He was billeted with the family of the British long jump champion, W.E.N. Breach, who had competed in an international with Germany just a week before war broke out. Later, Breach was to become President of Reading AC. Ted returned to London after only a few months and spent the war years living in Balham. He became a patrol leader in the scouts, and had a memorable time in the blitz helping out in hospitals, and erecting Anderson shelters for old people. He attended Battersea Central School till the age of 14 when he left to become an apprentice electrician to a firm in Chelsea. He remembers earning 4¾d per hour! He qualified the hard way, by attending night school, and later gained a place at Battersea Polytechnic, now Westminster College. Ted remembers the war being a very grey time, with rationing, bombing worries and no men around between the ages of 18 and 40. But on the other hand, people were thrown together: they helped each other, there was less materialism, they talked, played cards, they had to make their own entertainment, there was no television. After the war, now in his late teens, Ted's social life continued to revolve around the church with dances and scout activities. In 1947 he began his two year's national service in the army, joining the Royal West Kent Infantry for his initial two months training. Then, typical of the army, as a trained electical engineer Ted was assigned to the medical corp, spending 20 weeks being trained at the army school of tropical medicine. He played football and cricket in the army and even boxed. For his last six months while stationed at Mytchett, Ash Vale, he met up with Arthur Bruce and Jock Rutherford the Scottish international footballer and did a great deal of running. Ted and Arthur used to travel back to Battersea together on leave. Ted came out of the army in 1949 and rejoined the same electrical firm for a short time but soon decided to "do the knowledge" and join his father in the taxi business. He continued to play football and cricket and trained in Battersea Park. When he moved to Ursula Street he lived next door but one to Dennis Jones and his father Bill Jones. They were two life long Belgrave members, and it was they who persuaded Ted to join the club in February 1957. All through the fifties and sixties Ted was very much part of the club athletics scene competing on the road, country and track. Never one of the stars, nevertheless, Ted enjoyed his athletics particularly the pack runs from Belgrave Hall with the likes of Gerry North, and battles with Charlie Henn in the "5¾". He also got involved with the social life of the club, became Social Secretary and organising the club dinner for five years in the late 'fifties and early 'sixties. They used to be held at the Dog & Fox in Wimbledon. In fact Ted has only missed two club dinners in the whole time he has been a member. He served on the committee undertaking various roles until 1965. After moving to Woking in the late 60's, life became rather hard for Ted, running his own taxi business and bringing up his two sons. But over the years he never lost touch and has been able to slowly give more time to the club again. Today, although he has bouts of ill health and is troubled by arthritis, he still manages to do ten minutes exercise each day and keep fit by swimming. Ted does not like to dwell on life's problems, we all have them, but he feels belonging to Belgrave over the years has kept him active both mentally and physically and has helped him through the difficult times. Since retiring in 1990, Ted has returned wholeheartedly to committee work managing to find time to chair the Membership Services committee as well as organise the club kit. He has also served on the SEAA committee and after travelling to Africa managed to help forge links with several African Athletic organisations such as the Gambian A.A.A. and the Soweto A.A.A. This has involved organising competitive trips and receptions for visiting clubs from these countries. So Ted comes to the Presidency with a wider perspective than most. Having never been a top athlete or a sectional secretary he has no axe to grind and would very much like to use his influence to spread harmony throughout the club. He recognises that clubs such as Belgrave have to change with the times and people have to accept that, and not harp back to the good old days. At the same time he feels it is vital that the club retains the sportsmanlike spirit of the past. September 21st 1963 and Ted strides out in the Polytechnic Road Relay at Chiswick. items.s: Photo of Derek Clack and Sue after their 920-mile John O'Groats to Lands End walk, which raised £1000 for the Tadworth Children's Trust. For years Derek Clack has said that in all the time he's been in the club he's not yet had his picture published. Sorry Derek - it's a case of too few photographers required to be in too many places at the right time. However, The Wimbledon Guardian seems to be a little better off in the way of human resource and sent their photographer to snap Derek and Sue after their gruelling hike from John O'Groats to Lands End. The 920 mile walk took our intrepid couple seven weeks but it was well worth it for they raised £1000 for the Tadworth Children's Trust. They got lost for a while at Loch Ness and nearly went over a cliff, got stranded out on the West Highland Way as night fell, suffered from blisters ... makes those training reps up Wool Road seem like a piece of cake! items.sum: Club news notes (Sidetracks and More Sidetracks): the World Junior Championships, the Cinque Ports Triathlon, helpers, members' health (Derek Jones, Gwen Couzens, Kassa Tadesse, Dave McMillan), a lecture, the Darts Championship, Gordon Doubleday, the Youth in Action award, social events, 1889 newspaper finds and George Piddington's South Coast Marathon.
items.s: Sidetracks Club news notes (Sidetracks and More Sidetracks): the World Junior Championships, the Cinque Ports Triathlon, helpers, members' health (Derek Jones, Gwen Couzens, Kassa Tadesse, Dave McMillan), a lecture, the Darts Championship, Gordon Doubleday, the Youth in Action award, social events, 1889 newspaper finds and George Piddington's South Coast Marathon. Clive Shippen saw Ernest Obeng amongst the TV crews at the World Junior Championships in Sydney but couldn't get close enough to speak with him. And of course Sir Eddie Kulukundis was a fixture to his seat throughout the Championships. Clive did manage to chat to Mark Shearman a couple of times and mentioned that we'd like a copy of a photo of Tom for The Belgravian. (See front page.) Young Belgravians tried something a little different on June 16th in the Cinque Ports Triathlon. Alice Ragouzaridis competed in the under 10 event - Swim 100m, Bike 2000m, Run 800m and was a clear winner from a field of 17 boys and girls in 15:17. Paul Graham went in the under 12s where the distances were 150/3000m/1200m. He was way down after the first couple of disciplines, racing his old bike against some hot machines but ripped through the 32 strong field in the 800 metre run before running out of track to finish 9th in 23:19. 15th was Brendon Jackson 24:33. Competing in the under 14 age group but actually just 12 years old, Aaron Jackson placed 25th out of 36 in his 200m/6000m/2000m event. Winn Shepherd writes to let us know how grateful she is to Snowy Brooks, Ray James and Ray Wilson for their assistance in helping her on and off the coaches taking our teams to their away fixtures and to Sue and Harry Porter, Jackie Stone, Gail Porter and Pat and Alan Mead for their help in providing transport - and of course Jean Hutcherson her main support. It's a pleasure Winn, and while we are at it, many thanks to you for your continued support and help in the running of our home matches. We hear from Derek Jones that it is extremely likely that he will have to undergo a spell in hospital followed by some extensive convalescence before too long. Derek had lined himself up to be Field Event Referee for many of our forthcoming home fixtures but in typical Belgrave spirit he says, " ... well I won't be able to do that but I will be able to do the announcing from the caravan ..." Well Derek, if you say so and promise not to overdo it. In the meantime all Belgravians will want to wish him well and a swift return to good health. We also understand that Gwen Couzens is undergoing a prolonged course of medical treatment at the moment. Gwen, we are all thinking of you and look forward to seeing you back in the pink again. Kassa Tadesse has been sorely missed this winter by our cross country team. After a period of knee and foot trouble he got back to some great road running in the Autumn only for his trouble to flare up again. Latest news is that he is back in training, looking for races and gearing himself for a return to top class running. More sidetracks More Sidetracks An interesting lecture was held at Belgrave Hall back in October. The subject was "Over use in the Adolescent" and the speaker Debbie Annett, who runs a local sports injury therapy service. It was a most interesting subject and we were reminded that young athletes are not mini adults and that there are many, many things to bear in mind when planning sports training for youngsters. It was a pity that more of our coaches could not attend, while coaches from other clubs were totally absent. Perhaps we can repeat the exercise some time. The thirty-fourth Belgrave Darts Championship was held as normal on the first Saturday evening in December. Again, as normal, Bill Couzens won it. That makes it the last five times in a row to go with the first three times the event was held in 1963-65 plus '69, '71 and '76. One thing that wasn't normal though, we had an all-girl semi-final and Gail Porter was playing with such assurance throughout the competition that it did seem possible that we might see our first ever female champion. But Bill is cool under pressure and he was ever in charge. Always looked forward to is a letter from our Past President Gordon Doubleday. Gordon tells us that he is keeping fairly fit although cutting back a little on his commitments. He helped timekeep at the Chippenham to Calne Walk and also helped at a Sprint Triathlon earlier in the year. Among social functions he has attended was the Club Dinner of his local athletic club, Somer AC. It was held at the Centurion Hotel, an apt venue for someone who during his athletic career earned himself the coveted Centurion Badge. Our Youth in Action Scheme has been applauded by Mr. Iain Sproat, MP, the Minister for Sport, Department of National Heritage. At a special awards ceremony held in 1996 where schemes from all across the Nation were taken into consideration, we were only beaten into second place by a very grandiose scheme being run by Warwickshire County Cricket Club. Well done to everyone involved in running this scheme. The New Orleans Jazz Night at the Hall in December was a great success as was the Burns Night Supper on 25th January. At the latter event we were again entertained by the Scottish Folk duo known as Ptarmigan, and with a piper, a kilted Lionel Mann overseeing cooking of the Haggis and MC-ing the evening plus some entertainment from our own members a great night was had by all. Eric Hall was at the British Museum Newspaper library some while back, and delving into the "Sporting Clipper" for May 11th 1889 noted that at the Polytechnic H & CC Meeting on 4th May 1889 at Paddington Recreation Ground - J. Gilbert of Belgrave Harriers was third in a mile handicap from a field of 138 out of 165 entries. What a nightmare for the track judges that must have been. A report in the same paper but dated 9th November 1889 on a meeting held seven days earlier at Tufnell Park by Spartan Harriers mentions that the four mile junior inter-club race was won by Beaumont H with Falcon H 2nd and Belgrave H 3rd. The newspaper mentions that athletic clubs were springing up all over the country. Eric notes that some sprung and stayed while others faded or merged. Of the early names mentioned he recognised Poly, SLH, London AC, Finchley and Blackheath but even he is too young to remember Reindeer, Beaumont or Falcon! The determined Dave McMillan continues to slowly improve after his awful accident early in 1996 when he was hit by a car while out training for the London Marathon. He has had great set-backs but is now out of his wheelchair, he attended the Club Dinner in November, and on New Year's Eve threw away his crutches. Dave continues to have severe problems with his arm and is full of pieces of metal holding him together but don't rule out seeing him in the Yacht '3' again one day - even if he has to strap his arm to his chest! Tough guys these marathon runners. George Piddington is now living in his own flat down in Hampshire and his local club Havant AC are planning something special for him. George never did do his 50 marathons but Havant are planning to push him in his wheelchair on Sunday 27th April 1997 in the South Coast Marathon at Gosport. Are there any of George's old Belgrave mates who would like to take part and help George to another marathon? If so contact Peter Spencer, telephone [phone number withheld]. Incidentally, as a coach at Havant for many years now, George must have been delighted when his team won the Southern Women's Cross Country Champs at Parliament Hill. items.sum: Obituaries of long-standing members Bill Merryman, Fred Denny, A.H. (Ben) Knifton and Lovell Cole.
items.s: Farewell to old comrades Obituaries of long-standing members Bill Merryman, Fred Denny, A.H. (Ben) Knifton and Lovell Cole. We are sorry to learn of the deaths of several of our very long standing members. Each in his own way made a valuable contribution to the Club. We will remember them for their sportsmanship and companionship and will mourn their passing. Bill Merryman was born in 1916 and joined us in October 1931 as a runner. For years he trained at Wimbledon and Battersea Park. He loved taking part in "mob" matches where everyone counted. When the days came for Club Championships and Track Matches he would turn up as an ardent supporter. When World War 2 (1939-45) came he was able to continue his running with the R.A.F. Always ready to lend a hand he helped at Track Meetings, particularly the Field Events, a job he continued to do long after his active running days were over. His enthusiasm for the Club was carried over to the social side and he was a regular attender at these functions. In recognition for what he did for the Club he was elected President for 1979/80. He eventually left London to live at Newhaven (Sussex) but his interest in the Club and its fortunes never faded. Fred Denny was born in 1930 and joined us in 1955. A powerfully built policeman he turned out regularly in Club and Open walks and, of course, for the "boys in blue" in their Championships and matches. A keen student of the mechanics of race-walking he took up judging after ceasing to be active. His prowess in this field saw him rise to the grade of Chief Judge. In addition to showing the Red Card (dq.) he would have a chat with the "offender" telling him/her of the fault in their style and how to correct it. He was elected President of the R.W.A. in 1993/4 and during his term he made an appeal for funds to assist the development of young walkers. He recently had a heart attack from which he was recovering when he took a holiday abroad. On the journey home he had another attack which proved fatal. Sadly we also recently received the news of the death of A.H. ("Ben") Knifton. His is a name few will remember and few current members will have known him in spite of the fact that he had been a Belgravian for seventy-one years and was a Vice-President of the Club. Born in 1907 he joined us in 1925; he was a strong and steady walker. During his career there was only one National Senior Championship, the 20 miles, and in 1929 at Hayes (Kent) he scored in our winning team. As part of his training he would often do an all day stroll in the country at week-ends. This gave him good leg strength and stamina, which, combined with speed work with Club "packs" made him a formidable competitor. Some may remember his son, John, who walked for us and emigrated to the U.S.A.where he reached the top ranks of walkers there. Several years ago Ben left the country to live at the sunny Algarve (Portugal). Knowing him he probably found some grand walks in that area. Lovell Cole has also passed on. He was 85 and in his 58th year of membership. So we say "farewell" to these stalwarts and think of their friendship and of the parts they played in the life and fortunes of the Club. items.s: Youth in Action 96 Report of the Youth In Action Presentation Evening at the Polka Theatre, Wimbledon, on 6 December 1996, with the list of awards. THE BELGRAVE Youth In Action Presentation Evening on December 6th was a highly successful affair. Last year it was held at Belgrave Hall but our HQ was bursting at the seams as we tried to squeeze getting on for 200 people into our function room. This time we tried something different having been offered the use of The Polka Theatre at the end of Wimbledon Broadway. It was just the job. Many of our young athletes and their parents came along and we welcomed special guests in the personages of Sir Eddie Kulukundis OBE (our Club Patron), John Hadley (Representative of The Sports Council), Mike Da Silva (Chairman of the National Young Athletes League) and of course our Club President Ted Pallant. A glittering array of bronze, silver and gold-ware was handed over to our young athletes, together with certificates and trophies ... so many that one had to keep reminding one's-self of the incredibly high standards at which these youngsters compete: 15 year-old 2 metre high-jumpers, 58 metre hammer throwers, 10.62 sprinters, 14 year-old 6.42m long jumpers ... it just went on and on. Having exceeded our four year targets in half that time one wonders just where it will end. Our Junior Men have been promoted to Division One, our Young Athletes placed 3rd in their Premier Division and went to the National Finals ... the only area where we have not achieved unqualified success is in being unable to break into the Girls' National YA League. Here, with YA matches scheduled for the day after Southern Women's Leagues, where events are also included for youngsters, we were unable to turn out more than half a dozen at a time - in matches where we really need about fifty athletes. Well done John Powell for organising the evening. items.label: February 1997
items.sum: Eric Hall's account of a trip to Australia: Sydney 2000 Olympic facilities, Belgrave expatriates, and the 40th anniversary of the 1956 Melbourne Olympics.
items.s: Bels down under ... Eric Hall's account of a trip to Australia: Sydney 2000 Olympic facilities, Belgrave expatriates, and the 40th anniversary of the 1956 Melbourne Olympics. Our roving reporter Eric Hall checks out the facilities for Sydney 2000, meets up with a few expatriates ... and relives Melbourne '56 Recent issues of "The Belgravian" have made mention of the Belgrave interests in Australia and with the run up to the Sydney Olympics, only three years and a bit away, more will occur. It was with this in mind that this reporter snatched at the Editor's invitation to go out to see for himself just what was happening! No expense spared I was told and so Mavis came as navigator, interpreter and general factotum. The starting point was Sydney and we were soon made aware of the importance of the year 2000 to the residents. Only one told us that they planned to exit the city for September when the Games are to be held! The reason was that accommodation will be at a premium and air flights out of Australia very cheap at that time so this young lady was all for making a killing. Everyone else seemed besotted by sport and determined to show the world just what could be done with an Olympic Games. We toured the facilities available at the moment and saw the hole in the ground which is to be the main stadium. As ever there is talk of the building unions applying pressure to the organisers in order to hike their wages! The Aquatic Centre, as with all facilities we saw during our trip, is very impressive - larger than ever and with plenty of training facilities alongside. Within the precincts of the Homebush area we watched a road walk in progress but were unable to get to chat with the officials. On our final day in the city we were entertained by Clive and Elizabeth Shippen. Not wishing to be overlooked in the crowd, and it being a blustery day, I wore a Belgrave sweater and Clive responded by the rather more essential Belgrave cap. (By the way Ted, Clive is still waiting for the three he ordered months ago!) A tour of the beaches north of Sydney and the NSW track and training area, was followed by an inspection of the Shippen's new abode. Just one word of warning for anyone challenged to a spin by Clive - make sure it is on the flat as his drive rises at 45 degrees from the road and I am sure he intends to use it for interval training! They both wish to be remembered to everyone in the Club and I know Clive would relish the Surrey Cross Country performance over his old home course of Coulsdon. First individual and team prize is a real tonic to everyone. We moved on to Canberra and I aired my Club kit on the Institute of Sport track. Whether it was my style, speed or elegance that caused the assembled group of budding internationals to stop and stare I don't know but I was delighted to hear a shout of "Come on Belgrave". Canberra has everything needed by an ambitious athlete. We were left wondering why Australia doesn't win all the gold medals? Belgrave Station, just outside Melbourne, has featured in this magazine before but we couldn't resist the photo opportunity by draping the club vest across the station bench - quite what the Japanese tourists made of it we don't know - especially as it was raining at the time. We then boarded the Puffing Billy steam train for a beautiful ride through the countryside at a speed much the same as that I used to manage up Copse Hill - I probably did rather more puffing! Melbourne will always have a special place in my heart and yet again - after 40 years - it turned up trumps. Apart from the Editor's kind invitation to tour Australia the motive behind our visit was to attend the 40th anniversary celebrations of the Olympic Games of 1956. This included a tour of the Village at Heidelberg and a dinner, attended by over a thousand, across the road from the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG). We were prevented from using the MCG as it was needed for a concert by an M. Jackson. We met many old sparring partners, Ray Smith, Ron Crawford and Noel Freeman to say nothing of chatting late into the night with John Landy, Merv Lincoln and Ron Clark. We finally got away about 1.45 am and wandered along the Yarra to find a taxi back to the hotel. A very emotional evening finished up by the taxi driver announcing that a countryman of his had won a gold medal in 1956 - who else but the late Norman Read who had been so much in our minds during our stay. A few days on the road, amid outstanding scenery, found us in Adelaide where we stayed with Terry Clark - Belgrave's national junior champion in 1958. Again he passes his regards to all who remember him. He made sure we had access to all manner of sporting venues and people responsible for spotting talent and developing it whether it be cricket, athletics, cycling or hockey. All were enthusiasts and took time off from whatever they were doing to explain the Australian system and philosophy to us. Somewhere along the line we had time to surf the Internet, with Terry's aid, and found a list of Olympic medallists. Browsing through this we came up with a real Belgrave surprise. It seems that the bronze medal in the 1960 20km walk was won by a Stanley F Vickers (no problem with that) but the nationality given was Germany! No wonder conversation was always a problem! Our final evening was spent at an Italian restaurant where the proprietor collects autographed photographs of his sporting clients. My publicity managers not only found an old photograph of yours truly but I was prevailed upon (in an inebriated state) to sign it and when last seen it was being placed on the wall by the side of one signed by a Donald Bradman but I am not sure what event he was in! items.sum: Note that 263 club records were equalled or beaten in the 14 months to 1 December 1996, with younger age-group walking records reprinted on pages 46-47.
items.s: 263 Club Records Note that 263 club records were equalled or beaten in the 14 months to 1 December 1996, with younger age-group walking records reprinted on pages 46-47. Two issues ago you were no doubt astounded to read that 115 Club Records had been broken during the nine months up to September 30th 1995. Well, your statisticians have recently fought their way from beneath a mountain of result sheets and have now come up with the even more startling news that since that date and up to the time of writing at December 1st 1996, a period of 14 months, no fewer than 263 Club Records have been equalled or beaten. Takes some believing doesn't it! We had promised to publish a list in the Belgravian showing each advance in our best ever marks - but quite honestly we just cannot do so - it would take five full pages of this magazine. We do, however, present a reprint of our younger age group walking records, almost totally rewritten during the last year. These can be found on pages 46-47.

items.sum: Death of Barry Jones, General Hon. Secretary of Hercules Wimbledon A.C. and a familiar timekeeper in South London.
items.s: "HW's" Barry Jones passes away Death of Barry Jones, General Hon. Secretary of Hercules Wimbledon A.C. and a familiar timekeeper in South London. We were very sorry to learn that Hercules Wimbledon A.C.'s General Hon. Secretary Barry Jones had died suddenly in January. Barry gave a great deal of his life to the sport of athletics and didn't just confine his efforts to his club. If there was an athletic meeting being promoted virtually anywhere in South London, Barry was sure to be found on the time-keepers' stand and athletics in Surrey will be very much the poorer for his passing. Our commiserations go to our friends at "HW". Barry Jones Barry Jones General Hon. items.h: Belgravians help improve National Walking Standards
items.sum: Race Walking Secretary Stephen Whorlow's review of the club's walking section in 1996, with a boxed list of N.U.T.S. track and road rankings.
items.s: Belgravians help improve National Walking Standards Race Walking Secretary Stephen Whorlow's review of the club's walking section in 1996, with a boxed list of N.U.T.S. track and road rankings. Race Walking The Race Walking scene in our Club is taking us up the rankings and we are now one of the Nation's Top Clubs in the Young Athletes sections with many successes coming our way. We are still missing out in the Senior's age group with only one of our walkers filling that gap but our Veterans are still reasonably strong and active. With luck this Senior gap will be filled within the next three or four years by our up and coming youngsters. The problem has been that it is almost impossible to introduce new blood into an age group (Seniors) that has hardly any representation. But with the growth of Race Walking again nationally, especially in the Junior sections, we shall hopefully overcome this problem. The Junior numbers are growing and this was noticed at the AAA Championships in Birmingham this year when there had to be a dual start in two of the events to enable the races to be accomodated on the track. Race Walking had some of the largest individual entries in these Championships and the RWA Road Championships held in Folkestone had the highest number of entries for many years (and remember they were held in what used to be a barren area for Walking). This has done away with the old idea that Race Walking Medals are easily won. Not any more, they are hard fought for, and against some very good competition. Mabon Dane has been our only Senior and has flown the flag all round the country. This year he has represented the South and Essex whilst among the Juniors Andrew Goudie become a fully fledged Belgravian and gained our first full Junior England Vest for a long time, along with his Southern, Kent County and London Schools representative honours and being Ranked number three in his age group. New to Walking is Mick Graham, one of the Club's Cross Country and Road Running stalwarts. Mick is already knocking on the door of future Veteran Representation and he says that he finds the friendship around the country in the Walking scene very refreshing. So why not try the event, those in the Walking Section will make you most welcome! In the Under 17 section Nigel Whorlow has continued to progress through the rankings, finishing in the top 7 on both Track and Road in the Under 20 section. He, along with Laura Fryer gained their RWA "Young England " Vests, as well as SEAA, Kent County and Kent Schools Vests. Both were also 3rd. in their respective National Road Championships. The Under 13 Age Group brought us the surprise of the year in young Paul Graham who has taken to Walking as well as his Cross-Country and Middle Distance track competitions. He is ranked at the top of his age group. The Veterans have also had their say in the walking scene. Dave Sharpe competing well in the World Vets. Championships and for his County, also being the first walker to complete 100 races in the LPR Blackheath Handicap series. John Hall also represented his County (Middlesex) during the summer. Overall the Walking scene has brought back to the Club numerous Championship Medals and Trophies. The most prized of all was the presentation of the Sparta Trophy for being the most Improved Club overall in the country during 1995. (The trophy not being presented until May this year.) We won many County, Regional and National Championships and gained places on both Road and Track in all age groups, along with County and National Schools Championships, giving us three international representatives, an ESAA Champion, 5 SEAA and 6 County Champions). When you note the size of our small team you will realise that this has been a great effort within only two seasons of walking being re-introduced into these age groups in the Club. We have also, because of our youngsters' success and with help of our friends in Dartford Harriers, managed to get Race Walking re-introduced into the Schools County Championships. This in turn has helped get the event going in various schools around Kent, which can only be good for the sport and the Club in the long run (or Walk!). One of the nice surprises of the year was the receipt by our "Miniature Walking Dynamite" Lucy Asling, of a book from the USA in which she has been used as an example of the perfect walking style. Not bad to get International recognition at the age of nine. Lucy had finished the 1995/96 year having beaten all comers at 1km. (and most of the boys as well) on the Track and Road. The Young Athletes Grand Prix season was exceptionally long, with 11 events, but we still managed to get competitors to all the races, with two competing at every one. As can been seen elsewhere in this "Belgravian" we finished very high up most of the Age group sections and the Club finished one place higher overall (4th) than in 1995. Having taken on the re-introduced Club Race Walking Secretary's job I am finding the task something of a challenge, both on the financial side, and with the many other aspects of the job. My main aim will be to get the Walking Section well represented at all levels and make sure that everyone who wishes to compete can find the event that will suit them; then make sure that they can get to the venue to compete. Finally may I wish all our Walkers established and new, young and well trod, a prosperous and successful year, and let's see if we can get more Teams out during 1997. Stephen Whorlow In the N.U.T.S. 1996 Rankings the Race Walking Section of the Club has faired as well, if not better than many of the other Young and Junior Athletes Groups within the Club. Whilst some may say that there are not as many Race Walkers as there are competitors in other events, you still have to be above the N.U.T.S. Standard to figure in their Rankings, as in all events. We managed the following Track Track Rankings - Under 13 Girls (2,000m.) - Laura Fryer 2nd. Under 15 Girls (3,000m.) - Laura Fryer(U13) 10th. Under 17 Ladies (3,000m.) - Kelly-Anne Parker-Smith 4th. items.sum: Report and results of the RWA race walking relays at Chesterfield, where Belgrave's men's 'A' team took bronze despite penalty cards.
items.s: RWA Relays Chesterfield, 19 Oct 1996 Report and results of the RWA race walking relays at Chesterfield, where Belgrave's men's 'A' team took bronze despite penalty cards. Belgrave entered one female and two male teams in this event and had high hopes of bringing back the event silverware, but as the saying goes, "The best laid plans of Mice and Men etc." It did not work out as well as we hoped. Team selection let us down in the end and even though all were very competitive it was over excitement, as in many relay events, that let us down. There were too many Penalty Cards! In the Female 16km event we came eighth, with Laura Fryer (2km), Kelly-Anne Parker-Smith (6km), Victoria Parker-Smith (4km) and Sue Porter (6km) making up the team. The Male 22km. event gave us a little more success with Danny Bond (2km), Nigel Whorlow (4km), Mabon Dane (6km), Andrew Goudie (4km) and John Hall (6km) making up the 'A' Team. The team took the Bronze Medal, to add to their 1995 Silver but should have been the Relay Champions. As previously mentioned the Team gained far too many Penalty Cards which pushed us out of first place. items.label: February 1997
items.h: Bradford YA Grand Prix 9 Nov 1996: The Longest Day
items.sum: Report and Belgrave results from the Young Athletes race walking Grand Prix at Bradford on 9 November 1996, an 18-hour round trip; the report gives Sam McNalley's Under 13 win as 2km, the results line as 1km.
items.s: Bradford YA Grand Prix 9 Nov 1996: The Longest Day Report and Belgrave results from the Young Athletes race walking Grand Prix at Bradford on 9 November 1996, an 18-hour round trip; the report gives Sam McNalley's Under 13 win as 2km, the results line as 1km. BRADFORD YA GRAND PRIX 9 NOV 1996 The Longest Day An early start to what is possibly the longest trip (18 hours) the team will make during the coming Grand Prix League Season was made on a cold and wet Saturday morning. Nine trains and two bus journeys were the order of the day. Because of the distance and other commitments the team was depleted but we still had 7 Young Athletes and one Senior competing and we came home with a trophy for each that completed the event. The Under 11 Girls 1km gave us a third place to new member Emma McNalley, whilst in the Under 13 Boys event her brother Sam took his first Grand Prix Title by winning the 2km with a personal best. With no Under 15 Boys competing we relied on Laura Fryer in this age group. Laura finished the 1995/96 season Nationally ranked no. 2, and she confirmed her status as one of the leading Under 15 Girls by bringing home the 'goodies' in her 3km race by placing third. More was to come in the Youths 5km event where Nigel Whorlow confirmed his top National ranking in his second year in the age group, taking his second consecutive Grand Prix win and making himself favourite for the Grand Prix Title at the end of next summer. In third place was fast improving Chris Stanford gaining a massive personal best. Unfortunately Danny Bond had a bad day and had to withdraw after 3km while Robert Matelle never got started after gashing his leg while running to the start. He required 10 stitches for his troubles. To add to the successes of day, Mick Graham (M45) gained a 7th place in the Seniors 10km and is fast becoming a force in the Veteran Races around the country. These results have put the Club into a very secure second place in the overall team category of the Grand Prix National League. Under 11 Girls' 1km: 3, E.McNalley 7:42. items.sum: How the Graham family and their schoolfriends turned West Suffolk into a hotbed of Belgrave race walking, noticed by the East Anglian press and TV.
items.s: Belgrave dominate season's debut event How the Graham family and their schoolfriends turned West Suffolk into a hotbed of Belgrave race walking, noticed by the East Anglian press and TV. No not a headline taken from the South London Press, not even Athletics Weekly - but the Colchester Evening Gazette! It's not the only East Anglian paper to pick up on Belgrave's activities in their area either, for the East Anglian Daily Times also recently devoted three columns of its sports pages to the phenomena of Race Walking taking off in the Suffolk area in spite of the lack of local facilities. Even the local TV station has featured our young Belgravians going through their paces during training sessions. Mick Graham has been taking part in our cross country and road races for years. With his son Paul showing an early aptitude for all sports but in particular those of running and walking, it was natural that Belgrave should soon take on another recruit. Then Philip and Andrew quickly followed the course taken by their older brother and in turn schoolfriends at Chalkestone Middle School were impressed by the success that came the way of our young members. Before long West Suffolk had turned into a little hotbed of Belgrave activity. With top walker Mabon Dane on hand to advise and coach, and Dave Sharpe throwing in his expertise, Mick Graham himself was soon encouraged to have a go and now it is not at all unusual to see the claret and gold dominating the Colchester Track Handicaps and winning medals in all age groups from Veterans down to Under 11s. On a good day for walking and on a course that was fast enough to pull out early season PBs, the Club only had 3 walkers out. This did not hinder Under 17 Nigel Whorlow who improved his 10km. time by exactly a minute, although he had hoped for a 'sub-50', and he came home the leading Under 17 and 3rd Under 20. His actual race position of 8th in a field full Seniors with over 30 finishing was excellent. Danny Bond, competing in only his third 5km race since moving up an age group in October, found the the course hard going. He nearly pulled out after 3km but managed to continue on to finish and add to his league score ready for the final match to follow in December. items.s: Midland RWA Winter League Match 3 Tamworth, 1 Dec 1996 Report and Belgrave results from the third Midland RWA Winter League match, moved from Draycote Water to Tamworth, on 1 December 1996. This match was originally scheduled to take place at Draycot Water, Rugby but because of last minute problems it was moved to Tamworth, to be held over the same course as used for Match 1. This caused travel problems for our team of four but thanks to the Midland's Walking fraternity we managed to get lifts from Birmingham to the course. Nigel Whorlow, who had already taken over a minute and a half off his best during the previous two matches went out to break the 50 minute barrier but after only 3km suffered hip problems and had to pull out. Danny Bond, being the only Bels walker left to complete all three races came home 4th and took the Overall 3rd place in the Handicap section of the league. Chris Stanford, who missed the second match, came in 3rd. Laura Fryer took part in the U15 Girls race and managed to beat some of her new rivals in her new age group, coming home third. Also travelling over for the match were four of our Suffolk youngsters. Emma McNally surprised everyone by coming home first in the U11 Girls' event and another pleasant surprise was young Andrew Graham who took second place in the U11 Boys race. Not to be out done by their younger brothers and sisters, Paul Graham beat fancied favourite Luke Finch in the U13 Boys taking around two minutes off the Club record, with his team-mate Sam McNalley filling third spot. The Midland League, which was undertaken as a competitive training exercise, produced three PBs for a League medal. Under 17 Men's 5km: 3, C. Standford 29:29; 4, D.Bond 29:47.
