items.s: South of Thames “Junior” Champs. Pyecroft, Nr. Aldershot, 9 Nov 96: Roger and out ! Report of Roger Alsop winning the South of Thames "Junior" cross-country championship at Pyecroft, with results and a photo of him finishing. Banned at last! A first place for Roger Alsop means that we will have to look elsewhere for the cornerstone of our South of Thames “Junior” team for 1997. When interviewed by AW's Martin Duff when the race was over and asked “When did you think you could win it?” Roger, not normally known for hiding his light under a bushell, had to bite his lip to stop himself from replying, “As soon as I got out of the car!” Frankly though, that's how confident he felt going into the race. What a shame that we were unable to supply our cross-country Vice-Captain with a full team to back him up and gain a set of team medals. Said Chettati was up 16 places on last year and Kevin Quinn ran to a superb 20th in his first outing in this event. We only needed another runner in the top forty to win team silver while anyone in the top 70 would have given us bronze. To be fair, we had runners at home who had offered to turn out if necessary to complete a team but with the expectation of there being some six Belgravians on the start line without them, and being in the middle of a busy period of races week in and week out, it was felt that there should be no arm-twisting. In clear and bright conditions our man was quickly on the shoulder of the leader as the pack left the DERA sports ground and headed off for two laps of forest paths. Mick Wood's Aldershot boys were all to the fore on their home territory and they hassled Roger with their six men in the first ten: a gentle push here and there had to be administered by the Belgravian as they chopped and changed their pace around him. By the end of the first lap two men had gone clear, AFD's schoolboy champion Alan Barnes with Roger sticking close to him. The younger man just had to be in front and when Roger occasionally drifted alongside to pressure him, Barnes played right into the Belgravian's hands by trying to forge away again when in actual fact he was already at nearly full throttle with the needle swinging over towards ‘empty’. Two-thirds of the way into the race and it was time to go. Still running within himself Roger stepped up a gear and although Barnes could be heard breathing heavily just behind for a while, when the hills were reached, all became silent as the claret and gold vested figure went into an ever-growing lead. Only a particularly deep and flooded pothole gave him any trouble from here on and Roger's lead was over 20 seconds as he swung back onto the playing field for the finish. Both Kevin and Said enjoyed themselves as they worked their way strongly through the field and with Roger now barred from the competition they will form the nucleus of next year's team. 154 finished. 23 teams closed in. items.h: Reebok Surrey CC League Division 1 Race 2 Kingston Vale, 16 Nov 1996: Mixed fortunes on the Common
items.sum: Report and results of the second Surrey League Division 1 race at Kingston Vale, won by guest Richard Nerurkar, with Belgrave fifth team and youth results.
items.s: Reebok Surrey CC League Division 1 Race 2 Kingston Vale, 16 Nov 1996: Mixed fortunes on the Common Report and results of the second Surrey League Division 1 race at Kingston Vale, won by guest Richard Nerurkar, with Belgrave fifth team and youth results. Having gone to an unexpected 3rd team place in race one and with the team, if anything, promising to be a little stronger this time out, we could be forgiven for starting to look for a 2nd spot behind the strong Hounslow outfit. Matt Yates had completed his week's training by lunchtime but still turned out to spearhead the team and Graham Adams was back in the squad after sitting out the opening match with a calf injury. Yep, surely we could sneak a 2nd on what was more or less our home patch ... but the race was to be full of surprises and as the team declaration was handed in we were missing two of our key men in Dave Pamah and Dave Beaver although boosted by the very welcome return to the fold of a gaunt and fit looking Ray Foley. Again we had a large contingent on the line and as the starter called, “Ready,” our Captain showed his race intentions by streaking off and taking the field with him; a belated, “Go,” accompanied the tail-enders over the line. Guest runner and Sunday morning visitor to Belgrave Hall, Richard Nerurkar had looked ominously confident as he had loosened up before the start, declining with a smile the offer of a claret and gold vest to race in. As befits a triple-National winner he was immediately at the head of the field that had Aldershot's Garner and Jackson, Herne Hill's Jon Solly, our own Matt Yates and Croydon's McCallum all vying for forward positions. But climbing the hill to the top of the course only a mile out, Nerurkar decided that it was not going to be a social event and by the mid-race point a mile and a half later had gone 50 seconds clear. Further drama was unfolding back down the field. Graham Adams had quite uncharacteristically completely “blown up” after a mile and for him the rest of the race became purgatory. Another to suffer miserably when he thought he had fully recovered from a cold was Donal O'Riordan, so at half-way, two of our expected scorers were right out of it. Roger Alsop and Jim Estall had both had hard races the previous week but were comfortably up around the 20 mark but the gap between them and the majority of the Belgrave team was obviously going to be too much for that 2nd team place. At the finish positions were much the same. Bruce Barton had fallen heavily but gamely ran on well to lead home the engine-room men three places up on his Brockwell Park outing - and this in a higher standard field. Ray Foley was next in - great to have him back - just ahead of Steve Hewes who this time listened to wise old harrier Charlie Dickinson and worked his way through instead of blasting it from the start. Our 7th and 8th men, Said Chettati and Mike Kazimierski, also improved. Sadly we couldn't count Demetrius Onoufrio, our 2nd-claimer from Southampton Runners who had not been registered, so it was left to Phil Carstairs (still with the New York marathon in his legs) and Mark Anderson to close in the team. A quick tally up showed that we were 5th. It was a little disappointing at first but a measure of what we are now expecting of ourselves; and looking back we had done pretty well, getting within 20 points of our opening score in spite of problems. Aldershot had surprised while Borough of Hounslow slipped back a little, their 10th man coming home behind ours but with five men between 23 and 27 crossing the finish in line abreast formation, they kept their overall score down. The Boro' men seem unlikely now to lose their league lead but only 177 points covers the next five clubs so there is plenty left to run for. Unfortunately, while the seniors seem to have an enthusiastic and swelling pool of runners to call upon, our youngsters' numbers have dwindled. items.s: Surrey Cross Country Champs. Happy Valley, Old Coulsdon, 14 Dec 1996: Thirty barren seasons come to an end Report of the 1996 Surrey Cross Country Championships at Happy Valley, where Gary Staines won and Belgrave won the senior team title by four points from Boxhill Racers, their first for thirty years, with results and a photo. The boys were geared up for a set of medals. There was no way they were going home without something on this day. Roger Alsop's winter had been tailored towards a forward position in this event but the onset of a cold during the week meant that he was now only turning out for the team's sake. Jim Estall was taking a well-earned break after successive week's of road and country battles - but still the mood was one of determination. And then when Gary Staines showed up for his first race since Chicago, putting himself up as a target for Solly and Croydon's young McCallum to have a pop at, a quiet ripple of excitement went through the team. Maybe we could nail Boxhill! When the 200 plus runners surged across the frosty field and down into Happy Valley, Belgrave vests were already prominent in the top thirty with Jon Solly leading the charge. (Little known fact: Jon was actually born in Denmark Road Wimbledon.) SLH's Stuart Major, a favourite before the big boys showed up, took a turn at the head of the field after a mile or so, with first year Senior McCallum, Staines, Solly and Boxhill's Haywood in full cry behind. The Belgrave team was holding up well with Dave Beaver our second man in the late ‘teens and the other lads queueing up behind - except Ray Foley who was surprisingly lying about 80th. It looked as if he would be the Belgrave man to miss out on a medal. Halfway. Now Solly was making his bid; Mr. Staines was not going to find this an easy race by any means. A five metre gap was opened up and before long it had doubled, the Herne Hill Harrier racing away on the downhill and flatter stretches with Gary painfully recovering a metre or two with every climb. Dave Beaver now had Roger and Graham Adams in close attendance and Bruce Barton followed by Said Chettati were also moving well not too much further behind. Simon Fairbrother had eased his way through to join club-mate Haywood and with another man in 11th the Boxhill Billies were having another strong team run - but, fingers crossed, had to go back too far for their 5th and 6th men. Amazingly Ray Foley was now into the 40's; he'd been picking off runners like cherries from a tree - and his basket was still far from full. One more lap of Happy Valley to go and Solly's lead had, if anything, grown a little more. True there was a slight hesitation as he asked a pointsman if it was time yet to turn off up the long climb to the finish but his raking stride was relentless down the slope into the last circuit and Gary later confessed to severe doubts as to whether it was all over. Teamwise we looked better than ever. Said was suffering, slowly falling towards the back of the 30s, but Ray was running like a dream; with arms and legs pumping he was flying past man after man, seemingly feeling no pain. With five men now between 17 and 28, and Gary up ahead, surely the race was ours. But the fat lady was in no mood to sing just yet. Your correspondent and other supporters scurried to the top of the course and awaited the arrival of the runners. Frenzied shouting from spectators who could see down the slope told us that it was far from being all over and as the runners burst onto the finish field it was Gary's distinctive figure leaning into the climb a few paces ahead of the Herne Hill man. He'd used every ounce of his strength on that final incline and in the last minutes Jon Solly had crumbled. What a race. Everyone seemed to have run themselves into the ground. McCallum came home a minute later, eventually getting the better of Major and then it was three Boxhill men in quick succession before the finishers went into double figures. Steaming up the straight and still taking places to the line came our second man Ray Foley - a super run - and another tremendous performance came from Dave Beaver who just had the edge over Roger, but where was ‘Gerry’ Adams? Bruce finished strongly, delighted with his effort and still no ‘Gerry’. Five Belgrave in and then five Boxhill. Said painfully made his way to the funnel, grittily keeping ahead of Boxhill's last man and it was time for the maths. It seemed we'd done it by one point! A disconsolate ‘Gerry’ limped back but out of the race. He'd badly turned an ankle in the woods only a mile from the finish and now had to face the fact that as Captain he was going to be the man who didn't get a cherished ‘Surrey’ gold medal. When the non-scorers were taken out our winning margin became four points and after the presentation Boxhill's Robin Batchelor ruefully had to hand over the Cup. Wrapped in a plastic bag and lying with their kit-bags the trophy hadn't been handed in to the officials before the start - perhaps they'd not expected to lose it! Belgrave activity had been a bit sparse in the rest of the day's events. Nikki Haines ran to a fine 5th place in the Senior Women's 4 miles and it was good to see Morag Andrews and Jacinta Moore back out - but no team. No team either in the Under 20 Men's race. Adam Jones had been racing well in college events and was looking to go out of the age group in style. An untimely bout of ‘flu’ in the days before put paid to his plans, however, and he was forced to withdraw. This left us with Kevin Quinn and Simon Alexander to run as individuals - both finishing above the winning team's first scorer. From a large Under 15 Boys' field, Stephen Beaver's 7th proved that regular steady training is paying off and he may well have earned himself a trip to the Inter-Counties. items.label: February 1997
items.sum: Comment on what winning the Surrey Cross Country team title, for the first time in 30 years, means to Belgrave Harriers.
items.s: It's coming home ... Comment on what winning the Surrey Cross Country team title, for the first time in 30 years, means to Belgrave Harriers. “ ... it's coming home ... ”. We're pretty sure the soccer fans among you won't mind us borrowing the opening lines from the Euro '96 anthem - but frankly, the phrase just about sums up what winning this event means to Belgrave Harriers. Whatever success we gain in Track & Field and however you measure the prowess of an athletic club, we know that underlying it all we started as a Harrier club - and it hurts when we are no longer seen as one. When Surrey County's magnificent F.N.Pickett Cup was displayed at Committee two days after our Surrey team win, the look on Bill Lucas' face was an absolute treat to behold; and wouldn't old Tom have been delighted. As you will see from the list of previous winners, we have to go back 30 years for our previous victory when our outstanding runner of that day was Gerry North. In 1967 we went on to place 2nd in the ‘Southern’ and 4th in the ‘National’, winning the Surrey League on the way - so let's not get too excited, we don't expect that just yet! There's also a lot of difference between winning it once off and maintaining a vice-like grip on it for a few years. But nevertheless, we can feel very pleased with our progress and the fact that our runners are beginning to move in the right direction, together. Good on you boys and well done Gary Staines for spearheading the team! items.h: Reebok Surrey CC League Division 1 Race 3 Lloyd Park, Croydon, 4 Jan 97: The “Engine-room” packs to 2nd
items.sum: Report and results of the third Surrey League Division 1 race at a frozen Lloyd Park, where Belgrave packed eight men into the top 40 to finish second team and move to third overall, and James Venning won the Under 17 race.
items.s: Reebok Surrey CC League Division 1 Race 3 Lloyd Park, Croydon, 4 Jan 97: The “Engine-room” packs to 2nd Report and results of the third Surrey League Division 1 race at a frozen Lloyd Park, where Belgrave packed eight men into the top 40 to finish second team and move to third overall, and James Venning won the Under 17 race. Lloyd Park manages to throw up a variety of conditions over the years and this time it took on the disguise of an Arctic waste. With the ground already frozen to a depth of several inches, the still conditions had brought down a hard frost which had bushes, trees and grassland alike covered in a white mantle and with daylight already seeming to fail as race-time approached and with a hint of snow in the air - was it cold! It was a day only for the hardy and as the teams were registered it was apparent that some clubs, what with ‘flu’ and mid-winter apathy, were struggling to declare ten names. That put the Team Manager in jovial mood for he knew that he already had ten men jogging round the course to check out the icy spots. Gary Staines was suffering from a cold but had turned up to watch and gee up the lads, as had Stuart Paton, so with supporters on hand as well, the team was in good spirits and looking for another improvement in our fortunes. Spirits were lifted higher still when James Venning stormed to a convincing victory in the under 17 race. A tough looking runner this one and we'll be keeping an eye on his progress over the next few years. James just had time to give further reports on the course before the Seniors were lined up ... and away. A good circuit for spectators this one but with only part of the first lap gone we were startled to find that no Bels. featured in the top twenty while Hounslow and Aldershot seemed to be packing them in. Dave Beaver, clad only in singlet and shorts while many of the runners were sporting tights if not track-suits and woolly hats, was working his way through nicely as was Jim Estall but positions were much the same as the field set out on the second circuit. Climbing the steep, slippery slope before heading out on the last long loop we still only had Dave and Jim inside the first score but then the Bels came flooding through too fast for numbed fingers to keep a team tally. It was going to be interesting. England Team Manager Dave Clarke was using his experience and making a determined run through the field for Hercules Wimbledon but Hounslow's Simpson was dominating the race with McCallum, on his own ground, also looking comfortable. All around that last lap our team continued to consolidate but even en masse they were unable to break into the top dozen or so runners. But now it was time to dash over to the finish and check off the runners as they came home. The leading two had maintained their positions but Clarke had put on a real charge to get up to 3rd. Already providing the winner, Hounslow then had Usher in 4th and another man in 10th but apart from them the top ten finishers were evenly distributed between every other club - except the Bels. Fifteen men home and still no claret and gold ... and then, with Dave Beaver leading the way, it was all Belgrave. Eight men home in 40 and then, just over two minutes after our first man had entered the funnel, the team was closed in by Junior Galley and Mike Webb. Only Aldershot had got their complete team home ahead of us while Hounslow, Boxhill and Thames Hare & Hounds waited ... and waited. What a close race and what a great score for us. With second team place on the day and moving into 3rd overall we confirmed something that we have known all along but have hardly dared speak of: we can win these races. James Venning, seen here in middle-distance action in the McDonalds YA League during the summer, has carried his form over nicely to the winter. items.label: February 1997
items.sum: History of the Christmas Day Paarlauf two-man relay on Wimbledon Common, from its start in 1954 by Charlie Smart and Arthur Whitehead to the 1996 race, with its records, folk-lore, all-time and Belgrave top-20 tables and photos.
items.s: The Christmas Day Paarlauf History of the Christmas Day Paarlauf two-man relay on Wimbledon Common, from its start in 1954 by Charlie Smart and Arthur Whitehead to the 1996 race, with its records, folk-lore, all-time and Belgrave top-20 tables and photos. “FRIENDLINESS was, as befitted the season, the keynote of a highly successful Paarlauf, a newly instituted Christmas feature, run around the green at Wimbledon Common on Christmas morning.” That was how The Belgravian introduced its report on the inaugural half hour two man relay held on that most familiar of territory in 1954. Then, in fine and warm conditions, but with a wind from the north-west, 12 runners turned out to gain their first experience of what was described as a comparatively new type of relay. The race owes its origin to Charlie Smart, the Belgrave international distance runner who served with the Control Commission and competed in Germany after the war. He brought back the Continental idea of two man teams competing in an event known as the Paarlauf, or paired run, and Arthur Whitehead, owner of Lauriston Cottage on the edge of Wimbledon Common and always a fan of Charlie's, took up the concept and helped bring it to fruition. To ensure reasonably even pairings, the names of the six best runners were placed in one hat and the remainder in another; this method turning out to be, “quite satisfactory as the field kept surprisingly close together throughout the race, 332 yards covering them all at the finish.” This was in the days before Arthur Whitehead had opened Lauriston Cottage to all athletes and only Belgravians took part in the first race. However, it was the late Aubrey Reeve, the Hon. Secretary of Wimbledon AC who made the draw and the race was started outside the cottage by John Jewell, the Assistant Hon. Secretary of the Road Runners Club. Of course Arthur Whitehead and Charlie Smart also officiated. The 1,415 yards circuit was conveniently divided into two legs by the short recovery across the green adjacent to Rushmere Pond to Cannizaro Road and vice versa. The format established The inaugural winners were Len Bishop and Eric Gebbett with 6 miles 145 yards, a modest distance as later events were to show, caused perhaps by inexperience but certainly affected by the whistle being blown at 27 minutes, after which no further change was allowed, instead of the now used 28 minutes. One of the first to suffer the long last leg was Gordon Biscoe as his ‘senior’ partner Charlie Walker, reported as being caught napping, left Gordon in possession of the baton. After the race everyone adjourned to the cottage to wash down and partake of an enormous baking of mince pies with a hot and rather alcoholic witches brew concocted by Arthur Whitehead. And as the format for this popular event was established, it has remained virtually unchanged ever since. The following year the event took place on Christmas Eve and the famous exploding dustbin was born when, as The Belgravian reported, “ ... dispensing with the usual method of starting, Arthur Whitehead and Arthur Penstone had rigged up a small explosive charge inside a dustbin and the explosion which started the race brought back memories of the war when the Common was an exercise ground for the Army.” In later days, the dustbin was only used to sound time for no further changeover and then for the 30 minute finish. A more effective way of ensuring that everyone heard was difficult to imagine at the time although the Christmas Day explosions were brought to an end years later when a Wimbledon Common Ranger objected due to the noise frightening the horses. Today's solution, when explosions of any kind are frowned upon, is an easily carried klaxon driven by a canister of compressed air. Word of this interesting event quickly spread and in 1956 three Hercules AC pairings and one from Herne Hill Harriers joined eight from Belgrave to contest the event which was retained for the Bels by the two Charlies - Walker and Henn - in a more respectable 6 miles 656 yards. But it was inevitable that as Belgrave continued to draw for partners, in the spirit of the festivity, that we would soon lose a hold on the race to a nominated pairing from another club. The following year, a Ranelagh pair of Bill Bird (now Secretary of the Reebok Surrey Cross Country League) and Brian Nott (to become a second-claim Belgravian in the years ahead) set a new record of 6 miles 947 yards. In 1962, The Belgravian records that 18 pairs took part with 12 of these from visiting clubs. “This was the 9th year of the race and its popularity grows on each occasion. The winning pair, Gowan and Derham, were the only ones to complete 8 circuits for a new record of 6 miles 1,094 yards.” The first Bels pairing was 8th and it was commented upon that “the time has probably come for our stars to partner each other.” A Belgrave record of 6 miles 697 yards was set by Pat Newell and David Baines. Lauriston Runners On 30th October 1966 a meeting was held in the changing rooms at Lauriston Cottage at which it was agreed that those present would form a new club, Lauriston Runners. With the informal group of runners using the cottage as a training base now banded together as an open club, it was natural that the race should become organised under their auspices and at the same time the need for the Bels to change their ‘A’ and ‘B’ formula disappeared as at that inaugural Lauriston Runners meeting it was proposed by Bob Holt of Hercules AC, now second-claim Lauriston as well, that pairings for the Paarlauf should be made from ‘A’ and ‘B’ competitors to mitigate the disparity in competition. This had reached a peak the previous year when Millard and Taylor of Cambridge Harriers set a record of 6 miles 1,406 yards (4mins 24secs. miling pace) to leave all the Belgrave pairings way behind. That distance naturally still stands as the record as it is a rare occurrence for a genuine ‘A’ and ‘B’ pairing to exceed 6 miles 1,000 yards. Bels first pair of Steer and Walker set a Belgrave best of 6 miles 879 yards in 11th place that year. 1966 therefore saw the start of what might be described as the general hubbub and banter that is thrown up when the pairings are drawn - “What's ‘e doing in the ‘B’ hat!?” - as much a highlight of the event as the race itself! For Graham Taylor the rule change made no difference. Then at the top of his form, in a year which had seen him clock a sub-1hr. 40min. Belgrave ‘20’, it made no difference whether he ran with another ‘recognised’ runner or not. Drawn with ‘B’ runner Cheeseman of South London Harriers he was first again with 6 miles 1,067 yards. Athletic folk-lore The years drifted past and stories connected with the event have become part of local athletic folk-lore. John Phelan (Hercules Wimbledon) ran his first Paarlauf in 1962 and he also ran in 1996 - a span of 34 years in which he has competed 20 times, twice as a winner. But John's 34 year love affair with the race was easily eclipsed when Belgrave's Alan Black returned to the race this winter after a lapse of 14 Christmas-tides. Alan's first Paarlauf was in 1955 - giving him a span of 41 years in which he has clocked up 24 runs - also with two wins. Jocular accusations of “rigging” were made in 1978 when Alan, a one-time Scottish International, was classed as a ‘B’ runner. He found himself paired with “HW's” Dave Clarke, three times National Cross Country Champion and twice runner-up. It was the 25th running of the event and as the only man from the early races still turning out it did seem fitting that he should share in a “silver jubilee” victory. However, with 48 runners that year there were some other very good ‘B’ runners around including our own Pete Gilbey, then Surrey AC, and “HW's” Mike Kortenray and Pete Clarke. It was all above board. One further note regarding Alan Black: in the latest running of the event when paired with Paul Warburton they achieved the distinction of being the first twosome ever not to exceed 5 miles! As befits a National Champion Dave Clarke is the man who has the most victories to his name with five. Next comes Ealing & Southall's Pete Barratt whose three wins came in consecutive years, each time with a different Ranelagh partner, and Belgrave's John Gladwin, also on three. Ken Ashby (Hercules Wimbledon) has won twice as a ‘B’ runner, partnering his club-mate John Sullivan in 1969 and Bob Richardson of Blackheath in 1974. Ken's were fitting victories as his birthday also falls on December 25th. The rumour that, like a former celebrant of this birthdate, he could walk on water and used this ability to take a short cut across Rushmere Pond between his stages has been refuted by those who were present. The first woman to run was Angie Thomas who partnered her Thames Valley Harrier husband Clive in 1977 and there have been many other occasions of the race being used as an energetic Christmas morning family outing. In 1966 the Beard brothers turned out in force - Mike, Paul and Dave, all of Hercules AC (the Hercules and Wimbledon clubs amalgamated on 1st September 1967). And this feat was repeated by another threesome from “HW” in 1978 - Chris, Dave and Pete Clarke. There has only ever been one family victory and this way back in 1958 when the brothers Bird, Bill and 14 year old David took home the prize. Fathers and sons have taken part (eg. Belgrave's Keith and Mark Sinclair) and in 1995 there was a Belgrave father and son pairing when Dave and Steve Beaver took to the road. A sensation occurred in 1987 when the team of South London's John Roberts and Belgrave's John Wasborough found themselves both running at the same time! It seems that “Wassy” thought Roberts would have been among the leaders at the first takeover and not seeing him among the early arrivals, thought he must have missed him so away he went. Meanwhile Roberts, who had made a steady start, arrived at the changeover to find no “Wassy” and decided to continue. A few minutes later Roberts found himself passing “Wassy” who was then told in no uncertain terms to carry on! The Kenyans The Kenyans arrived in 1990 and what a baptism they received. Conditions were atrocious as a cold westerly wind brought heavy rain and sleet throughout the race. The recording of the number of laps run and the final measuring up was impossible. Only the first five places could be guaranteed as being correct and approximate measurements only could be made for the first three home. Osoro Ondoro of Kenya shared his win with Crawley AC's A. Reader with a string of famous African names relegated to the main and unrecorded body of the field: John Ngugi, Richard Chelimo, William Mutwol, Susan Sirma, etc. In spite of the weather they all enjoyed themselves, especially the after race refreshments, and they surprised the “regulars” no end when they washed themselves down by making use of the ice-cold water hose. They didn't show up the following year but were back in ‘92 and ‘95. These multi-world record holders and stars of tracks around the world all pay their £1 race entrance fee, enjoying the banter and happy to share their runs and Christmas mornings with unknown club runners. Surprisingly, there seems to have been a noticeable drop in standards over the years and this in spite of the appearance of the Kenyans. In 1965 no fewer than 26 of the 32 teams beat 6 miles, a figure that was equalled the following Christmas, the first year of the ‘draw’. In 1994 only one pair achieved that feat and only two in the latest running of the event. One must remember though, that in the mid ‘sixties Surrey boasted the finest distance runners in the country, a fact borne out by victory in the Inter-Counties Cross Country Championship. But as far as the Paarlauf is concerned no-one is the slightest bit bothered about the situation, it being generally agreed that the main point of the race is for the runners to enjoy themselves in a light-hearted Christmas event where despite “professionalism” the first three pairs only receive small token prizes. As Lauriston Runners' General Secretary Dave Beard says, “The prize for all those involved is the enjoyment in taking part whether actively or helping out or merely spectating”. With the race now well into its 5th decade, long may these sentiments prevail. * The 1967 race ran for 31 minutes 1996 Belgrave placings: 1, S.Fairbrother (Boxhill)/D.Anderson (Bel) 6m 377y; 4, G.Adams (Bel)/R.Owens (Met.Police) 5m 1655y; 6, D.Beaver (Bel)/M.Doogan (Woking) 5m 1579y; 7, R.Alsop (Bel)/P.Williams (Herc. items.sum: Charlie Dickinson's review of Jim Estall's 1996 season, from an ill-fated London Marathon to England selection and individual bronze and team gold at the Veterans Home International cross country in Irvine, with three photos.
items.s: Jim Estall, Belgrave Harriers & England Charlie Dickinson's review of Jim Estall's 1996 season, from an ill-fated London Marathon to England selection and individual bronze and team gold at the Veterans Home International cross country in Irvine, with three photos. CHARLIE DICKINSON updates us on the 1996 season of one of Britain's top veteran runners. Most runners are used to high and low points in their career, but few can have experienced such a turbulent season as Jim Estall in 1996. His worst London Marathon performance for many years in the heat of April was followed by weeks of illness and injury. But slowly, Jim picked up the pieces, started to run well again in the summer, and a series of fime Autumn performances saw him selected for the England Veterans Cross Country team for the Home International in Irvine where he won team gold and individual bronze medals. Perhaps the Marathon disappointment, where he ran 2hr 35min maybe ten minutes slower than expected, was all the worse after such a promising build up throughtout the late winter and early spring. Added to his usual consistent cross country performances were a fine 68:15 half marathon, 1hr 50min in the Worthing ‘20’, and his best ever time in the South of England 12-stage at Thurrock after a mid-week 32 minute 10km in the Civil Service Championships. However, two days before the London Marathon he started to notice a sore throat. He managed to run at 5 min. 30 sec. miles to Greenwich, but then began to slow, reaching half way in 74 minutes. By the end, feeling very unwell and dehydrated in the unusually high temperature, he dropped to 6 min. 15 sec. miles and eventually was just glad to finish. The first place team prize along with Paul Evans, Gary Staines and Junior Galley was at least some compensation for sticking it out but Jim was left ill and deflated for several weeks after the race. Nor was his recovery helped when he injured his foot while doing some fencing work in the garden. In fact it took him even longer to get over the accident than the effects of the marathon and it wasn't until June that he felt fit enough to race again. Answering a late call to run the 5000m for the British League team at Copthall, Jim surprised himself by running 15:37 off just a few weeks of steady running and no track work. He followed this with a 15:20 in the Southern league and a progression of excellent midweek VAC 5.2 mile runs in Battersea Park. In August he ran a solo 26:29, only a couple of seconds slower than Laurie O'Hara's course record. Jim was back with a vengeance. Two weeks later he ran away from the field in the VAC/Belgrave 10000m Championships, breaking the record in 31:31.6, a time which ranked him second M40 in the country. He then began to think again about the Veterans International cross country to be held in Scotland in November. He had first thought about the possiblity of selection back in the previous Autumn after beating the then British veterans cross country champion Barry Atwell in the Surrey Championships in December 1995, and again in the Surrey league in the new year. The Autumn saw a wonderful series of performances from Jim. 60th in the Great North run in 70:38, an 18:57 relay leg for the senior team at Aldershot in the South of England 6-Stage, a time which would have placed him second only to Mike Gratton if he had run in the Veterans race. Then on October 6th perhaps his finest ever race in the British veterans 10km road championships at Solihull. Here Jim finished second to supervet Nigel Gates, beating all the rest of the best veterans in the country and running 31:31 on an undulating course. It was here that Jim earned his England vest. So to Scotland for the Veterans International cross country on November 10th. On a beautiful sunny day on a rich green hilly four lap course overlooking the Isle of Arran Jim was determined to “give it a real go”. He did just that, chasing the in form Derek Mullin after the initial mad rush. At the end of the first lap Peter Yeomans had briefly taken the lead but by the time the field reached the awesome hill at the back of the course for the second time Mullin was beginning to pull away from Yeomans and Jim. Jim Estall showed great determination over the next lap and a half, never giving up the chase, with the first two shorter striding and lighter runners perhaps more suited to the sharply undulating terrain. Eventually, Mike Hager the real tough guy in veteran athletics and leading the England M45 team, came past Jim and finally Yeomans to snatch second place. When it looked as if Jim could still just about catch Yeomans with a quarter of a mile to go he felt his calf muscles tie up and had to settle for fourth. However, as Hager was an M45, this wonderful performance earned Jim the bronze medal and with the first four England M40's closing in 5th place, the result of the team was a foregone conclusion - gold. The weekend in Scotland was perhaps the highlight of Jim's running career and proof to all of us that we should never give up. Above: British League 5,000 metre duty at Copthall Stadium. Right: It's August, and Jim runs 26:29 for the VAC 5.2 mile race. The Battersea Park Peace Pagoda has only ever witnessed one faster run - and that by another Belgrave super-vet Laurie O'Hara. March 1998 The Belgravian The official gazette of Belgrave Harriers Number 226 Cover photos. Race Walking is alive and well in Belgrave Harriers. Our young men and women show every sign of re-establishing the club as force to be reckoned with thanks to the efforts of the 'Whorlow' camp from down South and the 'Graham' crowd from East Anglia. Front page: It's seven years ago since a little shrimp from the South Coast arrived at Battersea Park to take part in the national Run for Africa. He saw the coloured photographs of top Belgrave athletes cut from the pages of this magazine and pinned on the notice board. He declared there and then that he was going to join the Bels. The intervening years have seen Nigel Whorlow grow to well over 6 feet and make a huge impact as one of Britain's top young walkers. Already an "age-group" international and still only 17, he has a tremendous future ahead of him. We take great pleasure from the fact that it was images from this magazine that set him on the road to success - now it's time for his own picture to go on the board! Back page: Laura Fryer is also making a name for herself, winning races all around the country and ranking among the very top athletes in her event. Both pictures taken at the Belgrave Open Seven Miles at Wimbledon on 22nd November by Alan Mead. items.sum: Editorial thanking donors to the magazine, summarising the 1997 track and field and youth season, and reviewing the cross-country season and the coming road relays.
e: South of Thames Cross Country Championships
items.s: Editorial thanking donors to the magazine, summarising the 1997 track and field and youth season, and reviewing the cross-country season and the coming road relays. Many, many thanks to those Belgravians who have donated sums of money towards this magazine's production. We can't name you all – and we know that some of you don't want public recognition – but without that little extra contributed alongside your subscription, the 344,315 characters making up 70,870 words in these pages would never have seen print. We mention "that little extra", and certainly every £1 helps, but some members have been very generous indeed. It's been another marvellous year of athletics for Belgrave Harriers with the Track & Field squad carrying off the 1997 Gold Cup and British Athletics League Division One title. Among the Junior Men we have some truly amazing athletes who individually gained international honours with Dwain Chamber's European 100 metres win in World Junior Record time being the highlight. Combined as a team they contributed greatly towards the Club's promotion to the National Junior League Premier Division. But we are tight for space in this magazine and have therefore regretfully had to omit the full details of our progress in the Under 20 Track & Field team competitions. Those areas are covered in depth in Belgrave's Youth In Action magazine but we must at least record in these pages that apart from the Junior men's promotion: The McDonald's League Team (under 17 men, under 15 and under 13 boys) placed 6th of the sixteen teams in the Southern Premier League and thus just missed out on going to Birmingham for the Auxiliary National Final. The Thameside League saw our under 15 girls place 5th and the under 13s 7th, while both boys teams were 5th. If you want to know more about these activities then get in touch and while stocks last we will attempt to get a Youth In Action to you. Now, for all the Senior action and for Road Running, Cross Country and Race Walking for all ages – read on! As we have said, we are tight for space. As the originator of these pages also has a strong bias towards running of the cross country variety he now makes no apology at all for high-jacking the rest of the white space on this sheet for his own purposes. We have just about come to the end of the second of two successful seasons on the country. We've slipped a little in the Reebok Surrey League – from 2nd in 1996-97 to this winter's 4th – but to be honest, that is not so important as the fact that we have solidly entrenched ourselves again in the top division. The South of Thames Cross Country Association victories were superb. It's most unusual for a club to carry off both titles in one season, the sort of thing that comes from a team on the way up, but the amazing thing is that we could do it again next winter if we put our minds to it. We do need to strengthen our middle order up a bit (health problems and injuries hit us here) but top guns Gary Staines and Kassa Tadesse have done us proud. Clive Gilby has fitted into the team very nicely while tough guy Jim Estall has had an astonishing few months. Now for the big road relays. We may be missing a few faces for the 12-Stage events as the alternative attractions of warm weather training and the London Marathon kick in. However, it's about time that we avoided getting hung up about the Thurrock event and remembering that it is only the 'Southern' – the qualifying race for the National 12-Stage at Sutton Coldfield. We must treat it as just that and when success in the event comes along one day then all well and good. But some of our guys have never once run around Sutton Park and measured themselves up against the lads from clubs like Tipton and Bingley. Let's qualify and pencil in a good day out at Sutton Park on April 18th. items.label: March 1998
items.sum: Column reprinting items from 25 years ago (1973: Alf Harley's death, the Surrey League, the National Veterans' title, Sandy Law's shoe shop) and 50 years ago (1948: Southern and English cross-country titles, the National 20 walk and Harry Churcher's 5-mile world record).
items.s: From the Belgravian Column reprinting items from 25 years ago (1973: Alf Harley's death, the Surrey League, the National Veterans' title, Sandy Law's shoe shop) and 50 years ago (1948: Southern and English cross-country titles, the National 20 walk and Harry Churcher's 5-mile world record). FROM THE BELGRAVIAN 25 Years Ago ...1973 IT IS WITH GEAT SORROW that we have to record the death of Alf. Harley, a man who worked tremendously hard for his Club and athletics in general and who in return was held by all who knew him in high regard. Whatever the event, Alf. Harley always seemed to be there and it is almost impossible to visualise Belgrave's future without his dignified presence. SURREY C.C. LEAGUE DIVISION 1. With the coming of Aldershot, Farnham & District to the Surrey Cross Country League it was hoped that a little more excitement would be injected into what, for the past seven years, has become a bit of a procession. It certainly was! In the 3rd match at Streatham Common we were beaten by a mere 8 points with Les Presland, running with even more vigour since his move from Surrey A.C. [to A,F&D], providing the individual winner. So, we went into the final act of this desperately close struggle just 18 points up and with our grip on the trophy gradually being loosened. With Gerry North still suffering from tonsillitis, John Stow stuck in a train at Raynes Park and our veterans girding themselves for the following day's National Veterans' race, our chances became even slimmer. Over the Coulsdon course, still patchy with snow, the men from west Surrey romped home 30 points clear and gained an overall lead of 12 points. Final League Position. 1, Aldershot, Farnham & Dist. 863; 2, Belgrave H 875; 3, Hercules Wimbledon AC 1464; 4, South London H 1466; 5, Croydon H 1481; 6, Herne Hill H 1793; 7, Ranelagh H 1998. [Editor: Belgrave H have found themselves unable to win this competition ever since ...] NATIONAL VET'S CHAMPIONS. February 18th 1973 - Perry Bar Park, Birmingham. By winning the third National Championship for veteran runners on this cold and windy Sunday afternoon, Belgrave annexed the team trophy for the first time and furnished the individual champion also in the sprightly form of Laurie O'Hara. Laurie didn't just win - he slaughtered the opposing runners. Belgrave didn't just win - they annihilated the opposing teams. It was that sort of day, Claret and Gold all the way. And it was really like the old days to hear the whistles of surprise at the presentation ceremony when our winning score of 29 points was announced. 1, L.O'Hara 32:35; 10, C.Shippen 34:30; 18, P.Newell 35:08. Teams: 1, Belgrave H 29; Springburn 87; 3, TVH 94. THE CLUB have been pleased to accept the kind offer of Mrs. Churcher of the late Harry Churcher's medals and have agreed to hold them in trust during her life time, after which they will become the property of the Club. THE END OF AN ERA ... Sandy Law closes up his shoe making business to move to Eastbourne. For many years athletes have gone to Sandy's shop in Revelstoke, Road Wimbledon for a pair of hand made to measure running shoes, possibly his most famous customer being Roger Bannister, the first man to run a mile in under four minutes. Unfortunately in today's world manufacturers like Sandy find it increasingly difficult to compete with the mass production of shoes by the giants of the sports shoe business. and, 50 Years Ago ... 1947/48 THE SOUTHERN COUNTIES C.C. CHAMPIONSHIPS. ... were held at Aylesford on February 28th ... The senior race was over a 10 miles course and from the start Sydney Wooderson went in front followed by Vic Blowfield, with Ted Stimpson also well up. Len Herbert was coming through well and Frank Abberton and Tom Clinton were also well placed. Albert Frost unfortunately had a bad time but Tom Carter was running well and eventually became our sixth scoring man with Les Stokell unluckily missing a winner's medal by two places. We also won the Odling-Smee Cup, awarded to the first Surrey club to finish a complete team of twelve. Our positions were as follows:- 3 V.S.Blowfield 56:46; 4 E.S.Stimpson 57:24; 7 L.W.Herbert 57:50; 10 F.J.Abberton 58:05; 15 T.P.Clinton 58:20; 36 C.T.Carter 60:01; 38 C.L.Stokell 60:05; 65 R.W.Tobin 61:37; 84 S.R.Eales 62:25; 90 A.E.Frost 62:50; 106 A.F.Mitchell 63:28; 132 G.M.Pearson 64:15. Team result: 1 Belgrave H., 75 points; 2 Blackheath H., 113. THE ENGLISH C.C. CHAMPIONSHIPS. These were held in Graves Park, Sheffield, on March 13th, and being a fine day a very large crowd watched the racing. Once again Sydney Wooderson was up the front but this time there was a small bunch of runners with him including our own Vic Blowfield. On the last lap Wooderson made his effort but Vic kept with him stride for stride and then about half-a-mile from the finish Vic made a gallant attempt to get away from his man and succeeded up to a point. The only snag was that there was further to go than Vic had thought and Wooderson came again to beat Vic up the finishing straight. Len Herbert had run well throughout as had Ted Stimpson, now getting back to his pre-war form, and with Frank Abberton also making a last lap effort, and Tom Carter and Tommy Clinton coming along well we found to our satisfaction that we had beaten Sutton Harriers, the holders, to record our fourth National victory. Les Stokell was once again a good 7th man and Albert Frost and Dick Tobin completed our team. Positions were: 2 V.S.Blowfield; 12 L.W.Herbert; 15 E.S.Stimpson; 27 F.J.Abberton; 41 C.T.Carter; 57 T.P.Clinton; 64 C.L.Stokell; 95 A.E.Frost; 132 R.W.Tobin. Team scores were: 1 Belgrave H., 154; 2 Sutton H., 174; 3 Blackheath H., 183. In the Junior race Eddie Short was again our first man home in 7th position, and to gain such a high place in this race speaks well for Eddie's strength and determination. Mike Heard also ran well in finishing 40th and Arthur Bruce ran pluckily on a damaged foot to be 56th, with Eric Bishop 65, R.Garwood 112, L.C.Bishop 117, and L.A.Adams 138. In the team race we were placed 8th out of an entry of 30 clubs so can be well satisfied. WITH THE WALKERS. And so to the National 20 at Sudbury. Our teams were supported by what must have been the biggest crowd of Club Members and friends ever seen at a road race. Our Road Captain Charlie Churcher surprised most people by not adopting his usual get-a-way method and the opening stages of the race were unusually slow. Later on, however, Charlie developed stomach trouble and was obliged to fall back. About the same time Colin Sutton had trouble with his shoes and lost a lot of ground. In the centre of the field, however, our Vice Captain, Jack Bidgood, was doing some excellent work holding together about half a dozen of our walkers which no doubt had much to do with the ultimate result of the race. On recovering from his trouble, Colin Sutton battled bravely on recovering position after position and eventually caught up on Jack Bidgood and Co. Charlie, however, had continued to drop back and with our old friends, Surrey W.C., holding two places in the first five, a win for us seemed out of the question. Eventually our lads finished in a procession with five consecutive placings from 18 to 22 and backed up by George Bentley, Joe Wilson and Joe Coleman, we succeeded in taking the Nijmegan Shield with our eight walkers in the first 48, an excellent performance on which all are to be congratulated. WORLD'S RECORD FROM HARRY CHURCHER. And so to the most notable success in the Club's history for many years – our Track [Walking] Captain's achievement in setting up a new World's Record for 5 miles. items.sum: President Lionel Mann's message halfway through his 1997-98 presidential year, thanking committee members and his predecessor and listing the year's social highlights.
items.s: The President writes President Lionel Mann's message halfway through his 1997-98 presidential year, thanking committee members and his predecessor and listing the year's social highlights. The President writes:- I find that I am now about halfway through my presidential year and am amazed at how quickly the time has passed. It is a great honour to be elected to the office of President of our famous club and I much appreciate the fact. During the past few months I have tried to attend as many committees and functions as possible. While attending committee meetings I have been pleased to see how many hard working and diligent committee members we have, working for the good and upward mobility of Belgrave Harriers. These several committees are of course run by their separate secretaries but so well held together by the Belgrave Committee Chairman (Alan Mead) that the club has a great sense of united direction. I believe that it is of paramount importance to our club that we do maintain this sense of union amongst our various athletic disciplines and club interests. It would be a poor reflection on Belgrave Harriers if we should be seen by people outside the club to be disunited within. As officers and members we should always be so aware that by working ever closer together whether in committee room or the competitors' arena, we can retain and even improve the greatness of Belgrave Harriers. In this, my first opportunity of a "Presidential Address", I would like to thank immediate Past President Ted Pallant for the smooth efficiency of his handover to me, with all his helpful advice and support. Thanks also go particularly to all those other club stalwarts who have been my friends over so many years and especially over these past few months of my presidential term. Highlights of my year so far have been, and I must of course start with, the proposal and election to President, quickly followed by a superb Club Dinner and the Youth Awards evening at the Polka Theatre – all this before Christmas. Since then we have enjoyed the increasingly popular Burns Supper which I am pleased to help organize with the ever-energetic Derek Manning and his team. I was amazed at the quality and content of the Youth Scheme's magazine, a really superb production which can only complement the Belgravian; although the thought does cross my mind that they could both reach a wider audience if they were put together and perhaps produced twice a year. Food for thought perhaps. In closing I would like to extend to all Belgravians everywhere my very best wishes for a successful 1998 season, whatever your particular discipline or standard of competition. Lionel Mann R.V.M. items.sum: Profile of club president Lionel Mann, from his recruitment at Battersea Park in 1965 through his running career, personal bests, club offices and career as Chief Chef at Buckingham Palace.
items.s: A Profile of The President Profile of club president Lionel Mann, from his recruitment at Battersea Park in 1965 through his running career, personal bests, club offices and career as Chief Chef at Buckingham Palace. A Profile of The President written by Gordon Biscoe It was during the anniversary celebrations for Bill Lucas last April when it was realised that an almost complete London to Brighton relay team of yesteryear was present and that a reunion photograph would be a good idea. It fell to me to try and get them all into one place for a few moments, but when I tried to shepherd Lionel alongside the others I was told "But I never ran the Brighton – before my time!" The point is that Lionel has become such a part of the 'Belgrave furniture', such an integrated member of the road and cross country scene that, in spite of all those years as secretary and team manager I could not reconcile as to him not having been in the team. It was in fact 1965 when Lionel was spotted training at Battersea Park by our immediate Past President Ted Pallant and Joe Dooley *. They were told, when they approached him, that he was only training to keep fit for football. Always on the look out for potential talent,Ted's persuasive tongue went to work and Lionel was duly signed for Belgrave – and what a signing that turned out to be. Never one to stand on ceremony or do things by halves, Lionel quickly made his mark in our teams, both on the track and the road, as well as over the country. No mean feat in itself considering the middle and long distance talent we had in those days. By 1967 he was 'runner up' in the Club 20 mile Road Championship and earned himself his first representative appearance for his native county Beds & Hunts. So started an outstanding career in athletics with some of his achievements only just falling short of international recognition, as the recorded times below bear witness. Space does not allow a complete examination of his successes over the years but a brief summary, which must suffice, shows Lionel as having: – ◆ Competed on road, on the track and over the country at all distances from 400 metres to 37½ miles, as well as a number of hill races in Scotland – only small things mind you, like Ben Nevis at 4,406 feet in 2hrs 18m 33secs! ◆ Been Club Champion sixteen times (and runner up on another eighteen occasions) at 5 ¾ miles; 20 miles and Marathon on the road; 5km and 10km on the track and 7½ and 10 miles cross country. ◆ Been Bedford & Huntingdonshire County Champion four times over 5km, 10miles and 20 miles; Civil Service Champion at 5km and Marathon and Vets AC Champion three times at different age groups over 10 miles on the road. ◆ Represented the Civil Service, Kingston Borough and HMY Britannia on numerous occasions. Lionel leads Bob Smith, Dick Piotrowski, and Adrian Major during the Belgrave 7½ miles Cross Country Championship of 1968 but all four had to give way to Tony Fairclough (1st), Laurie O'Hara (2nd) and Pat O'Connor (3rd) by the finish. The field was 36 strong. ◆ Achieved personal best times of: ◆ Has to date run around 1720 races and a total distance of approximately 85,000 miles – equivalent to 2½ times round the world – these figures subject to 'update' as he has not stopped yet! Alongside this active career, which earned him a Club Honours Badge in 1968, he has combined official duties as well. Lionel was a committee member 1968/69; Road Running Captain 1969/76 and medals secretary 1987 to the present day. His club efforts were rewarded with election to Life Membership in 1989. While all this was going on, Lionel still found time to marry his charming wife Pat, raise a family, (Robert, Katherine and James who have also turned out in Club Colours) and advance his career as a chef with the Royal Household. This he has done with great success, having now attained the position of Chief Chef at Buckingham Palace and the award of the Royal Victorian Medal. Needless to say such a career has led to many unsociable hours and days but from the start Lionel was determined not to let the training suffer, so whenever he goes on Royal duties throughout the world, the kit goes too. In his more competitive days when alongside the likes of Pat O'Connor and Bill Weller they were the scourge of the road running scene, Lionel could often be spotted by the early riser, keeping the mileage up by running, cycling or even pushing the bike between his home in Molesey and Buckingham Palace! As if all this was not enough he has for many years helped run a Scout Venture Group near his home and acted as a lynch pin for the Royal Household Sports and Social Club, organising many of their functions and occasionally returning to his first love by turning out for their football team. In latter years he has also been joining forces with Derek Manning in master-minding the Club's Burns Night suppers. Lionel Mann is now known throughout the athletic fraternity, particularly 'on the road' where he was at his formidable best. During his time he has not only been an uncomplicated loyal member, but a great ambassador for Belgrave as well as for athletics in general; truly an athletes, athlete. It was typical of Lionel when told of his nomination as our President for 1997/98 to comment, "well, if I am going to do the job I aim to do it properly". We could want for no better man for the task! * Older members may remember Joe Dooley, referred to above, who regularly trained at Battersea and who for many years owned and wore that 'famous' Club vest which was a series of holes, held together by pieces of material in faded Belgrave colours! 800m 1:57.8 1 mile 4:16 10km 30:45 10 miles 48:48 Half Marathon 1:08:53 20 miles 1:44:45 Marathon 2:24:07 Lionel leads Bob Smith, Dick Piotrowski, and Adrian Major during the Belgrave 7½ miles Cross Country Championship of 1968 but all four had to give way to Tony Fairclough (1st), Laurie O'Hara (2nd) and Pat O'Connor (3rd) by the finish. The field was 36 strong. items.sum: Club news notes across two pages: Pam Davies's stroke, births in the Gilby and Staines families, walking and coaching news, retiring officials, corrections from readers, Dwain Chambers's awards, Arthur Penny's 90th birthday, and news of former members Steve Williams, Peter Hall, John Thresher and Doris Nice.
e: South of Thames Cross Country Championships
items.s: Sidetracks Club news notes across two pages: Pam Davies's stroke, births in the Gilby and Staines families, walking and coaching news, retiring officials, corrections from readers, Dwain Chambers's awards, Arthur Penny's 90th birthday, and news of former members Steve Williams, Peter Hall, John Thresher and Doris Nice. Sidetracks We were very concerned to hear that Pam Davies had been taken ill while running from Belgrave Hall one Saturday in late January. Pam was taken to St. George's Hospital where she was soon discharged. The following day, at home, she didn't seem too bad at first but as the day progressed she did become very unwell and eventually suffered a stroke. After a week in intensive care Pam was allowed out of bed and at the time of writing, at the end of February, she is undergoing physiotherapy. Still in hospital, steady progress is being made and all Belgravians will want to join in sending her best wishes for her journey down the road to full fitness and health. We look forward to seeing you back at the Hall again soon Pam. The cross country crowd is growing. Recently we welcomed two week old Matthew Gilby to his first cross country race where his dad ran to 5th in the South of Thames Championship. Congratulations to Jodie and Clive on the safe arrival of their baby Matthew, a brother for Daniel. Baby Thomas Staines made his entrance on Sunday 22nd February and weighed in at 7lbs 2oz. We hear that he's got a fair old pair of legs on him – but then with a mum and dad like Linda and Gary he would have, wouldn't he. Our very best wishes to the Staines family. We are very pleased for you. "Suffolk" Mick Graham has recently passed the first stage of his Race Walking coaching examination; we hear that he is well on the way towards qualifying as a judge as well. All this alongside finding himself, in the space of a couple of seasons, promoted from cross country "also ran" to county champion walker. Yes – he picked up the Suffolk 10 mile title to go with his track 3k title a few weeks ago. Who says you can't teach an old dog new tricks! Dave McMillan is training well. The last time we heard, he was regularly up to 10 miles on a Saturday afternoon in his quest to return to the London Marathon field. He recently completed the Hogs Back race and a small celebration was held afterwards to salute his progress. Some might not have walked again after those awful injuries. Incidentally, the paramedic who saved his life at the roadside received an award for his marvellous work. We must record our thanks to Mervyn Dessa for many years work as a track judge. Mervyn, who has not been keeping too well of late, has decided to retire from judging this summer and will be sorely missed. He tells us that he has been with the Club for seven years during which time he has greatly enjoyed our company and friendship. Win Shepherd is another stalwart at our track meetings, churning out the result sheets in the "caravan". Win is troubled badly by arthritis in her hands which makes recording the results very difficult. She would very much like to pass on her expertise to someone else. Any offers? Many thanks to you also Win – how many points you totted up for us over the years? Yet again Bill Couzens carried off the Denmark Pot for the Darts Championship. It was Bill's eleventh win in the 34 years that the event has been held. Next nearest is John Martin on five wins. More sidetracks on page 9 Sidetracks Eagle-eyed Pete Mulholland spotted a little howler in our last issue. On page 59 we showed Jim Estall runing past the Peace Pagoda during a VAC 5.2-miler and mentioned that the edifice had only seen one faster run by a veteran – and that by Laurie O'Hara. Knowing that we are sticklers for accuracy, Pete says, "I would point out that Laurie's 26:26 for the Veterans 5.2 in Battersea Park was set in 1976 – before the Peace Pagoda was built!" It's good to know that every word of our magazine is devoured by those outside our club as well! Another non-Belgravian to read our mag., Dave Cocksedge, points out a couple of adjustments that should be made to our 1996 T&F Rankings. Phil Goedluck's 10.88 100m was windy (+3.3) while we failed to record that Jon Ridgeon had a 47.7 400m at Barn Elms on 8 Sep and Ben Cascoe a 52.22m javelin throw at Croydon on 8 Jun. Thanks Dave. Deniz Gezgin, our popular young 400 metre runner, returned to his home country of Turkey for the summer and at Ankara ran in Junior European Clubs Cup 200 metres where he clocked 21.8. Not one to let grass grow under his feet he is now at Arkansas University but is keeping in touch via coach Bob Bridges. Janine Brown from Folkestone became an outstanding young middle-distance runner during her time with us. She is now competing for her local club Ashford AC and we were delighted to see her representing them in the SMC National Junior League promotion match. She sends her best wishes to all those in the Club who knew her. Not surprisingly Dwain Chambers received plenty of accolades after his success in retaining the European Junior 100m Championship in World Junior Record time. Among his awards were the George Hogflesh Trophy as the top English T&F Junior of 1997 (World Junior 100m record 10.06) and the Joe Turner Memorial Trophy for best male U20 AAA Champion (100m in 10.32). Seen training from Belgrave Hall: Hendrick Ramaala, Republic of South Africa 10k record holder and winner of the Great North Run ending a run of six Kenyan victories. Pity we can't turn him out for the "12-Stage". We hear that Ron Severn has regretfully had to step down as organizer of our Annual Club Dinner. We thank you greatly Ron for your efforts in making sure that this event has continued to be among the highlights of our club year. Good news is that someone has already stepped in to take up the reins – our ever energetic Hon. Treasurer Derek Manning. Derek informs us that the 1998 Dinner will again be held at The Preston Cross Hotel, on Saturday 14th November. Ticket prices remain unchanged at £27. Jacqui Smiter has had a short spell in hospital for a wrist operation. We hope that her recovery is swift and look forward to her teaming up with Cynthia James again this summer to capitalize on our promotion the the Women's Southern League Division Two. Arthur Penny, Empire Games 6 miles Champion in 1934, recently reached his 90th birthday and is just coming up to 70 years of continuous club membership. Arthur underwent an operation for gallstones recently but we hear that he keeping well and we are looking forward to a little get-together at the Hall soon when we can celebrate his long and illustrious time as a Belgrave Harrier. Talking of birthdays – here's a few that might stun you: Charlie Manning, Charlie Walker, Arthur Bruce and Reg Hopkins all reach their three-score and ten in 1998. Just think, a whole new age-group in which to record Club Best Performances! Does anyone know the whereabouts of Frank Ward, our Life Member and ex-Hon. Treasurer? Please contact the Membership Secretary Carl Lawton [phone number withheld] if you have Frank's 'phone number or address. Steve Williams writes from deepest Sussex. A true statistician, the article about the Christmas Paalauf in our last issue prompted him to inform us that he has now, on his own, achieved the combined ages of John Gladwin and himself when they won the event (and it seems like yesterday). Having taken early retirement, Steve says that the days and weeks run into one another at a pace never experienced when getting on the Northern Line five days a week! In spite of being surrounded by superb downlands and cliffs, he no longer runs or jogs due to a hip problem; his heart and mind are willing but his skeleton isn't. Nevertheless, he and Sue get in plenty of walks, especially now that they have re-housed a 5 year-old Labrador/Golden Retriever cross. Work now seems an even dirtier word than ever it was and although they live their lives along principles established by Mr. Micawber, Steve says that there's a smug look on his face when he reflects on former colleagues now chained to desks in Coventry when, on a sunny afternoon, he sups his half of Sussex bitter at the Golden Galleon while overlooking the meandering Cuckmere River. Steve and Sue send their best wishes to all. A member of our veterans' T&F team in 1996 was Ian Vaughan-Arbuckle, a member of Ryston Runners but second-claim Belgrave due to the fact that he lived and worked in London during the week. Unfortunately our old friend "Von Carbunkle" has been forced to quit running due to persistant knee problems. At a southern league match last summer we ran into old second-claim Belgravian Peter Hall, now a stalwart (and field event referee) with the host club on that day, Milton Keynes. It wasn't long before tales of the "old days" were being recalled. As a Polytechnic Harrier he was a keen supporter of the London–Brighton relay where Belgrave, Poly. and other rival clubs met up at the Black Swan at Pease Pottage on the way back to town. There they would attempt to out-sing each other with ever more doubtful ditties. One year even the coach driver got so drunk that a Poly member with an HGV licence had to drive the Poly bus back home. Peter passes on his best wishes to old training mates, particularly those from the Hurlingham days: Fred Paget, Lionel Mann, Pat Newell and Chas. Walker. Too late for the Winter Fixture List we received the names of the Captains of our young women's winter teams: Under 20 Women – Debbie Hearn and Under 15 Girls – Rebecca Lester. We have recently heard from John Thresher a regular first team man on track and country in the '60s who has been living in Toronto, Ontario for many years now. John has remained very much involved with the sport of athletics and has just accepted the position of President and Chief Executive Officer of Athletics Canada. What a hot seat to sit in. John will be establishing a new executive office for Athletics Canada in Toronto but the national office will remain in Ottawa for the time being so he'll have to get used to a fair bit of commuting. And then there's the Commonwealth Games in Kuala Lumpur, the "Worlds" in Seville, the Olympics in Sydney – tough eh! John is still running four times a week but only about four miles at a time. Our Life Member Doris Nice tells us that she enjoys reading the Belgravian, particularly the bits and pieces about the older members she has known through many years in the sport. When she read the feature on our immediate Past President Ted Pallant she felt that it was like reading her own history. "I always thought I knew the name when I saw it on the fixture cards," she writes, "but now I can see that Ted and I went to the same schools." Doris was born in Battersea and trained regularly for athletics in Battersea Park but as Belgrave didn't have a ladies section in the '50s, joined Surrey AC. Then, as a respected member of Surrey AC she automatically became a Life Member of Belgrave when both clubs amalgamated. items.sum: The Hon. Secretary's report to the 1997 AGM, dated 18 September 1997, covering deaths of members, a new disciplinary procedure, senior and junior successes across track, cross country, road and walking, and a call for more officials and helpers.
e: South of the Thames Cross Country Championships
items.s: Hon. Secretary's Report to the 1997 Annual General Meeting The Hon. Secretary's report to the 1997 AGM, dated 18 September 1997, covering deaths of members, a new disciplinary procedure, senior and junior successes across track, cross country, road and walking, and a call for more officials and helpers. Hon. Secretary's Report to the 1997 Annual General Meeting Sadly, three long-standing members of the Club died during the year: Lovell Cole, Jack Goswell (President 1964/65) and Laurie O'Hara. One matter of Club administration: the Committee have approved a procedure for handling any future disciplinary case. It includes among other things the right to appeal to a panel made up of Committee members who took no part in the original disciplinary hearing; it will be for this panel to decide in the light of the written appeal whether there are grounds for an actual appeal hearing. I will provide a copy of the statement of procedure for any member who wishes. In terms of athletic competition, the past year has overall been possibly our most successful ever. I will start at senior level. Our men have had yet another extremely successful track and field season. Under the team management of John Jeffery and Bill Laws they won both the First Division of the British League and the British League Cup by big margins. Despite the difficulties caused by the British League team always having first claim on athletes, the men's Southern League team managed by Bob Bridges have maintained their membership of Division 2 to which they were promoted last year. In the Rosenheim League, with Pat Mead as team manager, we won all but one match in our division and went on for the fourth successive year to win the league final. Our women's Southern League team, managed by Jacqui Smiter and Cynthia James, have subject to confirmation achieved their aim of gaining promotion to Division 2; and Sarah Roberts (400m) became our first female T&F international for a good few years. Seven first-claim members of the Club were selected for the World Championships in Athens: Darren Campbell (100m); both he and Dwain Chambers (still a junior) in the 4x100m relay, for which they received bronze medals; Chris Rawlinson (400m hurdles); Brendan Reilly (HJ); Dave Smith (hammer); Andy Tulloch (110m hurdles); and Matt Yates (1500m). Add to that Adrian Passey, second-claim, in the 5000m. And Geoff Dearman (4x400m), Matt Douglas (400m hurdles) and Stuart Faben (javelin) gained selection for the European U23 championships. Last year's very welcome improving trend over the country has continued. Our senior men, managed by Alan Mead, were second in Division 1 of the Surrey League, and indeed won the last match. We were second team in the South of the Thames Senior, and became Surrey team champions for the first time since 1967, with Gary Staines winning the individual race. The women, managed by Harry Porter, did enough to remain in Division 1 of their Surrey League. On the road, Belgrave won the men's team race in last September's Great North Run; and Paul Evans went on to win the Chicago Marathon in a very fine 2:08:52 (with Gary Staines fifth) and to return 2:09:18 in the London Marathon in April. I turn to the younger age groups. What we hope will become the highlight of the season for our younger teams is still to come – at Copthall Stadium on Sunday 21st September, in the promotion match in the National Junior League. Finishing in the top two [in the event they were first!] would see the Belgrave U20 men's team, which has been managed by John Powell, into the Premier Division for the first time ever. The young athletes team, now managed by Laurence Rogers, fell marginally short of equalling last year's feat of reaching the McDonald's Young Athletes League national finals, but remain one of the top sides in the country. Individually the highlight of the season at junior level was Dwain Chambers's gold medal in the European Junior Championships, in the world U20 record time of 10.06 seconds. (You can see Dwain in action at Copthall on Sunday, where he has agreed to run 100m, 200m and the relay for the Club.) Three other Belgrave Harriers were selected for these championships: Philips Idowu, who narrowly missed a medal when fourth in the triple jump, Michael Parper (400m) and James Hilston (4x400m). Other very fine performances during the season included Michael Parper's win in the Surrey County senior 400m, while still a junior, in a championship best time; and Philips Idowu's championship best triple jump at the English Schools' meeting. Marlon Kerr and Chris Lambert also gained selection for England in the schools international meeting. Our young walkers, from the youngest age-groups through to the U20s, have also gone from strength to strength under the management of Steve Whorlow, and latterly also Mabon Dane. Times have been set that have not been seen since the '60s and '70s, and international honours have been awarded to several, spearheaded by Nigel Whorlow. The Schoolslink project has again been a great success, with Belgrave coaches visiting many local schools, and our relationship with the local authority in Wandsworth has been further cemented with a second year of the borough's schools track and field competition. A schools liaison officer has now been appointed. After this story of success I need, I am afraid, to end by repeating the concluding remarks of my report at the last AGM. More help is needed in the work that it takes to operate the Club and to provide the services – of all kinds – that members expect. All too few people are doing the jobs that need doing – on the Committee, as coaches, managing teams, or officiating at meetings. Several are doubling up on jobs in the Club, and frequently they are working full time to earn a living as well. As you can see from the agenda, a number of Committee posts remain vacant. We are beginning to be recognised as a club that never fails to turn out its quota of officials, and a good number of them are making the effort to reach higher graded status; but we take part in so many fixtures that we have to draw very deeply – too deeply – on the time of our most dedicated men and women, one or two of whom have judged at over 40 club matches. We badly need more officials, especially those prepared to travel to away meetings. Moreover, some of those coaching and team managing – particularly among the younger age-groups – are extremely hard-pressed. I gather very worryingly that nobody is prepared to manage our young male cross-country teams in the season that is shortly to begin. [In fact Reg. Hopkins stepped in to fill the breach.] In any of these areas, if you think you can help, or even know someone who might, please let the appropriate person know. Anyone who can spare the time to help in any of these roles will be very welcome. C. Henn 18 September 1997. C. Henn C. Henn Hon.
