items.sum: Note on a 1935 British Games programme bought by Eric Hall, recalling Belgrave's 3 Mile Match against Birchfield (won individually by Jim Ginty) and an Open Flash Relay.
items.s: Belgrave vs. Birchfield 1935 Note on a 1935 British Games programme bought by Eric Hall, recalling Belgrave's 3 Mile Match against Birchfield (won individually by Jim Ginty) and an Open Flash Relay. Belgrave vs. Birchfield 1935 Continuing his quest for items of sporting historial interest Eric Hall recently purchased a programme for the British Games of 10th June 1935. There was a 3 Mile Match between Belgrave and Birchfield and the introduction states that Belgrave "prior to the Great War did little ....since, however, their rise to fame has been remarkable" . It then lists the various wins both cross country and walking. The Captain that day was Bert Footer and the rest of the team were Allum, Carter, Flower, Ginty, Parker, Patience; Shaw, Ring, Rice, Shields and Taylor. The June/July 1935 Belgravian reports that "the race will be long remembered by those who had the pleasure to witness it. At 1 mile Birchfield led; at 2 miles we were leading handsomely, but in the last lap our Midland friends managed to pack in together and inflict a 4 points defeat upon us." Jim Ginty won the event with a time of 14 mins 43 secs. Another item in the programme took my eye and seems quite relevant even today! An Open Flash Relay provided a "novel competition....and ideal practice for fast passing of the baton. Errors in this respect have more than once put us out of Olympic and International events". The race was for teams of three with a run up of 40 yards; exchange 15 yards; run 40; exchange 15 and run in 40 yards. A Belgrave team of Dyke, Bone and Mewes was entered. Evidently it was a regular race as previous times of 10.8 etc are given and winners had been Poly and Blackheath. It does seem, however, that although it was well intentioned the lessons on baton changing need to be revived! The Surrey AC team included a G. H. G. Dyson who became the national coach post war and was then responsible for the relay teams who still, occasionally, made a mess of things. items.sum: Report, adapted from Havant AC's Track Record, of George Piddington completing his 50th marathon in a wheelchair pushed by Havant AC clubmates at the South Coast Marathon.
items.s: George's 50th Marathon Achieved Report, adapted from Havant AC's Track Record, of George Piddington completing his 50th marathon in a wheelchair pushed by Havant AC clubmates at the South Coast Marathon. George's 50th Marathon Achieved As previously reported, George Piddington, a member of the Bels. for nigh-on 40 years, suffered a heart attack while out running and training for that elusive 50th marathon. Left with Parkinson's disease one might have been forgiven for thinking – "Well that's it, he'll never do it now". Never underestimate a marathoner, however, and also, never underestimate the friends one makes in this great sport of ours. Living on Hayling Island since 1965, George has also been with Havant AC for the last twenty-seven years and nine of his gallant colleagues from that club rallied round and took turns to push him around the South Coast Marathon, collecting for the Parkinson's Disease Society along the way. In his NHS Mk I rear-engined wheelchair, George clocked 3 hrs. 31 mins., eight minutes short of his pb, with his team of "pushers" truly delighted to take on three mile stints each to help him complete his 50th. "He has done so much to help athletes at the club over the years and it was a great way of saying thankyou to him." The run was not without incident. At one changeover point the support car's doors became locked with the car keys on the inside and the support team on the outside. As a "pusher" and George sped off into the distance the next leg runner was left behind – with transport but unable to get inside it. After some quick thinking she raced off after George on a borrowed bike, leaving behind a panicking support crew. The RAC were summoned but couldn't promise to arrive for three quarters of an hour. An Irish runner, stopping to unwrap a boiled sweet, offered some advice, and after poking about with an old coat hanger, miraculously sprang all the car door buttons. Faster than one could blink (or remove the coat hanger) the car was full and being driven off in hot pursuit. The rest of the changeovers went like clockwork and the team, consisting of George and all nine of his club-mates, crossed the finishing line together – with George just a fraction ahead. You know, it didn't seem to matter how hard they ran, old George always seemed to maintain his position in front! Adapted from an article in Havant AC's Track Record George Piddington George Piddington completed 50th marathon (South Coast Marathon) in wheelchair in 3 hrs. 31 mins.; member for nigh-on 40 years George Piddington George South Coast Marathon Hayling Island Havant AC

items.sum: Obituary of Gwen Couzens, wife of Bill Couzens and long-time helper at club social events, followed by Bill Couzens's thanks for members' sympathy.
items.s: Gwen Couzens Obituary of Gwen Couzens, wife of Bill Couzens and long-time helper at club social events, followed by Bill Couzens's thanks for members' sympathy. Gwen Couzens Very sadly we must announce that Gwen Couzens passed away before Christmas after a prolonged and courageous battle with illness. Like many another lady who married a member of our club, she immediately became a "Belgravian", long before our doors were officially officially opened to female members. Looking back over the years we can see her helping our club in so many ways. She was there lending a hand when the jumble sales were one of our methods of raising additional cash. Social functions just did not seem to take place without Gwen's cheerful presence. She supported Bill through his athletic days in the Southern League, hosted those marvellous New Year parties, saw both her children become members of the Club and was bound up with the fortunes of the Bels. as we rose through leagues. A true sign of our regard for Gwen was that the chapel at Lower Morden was packed with family, friends and club members, many of those present falling into more than one of those categories. We will all miss her and we offer our deepest sympathy to her family, particularly Bill, Tina and David. Bill Couzens writes: To my fellow Belgravians and friends, Thank you for the many cards and letters of sympathy and the lovely floral and written tributes in memory of my dear wife Gwen. This has been a great comfort to myself and my family at this sad time. Your kindness is deeply appreciated. items.sum: News from Clive Shippen in Sydney about his coaching at Homebush and his chance meeting with former Belgrave decathlete Jim McGrath, who emigrated in 1961.
items.s: Clive Shippen writes from Sydney News from Clive Shippen in Sydney about his coaching at Homebush and his chance meeting with former Belgrave decathlete Jim McGrath, who emigrated in 1961. Clive Shippen writes from Sydney How time flies: we have to remind ouselves that it will soon be two years since he left these shores. Clive's business is now off the gound and he is a Fellow of the Institute of Engineers Australia. Still jogging three times a week, he also finds time to assist in pole vault coaching at Homebush track where he advises Peter Banks who won the Aussie decathlon title with 7915 points. Peter is being tipped to reach 8500 by Sydney 2000. Another lad aided by Clive also has outstanding potential – a 6'2" 17 year-old whose talent has already taken him to a 49.50m discus throw, an 11.05 100m, 6.80m long jump and 17.2 high hurdles. Note the name – Peter Elvy. Clive tells us of an old Belgravian that he ran into: ' I attended Homebush recently for a pole vault session with Peter. I was wearing my Belgrave track-suit, cap and carrying a Belgrave bag (how ostentatious!). An old grey-haired gentleman, in the process of coaching a girl vaulter, spotted my track-suit, approached me and said, "What's Belgrave doing out here then?" I looked baffled. "Jim McGrath is the name," he said. "You probably won't know me but I used to belong to Belgrave before emigrating in 1961." It took a while for the penny to drop and for my brain cogs to turn back to that era, and then I remembered. Impossible to recognize him of course, but I well remember how invaluable he was to us in trophy meetings with his decathlon skills. ' Jim featured well up in our ranking lists for 1959 in every field event except the triple jump and hammer and was also our best high hurdler for the year. By 1960 he was our top high jumper, long jumper, discus thrower, pole vaulter – and need we say – decathlete. items.s: Mabon gets a boost Mabon Dane's walking sponsorship from Crowe Insurance Group and his upbeat view of Belgrave's senior and junior race walkers. Mabon gets a boost Mabon Dane writes to tell us that he has had a boost to his walking thanks to a sponsorship deal with his employers Crowe Insurance Group who are covering some of his travel and kit costs to the tune of £1000. Attracted to the club after seeing the successes of the club's juniors and the enthusiastic turnouts of the seniors in races during 1995. Mabon joined early in 1996 and was followed within months by the current junior international Andrew Goudie. Full of enthusiasm, Mabon tells us that the Belgrave walking section from U20 above is about to see its best period in well over 10 years in the forthcoming season. Fast improving Nigel Whorlow moved up to the U20 age group in September 1997 while Andrew Goudie, already an U20, recently gained a second international vest when he represented Great Britain in Germany. Mick Graham, father of the current U13 National Champion, Paul Graham, is another fast improver having recorded his first sub 15 minute 3 km walk at the 1997 Belgrave track championships. He will be a force to be reckoned with over the next year. As for Mabon, he hopes to significantly improve on his existing times in a quest for selection for the 1998 Commonwealth Games. items.s: Brief obituaries of former members Len Adams and Tony Whincup. We also regret to record that two other Belgravians have passed on recently. Len Adams had not kept up his membership in recent years but was a regular runner with us in the 'fifties and 'sixties and was a good friend of the late Tom Carter. He must have always kept Belgrave close to his heart for his last wishes were that "... there should be no flowers but donations to be made to the Belgrave Harriers". Leo Coy kindly represented us at his funeral in Dartford. Tony Whincup died in October aged 75. We hadn't seen a lot of Tony in recent years but, a Belgravian since 1948, he was one of those myriad members who have remained true to his club over a long period. Like many others he got little back for his annual subscription other than the pleasure of knowing that his contribution went towards keeping the club moving forward. items.sum: Obituary of veteran middle-distance runner Laurie O'Hara, recalling his late start in athletics, his veterans' titles and world rankings, with two photographs.
e: British Veterans National Cross Country Championships
items.s: LAURIE O'HARA (1932-1997) Obituary of veteran middle-distance runner Laurie O'Hara, recalling his late start in athletics, his veterans' titles and world rankings, with two photographs. LAURIE O'HARA (1932-1997) It is with much sadness that Belgrave Harriers announce the death of Laurie O'Hara at the age of 65 years. He died only the day after attending a social function at Belgrave Headquarters. Laurie was probably the most consistent middle-distance veteran runner during the period 1972-75 when he recorded personal bests of 3:58.5 (1500m), 8:22.0 (3000m) and 14:28.2 (5000m). In 1973 he won the British Veterans National Cross Country title and led Belgrave to the team title in 1973 and 1974; it was in that latter year that he topped the World rankings at 3,000 metres and 5,000 metres. He was a late starter. During his twenties he played football for Harrow, Leatherhead and then, on amateur forms, for Reading FC. He kept fit during the summers by running at Hurlingham track and it was there that a Belgrave training pack discovered just how good he was at interval work. Laurie was a natural at such training and soon abandoned football to take up athletics at the late age of 29 years. Within weeks he was competing for the first team and after only a few months he recorded a fastest stage time in the London to Brighton Relay, gaining a team gold into the bargain. For the next ten years he was a familiar figure up and down the country; running through each year's fixture list with gay abandon, making up for his late start. Laurie reached veteran status in 1972, just as the World Veteran Association was formed. The inaugural international meetings at Crystal Palace and Cologne brought together for the first time teams from Canada, USA and Australia, sparking interest across Europe. Laurie made his mark on the International scene swiftly by scoring fine wins in the 5,000 metres events at both venues. Housed inside that diminutive 5 foot 4 inches, 8 stone frame of his was a ferocious finishing kick. Many of his winning margins were achieved in the last 150 metres and for this he gained quite a reputation. Medals continued to come his way as he moved up through the age categories but a persistent virus problem never gave him the chance to tackle the M65 group. Laurie was a quiet unassuming man, well respected and much liked. He will be sadly missed by his club and the veteran fraternity in general. Belgrave Harriers extend their condolences to his wife and family. Clive Shippen We will always remember Laurie O'Hara as a winner. The Dysart Dash 10k at Petersham on June 30th 1996 was one of Laurie's very last races and yet again he was the first man home in his category. Laurie O'Hara traverses Farthing Downs, Coulsdon, during the final Surrey Cross Country League fixture of the 1969-70 season. Belgrave took the team race and topped the League for the 5th consecutive year. We will always remember Laurie O'Hara as a winner. The Dysart Dash 10k at Petersham on June 30th 1996 was one of Laurie's very last races and yet again he was the first man home in his category. items.sum: Two short reminiscences of Laurie O'Hara racing in the TVH Road Relay in the mid-1960s and the 1963 Southern Road Relay, signed with initials.
items.s: Memories of Laurie ... Two short reminiscences of Laurie O'Hara racing in the TVH Road Relay in the mid-1960s and the 1963 Southern Road Relay, signed with initials. Memories of Laurie ... TVH Road Relay, Cranford, mid '60s. One hears runners talking of 'flying' when they are running at their best. Whilst among the runners milling about near takeover area I looked up and saw the leaders come into sight over the bridge. The sun was low in the sky and there was Laurie's distinctive and diminutive figure, silhouetted for a brief moment as he crested the rise. He was in full flow and I would swear that not once did his shoes touch the ground as he headed for home. A full twelve inches of golden sunlight shone between his shoes and the tarmac. Laurie was flying! (CEM) Southern Road Relay, London – Brighton, 1963. Portsmouth AC with their international runners were the team in those days. In the Southern Road Relay Laurie was on the 7th stage and took the baton from a youthful Tony Fairclough who had run his socks off to move up to within ten seconds of the leader. Laurie set off like a man with a mission and as the Gatwick Airport stretch was reached, came up to the Pompey runner's shoulder. The whole thing was recorded by a Belgrave movie camera team on a motor-bike. As the two runners approached a short underpass our man's last action before the two runner disappeared for an instant into the shadows was to turn his head and cheekily wink at the camera crew. Ten seconds later and out into the sunlight again – Laurie was 5 yards ahead and going away. Belgrave went on to win the Southern Road Relay that day to interrupt Portsmouth's domination of the event. items.sum: Obituary of Jack Goswell, Past President, Life Member and long-serving race walking secretary and team manager of Belgrave Harriers and R.W.A. official, with a photograph from 1974.
items.s: JACK GOSWELL, R.I.P. Obituary of Jack Goswell, Past President, Life Member and long-serving race walking secretary and team manager of Belgrave Harriers and R.W.A. official, with a photograph from 1974. JACK GOSWELL, R.I.P. Just before Easter, Jack Goswell, Past President and Life Member of Belgrave Harriers, died after a short period in hospital. Jack was a great Belgravian. He had two driving ambitions; to enhance the name of Belgrave and improve the organisation of the Race Walking Association Championships. Although not a top competitor, he was one of the all-time greats of race walking. He did take part in a few club races and the Nijmegan Marches. Jack joined Belgrave Harriers in April 1951 and within 17 months became the Hon. Race Walking Secretary. But he was much more than a Secretary, being coach, adviser and a brilliant team manager. Around a nucleus of champions like Stan Vickers, Eric Hall, Ray Middleton and Ray Hall, he built teams which, during his 15 years as Walking Secretary finished first on 18 occasions, second 13 times and third on seven occasions for Belgrave Harriers in Senior R.W.A. national road walking championships. In 1957 the club, under his guidance, took first place in all the R.W.A. championships in one year; 10 miles at Coventry, 20 miles at Hendon and 50k at Leyland, a feat never achieved before by any club. The 20k championship was not added to the championship programme until 1965. One can only marvel at the drive and enthusiasm which formed those teams and those which, on eight successive years between 1955 and 1962, won the Nijmegan Shield awarded then to the first club finishing a full team of eight walkers in the National 20 miles. Belgrave's and Jack's success was incredible when you remember that every walker who started must finish and none could afford to incur a judge's displeasure as each judge in a national championship then had the power to disqualify a competitor. Today the team size has been reduced to 6 and it takes 3 judges to disqualify a competitor. Jack's success was due to his in depth knowledge of his walkers and the opposition, an ability to generate intense team spirit, absolute faith in his team selections, enough determination to drive exhausted walkers to give 101% and to take full advantage of the rules of competition. In those days feeding stations were far apart so competitors had to depend on help from club supporters or on the generosity of others to survive. Today national championships are held on multi-lap courses with fixed feeding stations every 5kms. The Milan Trophy was awarded for the first time in 1962 to the club finishing the first full team of eight walkers in the R.W.A. 50k Championship. Belgrave, spearheaded by Ray Middleton, 2nd and Ray Hall, 3rd and marshalled by Jack, took the trophy. Another job performed by Jack, with the help of his wife Joan, was organising the annual Belgrave Open 7 Miles Road Walk each November at Wimbledon. He undertook this task for over 25 years. He was President of Belgrave Harriers in 1964–65 and for many years organiser of the '200' Club which helped to ensure that the club's finances were kept on a sound footing. In December, 1953 Jack was elected to the R.W.A. (Southern Area) Committee. He became Chairman in 1961–2 and President in 1963–4. On the death of Alf McSweeney (Highgate H) Jack became R.W.A. Hon. Championships Secretary in September, 1962. His experience of organising the Belgrave Open '7' and various other road walking races in the South, coupled with the invaluable support of his wife Joan, enabled him to carry out the duties of Hon. Championships Secretary with distinction. He held the post until the R.W.A. A.G.M. in September, 1967. For over 20 years Jack and Joan compiled the results of all 'nationals' and produced on-the-spot results for distribution to everyone free of charge. In 1971–72 Jack became R.W.A. National President and in September, 1973 he was made a R.W.A Life Member for long exceptional and meritous service to the Association. His wife Joan received the same honour a few years later. Jack was a perfectionist, which meant some people found he was not easy to work with when producing results. Finishing lists (numbers and times) had to be checked and re-checked. He expected all names, numbers and times to be accurate, no matter what the weather conditions on race day. He expected everyone helping to compile results, including Joan (usually the 'typist), to be constantly alert. As I was frequently one of those involved I saw Jack's annoyance when some mistake caused a hold-up in the production of results. I discovered that Joan was a lady of infinite patience. Over a period of some 25 years I had the privilege of serving on the R.W.A. Southern and National committees and various sub-committees with Jack and found him to be a very hard worker with a wide knowledge of current and past walkers and personalities in athletics. I think that he was disappointed that his abilities as a team manager were not put to the test as a G.B. walking team manager. Unfortunately during the last few years constant leg trouble made it difficult for Jack who was a Grade I walking judge to attend races. This, combined with the fact that he was a very independent character who liked to keep his personal life private meant that he had very little contact with the race walking scene in recent years. I, like many of those who attended his funeral, was surprised to learn that Jack had a twin brother Tom. Our condolences to Tom and his family. I shall always remember Jack as a great Belgravian, a man of great integrity who made sure that any task which he undertook for the Club or athletics was tackled with great drive and enthusiasm and completed satisfactorily. May his soul rest in peace. items.sum: Eric Hall's personal tribute to Jack as Belgrave's race walking secretary and team manager from 1951, with memories of training, outings and the Nijmegen Shield wins, and a 1953 photograph of Jack racing.
items.s: . . . he was "Mr. Belgrave" Eric Hall's personal tribute to Jack as Belgrave's race walking secretary and team manager from 1951, with memories of training, outings and the Nijmegen Shield wins, and a 1953 photograph of Jack racing. . . . he was "Mr. Belgrave" For those of us who were lucky enough to be members of Belgrave during the period when Jack was Race Walking Secretary he was the man we looked to for everything to do with our sport - he was Mr. Belgrave so far as we were concerned. Recollections flood in and they cover the whole range of sporting activity and emotions. He took over as Race Walking Secretary at a time when our fortunes were, comparatively, low. We had great teams pre and post war but by the early fifties many had retired. Jack's arrival on the scene, firstly as a competitor in 1951, and then only a short while later as Secretary changed all that. It is easier to give reasons for the change than it is to point to a date when things changed. Jack was first and foremost a motivator, a man you could not let down. Normally quiet encouragement was all he required but if need be he could use the whip to good effect. Jack always knew instinctively just what I needed, and I am sure I speak for many others. He was the team manager and unofficial coach who persuaded us to apply discipline to our training methods. Tuesday evenings, in the winter, almost without exception, found him at Wimbledon. He counted us out and waited patiently for us all to return! A quick cup of tea and a rush down hill for the train home. In the summer he watched us on the track while the longer distance men did "the bridges". Once home he had to reconcile his little black book with the money he had collected for race entries, outings, the Race Walking Record or the Club football competition. We would often hear of how late he, and Joan, worked to ensure that all ran smoothly. Race days saw him arrive early to organise our teams and, if it was a home fixture, sort out the officials and recording in readiness for the printing of the results and the prize giving. He took great pride not only in Belgrave's sporting successes but also in maintaining a very high standard of race promotion. He was more than ably supported by his wife, Joan, who was often to be found in cold, uncomfortable, venues ever ready with the typewriter and duplicator to ensure we all had a fully completed result sheet before we left for home. The pair of them were also a very formidable Belgrave team. Naturally enough both were pressed into service by the RWA, and other bodies, and so they became a corner stone of race walking at many venues. An all day stroll with Jack was an entertainment especially if Harry Shields was in the party. No matter how short of breath, or how tired the legs, one or other was ready with a quick remark which not only made it all worthwhile but also took our mind off what later became known as "the pain barrier" ! we were not averse to playing tricks and I will always remember the day when Jack, this time on his faithful bicycle, rode ahead of us to the next cross roads to take a rest. We found a short cut across a field which meant that we avoided the cross roads and it was some while before we heard Jack's voice some 400 yards behind us telling us exactly what he thought of us! As he was carrying our lunches he would have had the last laugh anyway. It was not unusual for one or other of us to 'phone him on a Thursday to talk about the Saturday race and just before putting the receiver down we would assure him that we would be at Waterloo in good time for the 8.30am to Salisbury – the race being in Sheffield! Only Joan knew just what he had to put up with from an unruly pack of athletes all intent on having a good time – Jack it was though who added the necessary ingredient to ensure that success came our way. During a race he would inform you of progress if he thought you needed to know or could do something about improving the position. For some of the time I was Club Captain which was a sinecure and Jack never once gave me bad news – always encouragement, always persuasion but never ever a moan. He led us to great heights during the period from 1955 to 1965 and I was very fortunate to be a member of many of those teams and please bear in mind that, in those days, Belgrave turned out nearly 60 walkers – rather more than many total fields these days. Jack organised the teams and had in mind handicap prizes as well as National titles. We had more than our share of both and to us went the glory, the trips overseas and the prizes, but Jack shared in our satisfaction and fulfilled the prophesy made by Alf Harley, when he took the job on, that in a year or so he could have a great team! Given that you could wear a British vest and not make the Belgrave "A" team it was a fair forecast but if anything pleased Jack most of all I like to think it was the long sequence of wins in the Nijmegen Shield given for the first team to get all eight men home in the National 20 mile walk – Belgrave won it eight years in a row! He was also very proud of the National Championships he put on at Wimbledon which meant a considerable amount of work – including course measuring involving sweeping snow off the road in order to paint white mile marks! The only occasions when Jack was absent from an event was if it clashed with an international at Twickenham – somehow he managed to get tickets every time but would never reveal the source. Well Jack, as I have said in the past, Many Thanks for just being there and doing so much for so many of us. I am confident that you will soon be organising the recording angels into some sort of order with the aim to beat everyone else in getting the celestial handicap results out! You could get contributions from many people and mount an issue of The Belgravian just dedicated to him – I have enough memories to fill a small book myself. Eric Hall The Competitor: It's 1953 and Jack, wearing no. 2, competes alongside Patsy Logan at Parliament Hill in the Highgate Harriers 1 Hour Track Race. items.label: March 1998
items.h: The light at the end of the tunnel is now dazzling
items.sum: The Young Athletes Race Walking Team Manager reviews Belgrave's revival in race walking during 1997, its young walkers' international, national and county honours, and thanks the seniors who coach them, with a photograph of young walkers at the Belgrave Open '7'.
items.s: The light at the end of the tunnel is now dazzling The Young Athletes Race Walking Team Manager reviews Belgrave's revival in race walking during 1997, its young walkers' international, national and county honours, and thanks the seniors who coach them, with a photograph of young walkers at the Belgrave Open '7'. Race Walking The light at the end of the tunnel is now dazzling Two years ago I said there was a light at the end of the Club's Race Walking "tunnel". That light is now shining bright and the Club has regained its status as a major force in the event. The Young Athletes Walking section has played a large part in this renaissance. They have joined the other sections of the Club in making the Bels one of the most successful all-round athletic clubs in the U.K. 1997 was expected to be fairly quite for the club after one or two of our teenage walkers had found life a bit more interesting elsewhere but it didn't turn out that way. The youngsters have gone from strength to strength, bringing back the spoils of competition time after time. It has been a busy year, with visits to the Midlands and the North being a regular occurrence. Sheffield was the venue for a Grand Prix, the National Road Walking Championships and the Inter-Area Match. The Club has produced county road & track champions, regional road champions and national champions and medallists. We are now gaining rewards throughout the country and with others coming in at the lower age groups and some joining at senior level, the new athletic year will hopefully bring even further success right across the age range. Andrew Goudie gained his Great Britain Junior Vest this year in a match in Germany and was joined by Nigel Whorlow who received his call to represent England at the end of September. Our younger athletes also got a taste of International racing by competing for the RWA 'Young England' team vs. Ireland in Dublin; Laura Fryer (for the second time), Paul Graham and Sam McNally were the Bels representatives in this match. For first time Race Walking was included in the Schools International Athletic Match (England vs. Ireland vs. Scotland vs. Wales). The event was held in Dublin and Nigel Whorlow represented the English Schools and gained the bronze medal. To compete in this event is the highest representative honour available in Schools Athletics. Six of our youngsters were picked for the Southern Area in the Inter-Area Match but due to prior engagements only two of them were able to take up the invitation. This did not stop Paul Graham winning the U13 Boys event. We also had representatives in the U15, U20 and senior Inter-County matches, with Nigel gaining a U.K. All-Time Top Ten time in the 3,000m at Crawley. Our regional and county representation is strong and is likely to get even stronger over the coming year. We also had many national, regional and county champions - too many to name them all here but they are all listed in the race reports. Overall we have gained 4 county golds and 2 silvers followed by 2 regional golds, 3 silvers and 2 bronze. On the national ranking scene we have quite a few young athletes at or near the top of the lists All looks well for the future of Race Walking within the Club. We have now established ourselves as one of the top three walking clubs in the country, both of the clubs above us being dedicated solely to walking. With the success we have been having the Race Walking section within the Club now stands proudly alongside all the other sections who have done the Bels proud over the past couple of years. One of the problems with Race Walking is the lack of encouragement from other sections of the Club. Youngsters who want to try out various events rarely get pointed in the 'walking' direction. It must seem very strange to those outside our Club when they see that all our youngsters in the race walking section live miles from London. I am sure that we must be able to get some of our other young athletes interested in the event. We have young walkers in Kent and Suffolk but none from our home county of Surrey. Finally thanks must go to those seniors who have helped coach our youngsters to their present high standard. They include Mabon Dane, Mick Graham, Dave Sharpe and Ray Hall. I look forward to another successful year. items.s: MICKY BROWN OPEN & YA GRAND PRIX STEYNING, 22 JUN 1997 Report and results of the Micky Brown Open and Young Athletes Grand Prix walks at Steyning on a wet day, with Belgrave second in the M.Brown Trophy; the text gives Mick Graham as M50 while the results list him as M45. MICKY BROWN OPEN & YA GRAND PRIX STEYNING, 22 JUN 1997 The trip to Steyning was made very difficult due to the races being held well off the beaten track. Nevertheless, with three trains and a bus journey for the Folkestone Squad and our boys from Haverhill staying overnight nearby to ensure they were there on time, the Club did very well to get the numbers out and provide the other teams with some stiff competition. It was well worth the effort as nearly everyone scored a pb. in spite of it being one of the wettest days of the year and many of the day's spoils went to the Bels. team. Starting with the under 11 girls, Lucy Asling had not only to contend with the worst of the weather but with some of the competitors who still needed a bit more coaching in the 'niceties' of Race Walking. She managed to come home in 2nd place with a big pb. In the under 11 boys' event we had our young 7 year old Andrew Graham showing how the event should be walked and he joined Lucy as one of the best stylists in the younger age groups as well as also getting 2nd place in another pb. Newcomer Jeremy Dawson also showed that he has the stamina and courage for the event. Among the under 13 boys young Paul Graham has started to put plenty of space between himself and the rest. Again he was 1st and with Sam McNally 3rd and Stephen Whorlow 5th (with a massive pb knocking over 1½ minutes off his previous best) the winning team prize was theirs once more. Laura Fryer's was the best race of the day. In the under 15 girls' event she chased the National Champion, Nicola Phillips of Dartford, all the way to the line. Laura had actually beaten her rival and friend the previous week in the Kent Schools Championships but here just lost out by 10 metres in spite of reducing her best ever time by another 18 seconds. The under 17 men's 5km race went to Nigel Whorlow who learned a lesson about even paced racing. He had worked out his lap times exactly and kept to them for the whole race but couldn't understand why he had not achieved his expected time. Oh dear! He had forgotten to add on a bit for the additional 200m at the beginning, making it a costly mistake in respect of his time. Racing at the same time, but in the U20M group was Andrew Goudie who gained a very respectable 3rd place to become our first member home in a race that also included the senior men and veterans. In the senior event Mick Graham (M50) set off like a train but was caught by Carl Lawton half way through the race. Mick, now one of the country's top veterans, also finished with a best ever time. A good day's racing was had by all our youngsters, with 5 first places and 5 others of our 13 entries getting into the frame. items.s: AAA U15/U17 CHAMPS. BIRMINGHAM, 17 AUG 1997 Report and results of the AAA U15/U17 race walking championships in Birmingham, with bronze medals for Laura Fryer and Nigel Whorlow. Race Walking AAA U15/U17 CHAMPS. BIRMINGHAM, 17 AUG 1997 We were well represented in the Championships this year. As previously the under 13s had to compete as under 15s and again they acquitted themselves well. But it was in the older age groups that we took our medals. Laura Fryer fought for the whole of her 3,000m race with Dartford's Nichola Phillips and Solihull's Kelly Mann. Unfortunately her early race tussles with the Dartford girl used up her reserves and her rival from Solihull caught and passed her on the last lap. Nevertheless, Laura can be very proud of the bronze medal she took home. In the under 17 men's event Nigel Whorlow decided that the position was more important to him than the time. As the day heated up it was decided to put water out in this 5,000m event. The Irish had sent over their big gun in the guise of David Kidd and with Tommy Taylor of Leicester also in the race it was to be a repeat of the Schools International only three weeks earlier in Dublin. Taylor blazed off but after 5 of the 12½ laps Kidd caught him and the positions stayed that way until the end, although as the Leicester man flagged Nigel began to get his sights on him until he ran out of time. items.sum: Report and results of the 78th Belgrave Open Seven Mile Walk at Wimbledon, won by Mark Easton of Surrey Walking Club, with Belgrave narrowly taking the team race and young Belgrave walkers winning most of the 2km races; with photographs of Andrew Goudie and Matthew Hales and of Paul Graham pipping Kevin Baker.
items.s: BELGRAVE OPEN '7' WIMBLEDON, 22 NOV 1997 Report and results of the 78th Belgrave Open Seven Mile Walk at Wimbledon, won by Mark Easton of Surrey Walking Club, with Belgrave narrowly taking the team race and young Belgrave walkers winning most of the 2km races; with photographs of Andrew Goudie and Matthew Hales and of Paul Graham pipping Kevin Baker. BELGRAVE OPEN '7' WIMBLEDON, 22 NOV 1997 The 78th edition of the Belgrave Open Seven Mile Walk resulted in a close win for the home club. Mark Easton of Surrey Walking Club stamped his authority on the race from the very outset. He was tracked by Steyning's Gareth Brown for the first half of the race but took the West Wimbledon hills in his stride as he went on to win by nearly a minute. The Sussex based club provided the second and third men home and with only four to score the team race looked to be heading Steyning's way but although out of the individual medals, the Belgrave squad packed their top competitors into 5th, 6th, 8th and 9th places to pip the Sussex men by three points - 28 points to 31. Junior Andrew Goudie was the Bels. first man home (54:45), one place ahead of club-mate Nigel Whorlow (55:37), still only an under 17. Mabon Dane was 8th (58:30) with veteran Team Manager Carl Lawton closing in the quartet (58:49). It was a tremendous effort for Carl who had been up until 4am dismantling the scaffolding and seating erected in Covent Garden for the Children in Need appeal. With little rest he then masterminded the race - and took home a first team prize to boot. Many of the Club's younger walking stars were also in action over the 2 kilometre course and between them they made virtually a clean sweep by winning every age group but one. Kevin Baker was the first under 17 in 10:41 but was actually pipped on the line by the outstanding Paul Graham whose 10:40 gave him the under 13 boys' title. Laura Fryer won the under 15 girls' event in 10:54 while Steve Whorlow took the boys' race in 13:12. Lucy Asling, only in her eleventh year, was 3rd in the girls' under 13 event in 14:04. 4, Surrey WC 54; 5, London Vidarians 127. Pipped on the line! items.s: INTER-COUNTIES MATCH CRAWLEY, 30 AUG 1997 Report and results of a 3,000m track walk at the Inter-Counties Match in Crawley, with four Belgrave walkers representing three counties and Nigel Whorlow setting a top-ten UK all-time U17 time. INTER-COUNTIES MATCH CRAWLEY, 30 AUG 1997 In a 3,000m track race with four Belgrave athletes competing for three different counties it was hard to know who to shout for, but the race did produce one of the finest inter-counties races for a long time. As far as the Bels athletes were concerned it developed into two separate races. Andrew Goudie vs. Nigel Whorlow (both Kent), and John Hall (Middx) vs. Mick Graham (Suffolk). Nigel and Andrew were side by side for the first 3 laps and then, as if something had startled him, Nigel took off and produced his race of the season. He almost passed Andy O'Rawe from Essex and produced a time that puts him in the top ten Under 17 All Time U.K. List. Andrew followed him home in 5th place while Mick decided that tagging closely onto John would give him a personal best. 4, (3rd in match) N.Whorlow 13:11.5; 5, A.Goudie 13:24.6; 7, J.Hall (M45) 14:22.8, 8 M.Graham (M45) 14:25.4. items.h: BILL LUCAS "... a bold spirit in a loyal breast"
items.sum: Clive Shippen's tribute to Bill (W.E.) Lucas, recalling his 3rd place in the AAA 3 miles that won him a 1948 Olympic place and his 61 years of service to Belgrave, with photographs from a club function; the piece dates both the author's first sight of Lucas and the following year's Olympic trials to 1948, as printed.
items.s: BILL LUCAS "... a bold spirit in a loyal breast" Clive Shippen's tribute to Bill (W.E.) Lucas, recalling his 3rd place in the AAA 3 miles that won him a 1948 Olympic place and his 61 years of service to Belgrave, with photographs from a club function; the piece dates both the author's first sight of Lucas and the following year's Olympic trials to 1948, as printed. BILL LUCAS "... a bold spirit in a loyal breast " It was in 1948 in the AAA Championships at White City that Bill first came to my notice. My 14 yrs. old classmates and I had been taken there by our enthusiastic P.E. teacher ("killer" Clark of SLH and later Hercules AC) to witness our first major meeting. We knew no-one of course, so when the 3 miles field swept round the first bend we decided to pick our winners rather like viewing horses in the pre-race paddock. I opted for a tall, stylish runner who looked a thoroughbred compared with many of the others. He was entered in the programme as W.E. Lucas, Belgrave H.; right next to G.F. Lucas of the same club. My ignorance soon became apparent when Sydney Wooderson became the first Briton to break 14 minutes for the distance, closely followed by the flying Dutchman Willie Slykhuis. Fortunately betting was strictly forbidden, as Bill was well out of the medals. Not until the following year's visit did W.E. Lucas come to mind again. There he was once again in the programme together with G.F. Lucas (Bels) and L.W. Herbert (Bels). Once again I was out of luck; Lucas was in the medals alright (3rd) but it was the wrong Lucas! In 1948 I hovered. This year the Championships were also the Olympic trials. Willie Slykhuis must be favourite surely and Alec Olney was already making a name for himself. I decided to back Bill for 3rd (one of my class-mates had decided to run a book this year). This time my loyalty paid off: Bill finished a brilliant 3rd and I made 5 shillings! As a result of his run Bill was selected for Great Britain in the 1948 Olympic Games. Four years later, coincidentally, I found myself a member of Belgrave Harriers. An early visit to Belgrave Hall found me enquiring who the fellow was with the clip-board: he looked familiar. On being told it was Bill Lucas I can still remember bursting out with "Not the W.E. Lucas". I was looked at rather oddly as Belgrave Harriers were blessed with several classy runners at that time and Bill would have been ribbed no end if Tom Carter, Footer and Co. had heard my utterance. Fortunately they didn't hear about my five bob win either. For the next 40 years or so Bill's imposing figure strode the stage of athletics fixtures and committees throughout England and I often wonder how many others have said "Not the W.E. Lucas!" There would have been many different reasons for saying this of course, for Bill has always been noted for speaking his mind; whether it be to a recalcitrant team member or the fully arraigned South of England Committee. He has been respected for it. But above all is his deep loyalty to Belgrave. He could so easily have become an international track referee, but he preferred to support Belgrave fixtures. He fought for Belgrave's interests in every forum. And can anyone remember a Belgrave Dinner without his presence? The Club has benefitted immensely from his membership these last 61 years. And should he ever reach those Pearly Gates and announce himself in his toastmaster style, no doubt a voice will be heard to boom "Not the W.E. Lucas!" items.sum: Eric Hall describes researching Olympic reports at the Olympic Museum in Lausanne and finding conflicting official accounts of Tommy Green's Olympic 50km walk win and Stan Vickers's 1960 Rome walks.
items.s: You Had Better Believe It! Eric Hall describes researching Olympic reports at the Olympic Museum in Lausanne and finding conflicting official accounts of Tommy Green's Olympic 50km walk win and Stan Vickers's 1960 Rome walks. You Had Better Believe It! Memory plays funny tricks – or so it is said. Can we believe what we read? The facts are twisted on occasions no doubt but when they are recorded in official reports it should be possible to rely on them, or at the very least there should be some acceptable explanation for the discrepancies. For many years one of my hobbies has been historical research, and, as some may recall, an earlier interest was race walking. This last year gave me the chance to combine the two and given that during a visit to an Internet site a year or so ago we found that our own Stan Vickers was said to be German I was ready for anything. The Olympic Museum in Lausanne, Switzerland, has a marvellous collection of exhibits depicting all aspects of the history of the Games and, in addition, there is a fine library and film archive containing records of every Games of the modern era. The library is open to all during normal opening hours and some video footage is available on screens either free of charge or for a small fee. In addition, by prior notice, it is possible to view other films from the archives and, if your pocket is deep enough, one may also purchase copies for personal use. During two days spent in the library and studios Mavis and I were able to relive our visit to Rome in 1960; see the Melbourne footage of my own and Stan's events, plus we had time to look through Games reports produced by the host cities and other National Olympic Committees. It was here that my memory proved fallible – or was it? Starting with an event which means much to a Belgravian but which took place in the year I was born we checked the Tommy Green story in two publications. The British Olympic Association report states that only seven of the fifteen starters finished and that Tommy and Dalinsch of Latvia were together only a mile from home. "The Latvian complained of cramp in his side, and the Italian (Frigerio) began to catch him. Dalinsch, responding gamely, fought off the challenge but, meanwhile, Green was forging ahead to finish more than seven minutes in front of the Latvian, who had a two minute lead of Frigerio, who collapsed on crossing the line". The German Olympic report on the same race has much the same story except that Tommy got away in the last three kilometres but it shows ten finishers! The other interesting point about the German report is that there are two photographs purporting to be of the same event – in one Tommy is wearing his British vest and number 98 (on his shorts which is not allowed today!) and in the other he is wearing a half sleeved vest, no number, but, possibly, a Belgrave badge! This latter picture also appears in the British report and is likely to have been an agency photograph I would think. Moving on to 1960, and the 20 kilometre walk, there may be some members of the Belgrave party who made the trip to Rome who would like to know that according to a photograph in the German report Stan Vickers is shown as winning the 50 kilometres although the title is Don Thompson! The American report of 20 kms. notes that "Vickers sinks exhausted to the turf. Two over-zealous Italian medical orderlies lift him up and before he knows what is happening he is whisked off in a Red Cross van to hospital where some British officials discover him hours later in perfect health. The Italian orderlies had failed to understand Vickers' protestations – in English – that there was nothing on earth the matter with him". Garbled to say the least but it must be official – the Americans say so! For those of you who have been brought up on a different account of events I prefer the British report which, correctly, states that it was Matthews who finished up in hospital after retiring at halfway. It is true that Stan's Italian was not too good but then what could you expect of someone who was described as being a German anyway! Don't always believe what you read – the truth is stranger than fiction but fiction is said to be more interesting – sometimes! items.sum: Report of the gathering at Belgrave Hall on April 19th to celebrate Bill Lucas's 80th birthday and over 60 years of service to the club, with photographs taken on Ted Pallant's camera.
items.s: Bill Lucas's 80th birthday Report of the gathering at Belgrave Hall on April 19th to celebrate Bill Lucas's 80th birthday and over 60 years of service to the club, with photographs taken on Ted Pallant's camera. A fine gathering of Belgravians turned out at Belgrave Hall on April 19th to celebrate Bill's 80th birthday and over 60 years of continuous service to the Club (with no signs of his letting up just yet!). A succession of articulate speakers took us back to the days of Bill's running, his selection for and appearance at the 1948 Olympics in the 5,000m, then his years of announcing at the White City. Verbal battles at Southern Counties A.A.A. were recalled, anecdotes of his exploits as an official: "... get those toes behind the line Ovett or I'm disqualifying you and your whole team!" – and two terms as President of our Club. Thanks to the wonders of modern technology Clive Shippen was able to telephone from Australia at exactly the right point in the proceedings with his words being broadcast to all present. With Bill having spent a considerable period as Belgrave's and Surrey's Cross Country Team Manager it was fitting that many of his team were able to attend or send messages: Gerry North, Alan Black, Laurie O'Hara were there – even Chris Steer had managed to fly in from North America. How wonderful to see George Piddington back at the Hall as well. Gordon Biscoe and Charlie Manning masterminded the event with Derek Manning arranging the catering. Well done chaps – and well done Bill. Below: Snowy Brooks, Ted Pallant and Sheila, Bill Lucas and Sheena enjoy the festivities at Belgrave Hall on April 19th. Above: Ted Pallant and Denis Brickwood recall old days and enjoy the 'spread'. Photographer unknown. It was Ted Pallant's camera that produced these shots but he couldn't possibly be the man clicking the shutter - he's in all the pictures!
