items.sum: Alan Mead's account of Belgrave member Etienne Gailly, the Belgian who led the 1948 Olympic Marathon at Wembley but was passed in the stadium and finished third, with sources and result; some foreign names are spelt differently in the text and the result box.
items.s: So Close to Olympic Glory Alan Mead's account of Belgrave member Etienne Gailly, the Belgian who led the 1948 Olympic Marathon at Wembley but was passed in the stadium and finished third, with sources and result; some foreign names are spelt differently in the text and the result box. Marathon Men - Etienne Gailly Fifty years ago, at Wembley Stadium, a young Belgian with strong Belgrave affiliations came within 42 seconds of Olympic immortality by Alan Mead The young Belgian Etienne Gailly seemed to have already packed more excitement into his twenty-five years than most of us see in a lifetime but fifty years ago this young man lined up for the 1948 Olympic Marathon with his sights set on a high placing. Just over two and a half hours later he was involved in a desperate finish that bore great similarities to the drama of that previous London Olympic Marathon of 1908 when Italian Dorando Pietri struggled to the finish in dire straits, only to be disqualified. In 1943 at the age of twenty, with his native Belgium occupied by German forces, Etienne had left home and travelled through France with the idea of somehow reaching Britain. There he intended joining some of his free countrymen with the aim of returning to his homeland one day to help drive out the invaders. He crossed the Pyrenees but was then arrested and spent the next six months incarcerated in a Spanish gaol. In due time he was released, the intention being that he should return to Belgium but Etienne still had other ideas and his travels took him on to Portugal, Gibraltar and finally England. Immediately he started training as a parachutist with the Brigade Belge but a tough paratrooper's training was not enough for this young man and having already done a little athletics at home he decided to join a British club. On April 29th 1944 Etienne (immediately becoming known as Steve) was elected a member of Belgrave Harriers and he found himself running alongside such notables as Carter, Cohen, Shields and Doubleday. Soon plans were being laid for the liberation of Europe. Second Lieutenant Gailly played his part and before too long was reunited with his family, although still managing to get back to see his running friends in England. With the War over and settled back in Belgium, Etienne raced for the famous l'Union Saint-Gilloise which numbered another Belgravian among its members—top miler Bill Nankeville. His athletics progressed and by 1948 he was not only the Belgian Marathon Champion but in a match vs. the French team Stade Francais, held to celebrate the 50th anniversary of his club, Etienne lapped the field to win in 31 mins. 52 secs.— not bad for a man now considered to be a marathoner. Entries for the marathon of the XIV Olympiad included some famous names. There was the diminutive Korean Yun Bok Soh who had set a World's Best of 2 hrs. 25 mins. 39 secs. in 1947, the Americans Ted Vogel and John Kelley, Boston winners Gérard Côte of Canada and Stylianos Kyriakides of Greece, Johannes Colemann from South Africa and a trio of Flying Finns — Viljo Heino (10,000 metre World Record breaker), Jussi Kurikkala and Mikko Hietanen (the European Champion). Britain's team included the redoubtable veteran Jack Holden, four-times winner of the International Cross Country Champs. and three times "National" champion, and the tough Welshman from South London Harriers, Tom Richards. Wembley Stadium was full to the rafters on Saturday, August 7th, the final day of the games, as the forty-one marathon runners circled the track and were directed out of the arena by the first (and last) pointsman of the race, our own George Chantler. Of the Belgrave competitors in the Games, Bill Lucas had gone out in the heats of the 5,000 metres earlier in the week, Bill Nankeville had placed 6th in the final of the 1500 metres, run in a down-pour, and as the marathon was taking place on the roads, the 10,000 metres Walk saw a below par performance from Harry Churcher who finished 5th. Interestingly, discussions at a Club "committee meeting", held while rambling the South Downs, had resulted in an agreement that as Etienne was not now living permanently in the U.K. he would not be considered one of our "internationals" even though he was racing in the colours of Belgium; a great shame. Under heavy skies and in humid conditions with an uncomfortable wind, the marathon field reached the Kingsbury Cross Roads and then headed on towards Stanmore. Etienne was surprised to find himself among the leaders. Together with his coach he had decided beforehand to totally ignore the other runners and follow a schedule which would bring him home in 2 hrs. 30 mins. He carried a stopwatch and regularly checked it to ensure that he was on schedule. Gradually the opposition fell away and although he was somewhat concerned that he had taken the lead so early, he decided that as he was following a schedule that he was convinced he could manage, he would stick to his plan. The marathon route had been gradually climbing from the start and after going through Stanmore and the 6 miles point in 34 mins. 34 secs. the inclines became ever steeper as Stirling Corner and Elstree were approached. At 13 miles he held a 24 second advantage over the unknown Lou of China and over a minute on the Argentinian Guinez and Frenchman Josset. The favourites were way down the field and it began to look as if Etienne, one of the youngest men in the field, was going to bring about an almighty upset. Unfortunately Gailly and his coach had based their calculations on a level course but the route chosen for the 1948 Marathon was later described as: " ... one of the most punishing ever selected for the Olympic Games. Only on the track of the Empire Stadium itself did the runners get respite from the up hill and down dale of the hard metalled roads." Etienne was coping well with the climbs but the extra energy he was expending was to cost him dear in the later stages. In his own words, reported later in World Sports magazine he tells us: "Surprised when I saw that I was ahead of the entire field at such an early stage I was convinced the others would soon re-establish contact with me. In fact I was often glancing back, expecting Heino and Holden to appear at my side. I considered them my most dangerous rivals and it was baffling not to see them coming to the fore. ... When after about 32 kms. the Korean, Choi, passed me and I could not respond, I asked myself: 'Is he travelling so fast or am I fading?' I had to admit to myself that my strength had left me temporarily. I could only watch how fast Choi was running. Although I hated this tiredness, I was not unduly alarmed. I had been alone in the lead for 27 kms: things looked not quite so good now but, after all, I felt nothing more than a normal tiredness which I hoped to overcome soon. Next the Argentinian Cabrera passed me. This, however, did not discourage me, not even when he gained some 60 yards on me, because just at this time I felt my rhythm coming back. I had got my second—or was it my third—wind." The Korean had run an amazing middle part of the race but no sooner was he beginning to look a likely winner than he began to limp and before long was forced to drop out of the contest. Tommy Richards was looking stronger as the race progressed and with just 2 kms. remaining it was impossible to predict the winner as just 16 seconds covered the Argentinian, the Belgian and the Welshman. Etienne takes up his story once more: "I joined issue again ... and closed quickly ... No sooner had I got into the Argentinian's slipstream than I decided to spurt without delay. I no longer felt powerless: on the contrary, I thought that now was the time to square the account. ... I passed Cabrera, and having regained the lead, seemed to be travelling well. Certainly I was tired, but quite convinced that I would last the distance. "It was then that I committed my biggest blunder ... To rejoin Cabrera I had to make good some 70 yards. Having achieved this I drew away from him too quickly because after about 1 km. I had left him 60 yards or so behind. This works out at over 100 metres overtake in only 2kms." The damage was done. Etienne was terribly exhausted—far more so than he realised. He still led as the stadium was approached but was mercilessly exposed to the two men doggedly trailing him. Sheridan tells us: "... with only a few hundred yards remaining it became apparent that all was not well ... Etienne Gailly was in obvious distress. Ashen faced with eyes bulging, he lost his sureness of stride and was almost staggering. Was he to undergo the same fate as had befallen Dorando Pietri forty years earlier?" And Etienne again: "I had no premonition of collapsing. At the very moment, however, when I stepped on the track, exhaustion overcame me like a powerful drug. Immediately after I had crossed the normal finishing line—unfortunately this was not the real finish—this lay 400 metres further on—I knew that I was going to be passed. I cannot deny that this last lap was hard for me. It was like the progress of a martyr. I was horribly weak, indeed, I almost fainted ... First Cabrera and then Richards passed me, as behind a veil. I was no longer fighting them but that awful engulfing weakness, wanting more than anything to get to that unbelievably distant finishing line. I got there ... somehow." The previously unrated Cabrera had run a perfectly judged race and seemed so strong at the end in comparison to the tottering Gailly. Afterwards he revealed that he ran no more than 36 miles a week in training. Thrilled as the spectators were with a British silver medal for Richards, Gailly's heroic struggle endeared him to the crowd and to all the athletics writers of the day. Within a week he had recovered enough to take part in a 3,000 metre race in Belgium and then he was 2nd in an inter-Allied Games 5,000 metres held in Antwerp. By September, in Prague, he was on international duty for Belgium again as he ran to 2nd in the 10,000 metres vs. Czechoslovakia. What a man. In Belgium he was awarded the Grand Prix d'honneur as the outstanding athlete of the year and the Trophie National du Merite Sportif for his performance in London. With youth on his side he surely would have been a red hot favourite for the 1952 Olympic Games in Helsinki and then there was 1956 and even 1960 when he would still be of an age similar to many of the pre-race favourites in the London event—but it didn't happen. Lieutenant Gailly was, after all, a soldier first and foremost and his adventures went on. In November 1951, while with his regiment of paratroopers in Korea, he was wounded when an exploding mine shattered seven bones in his left foot. He was flown to Tokyo for hospital treatment and later returned to Belgium for convalescence before his anticipated return to South East Asia for further duty. He was expected to have a permanent limp for the rest of his life and, as far as we know, Etienne never competed again. Sources: • Good Reasons: 100 years of Olympic Marathon Races by Michael Sheridan; published by the author 1996, ISBN 0952819201, obtainable from the author at [address withheld]. • World Sports Magazine 1948 and 1952. • The Belgravian, 1948, 1949. • Athletics, 1948. • The Miracle of the Mile, Bill Nankeville, Stanley Paul 1956. • Olympic Games, Tom McNab, Knight Books 1971, ISBN 0340150637. • Conversations with Charlie Jones. items.label: March 1999
items.h: Newsman who will be a winner in the long run
items.sum: Reprint of a Times article on Belgrave Harrier and journalist Dave McMillan, a London Marathon ever-present until a near-fatal road accident in 1996, before his return to the 1998 race.
items.s: Newsman who will be a winner in the long run Reprint of a Times article on Belgrave Harrier and journalist Dave McMillan, a London Marathon ever-present until a near-fatal road accident in 1996, before his return to the 1998 race. Marathon Men - Dave McMillan This article appeared in The Times of April 20 1998, just prior to Dave McMillan's return to the streets of London where he covered the 26.2 miles in 4 hrs.23 mins.02 secs. David Powell on the club athlete whose dream of sporting glory ended when he almost died after a horrific accident Dave McMillan was an ordinary club runner with the chance to achieve celebrity status. It might have taken him another 25 years or more, but he was determined to persevere. The first sign of interest in his one shot at sporting glory came in a letter from The Times. This newspaper was seeking information on the 42 runners — all men — who had completed every London Marathon and wanted to know how many would be lining up for No 16 that spring. McMillan's reply was dated January 31, 1996. In it, he said: "I'll run London again, I wouldn't miss it for the — world." Well, he did miss it, and got nothing in return, except a story about the day that running almost cost him his life. Only four days after penning his reply to The Times, McMillan was involved in an horrific road accident while out running. So serious were the injuries from his collision with a car that the paramedic in the ambulance decided that his patient would die before reaching hospital. The only hope was to pull into a lay-by and perform emergency surgery. Even then, McMillan's chances were slim. The operation, a needle thoracotomy, had a track record of 100 per cent failure. "Three paramedics before mine all lost their patients," McMillan said. "Mine was the first successfully to carry it out." McMillan had been found with fractures to his right arm, right leg, ribs and shoulder, but it was not until the ambulance was on its way to hospital that Graham White, the paramedic, became aware of extensive internal injuries. White discovered that oxygen was not getting through to the blood and that McMillan's right lung was collapsing. Dave McMillan had his right leg broken in four places, bone smashed in his right arm and nerve almost severed, five fractured ribs, shoulder blade broken in two places, and a punctured lung "He had to pierce through the chest wall into the lung with a steel syringe to drain the lung, which was filling up with blood," McMillan said. "The paramedic only has to be a quarter of an inch out and the patient has had it. Graham was voted Paramedic of the Year for saving my life." McMillan spent four days in intensive care, a month in hospital and returned for further surgery while the sixteenth London Marathon was taking place. Having never missed the race, he was now forced to watch from a hospital bed. "I wanted to get up and run it," McMillan said, recalling his frustration. "I thought that, if I could keep on doing the London Marathon, I might eventually be the only person who has run them all. Once I saw that race going ahead without me, I knew I had lost that chance." McMillan's instinct as a journalist told him that the last person left with a 100 per cent London record would attract big media attention. It may be another 25 years or more, given that the youngest is still only 39, but it meant everything to him to remain a contestant. Those who have kept going are showing a reluctance to fall by the wayside. Of the 42 ever-presents who ran in 1995, all but McMillan lined up in 1996 and 1997. Being a journalist, McMillan also understands the interest in him now. On April 26, he will be back, for his first marathon since his accident. "I cannot wait," he said. "It is going to feel fantastic." McMillan, a Belgrave Harrier, uses running as a vent for the pressures of work. In 15 London Marathons, he has finished between three and four hours every time. When he was out for a 14-mile run that eventful January morning in 1996, his mind was set on breaking three hours for the first time, having run 3 hrs. 5 mins. the year before. The competitor in him remains. To finish would be remarkable, but McMillan, 50, has higher goals. "In the 15 I have run, I have never been over four hours. My aim is to keep under four hours. When I applied to run in the first race, I had never run a marathon, but I finished in 3:42. My slowest is 3:56 in 1991. "Though he has set sub-four hours as his target, he is taking nothing for granted. How can he when he recalls that it was 11 months before he was allowed to walk and 20 before he returned to running last October. "The greatest fear every time I go out is that the leg will give way," McMillan said. However, he has the added incentive of using the marathon as a vehicle to raise money for the trauma unit at the John Radcliffe Hospital, Oxford, where he arrived after his roadside surgery. McMillan's record of never having missed a London Marathon may have disappeared into the back of an ambulance, but at least others may now benefit from his will to return. Sunday, 17th May 1998, and Dave McMillan completes the Oxford 'Town & Gown' 10 kms. items.label: March 1999
items.h: Belgrave Stars of the Silver Screen
items.sum: John Jeffery's humorous account of Belgravians running a filmed 1500 metres race at Crystal Palace for the International Museum of Sport in Munich.
items.s: Belgrave Stars of the Silver Screen John Jeffery's humorous account of Belgravians running a filmed 1500 metres race at Crystal Palace for the International Museum of Sport in Munich. — John Jeffery writes — An interesting side-line of being members of a large and successful club like Belgrave is that we are often asked to provide athletes for advertisements and sports programmes. So it was, that on a cold and gloomy day at Crystal Palace, half a dozen Belgravians gathered to compete in a 1500 metres race which would be filmed and later converted, using computer technology, into an interactive entertainment for youngsters and budding athletes. It would be initially shown in Munich at the International Museum of Sport and subsequently sent to various Sports Academies around the World. Briefly, the idea was that a motor-bike with a cameraman on board would film the race as if he were one of the competitors, finishing in 3rd or 4th position, and with careful editing it would appear to be a genuine race. And so they lined up! Wearing assorted vests, including some Belgrave ones, we had Matt Yates, Junior Galley, Clive Gilby, Dave Pamah and Kevin Quinn. To add to the international theme I twisted John Bicourt's arm and he supplied three of his Kenyan all-stars. The gun went and the race began. The cameraman was left at the start and had to spend the first lap weaving through the field to catch up. Matt Yates broke the habit of a lifetime and was up with the leader Clive Gilby. As the race unfolded various athletes took the lead until coming off the final bend, Matt broke away and held off the Kenyans to win in 3 mins. 54 secs. If only real life was as easy! The Director of the film was impressed with the initial results and it only remained for he and I to review the action and release the athletes. The first lap looked great with a group of athletes fighting for the lead in typical middle-distance style. And then, in growing horror, we saw that emerging from the corner of the screen was the lovely Mrs. Gilby (Clive's Mum) pushing his little boy into the second lane to cheer Daddy round the track. The Director turned several shades of puce before frantically using all his expertise to work out how to delete Grandmother, baby and pushchair from the action. We went into hasty conference. There was only one answer, we would have to do it again. I was delegated to break the good news to the athletes who were already warming down. Being loyal and true Belgravians they were all very phlegmatic and reconciled to the situation, treating the thought of running again with jovial banter. Did I really write that! No, let's be truthful, they went ballistic. There were immediate threats that included water jump, Mrs. Gilby, baby, pushchair and finally even the innocent Clive. Eventually we calmed them down and after much deliberation and careful scripting commenced the strangest 1500 metre race in history. Half the athletes started the race followed by the cameraman and bike. They ran the first lap and were then replaced by the rest of the field who were hiding at the start of the first bend. This went on for 3 laps with athletes filling in and dropping out until more by luck than judgement we had enough athletes on their feet to finish the race. Apart from two athletes (who shall remain nameless) being unable to catch up at any stage, it all worked very well and any of you visiting the Munich Museum will have the chance to peruse the finished product. If that is too far to go, the producer is sending me a copy which I will be delighted to lend to interested parties. Unfortunately I have been unable to persuade Mrs. Gilby to sign a copy for me. Who won the race? I'm sorry you asked that as, to make up the numbers, we brought in Mark Death who is one of the Senior Managers at Crystal Palace and a middle-distance runner. In the scramble for the line he dipped first. What's wrong with that I hear you ask? He's a member of Blackheath! items.label: March 1999
items.h: Cynthia James - Life Member of Belgrave Harriers
items.sum: Tribute to Cynthia James, joint women's team manager and tireless helper, elected a Life Member at the 1998 A.G.M.
items.s: Cynthia James - Life Member of Belgrave Harriers Tribute to Cynthia James, joint women's team manager and tireless helper, elected a Life Member at the 1998 A.G.M. In 1983 the James family first came into contact with Belgrave Harriers when 12 year old Cindy joined our women's team. Cindy brought with her more than her own athletic talent for within a very short space of time her mum and dad, Cynthia and Raymond, were helping out at track and field meetings and as time went by even young brother Richard found himself racing in Belgrave colours. Now, fifteen years later we can look back on the very valued help and friendship that this family has brought to our club, but in particular it is time that we officially recognised the work that has been put in by Cynthia. It was no time at all before Cynthia began to assist our Women's Team Manager, taking on ever more of the pre-match 'phone calls and hassles; ensuring that the girls got to their starting marks in time for their events; stepping in herself to heave a shot, discus or hammer should the need arise. She officially became Joint Team Manager with Harry Porter and continues in that role today with Jacqui Smiter. But Cynthia hasn't confined herself to looking after her athletes and chasing about with her team sheet. Countless times a thirsty track or field judge has had cause to thank her as she has provided seemingly unlimited supplies of tea, coffee and a veritable haystack of fruit cake and biscuits. It would be true to say that, thanks to Cynthia, we are now regarded as a club that always "look after their officials". It was not always so. Remember that all this team managing is not just for the Women's Southern League Team but for our Thameside League as well. And Cynthia has not confined her role to one of helping out the women's team only. Our men's matches always run better for Cynthia's presence and she soon has the lads carrying refreshments around – as meek as any lambs. None of this is a once a week activity either. A whole Saturday can be spent organising her team in the driving rain in Huntingdonshire or Cornwall; the whole of the following Sunday might be spent competing for our Veterans' team at Colindale, while Wednesday night might involve catering for the Rosenheim officials and Friday night a Track & Field Committee Meeting ... it goes on and on. Congratulations to Cynthia James, elected Life Member of Belgrave Harriers at the 1998 A.G.M. and pictured here with husband Ray. items.sum: Report on the Belgrave athletes at the 1998 European Championships in Budapest, led by Darren Campbell's 100m gold and Dwain Chambers' silver, with results for each event.
items.s: Gold & Silver at the Nepstadion Report on the Belgrave athletes at the 1998 European Championships in Budapest, led by Darren Campbell's 100m gold and Dwain Chambers' silver, with results for each event. Track & Field - European Championships - Budapest — The 17th European Championships in Athletics, Budapest, Hungary, 18-23 August 1998 — What a superb arena the Nepstadion is. Plans for a stadium on this site were originally drawn up when Budapest was asked to host the first Modern Olympic Games in 1896. As it turned out those games eventually went to Greece and what was to become the chief sports facility of Hungary was not begun until 1948 with completion in 1953. Since then some outstanding events have been hosted: Davis Cup Tennis, European Basketball, many international Soccer matches including some graced by the legendary Puskas. Evangelist Billy Graham and Pope John Paul II have both filled the stadium—as did rock bands Queen and Genesis—but athletics has been far from overshadowed with no less than 23 World Records being set here. One thousand four hundred and ninety four athletes from 47 countries gathered together in this inspiring environment to compete in the 17th European Championships in Athletics—including eight Belgravians. 100m ~ Darren Campbell (Gold) and Dwain Chambers (Silver) As heats progressed to second rounds and then to semi finals, the 100 metres always looked like being a two horse race—and it still looked that way with 30-40 metres of the final gone. Then came Darren Campbell's electrifying finish that swept him away from his younger rival and across the line for a time four hundredths of a second faster than his coach Linford Christie's previous Championship Best and two hundredths faster than Dwain Chamber's Club Record. There had been many who thought that Dwain might have pulled it off himself. His starting was tremendous and his aggression during each race was plain for all to see, but at only 20 years of age he will surely collect further medals in the event. He's also proved that he's got the right temperament and that his World Junior Record of 10.06 from 1997 was far from being a fluke. It was the first ever British 1-2 in a European 100m final—and both of them Belgrave boys too! Tremendous. Round 1, 18Aug., 6 hts, q = first 4 + 8 fastest losers: ht4 (-0.3) 1, Campbell 10.40; ht5 (+0.6) 2, Chambers 10.28. Round 2, 18Aug., 4 hts, q = first 4: ht2 (-0.1) 1, Campbell 10.26; ht3 (-0.2) 1, Chambers 10.26. Semi-finals, 19Aug., q = first 4: sf1 (+0.3) 1, Chambers 10.15; sf2 (+0.5) 1, Campbell 10.11. Final, 19Aug.: (+0.3) 1, D.Campbell 10.04; 2, D.Chambers 10.10; 3, H.Papadias (Greece) 10.17. 1500m ~ Matt Yates It seemed a different Matt Yates in Budapest. We've seen him qualify for other games and then simply not do himself justice but this time he seemed so positive, qualifying confidently and then lining up with the other Britons Whiteman and Mayock to tackle the Iberian onslaught. Always right in the bunch, he was still prepared to charge at the medal positions as the final lap unwound but the early pace had been just right for the 'sprinters' and Estevez, Silva and Cacho were moving too fast for any ground to be regained over the final 200 metres. In 6th place (3rd Briton) Matt just failed to equal John Gladwin's 5th place from 1986. Round 1, 18Aug., 2 hts, q = first 4 + 4: ht2 3, 3:38.97. Final, 20Aug.: 1, R.Esteves (Spain) 3:41.31; 2, R.Silva (Portugal) 3:41.84; 3, F.Cacho (Spain) 3:42.13; 6, M.Yates 3:42.63. 110m Hurdles ~ Andy Tulloch Andy had been struggling with injury problems in the months before the games, only having raced once in seven weeks. To qualify for the semi-final with 13.81 and then improve again into a 2 metre wind was an honourable performance. Roll on the Commonwealth Games ... Round 1, 18Aug., 4 hts, q = first 3 + 4: ht2 (?.?) 3, 13.81. Semi-finals, 22Aug., q = first 4: sf2 (-2.0) 7, 13.79. 400m Hurdles ~ Chris Rawlinson In spite of an early season 49.81, 1998 has seen Chris Rawlinson only a shadow of the man who ran 49.69 the previous year to qualify for the World Champs. He must have been extremely disappointed with 7th place in his heat in Budapest and in fact this turned out to be an altogether lack-lustre event for Britain as both our other representatives failed to progress in similar fashion. Round 1, 18Aug., 4 hts, q = first 3 + 4: ht2 7, 51.11. High Jump ~ Brendan Reilly Twelve jumpers separated themselves from the non-qualifiers by clearing 2.24m, our own Brendan Reilly needing all three attempts to make the cut. Come the final and the Belgrave man oozed confidence as he ignored 2.15 and 2.20 and became the last competitor to open his account, sailing over 2.24m at his very first try. Missing 2.27m, Bren's next attempt was at 2.30 but two tries here while six other men cleared, showed that it was going to have to be all or nothing and in spite of having a season's best of 'only' 2.28 he took his final leap with the bar at 2.32. It wasn't to be. A clearance would have put him in the top five jumpers and shooting for a medal but nevertheless it was a good competitive performance from a man who only qualified for the games on the last possible day. Qualifying rounds, 19Aug., q = 2.27 or best 12: group B 5, 2.24 (2.20xo, 2.24xxo). Final 21Aug.: 1, A.Partyka (Poland) 2.34; 2, D.Grant (GB&NI) 2.34; 3, S.Klyugin (Russia) 2.32; ... =9, B.Reilly 2.24 (2.24o, 2.30xx-, 2.32x). Discus ~ Nick Sweeney A repeat of his 64.28m set in Helsingborg, Sweden, in July would not only have seen Nick through the qualifying round, it would have taken him to 5th place in the final. Two no throws came from our big Irishman, putting huge pressure on him, while Schult and Dubrovschik both reached out to 63 metres plus. The Belgrave man pulled himself together on his last attempt and got himself up to 8th in his pool with 60.36 but when the second pool had completed their throws it became apparent that our man had missed qualifying by a mere 23cms. Only three throwers had landed their platters beyond the qualifying arc, with Nick being an unlucky 13th overall and 12 being taken through to the final. Qualifying rounds, 22Aug., q = 62.50 or best 12: group A 8, 60.36 (x, x, 60.36). 4x100m Relay ~ Darren Campbell and Dwain Chambers (Gold) With five out of six sprint medals having gone to Britain, nobody doubted the ability of the GB boys to bring home another gold. The heats underlined that fact. A steady run, with Darren Campbell on his customary leg down the back straight and Dwain Chambers cruising the home stretch, clearly gave Britain the fastest qualifying time. Incredibly, when it came to the final, Devonish and Chambers were dropped in favour of a last pairing of 200m victor and bronze medallist Doug Walker and Julian Golding. Whilst not necessarily arguing about the inclusion of the latter two, one had to question the selectors' reasoning behind leaving Condon on leg one—a man a full 3.5 metres slower than Chambers. Apparently they wanted the same team that had run in the European Cup. British coach and selector Richard Simmons remained tight-lipped when being questioned while Dwain seemed mystified and just shrugged his shoulders. It made no difference to the result but the British winning time was slower than that of their heat and a chance of a 37 clocking was lost. A 45.5 clocking made him second fastest of the quartet but with top men Iwan Thomas and Mark Richardson taking a breather before the final, no-one had any complaints about the final selection on this occasion. Well done Sean. Round 1, 22Aug., 2 hts, q = first 3 + 2: ht2 1, GB&NI 3:02.37 (Hylton 45.7, BALDOCK 45.5, Wariso 46.1, Baulch 45.05). items.s: 10.03 from Dwain Chambers! Report on Belgrave athletes at the 1998 IAAF World Cup in Johannesburg, where Dwain Chambers ran 10.03 at altitude after a 0.063 reaction time (Thompson's time is printed as 69.87) and anchored the winning GB relay. IAAF WORLD CUP JOHANNESBURG, RSA, 11-13 SEP 1998 As European Cup victors the British men took their place in the World Cup final alongside teams representing six continents, USA and Germany, slotting in this meet between European and Commonwealth Games. The first day's competition saw Dwain Chambers take full advantage of the 1748m altitude. A sensational start had Dwain in the lead with Africa's Ogunkoya but recovering from a poor getaway, Barbadian Obadele Thompson, racing for the Americas, rocketed through to one of the sprint performances of the year 69.87. Dwain's time in 3rd was the second fastest ever by a Briton, making him once again the fastest Belgravian of all time; but the altitude wasn't the only helpful factor. His reaction time at the start was revealed as 0.063 when 0.100 is the fastest permitted, anything less being judged as an anticipated start and therefore illegal. The starter chose not to recall the athletes so the result stood but if, for comparison's sake, we adjust his reaction time to his more normal 0.130 we come up with something like 10.10. The National Union of Track Statisticians have taken his 10.10 from Budapest as his season's best with this 10.03 being classed as a "rolling start"; we must follow suit. Another to enjoy the thin air was Mike Edwards, called up for the pole vault on day two. First time clearances came at 5.00 and 5.20 while two attempts were needed for 5.40. A massive 5.60 was the next height to be attempted and with a best ever of 5.52 dating from 1993 it was not surprising to find that Mike had reached his limit. The hammer event saw a psyched up Mick Jones blasting it from round one. As he later said, it wasn't until he calmed down and concentrated that he managed to start putting his hammer out where it should have been going. He was pleased to put South Africa's Chris Harmse behind him though. Harmse was one of his main rivals for the following week's Commonwealth Games. Further great running came from Chambers as he anchored the GB team to a winning 38.09 in the 4x100 metres-a Championship Best-and Sean Baldock continued his tremendous season with a 45.1 leg in the long relay. a=11th, b=12th, c=13th. 100m a: (-0.2) 3, D.Chambers 10.03. items.h: Nick Sweeney sets another National Discus Record
items.sum: Photo feature on Nick Sweeney's 1998 discus season, including a 67.89 Irish Record at Helsingborg.
items.s: Nick Sweeney sets another National Discus Record Photo feature on Nick Sweeney's 1998 discus season, including a 67.89 Irish Record at Helsingborg. Above: Tremendous discus throwing came from Nick Sweeney throughout the summer of '98 and Helsinborg, Sweden, almost became a second home to the 30 year-old Irishman. Standing 1.95m tall and weighing in at 121kg, Nick previously had a best of 67.40 dating from 1996. Having travelled to the Swedish town to spin his platter out to 64.28 in July, he was back in August, this time reaching out to 65.59. Not at his best in Budapest for the European Games, Nick barely scraped over 60m but on September 4th, once more in Helsingborg, he launched a mighty 67.89 for his eighth Irish Record - a distance 2 metres in excess of the British Record. Two days later at the same venue he set his second best mark of the season with 65.70. Nick is a graduate of Harvard University and played Rugby Union for Irish Schools. Above: Tremendous discus throwing came from Nick Sweeney throughout the summer of '98 and Helsinborg, Sweden, almost became a second home to the 30 year-old Irishman. Standing 1.95m tall and weighing in at 121kg, Nick previously had a best of 67.40 dating from 1996. Having travelled to the Swedish town to spin his platter out to 64.28 in July, he was back in August, this time reaching out to 65.59. Not at his best in Budapest for the European Games, Nick barely scraped over 60m but on September 4th, once more in Helsingborg, he launched a mighty 67.89 for his eighth Irish Record - a distance 2 metres in excess of the British Record. Two days later at the same venue he set his second best mark of the season with 65.70. Nick is a graduate of Harvard University and played Rugby Union for Irish Schools. items.sum: Report and Belgrave results from the 1998 Commonwealth Games in Kuala Lumpur, with silver medals for Mick Jones and Ben Challenger, relay gold and silver and John Regis's 200m bronze.
items.s: Fifteen at the Friendly Games Report and Belgrave results from the 1998 Commonwealth Games in Kuala Lumpur, with silver medals for Mick Jones and Ben Challenger, relay gold and silver and John Regis's 200m bronze. Commonwealth Games - Kuala Lumpur - Track & Field Fifteen at the Friendly Games Commonwealth Games, Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, 16-21 September Late September, and at the "Friendly Games" a long athletics season drew to a close with some explosive performances. The sprints lacked only the Americans while the middle-distances were dominated by Kenyans. An unprecedented fifteen Belgravians made the long trip to the national capital of Malaysia, braving warnings of crippling smog and excessive humidity and temperatures to compete in the Bukit Jalil stadium. Gold and silver came our way in the relays and that old war-horse Regis came up with a bronze medal but this time it was the field events that gave us our closest shots at individual gold. A medal at last for Mick Jones For Mick Jones Kuala Lumpur was a dream come true. Twice before in Commonwealth Games competition he had finished just out of the medals in fourth place but in 1998 there was to be no mistake. The South African Chris Harmse led after round one, his 72.83 edging out Australian Stuart Rendell's 72.52 and Mick's 72.58. Dave Smith's 67.31 placed him 5th. But while the South African had launched his "big one", round two saw Rendell improve to 74.37 and Mick hanging on to silver medal position with 73.51. A lifetime personal best came from the Belgrave man in round 3—74.02 while Rendell fouled. That was it as far as the medals were concerned. The Australian backed up his leading mark with 74.33 for his fourth effort and then finished off with a winning 74.71for his sixth throw. Dave Smith heaved his best of the competition in round four to go back into 5th. Still only 24 he must have as good a chance as anyone to pick up that elusive gold in some future Games but he'll still have that man Jones to deal with for a while yet. For the first time in his life 35 year-old Mick is to go warm weather training this winter, travelling to South Africa with his coach Alan Bertram. If he can throw 74.02 after training in a Dorking field, thanks to a helpful farmer, the best could yet be ahead of him. Silver for Ben Challenger That man Dalton Grant and our own Ben Challenger were the men leading the way in the high jump. Dalton came in at 2.15 with Ben delaying until 2.20—both had first time clearances and then it was up to 2.24 where the pair went clear again, as did Brendan Reilly, while Australia's Forsyth, Lendis of South Africa and Naiko of Mauritius all needed two shots. Now it was 2.28 where Grant and Challenger continued their first time successes, this time taking Forsyth with them. Naiko cleared the bar on his third try while Brendan failed twice and saved his last attempt for 2.31. This was where it would be settled. Grant has a reputation for being a "big-time" jumper and he did it again. The bar was repeatedly rattled off the pegs by all remaining athletes until with his third attempt the Haringey man wriggled his way over to become the only man to go clear. Ben's silver medal was a terrific achievement. He had injured an ankle while competing in the European Cup and had missed out on Budapest in an effort to get himself into shape for this competition—and he was within an ace of carrying off the gold. Jason Lobo and Dave Pamah kept us represented in the middle-distance events. Jason was only just outside his season's best in placing 6th in his semi, while Dave, racing for his mother's St. Kitts & The Grenadines, started off a flurry of e-mails between the IAAF and The Belgravian "offices" as it became apparent that as a representative of those islands his performances of recent years made him national record holder for the 800 and 1,500 metres! Over the barriers, a lifetime best came from Northern Ireland's Matt Douglas in the one-lap race and Andy Tulloch continued his comeback from injury with a super 13.57, his best of the year, to reach the final where he placed 6th. Discus man Lee Newman took advantage of Welsh ancestry to take part in the discus competition. His season's best would have given him a fighting chance of 4th place but at 7th he nevertheless got the satisfaction of putting one over on British Record holder Perris Wilkins. For Ian Tullett it was not a happy time at all as he sufferred the ignominy of three fouls at his opening height in the pole vault. Roller-coaster ride for Ladejo In only his second full Decathlon, Du'aine Ladejo's 7th place has got to be considered a success but he will be far from satisfied with his performance. A near pb came in the 100 metres to take him straight to the top of the leaders board—and then came an awful long jump where two fouls nearly saw him exiting the competition before he popped out a mediocre but safe 6.92. The shot was passable but then the high jump resulted in a super pb of 2.04 and a season's best of 46.12 in the 400 metres rounded off day one with the Belgrave man lying in 3rd place on 4317 points. — And then came day two and the hurdles. How Du'aine got over the first flight after totally messing up his start we'll never know. Amazingly he still registered 14.91 but it could have been so much faster—and the rest of the competition was a mere recovery exercise. Putting it all together in just two days is going to be a real challenge but some of his performances are awesome and those in the know tell us that Du'aine is sure to register 8,000 points soon. Gold and Silver in the relays Again we were well represented in the sprints but Euro-Champ Darren Campbell, although reaching the final and consolidating on his new level of performance, had to give way to the might of Bolden, Fredericks & Co. Dwain Chambers was unlucky to get only 5th in his semi-final with a time the same as Campbell's. The 200 metres saw 'JR' back in the big-time following an achilles tendon injury. John Regis, a silver medallist at each of the preceding Commonwealth 200s was delighted with his bronze medal and in spite of 33 years now showing on the clock has vowed to go on until 2000! We had to wait for the relays for sprint gold where in the one lap race England romped to a Championship Best Performance of 38.20 with Dwain Chambers providing the start and Darren Campbell the glory leg. Sean Baldock contributed to the 4x400 squad's 'silver' by opening up for England in the heats but then missed the final again as the team was switched around. With so many talented one lap runners in this country he's going to have to wait a bit longer before he can get into the final four. 100m ~ Darren Campbell and Dwain Chambers Round 1, 16Sep., 8 hts, q = first 3 + 8 fastest losers: ht4 (-0.2) 3, Chambers 10.44; ht6 (-0.3) 1, Campbell 10.23. items.sum: Bill Laws recounts the troubled travel arrangements and funding for Belgrave's trip to the European Champion Clubs Cup Group 'B' match in Belgrade in May 1998.
items.s: Nightmare to Europe Bill Laws recounts the troubled travel arrangements and funding for Belgrave's trip to the European Champion Clubs Cup Group 'B' match in Belgrade in May 1998. Track & Field - European Champion Clubs Cup Nightmare to Europe — Bill Laws writes — The Journey The 17 hour trip from Heathrow to Belgrade was the final depressing stage of a planning nightmare. It all started well back in November '97 when we were informed the ECCC Group 'B' match was to be held in Belgrade on Saturday 30th May 1998. A quick check with WGT management, BAF's recommended travel group, showed that out of Gatwick with BA on the Friday and back to Gatwick on the Sunday was the easiest route. Great, we booked 36 seats at a special rate (and I mean special!) and in February we wrote to all our British League team giving them advance notice. As these letters were being delivered we received an urgent fax from PARTIZAN AC the host club. Due to a Yugoslav vs. Nigeria football match scheduled also for 30th May, could we agree to putting the match back to Sunday 31st May when it would be televised. "No trouble" we faxed, "if you pay for an extra night's accommodation." No problem was their reply, so back to WGT requesting the return flight be changed to Monday 1st June – at no extra cost. "Done", faxed Ian Dennis from WGT and again we sat back and relaxed. Towards the end of April we received a welcoming fax from the British Embassy in Belgrade requesting travel details. On receipt of our reply, HM Consul Bob Gordon phoned to say that he had good information that there was no BA flight to Belgrade on the Friday. We immediately checked with the World's Favourite Airline who informed us that although there was no Friday flight at present, it would be in the summer schedule due to start mid-May. This information was duly passed back to the British Embassy who was adamant that there would be no agreement to the Friday flight. They were right. Two weeks before departure BA informed us that we would need to take Thursday's flight out of Gatwick as the Friday one had not been introduced. Surprise, surprise! Things were getting out of hand. We were now looking at a 5 day trip for a 1 day match, more hotel costs and the athletes needing to take another day off work. What was the alternative? BA suggested a flight to Budapest on the Friday, which would then involve a 4 hour coach drive to Belgrade. OK but they would have to pay for the coach. BA refused this suggestion but a further reduction in ticket price kept us off the boil. Only just. WGT re-arranged tickets and organised the coach through Budatours in Budapest. Great, our troubles were over. Well, not quite. The day before departure (Thursday) Eurotours refused to accept VISA payment (we deduced this was because BAF was in Administration and had the credit rating of a block of concrete!) They wanted cash, 865 GBP to be precise. No cash, so 'your's truly' dashed to the bank, loaded up with a wad of the folding stuff and prepared for the next disaster. As a result of these changes, Chris Rawlinson was forced to withdraw due to an exam at Loughborough on Monday 1st June. Meanwhile, for those who remembered to bring passports to the first BAL match, we (John Jeffery) made four journeys to the Yugoslav Embassy in London. Others sent passports by post and by the time we had got all the Visa's, we knew our way about Kensington quite well. We had heard that the Yugoslav's were turning round anyone without Visa's, so the airlines were checking carefully all documents. The last problem came with the late replacement of Brendan Reilly by Ben Challenger. We flew Ben out JAL on the Saturday without a Visa. Fortunately, we had enough time having arrived a day earlier to ease the release of Ben's Visa and our minder – Marina – was proving a tower of strength. But back to the coach trip from Budapest to Belgrade. Scheduled for 4 hours, it eventually took 7 hours including a lengthy stop at the Hungarian–Yugoslavian border. We came to the conclusion that the drivers were on an hourly rate because they would not take the coach over 50mph even on a clear dual carriageway. Attempts to give them financial inducements failed and the frustration of being overtaken uphill by a fully laden cement lorry needs to be experienced to be appreciated. The team took it all in good spirits but the effects of a 17 hour trip on their bodies was to become apparent 36 hours later. The Finances In previous years we have managed to defray most costs of the ECCC matches by donations from the British League, BAF and the Sports & Arts Foundation. This year the League, although without a sponsor, donated £2,000, BAF couldn't and the Sports & Arts Foundation informed us that due to the Lottery creaming off football pools income, they too could not subscribe. At one stage, the Belgrave Committee decreed that even though we were the UK Clubs' representatives, it would not be possible for Belgrave to contribute from its own stretched budget. Withdrawal was a real possibility until our Patron and No.1 supporter, Sir Eddie, stepped in to meet the substantial outstanding balance. Sir Eddie travelled to Belgrade via Rome and once again gave the team tremendous support. We hope to repay him in 1999 with promotion to Group 'A' in Europe. As I write, it appears that the venue will be Athens. Let us hope the travel arrangements will be a lot easier. I couldn't face another fiasco so soon after the Belgrade trip! The Hammer competition at the European Champion Clubs Cup was held outside of the main stadium and with no cage! Who'd want to judge the event in those circumstances — and who'd want to be the photographer — we note that the man with the lens didn't get too close! Mick Jones had a good competition and threw 72.55 for second place. items.s: Most ambitious year yet Boxed introduction setting out Belgrave's 1998 targets, including promotion at the European Clubs Champions Cup in Belgrade. Most ambitious year yet Following last year's double victory in both the Cup and League Division One, our '98 targets included not only a repeat of the Golden Double but also the European Clubs Champions Cup Final to be held in Belgrade at the end of June. In 1997 Sale had been last in the 'A' Cup match and so the Great Britain representative team was now to compete in the 'B' Match. Promotion was on our mind. Because at our last appearance in 'A' Group two years ago in Istanbul we had finished in a creditable bronze position, we thought that promotion would be a formality. Oh boy, were we wrong! items.h: A jaded team ends up 4th in Belgrade
items.sum: Bill Laws's report of Belgrave's 4th place, representing GB clubs, in the European Clubs Cup Division 2 match in Belgrade on 31 May 1998, with team placings and Belgrave results.
items.s: A jaded team ends up 4th in Belgrade Bill Laws's report of Belgrave's 4th place, representing GB clubs, in the European Clubs Cup Division 2 match in Belgrade on 31 May 1998, with team placings and Belgrave results. European Champion Clubs Cup - Track & Field A jaded team ends up 4th in Belgrade EUROPEAN CLUBS CUP DIVISION 2 BELGRADE, YUGOSLAVIA 31 MAY 1998 Last year Sale were relegated in a tough 'A' Group final held in Moscow. Although not at their strongest Sale had reported that several central European teams had turned out national squads and the Russian contingent had trounced Larios who in previous years had proved invincible. This should have been a warning to us but conscious that we had finished 3rd in the 'A' Group final in '96, we planned for our visit to Belgrade content in the belief that it would be our honour to return a GB team back to the top level of European Club Competition. Nothing short of a win would be satisfactory. Team selection was to take place after the first British League Match and it was only following the season's opener at Watford, that we began to realise we might not have the strongest of teams for Belgrade. In the throws, Matt Simpson reported that his elbow injury needed surgery and the operation was planned for 1st June. Nick Sweeney, also based in the USA, had had surgery and was throwing discus comparable distances to both Lee Newman and Kevin Brown. There were rumours that javelin stalwart Nigel Bevan had moved to Birchfield, although he was still in the USA and was uncontactable and in the hammer Dave Smith's recovery from a broken ankle had not moved to a point where he could challenge a resurgent Mick Jones. The middle distance was presenting problems too, as Matt Yates reported that a warm weather training injury had not recovered. Tom Lerwill was having a year's break to recover from glandular fever and Paul Evans was still laid low from problems incurred during an extended overseas training trip prior to the London Marathon. Fortunately, Jason Lobo was eligible and although specialising at 800 we chose to bring Matt Kloiber for the 800 and move Jason up to 1500. New member James Ellis Smith was selected for the 5000, not because of his 3.42 1500m pb, but because he had wintered in South Africa and had some good road race results under his belt. With Justin Chaston tied by work commitments in the USA, Lee Hurst was to prove a valuable choice for the steeplechase. No problems with the jumps squad until a week before departure, when Brendan Reilly was injured in a car crash and there was a last minute panic to get a visa for welcome newcomer Ben Challenger, who was now destined to make his début in a Belgrave vest in the high jump in Belgrade. The sprints squad was strong with only Dwain Chambers unavailable due to a number of overseas engagements. Clearly the world junior 100m record holder was of interest to a number of early season meeting promoters. With hindsight it is difficult to comprehend why the ECCC committee chose a venue like Belgrade. You will read elsewhere of the travel nightmare. Suffice to say that on the day, a somewhat jaded team performed adequately but without much inspiration. What was achieved was outstanding under the circumstances with a few excellent performances. The experience and professionalism of what, after all, was a very young team, showed through and we all left a lot wiser vowing we would be better prepared for the '99 event should we be fortunate enough to qualify to represent the GB clubs again. Unlike the 'A' Group event, the 'B' Group was to complete all events in a single day. The 10,000m was removed from the 'B' event and the Yugoslavs, mindful of the publicity value of such an important event, had placed 16 TV cameras at the stadium and the match was televised and broadcast over a 3 hour period. Central Europe received the satellite TV programme. It was not until Saturday evening's Technical Meeting that we realised how strong the other Clubs were. The local team Partizan comprised a full Yugoslav squad and our interpreter, Marina, would not contemplate anything other than their victory. She would like it if Belgrave came second. As it turned out, so would we. Sporting Club of Portugal had a number of overseas members including former World Junior Sprint Champion Francis Obikwelu. Somehow, Panellinios of Greece had obtained the services of 400H World Record Holder Kevin Young. The Sunday was going to be interesting. A good start The match day dawned bright. There was not a breath of wind as temperatures soared and tree pollen fell intrusively like thick snowflakes. Several athletes succumbed to hay fever and were in such a bad way they needed medical treatment. Your team managers refused to let anyone be injected by the match doctors so it was cold wet towels and a prayer for those suffering. Realising a good start was essential we left early for the hammer competition. Not only was this not to be in the main Stadium but we were soon to discover there was no cage either. The competitors agreed to throw but it was the foot fault officials who won the plaudits. Luckily for everyone the throwers were careful but there could have been some serious injuries. Mick Jones threw exceptionally well in the circumstances with 3 throws over 70m and his longest, at 72.55m gaining second spot and 7 points – a decent start. Whereas the hammer had started at 10.00am the main programme started in the main Stadium at 16.40 to avoid the highest temperatures and to satisfy TV. We had taken advantage of the time gap to practice sprint relay takeovers and get in some starting practice. Darren Campbell was looking lethargic out of the blocks and we hoped race conditions would improve his reactions. But first to the pole vault. It was about now that we realised the large local crowd were not interested in good competition and sportsmanship. Partizan was an appropriate name for both the local club and supporters. First into the gladiatorial ring was Mike Edwards, not someone to be easily intimidated. As the competition progressed the crowd hurled abuse at all but their man. Mike loved it. The louder they shouted the perkier he got. Second place and another 7 points. Good man, but Partizan were first as they were in the next event the discus. Kevin Brown seemed to hurry his throws and finished fourth – one place lower than he could have expected. Nonetheless 5 more points. We lead after six events The long jump started as the pole vault reached its final stages. The runways were separated by a few metres and Julian Flynn was clearly affected by the crowd. Adrenaline rush or whatever, his only valid jump was in the 5th round by which time the team managers were reduced to nervous wrecks. Fifth place and four points. Then to the first track event the 400 flat. Brankovic was Partizan's Captain, the 1992 European Champion and the crowd's favourite. A long hold on the track in fierce heat saw the opposition wilt before the start and it was the Yugoslav who rushed into a commanding lead. Sean Baldock looked jaded and the crowds support for their man reached deafening proportions as he entered the home straight with a 5m lead. But what was this? Relentlessly inch by inch Sean was pulling back the big Yugoslav only to pass him with a desperate lunge 5m before the tape. The crowd groaned and we had recorded our first and only victory of the day. In the 100m, Darren Campell lived up to our worst fears and had a disastrous start. Seventh after 30m he then got into that liquid smooth, ground eating stride and was gaining fast on all but the leader as the line was reached. 10.03 was the winning time by Obikwelu with Darren in third. Twenty minutes later Andy Tulloch lined up against Schwarthoff in the high hurdles and was rewarded with a fine second spot in a legal 13.63. After six events we were leading with 41 points followed by Partizan on 39 and Lac Quelle Munich, the German Champions on 33. From then on it was mostly downhill. Stuart Faben managed just 2 throws in the javelin and should have finished at least 2 places higher than 5th. Matt Kloiber faded badly after leading the 800 for 600m and could only manage 7th. Then Philips Idowu withdrew from the triple jump after 3 attempts due to a slight injury. His best of 14.81 was probably his poorest competition of the year and only good enough for 7th spot. The abyss was beckoning. We realised it wasn't our day in the sprint relay when the second leg runner outside Jason Fergus pulled a hamstring and pushed our man across the track. With a side-step worthy of a rugby veteran, Jason continued and we recovered to 4th with a commendable 40.53. But again with a bit of luck it could have been so much better. Challenger close to 2.31m In the high jump things were looking better. Ben Challenger, like Mike Edwards appeared to be gaining inspiration from the raucous crowd. His 2.28 pb clearance was effortless and one of the 2.31 attempts was as close as you could get to a clearance without actually succeeding. Nevertheless, 2nd spot, 7 points and what a debut for Belgrave. James Ellis Smith went with the leaders in a very hot 5000. Castro of Sporting Club of Lisbon got outkicked as James succumbed to the heat and travelling and faded serenely to 6th spot. Matt Douglas struggled to find form in the 400H as Kevin Young cruised to 48.88 at the age of 32. Still plenty of time Matt! Next came Jason Fergus in the 200 still shaken after the sprint relay traumas. Actually, shaken and stirred by the looks of things, as he gained the bronze medal in a very creditable 21.01 legal. Obikwelu again won, this time in 20.50. Lee Newman performed well up to expectations in the shot that was won with a massive 20.71 by Peric of Partizan. This match was hot! Lee Hurst then stepped up for the steeplechase and, putting all thoughts of partying behind him, showed true grit to again get a bronze medal. His performance was clearly the best of the middle distance men who generally had found the long journey just too much – witness Jason Lobo fading to 7th in the 1500 and like Matt Kloiber mystified that there was no strength when he needed it. And so to the last event the long relay. Geoff Dearman and Michael Parper joined the drained Matt Douglas and Sean Baldock to finish with another bronze, by which time we had faded to 4th. With only two teams promoted we realised that this had been one of the toughest matches we had been in. Overall, 10 Group 'B' records had been set in this cauldron of a stadium. Considering that this event has been going for 25 years, this was a truly competitive and high standard match. There is no reason to believe it will be any easier in 1999 but you can bet that should we be there, we will be stronger and better prepared. items.h: End of the road for Larios
items.sum: News that drinks firm Larios was ending its sponsorship of the Spanish club Larios, dominant in the European Champion Clubs Cup in the 1990s.
items.s: End of the road for Larios News that drinks firm Larios was ending its sponsorship of the Spanish club Larios, dominant in the European Champion Clubs Cup in the 1990s. End of the road for Larios It was reported in Athletics International recently that as from November 1998 the Spanish drinks manufacturer Larios would not be continuing its sponsorship of the top Spanish athletics club that bears its name. It seems that Larios have poured some $1 million per year into the club since 1985 resulting in a massive international recruitment campaign that brought them Merlene Ottey, Javier Sotomayor, Brahim Boutayeb, Samuel Matete, James Beckford and a large proportion of the Cuban national team. Not surprisingly this tide of athletic talent took them to first place in six out of seven European Champion Clubs Cup competitions between 1990 and 1996. They were then second in 1997 and only fourth in 1998. The club, based in the Madrid suburb of Moratalaz were known to be searching for another sponsor with the possibility of disbanding altogether if another cash provider was not forthcoming. items.s: British Embassy Comes Up Trumps Account of the British Embassy barbecue in Belgrade for the Belgrave team on the eve of the European Champion Clubs Cup match. British Embassy Comes Up Trumps We knew the British Embassy in Belgrade was good. Even before our ill-fated trip they had been in touch to advise us that the direct flight from Gatwick would not be operated. A fact that BA only acknowledged a couple of weeks before our departure. Anyway, Bob Gordon, the Consul, invited the team and some of our Jugoslav hosts to the British Embassy for an excellent barbeque on the eve of our match. While Michael Parper led the 'horse races' for the children, Marlon Dickson worked his way through three meals. Up 'til then he had proclaimed a distinct dislike for local food and was on hunger strike. The numerous and huge bowls of strawberries and cream crowned a great evening. Mick Jones had been explaining to anyone who would listen that his training at Ockley Court Farm took place on a smooth concrete pad distanced some 75 metres from the nearest strawberry bed. So Mike's claim to fame was to reach the strawberries. No sooner the word! Team members were seen to smuggle out bowls of strawberries, not for consumption, but to give Mick some added incentive during the next day's competition. And you will see from the results that it worked. items.s: Winning ways at Watford Report and results of British League Division One Match 1 at Watford on 16 May 1998, won by Belgrave. British League Division One - Track & Field Winning ways at Watford MATCH 1, WATFORD, 16MAY 1998 This was a TVH home fixture. The 'Valley' have been having problems with their local Council and the once pristine West London Stadium has now become unusable for League fixtures. It is tragic that after the euphoria of re-naming it in honour of Linford Christie, the Council should keep its hands in its pockets and let it slide into gentle decline. So here we were at a new venue which proved to be very congenial, blessed with fine weather and eight teams eager for the start of a new season. Dave Smith, competing for the first time since breaking a bone in his foot was highly delighted to win the 'A' hammer. John Urquhart returned after a winter's retirement to win the 'B' event and so ensure that as usual the hammer squad got us off to a great start. The long jump proved a disaster in more ways than one with only three competitors clearing 7 metres and Commonwealth Games representative Chris Davison of Newham winning with a meagre 7.27m. The triple jump distances were also down and the flat jumps run-up was branded one of the slowest in the South by all competitors. Something to note if you're looking for a good competition! Good points in the first track race, the 400H, kept us in contention as the team scores were updated. Matt Douglas nudged towards his PB in his first outing of the year while Ian Wells pointed out that his 'B' selection was the first by right for three years. Ever a willing reserve, this promotion encouraged a pleasing 4th place. Following his tester in the previous week's Southern League, Darren Campbell won the 'A' 100 in style clocking 10.48 seconds into a 1.2m/s headwind. Jason Fergus was pipped by Alan Condon in the 'B' – but excellent points. Chris Rawlinson moved down to the sprint hurdles and 200m but it was clear that a long layoff with injury had affected his sharpness. Little were we to know that Chris' troubles would be increasing as the season progressed. Wins for Brendan Reilly in the high jump, Geoff Dearman in the flat 400, and by both vaulters and both shot putters made up for a disaster in the javelin and a dropped baton in the sprint relay. A fine win in the long relay eased the team to victory. A final leg by Sean Baldock timed at 45.7 was the highlight. Clearly the Baldock brothers are going to be a big asset in the years ahead. Thanks to the many youngsters who filled the gaps. items.sum: Report and results of British League Division One Match 2 at Birmingham on 6 June 1998, lost to Shaftesbury Barnet by one point despite a club record 4x400m.
items.s: Record 4 x 400 metres but Shaftesbury Barnet make their point Report and results of British League Division One Match 2 at Birmingham on 6 June 1998, lost to Shaftesbury Barnet by one point despite a club record 4x400m. Record 4 x 400 metres but Shaftesbury Barnet make their point MATCH 2, BIRMINGHAM, 6 JUN 1998 So much for my predictions. We lost this one by a single point – surprisingly to Shaftesbury Barnet who had only managed 5th place in Match 1. Once again the League was wide open and we would need to make a concerted effort in the next two matches. It wasn't difficult to find excuses. The previous week's ECCCF match in Belgrade had taken its toll – particularly on the middle distance men. Our paucity of depth in middle distance was cruelly exposed and we could not complete 'B' events in the 800,1500, 3000 steeplechase and 5000m. Ian Wells gamely started the 3000 steeplechase but was forced out with injury. Steve Baldock ran the 'A' 800 and 'A' 5000! But now for the good news. The hammer was first class with Mick Jones throwing a PB to beat Paul Head with both men over 73 metres. Matt Douglas clocked the same time as in Match 1 to win the 'A' 400H. Darren Campbell and Jason Fergus ensured good points in the 100 but a poor start cost Darren victory. Dwain Chambers made a rare appearance in the 200 and the dream sprint relay squad of Chambers, Fergus, Walcott and Campbell set an impressive early season time of 40.51 as they deadheated with the Newham boys. Even the camera couldn't separate the two teams. The even better news was that several newcomers made a noticeable difference. Julian Flynn, in both the long jump and triple jump, is going to be a major points contributor, Richard Sear had his first taste of Division 1 sprint hurdles and junior javelin thrower, Tim Kitney pipped stalwart Stuart Faben to provide a welcome points boost. Ben Challenger made his League high jump début with a steady 2.20m. With Brendan Reilly still sidelined, suffering from whiplash injuries, Samson Oni got carried away in the exalted company and opened at 1.95m – which he failed to clear. Ian Tullett turned the tables on Mike Edwards and once again we had maximum points in the pole vault. But the best news was a new club record in the long relay. Michael Parper, Geoff Dearman, Matt Douglas and Sean Baldock knew that only a win would give us a chance of victory. Their 3.09.26 provided a 2 second margin over second spot but it was Shaftesbury Barnet in second place which ensured they won the match by just 1 point. Ian Wells blamed his failure in the steeplechase for our demise but it was the absence of most of our recognised middle distance men that had placed an unequal burden on the rest of the team. 100m: (-1.6) 2, D.Campbell 10.55; (-1.5) 2, J.Fergus 10.71. 200m: (-1.9) 2, D.Chambers 21.44; (-2.1) 2, A.Walcott 21.74. 400m: 2, G.Dearman 46.93; 3, M.Parper 48.49. 800m: 6, Steve Baldock 1:54.1. 1500m: 6, J.Ellis-Smith 3:56.0. 5000m: 8, S.Baldock 16:16.37. 110mH: (-1.5) 7, R.Sear 15.05; (-1.7) 4, S.Scott 15.45. 400mH: 1, M.Douglas 50.90; 5, I.Wells 56.83. 3000mSC: 8, J.Galley 10:35.04. items.sum: Report and results of British League Division One Match 3 at Edinburgh on 4 July 1998, won by Belgrave to all but secure the League.
items.s: Wrapped up for '98? Report and results of British League Division One Match 3 at Edinburgh on 4 July 1998, won by Belgrave to all but secure the League. Track & Field - British League Division One Wrapped up for '98? MATCH 3, EDINBURGH, 4 JUL 1998 Although Edinburgh is a wonderful city this is a trip we prefer to avoid. Partly because it effectively means going up on a Friday and returning Sunday but mainly due to the enormous cost of travel. Shaftesbury and Newham flew up and estimated the cost of this match alone at £6,500 each. We travelled by train and stayed at Edinburgh University Halls of Residence which kept our costs to a modest £3,600! Bearing in mind that seven teams travelled, the total cost to all concerned was over £20,000. With no League sponsor and dwindling reserves, more attention will need to be paid by the British Athletics League to suitable venues for the 1999 season. On the bright side we had a great trip, good team spirit and a night in Edinburgh after the match where the taverns were full of revellers watching the World Cup Football on large screens. Tough old life isn't it? The weather had been bad north of the border this summer and by all accounts we had the best of it. Force 5 winds and intermittent squalls. Some of the events were of a remarkably high standard considering the conditions. Jason Lobo doubled up on his first League appearance for us and finished a fine second in the 'A' 800m with a surprised Kevin McKay of Sale back in 5th spot. Kevin made amends by winning the 'A' 1500m but newcomer Mark Miles caused a stir by hanging on until the last 200 where lack of training told and he drifted back to 4th spot. Immediately afterwards Jason again collected silver, this time in the 'B' 1500m to total 24 points in his first League outing. Matt Yates made his only appearance for us this year to win the 'B" 800m. In the throws we welcomed another newcomer Nick Sweeney. Nick couldn't compete for us last year due to an operation but proved his value by winning the 'A' discus and finishing second in the 'A' shot for big points score (30). Ironically, Matt Simson was still sidelined due to the elbow operation which he had after Match 1. A blast from the past was Fred Salle, surprising everyone to win the 'A' long jump. This allowed Julian Flynn to win the 'B' long jump, so more good points. With Fred around people were inquiring whether this was Commonwealth year? Chris Rawlinson won the 'A' 400H in a gamble to improve fitness before the AAA's Championships. He was still treading a very thin line between fitness and injury. Welcome back too to Haroun Korjie and Marlon Dickson in the sprints. Unfortunately, Haroun found the cold conditions unsettling and tore a hamstring in the sprint relay. Mind you it didn't stop him clubbing in the evening. And who else made a welcome return? None other than Neil Owen, glad once again to be sprint hurdling. After two frustrating injury ruined years, the 'long un' was back and pleased to be part of the team once more. With Nick Cooper also back from injury the sprint hurdles look brighter. Brendan Reilly too was back after his car accident and although he won the 'A' high jump, was not happy after failing at 2.20m. So much so that the large arc transcribed by his take-off shoe would have been a stadium throws record, except for the assisting wind. We avoided him for 5 minutes thereafter! Much better points in the steeplechase moved us into the lead in the late afternoon drizzle. Lee Hurst turned in his usual first class performance and newcomer Kevin Nash looked the part as he won the 'B' event. The match was well and truly won by the time the relays came round, which was just as well, as a combination of injuries and tiredness ensured that no records were in danger. Behind us the other teams were playing musical chairs which ensured that our lead extended to 5 League points which virtually wrapped up the competition. But I've been wrong before and Match 4 would still be a test of will. 100m: (+3.3) 5, H.Korjie 10.58; (+3.5) 4, M.Dickson 10.77. 200m: (+2.7) 8, H.Korjie 22.40; (+1.8) 4, S.Baldock 21.60. 400m: 3, G.Dearman 47.78; 3, M.Parper 48.77. 800m: 2, J.Lobo 1:50.19; 1, M.Yates 1:51.37. 1500m: 4, M.Miles 3:53.91; 2, J.Lobo 4:05.66. 5000m: 5, K.Tadesse 14:47.32. 110mH: (+5.0) 4, N.Owen 14.22; (+4.5) 2, N.Cooper 14.65. 400mH: 1, C.Rawlinson 51.52; 3, M.Douglas 54.29. 3000mSC: 2, L.Hurst 9:02.43; 1, K.Nash 9:07.97. items.s: 'JR' is back- 20.56! Reilly gets 'Euro' qualifier Report and results of British League Division One Match 4 at Copthall on 8 August 1998, won by Belgrave to take the League title with a record 1460 points. British League Division One - Track & Field 'JR' is back- 20.56! Reilly gets 'Euro' qualifier MATCH 4, COPTHALL, 8 AUG 1998 As we approached this match the AAA's Championships were well and truly done and dusted. There remained a few places yet to be filled for the European championships and the Commonwealth Games. Jason Lobo was chasing an 800m qualifying time in Brussels while Matt Yates was chasing a 1500m time in Spain. So once again we had a depleted middle distance squad. Also chasing a high jump qualifying mark was Brendan Reilly and Match 4 represented his last chance with final selections taking place that evening. True to form, Brendan produced the goods clearing 2.28 and narrowly failing at 2.35. A very happy bunny! But this was after a dream start with Mick Jones and Dave Smith going head to head to win maximum points in the hammer. Dave's 70.84m was best to date indicating a gradual return to fitness but he was still to take second to Mick, although he did get the valuable scalp of Newham's Paul Head. Good points too in the long jump but conditions and distances were poor. Kevin Brown continued to improve in the discus pushing the 59 metre mark but still down on qualifying requirements for England for the Commonwealth Games. Lee Newman, already picked for Wales couldn't get motivated but won the 'B' division. Excellent points came from both sprints, with John Regis making a welcome League return in the 200m after a gap of Lord knows how many years. Anyway, we were delighted to see him back in the team and he seemed to be pleased he came, after running a superb 20.56 which was to ensure his Commonwealth selection. Soon after, the sprint relay squad were being wound up by the Newham quartet who had dead heated with them in Match 2. This seemed to fire our boys . Junior Chris Lambert ran a superb first leg and John Regis responded with a huge rush down the back straight. Clean takeovers by Drew Walcott and Jason Fergus saw a season's best time of 40.43 with the Newham boys 5m down. And finally to the long relay which was to be a formality as our Match victory and League title had been assured much earlier in the afternoon. Newham finished runners up in the League and look to be the main opposition next year. Our total points score of 1460 was 55 more than last year and was our highest ever. And this from our youngest team too! The signs are good for next year. I'm looking forward to it already. Hope you are too because if there's one thing the team enjoys, it's your support. With more London fixtures next year, there's no excuse for not coming along and meeting the team. 100m: (-1.0) 2, J.Fergus 10.61; (-1.6) 1, A.Walcott 10.71. 200m: (+1.8) 1, J.Regis 20.56; (+1.7) 2, A.Walcott 21.29. 400m: 3, G.Dearman 47.18; 2, M.Parper 49.15. 800m: 6, C.Gilby 1:53.41; 7, D.Pamah 1:56.51. 1500m: 6, J.Ellis Smith 4:10.41; 7, D.Pamah 4:55.2. 5000m: 4, K.Tadesse 15:02.6; 4, J.Estall 15:30.0. 100mH: (+3.1) 3, N.Owen 14.10; (+1.5) 3, N.Cooper 14.79. 400mH: 1, M.Douglas 51.36; 4, I.Wells 55.92. 3000mSC: 1, L.Hurst 9:01.8; 4, K.Nash 9:47.0.
